n: Amos. His name is written in a different manner, in Hebrew, from that of the third among the minor prophets, (Worthington) though St. Augustine has confounded them. --- Ezechias. He wrote this title towards the end of his life, or it was added by Esdras, &c.
Earth. He apostrophises these insensible things, (Calmet) because they contain all others, and are the most durable. (Theodoret) (Deuteronomy xxxi. 1.)

Sad. This was spoken after Ozias had given way to pride, when the Ammonites, &c., began to disturb Juda, (4 Kings xv. 37., and 2 Paralipomenon xxvii. 7.) under Joathan, who was a good prince, but young. (Calmet) --- Enemies. At the last siege, (St. Jerome) or rather when Jerusalem was taken by the Chaldeans. (Calmet) --- Many, from the highest to the lowest, had prevaricated: but God always preserved his Church. (Worthington)
Cucumbers. Or melons, which grew in the fields, and huts were erected for guards, till they were gathered.
Sodom. Juda is so styled reproachfully, (Calmet) because the princes imitated the crimes of that devoted city, Ezechiel xvi. 49., and infra[Isaias] chap. ii. 6., and iii. 9. (Menochius)

Victims. Without piety, they are useless. God tolerated bloody victims to withdraw the people from idolatry, but he often shewed that they were not of much importance, in order that they might be brought to offer the sacrifice of the new law, which eminently includes all the rest. (St. Jerome) (Psalm xlix. 9., Amos v. 21., and Jeremias vi. 20.) (Theodoret)
Bearing. Hebrew, &c., "pardoning," (Calmet) or "bearing." Septuagint, "I will no longer pardon your sins." (Haydock)
Wash. Interiorly. (Calmet) --- He seems to allude to baptism. (Eusebius) (Theodoret)
Accuse me. If I punish you without cause.

Water. There is no sincerity in commerce. (Calmet) --- Teachers give false interpretations of the law. (St. Jerome) --- Iniquity abounded before the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans and Romans. (Worthington)
Ah! God punishes with regret. (Menochius) --- Comfort. I will take complete vengeance under Joathan, (4 Kings xv. 37.) Achaz, &c.
Tin. I will reform abuses in the reign of Ezechias, but much more by establishing the Church of Christ, which shall be the faithful city. (Calmet)
Judges. The Jews explain this of the judges, and priests, who governed after the captivity; though it refer rather to the apostles, &c. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

Idols. Protestants, "oaks, which ye have desired, and ye shall be confounded for the gardens," &c. (Haydock) --- The groves were sacred to Venus, and the gardens to Adonis, and were scenes of the greatest immorality and profanation, chap. lxv. 3.
It. The efforts of Achan and Ezechias against the enemy proved in vain. (Calmet)

Under Egypt he meant the world, and under things made with hands its idolatry, and under the shaking its subversion and dissolution. And the Lord, the Word, he represented as upon a light cloud, referring to that most pure tabernacle, in which setting up His throne, our Lord Jesus Christ came into the world to shake error.
Hippolytus Exegetical Fragments

When Hezekiah, king of Judah, was still sick and weeping, there came an angel, and said to him: "I have seen thy tears, and I have heard thy voice. Behold, I add unto thy time fifteen years. And this shall be a sign to thee from the Lord: Behold, I turn back the shadow of the degrees of the house of thy father, by which the sun has gone down, the ten degrees by which the shadow has gone down," so that day be a day of thirty-two hours. For when the sun had run its course to the tenth hour, it returned again. And again, when Joshua the son of Nun was fighting against the Amorites, when the sun was now inclining to its setting, and the battle was being pressed closely, Joshua, being anxious lest the heathen host should escape on the descent of night, cried out, saying, "Sun, stand thou still in Gibeon; and thou moon, in the valley of Ajalon," until I vanquish this people. And the sun stood still, and the moon, in their places, so that day was one of twenty-four hours. And in the time of Hezekiah the moon also turned back along with the sun, that there might be no collision between the two elemental bodies, by their bearing against each other in defiance of law. And Merodach the Chaldean, king of Babylon, being struck with amazement at that time-for he studied the science of astrology, and measured the courses of these bodies carefully-on learning the cause, sent a letter and gifts to Hezekiah, just as also the wise men from the east did to Christ.
Prologue to Isaiah

No one, when he will have seen the Prophets to be written in verses, would think them to be bound in meter among the Hebrews, and to have anything in common with the Psalms or the works of Solomon. But what is customary to be used in Demosthenes and Cicero, as they are written in words with divisions, who certainly wrote prose and not in verses, we also, providing ease of reading, have divided a new translation with a new kind of writing. And first, knowing of Isaiah what is presented in his speech, certainly as a man noble and of urbane elegance he does not have anything of rusticity mixed into (his) speech. For this reason it happens that in comparison with others the translation was not able to preserve the flower of his speech. And then adding this, that it is being spoken not only by a prophet, but by an evangelist. For thus all the mysteries of Christ and the Church are pursued to clarity, so that you would not think them to be prophesied of the future, but they covered the history of things past. For this reason I suppose the Seventy interpreters to have been unwilling at that that time to set forth clearly for the gentiles the sacraments of their faith, not throwing holy things to dogs or pearls to swine, which things, when you will have read this edition, you will note were hidden by them.
Nor am I unaware of how much work it is to understand the Prophets, or for anyone not to be easily able to judge from the translation, unless he will have before understood those things which he will have read, and we to suffer from the bites of many, who, being goaded by jealousy, what they are not able to follow, they despise. Therefore, knowing and being wise, I place my hand in the fire, and nevertheless I pray this for the scornful readers: that just as the Greeks after the Seventy translators read Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion, either for study of their doctrines or so that they better understand the Seventy through their collation, that these are deemed worthy to have at least one translator after the earlier ones. Reading first and afterward despising, they are seen not to condemn by judgment, but rather by the ignorant presumption of hatred.
And Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem and Judea when the ten tribes had not yet been led into captivity, and the oracle covered both kingdoms, now together, now separately. And while he sometimes looks at present history, and indicated the return of the people to Judea after the Babylonian captivity, yet is all his concern for the calling of the nations and for the coming of Christ. Who, how much the more you love, O Paula and Eustochium, the more strive for him, so that for the present disparagement, by which the envious incessantly tear me into pieces, the same One may restore a reward to me in the future, Who knows me to have exerted myself in the learning of foreign languages: the Jews might not jump all day on the errors of the Scriptures in His Church.
Commentary on Isaiah

Having at last, after a long time, completed the twenty books of explanations on the twelve Prophets, and the Commentaries on Daniel, you compel me, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, to pass on to Isaiah, and to render to you what I promised your holy mother Paula while she was living. I remember, indeed, that I promised it also to your brother Pammachius, a most learned man; and though you are his equal in affection, you surpass him by being present. And so I pay to you, and through you to him, what I owe, obeying the commands of Christ, who says: Search the Scriptures (John 5:39); and, Seek, and you shall find (Matt 7:7). Let me not hear, along with the Jews: You err, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the power of God (Matt 22:29). For if, according to the apostle Paul (1 Cor 1:24), Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and he who does not know the Scriptures does not know the power of God and his wisdom, then ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. Therefore, supported by the help of your prayers, you who meditate day and night on the law of God and are a temple of the Holy Spirit, I will imitate the householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old, and the bride who says in the Song of Songs: New and old, my kinsman, I have kept for you (Song 7:13); and I will so expound Isaiah as to show him to be not only a Prophet but an evangelist and an Apostle. For he himself says of himself and of the other evangelists: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach good tidings, who preach peace (Isa 52:7). And God speaks to him as to an Apostle: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And he answered: Here am I, send me (Isa 6:8).

And let no one think that I wish to comprehend the subject of this volume in a brief discourse, since the present Scripture contains all the mysteries of the Lord, and proclaims Emmanuel both born of a Virgin and the doer of illustrious works and signs, dead and buried, and rising again from the lower world, and the Savior of all the nations. What shall I say of physics, ethics and logic? Whatever belongs to the holy Scriptures, whatever the human tongue can utter and the understanding of mortals receive, is contained in this volume. Of its mysteries he who wrote it himself testifies: And the vision of all shall be to you as the words of a sealed book, which, when they give it to one who knows letters, they shall say: Read this. And he shall answer: I cannot, for it is sealed. And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and it shall be said to him, Read, and he shall answer, I do not know letters (Isa 29:11-12). Whether, then, you give this book to the People of the nations, who do not know letters, it will answer: I cannot read, because I have not learned the letters of the Scriptures; or whether you give it to the Scribes and Pharisees, who boast that they know the letters of the Law, they will answer: We cannot read, because the book is sealed. Why then is it sealed to them? Because they did not receive him whom the Father sealed (John 6:27), who has the key of David: Who opens, and no one shuts; who shuts, and no one opens (Rev 3:7).

Nor indeed, as Montanus dreams along with his mad women, did the Prophets speak in ecstasy, so as not to know what they were saying, and, while they instructed others, themselves to be ignorant of what they said. Of such the Apostle says: Understanding neither what they say, nor the things about which they affirm (1 Tim 1:7). But, according to Solomon, who speaks in Proverbs: The wise man understands what he brings forth from his mouth, and on his lips he will carry knowledge (Prov 16:23), they too knew what they were saying. For if the Prophets were wise, which we cannot deny; and Moses, instructed in all wisdom, spoke to the Lord, and the Lord answered him; and of Daniel it is said to the prince of Tyre: Are you wiser than Daniel (Ezek 28:3)? and David was wise, who gloried in the Psalm: The uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made manifest to me (Ps 50 [51]:8): how did the wise Prophets, like brute animals, not know what they were saying? We read also in another place of the Apostle: The spirits of the Prophets are subject to the Prophets (1 Cor 14:32), so that they have it in their own power when to be silent and when to speak. And if this seems weak to anyone, let him hear this from the same Apostle: Let two or three Prophets speak, and let the others judge; but if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent (ibid., 29). By what reasoning can they keep silence, if it is in the power of the spirit that speaks through the Prophets either to be silent or to speak? If, then, they understood what they said, all things are full of wisdom and reason. Nor was it air struck by a voice that reached their ears; but God spoke in the mind of the Prophets, according to what another Prophet says: The angel who spoke in me (Zech 1:9); and: Crying in our hearts, Abba, Father (Gal 4:6); and: I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me (Ps 84 [85]:9).

Hence, after the truth of the history, all things are to be taken spiritually: and so Judea and Jerusalem, Babylon and Philistia, and Moab and Damascus, Egypt and the desert of the sea, Edom and Arabia, and the valley of Vision, and finally Tyre, and the Vision of the four-footed beasts, are to be understood in such a way that we seek everything in the sense, and that in all of these Paul the apostle, as a wise architect, may lay the foundation, which is no other than Christ Jesus. And it is a task of great labor and toil to wish to expound the whole book of Isaiah, over which the talents of our elders have sweated: of the Greeks, I mean. Among the Latins, however, there is a great silence, apart from the martyr Victorinus of holy memory, who could say with the Apostle: Though I be unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge (2 Cor 11:6). For Origen wrote on this Prophet, according to the four editions, as far as the Vision of the four-footed beasts in the desert, thirty volumes, of which the twenty-sixth book is not found. There are also current under his name two other books on the Vision of the τετραπόδων, addressed to Grata, which are thought to be pseudepigraphal; and twenty-five Homilies, and Σημειώσεις, which we may call Excerpts. Eusebius Pamphili also published fifteen volumes according to the historical explanation; and Didymus, whose friendship we lately enjoyed, published eighteen tomes from the place where it is written: Comfort, comfort my people, you priests; speak to the heart of Jerusalem (Isa 40:1), to the end of the volume. Apollinaris, however, after his manner, so expounds everything that he runs through it all, and with certain points and intervals, or rather abridgments, flies past the stretches of a great road, so that we think we are reading not so much Commentaries as indexes of chapters. From this you perceive how difficult it is that our Latins, whose ears are fastidious, who are nauseated at understanding the holy Scriptures and are delighted only by the applause of eloquence, should pardon me if I speak at some length, since Isaiah, by the number of his verses, is either equal to the twelve Prophets or greater. And wherever, passing over the Seventy, I have disputed from the Hebrew, the reason is that most things are either the same as or similar to the others, and, having set forth the twofold edition, I did not wish to lengthen the books of explanation, which even in a single explanation exceed the measure of brevity. But now let us carry out what we have set before us.
Commentary on Isaiah

The vision of Isaiah, the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. For Judah, in which two tribes are signified, the Seventy and Theodotion put Judea, which denotes the whole land of the twelve tribes. And for what we have translated from the Hebrew, concerning Judah and Jerusalem, they translated, against Judea and Jerusalem. Symmachus, more plainly as is his custom, has about Judah and Jerusalem, so that he would have the title point to neither prosperous nor adverse things, but to those things which the prophetic word foretold about Judah and Jerusalem in either direction. Isaiah therefore speaks principally of two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, apart from the ten which were in Samaria and were called Ephraim and Israel, and which Pul king of the Assyrians had already begun to lay waste under Uzziah king of Judah and Jerusalem. Then, in the fifty-second year of his reign, while Pekah son of Remaliah was reigning in Samaria, Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians came and took Ijon and Abel, the house of Maacah, and Janoah and Kedesh and Hazor and Gilead and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them away to the Assyrians (2 Kgs 15:29). From this it is shown that all these things are told, when the overthrow of Samaria was near, as a warning to the two tribes.

Now Uzziah is the same man who is also Azariah, with a double name. And from the kings who are set in the title we learn that Isaiah, Hosea, Joel and Amos prophesied at one and the same time; but the beginning of the word of the Lord was in Hosea the son of Beeri. Amos, however, the father of Isaiah, is not, as most suppose, the third of the twelve Prophets, but another; and among the Hebrews they are written with different letters. This one has as its first and last letters ALEPH and SADE (אמוץ); that one AIN and SAMECH (עמוס); and this one, according to some, means strength or robust; that one a hard people or heavy: about which we have spoken more fully in Amos. And not only this prophet, but others too, though they have in their title: The vision which Isaiah saw, or Obadiah, do not go on to say what they saw (for example: I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and two Seraphim round about him), but they relate the things that were said, that is: Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth (Isa 6:1, 2). And: Thus says the Lord God to Edom. I have heard a hearing from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy to the nations (Obad 1:1). For the Prophets were formerly called seers, who could say: Our eyes are ever toward the Lord (Ps 24 [25]:15). And: To you have I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven (Ps 122 [123]:1). Hence also the Apostles are commanded by the Savior: Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for the harvest (John 4:35). These eyes of the heart the bride too had in the Song of Songs, to whom the bridegroom says: You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes (Song 4:9). And in the Gospel we read: The lamp of your body is your eye (Matt 6:22). In the old Instrument also it is said that the people saw the voice of God (Exod 20:18). So let the ravings of Montanus fall silent, who thinks that the Prophets spoke of things to come in ecstasy and in madness of heart; for they could not see what they did not know. I know that some interpret Judea and Jerusalem of heavenly things, and Isaiah as in the person of the Lord Savior: that he foretells the captivity of that province in our land, and afterwards its return and ascent to the holy mountain in the last days. We judge these things contrary to the faith of Christians and reject them altogether; and, following the truth of the history, we interpret spiritually in such a way that whatever they dream about the heavenly Jerusalem we refer to the Church of Christ, and to those who either go out from it because of their sins or return through repentance to their former seat; of which we think this too is said in this same Prophet: Be enlightened, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you; and, In you the Lord will appear, and his glory will be shown upon you; and kings will walk in your light, and the nations in your brightness; when all her sons come from afar, and her daughters will be carried on the shoulders; and the camels of Midian and Ephah will cover her, bringing gold and frankincense; and the flocks of Kedar will be gathered in Jerusalem, and the rams of Nebaioth will hasten, and they will be acceptable victims upon the altar of the Lord (Isa 60:1ff.)

And as for its being set in the title that he prophesied under Uzziah and Jotham and Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, this is not to be understood confusedly, as in other Prophets, so that we do not know what was said specifically under which king; rather, up to the end of the volume it is recorded in writing what was revealed to him by the Lord separately under Uzziah, and what under Jotham, and what under Ahaz, and what under Hezekiah. Let us know also that Hezekiah began to reign in Jerusalem in the twelfth year of Romulus, who founded in Italy the city of his own name, so that it may clearly appear how much more ancient our histories are than those of all other nations. Now Isaiah means saved of the Lord; Judah, confession; Jerusalem, vision of peace; Uzziah, strength of the Lord; Jotham, perfection of the Lord; Ahaz, holding or robust; Hezekiah, dominion of the Lord. He, then, who is saved under the Lord's protection, and is the son of Amoz, that is, of the strong and robust, spiritually beholds the vision of confession while he bewails his old sins, and of peace when after repentance he passes over to the light and rests in eternal peace; and all his times pass under the strength of the Lord and under his perfection and might. And when he has done all things, he will say that word of the Gospel: We are unprofitable servants; for we have done what we ought to do (Luke 17:10).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH, INTRODUCTION

The word of the holy prophets is always difficult to surmise. It is filled with hidden meanings and is pregnant with announcements of divine mysteries. The end of the law and prophets is Christ, as Scripture says. Those who want to expound these subtle matters must be diligent, I believe, to work in a logical way to thoroughly examine all of the symbols in the text to gain spiritual insight. First, the interpreter must determine the historical meaning and then interpret the spiritual meaning, in order for readers to derive benefit from every part of the text. The exposition must be clearly seen to be complete in every way.
ON PRAYER 2

Our Lord frequently proclaimed God as a Father to us. He even gave us an instruction "that we call no one on earth father, but the Father whom we have in the heavens." So, in praying ["Our Father"] we are likewise obeying the precept. Those who recognize their Father are blessed! This is the reproach that is brought against Israel, to which the Spirit attests heaven and earth, saying, "I have begotten children, and they have not recognized me."
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 44:8

All that exists was created by God, and there is nothing uncreated except the nature of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. God, who is good by nature, wishing to have those whom he might benefit and who might enjoy the benefits received from him, made creatures worthy of himself, that is, who could receive him worthily.
Discourses Against the Arians 1.11.37

The one who is [begotten] from another by nature is a true child, just as Isaac was to Abraham, and Joseph was to Jacob, and as the radiance is to the sun. But those who are called children only from virtue and grace are called so not by nature but because of what they have received by grace. They still are not of the same nature as the one who gave them [the gift]. They are the ones who received the Spirit by participation, about whom it is said, "I produced and exalted children, but they rebelled against me." Of course, they were never really children by nature, and because of this and the fact that they reverted [to their former ways], the Spirit was taken away and they were disinherited. But when they again repent, God will receive them again and give them light. He will again call them children who at the beginning had been given grace.
FESTAL LETTER 10

And if they had examined with their understanding the things which were written, they would not have carefully fulfilled the prophecies which were against themselves, so as not to make their city now desolate, grace taken from them, and they themselves without the law, being no longer called children but strangers.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth: for the Lord has spoken. Above, it was shown by the title who the prophet was, whose son, what he saw against Judah and Jerusalem, or concerning Judah and Jerusalem, and at what time; now he summons heaven and earth to listen. By heaven he signifies the supernal and angelic powers; by earth the race of mortals, μετωνυμικῶς, naming the things contained by the things that contain them. Or else because the Lord, through Moses, had called heaven and earth as witnesses when he gave his law to the people of Israel, and had said: Attend, O heaven, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth (Deut 32:1), after the transgression of the people he calls the same again to witness, so that all the elements may know that God has been justly roused to anger in vengeance for his commandments. For heaven the Hebrew SAMAIM (שמים) sounds heavens, in the plural number, especially since he said hear, that is, SEMU (שמעו), which is expressed in the plural number, not the singular. But some hold that it is indeed said heavens in the plural but understood in the singular, as we call single cities Thebes and Athens. And it is an idiom of the Hebrew script that all words ending in the syllable IM (ים) are masculine and plural, like Cherubim and Seraphim; and those in OTH (ות), feminine and plural, like Sabaoth. And this too is to be noted, that to the heavens it is said, hear, to the earth, give ear; for the things that are on high have greater understanding, while the lower ones are wrapped in earthly senses. Hence the Savior too says in the Gospel: He who has ears to hear, he says, let him hear (Matt 11:15). If anyone, then, is heaven and has his citizenship in the heavenly places, let him hear mystically the things that are said; if anyone is earthly, let him follow the simple history. This also is to be observed, that he did not say: Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, what the Lord has spoken to you, but what he has spoken to me, so that what I have heard in the spirit I may report to you, who do not deserve to hear him speaking himself. Some [the Origenists] think that heaven and earth are summoned to listen as if they were living beings, according to what is said of the earth in another place: Who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble (Ps 103 [104]:32); whereas this belongs to the power of God, not to an understanding in the earth.

Sons have I begotten and exalted, but they have despised me. For which Symmachus and Theodotion translated thus: Sons have I nourished, and exalted (Exod 4:22). From this point the Prophet relates what the Lord has spoken: that the people of Israel, whom he had created as servants under the common law, he changed into sons, and said: Israel is my firstborn son. Then too the Lord in the Gospel promises the Apostles that if they do his will he will no longer call them servants but friends (John 15:15). But if Israel should grow proud on hearing that he is the firstborn, let him understand that he is called firstborn for this reason, that second sons are signified from among the nations. For he is not called only-begotten, which would exclude other brothers, but firstborn, to show that others too will follow; and yet, according to the mysteries of the Scriptures, it is not the firstborn who receive the inheritance but the second. Cain was the firstborn, but the gifts of Abel pleased God. Ishmael was the firstborn, but Isaac received the inheritance. Esau was the firstborn, but Jacob the supplanter snatched away the father's blessing. Reuben was the firstborn, but the blessing of the seed of Christ is nevertheless transferred to Judah. Thus they were first according to the order of calling, and were called the head; we, the second, who were called the tail, have been turned into the head and are called sons of God. For as many as received him, to them he gave power to become sons of God (John 1:12). Nor have we received the spirit of bondage in fear, but the spirit of adoption, in which we cry: Abba, Father (Rom 8:15); for perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18). And it is better to read according to the Hebrew, Sons have I nourished, rather than begotten, lest it seem contrary to that saying which we read in the Epistle of John: Everyone who is born of God does not sin (1 John 3:9). For if these were born of God, how could they sin, since everyone who is born of God cannot sin?
Commentary on Joel

And so that we may know that hearing is more sacred than that which sounds in the ears, let us learn it from Isaiah, who says: Hear, O heaven, and perceive with your ears, O earth. Those who are old men and heavenly hear spiritually; those who dwell on the earth and are called earthly perceive with their ears. And this must be noted in all the Scriptures where these two words are placed together. We read this also in the case of Lamech, the sinner, who spoke to his wives Adah and Zillah: Hear my words, wives of Lamech, perceive my words with your ears, for I have killed a man to my wounding, and a young man to my bruising; he knew that what he was saying was obscure, and therefore he called his wives not only to the simple sound of the words, but also to the hidden understanding of what was said.
The Instructor Book 1

For how shall we not regard it fearful, if one who knows God shall not recognize the Lord? While the ox and the donkey, stupid and foolish animals, will know one who feeds them, Israel is found to be more irrational than these? And having, by Jeremiah, complained against the people on many grounds, God adds, "They have forsaken me, says the Lord."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 13

That was the manger of which the prophet prophesied, saying: "the ox knew its owner, and the ass the manger of its lord". The ox is a clean animal, the ass an unclean animal. "The ass knew the manger of its lord". It was not the people of Israel who knew the manger of their lord, but an unclean animal from among the Gentiles: "but Israel", he says, "has not known me, and my people has not understood me". Understanding this manger, let us strive to know the Lord and to become worthy of the knowledge of him, and to take up not only the nativity and resurrection of his flesh, but also the renowned coming of his second majesty: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.
Letter 36.6

What is more evident than that it is said of the passion of the Lord: "The ox knows his owner and the donkey his master's crib." Let us, then, know the Lord's crib where we are nourished, fed and refreshed.
Letter 59.93

[The righteous person] does not say, "My portion consists of herds of oxen, donkeys or sheep," except, perhaps, he counts himself among those herds which know their owner and wishes to consort with that donkey which does not shun the crib of Christ … [For this person] that sheep is his portion which was led to the slaughter and the "Lamb which was dumb before his shearer and did not open his mouth." In [Christ's] humiliation, judgment has been exalted.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 80

He calleth the action "glory," not only for Himself the Crucified, but also for the Father; since this was the case, for not the Son only, but the Father also was glorified. For before the Crucifixion, not even the Jews knew Him; "Israel," it saith, "hath not known Me" (Isa. i. 3); but after the Crucifixion, all the world ran to Him.
Commentary on Isaiah

The ox knows his owner, and the ass his master's crib. Israel has not known, my people has not understood. For which the Seventy alone translated: But Israel has not known me, and the people has not understood me; so that, according to the others and the Hebrew, Israel did not know his owner, and the people did not understand the crib of its master. And the sense is clear: I adopted them as sons, and made them a peculiar people, my portion and the cord of my inheritance, and called them firstborn; but they did not do even what brute animals do, so as to be won over by kindnesses and to recognize their shepherd and nourisher. Nor did he compare them to dogs, which are the most sagacious kind of animal and guard their masters' houses for a little food, but to the ox and the ass, of duller sense: of which the one, drawing carts, turns the hardest clods of earth with the ploughshare, the other carries burdens and lightens men's labor in walking; whence also they are called beasts of burden (jumenta), because they help (juvent) men. This passage can also be understood of God the Father, but it is referred rather to the Son, because the people of Israel did not know him nor receive him: whose day Abraham saw and rejoiced, and on whose coming the prayers of all the Prophets hung. He too says to Jerusalem in the Gospel: How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not (Matt 23:37)! Do we ask where we have read of the ox and the ass together? In Deuteronomy it is written: You shall not plough with a calf and an ass together (Deut 22:10). And in this same Isaiah: Blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread (Isa 32:20). Ebion ploughs with the ox and the ass together, worthy, for the lowliness of his understanding, of the poverty of his name; for he so receives the Gospel as not to abandon the ceremonies of the Jewish superstitions, which went before in shadow and image. But blessed is he who sows in the words of the Scriptures, of the old as well as of the new Instrument, and treads the waters of the letter that kills, so as to reap the fruit of the life-giving spirit. The ox, according to the anagogy, is referred to Israel, which bore the yoke of the Law and is a clean animal. The ass, weighed down with the burden of sins, is taken as the people of the nations, to whom the Lord said: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you (Matt 11:28). So while the Pharisees and Scribes did not believe, who had the key and the knowledge of the Law and were truly called Israel, that is, a mind seeing God, part of the people of the Jews believed, so that on one day three thousand believed together, and on another day five thousand. And while the wise of the world did not receive the cross of Christ, the unlearned crowd of the nations took it up. Hence the Apostle too said: See your calling, brethren: that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but the foolish things of the world God has chosen, to confound the wise; and the weak things of the world God has chosen, to confound the strong (1 Cor 1:26, 27). But these things are forced; the former interpretation is the true one.

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 103: WHY GOD COMMANDS SACRIFICES YET ELSEWHERE REJECTS THEM

HOW HAS THE LORD IN LEVITICUS COMMANDED THAT SACRIFICES AND LIBATIONS BE OFFERED, WHICH ELSEWHERE HE REJECTS? FOR IT IS CLEAR IN LEVITICUS THAT THE LORD COMMANDED THE FATHERS TO OFFER LIBATIONS OR SACRIFICES OR BURNT OFFERINGS: YET HE SAYS THEREFORE THROUGH THE PROPHET JEREMIAH: THEREFORE SAYS THE LORD, GATHER YOUR BURNT OFFERINGS WITH YOUR SACRIFICES, AND EAT FLESH; FOR I DID NOT SPEAK TO YOUR FATHERS, NOR DID I COMMAND THEM, IN THE DAY THAT I BROUGHT THEM OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT (Jer. 7:21–22) ABOUT BURNT OFFERINGS AND SACRIFICES. — If you look closely, there is really no question to be raised on this matter; nor should you think the Lord lied or changed, as if he commanded and later denied. For of this kind of sacrifices and drink offerings or burnt offerings, nothing is found that he commanded, regarding those of which he now testifies that he spoke. Notice that there are two kinds of sacrifices: one which was commanded to be offered for each specific kind, and another which was called voluntary. As for that which was commanded to be offered in various kinds, whether for sins or for firstborn, it was prescribed what it was, of what sort, and how it was to be offered. But the voluntary sacrifice was certainly not commanded, because it was left to free choice, so that if anyone wished to offer, he would offer what seemed good to him; for these sacrifices were voluntary. And because they offered these carelessly and rashly, without considering that whoever offers to one greater should offer chosen gifts, it is therefore said to them, I did not command you about these: but if you wish to offer, you ought to offer what is worthy. Therefore it is found that Cain also sinned, when he did not consider that what is better ought to be offered to God. For when they claimed to offer these to appease God, in that very act they provoked God to anger, so that in what they said they were doing well, they sinned by offering unworthy burnt offerings to God. Therefore he says in the prophet Malachi: “If you bring a blind or lame or sick animal as a victim, it is not good. Offer it to your leader or governor; if he will receive you, says the Lord almighty” (Mal. 1:8). From this it is that through Isaiah God complains of the same matter, saying: “What are your sheep of burnt offering to me? Nor in your sacrifices have you honored me. For I did not make you for this purpose, that you should toil over incense, or that you should buy incense for me with silver; nor have I desired the fat of your sacrifices: instead, you have stood before me in your sins and iniquities” (Isa. 1:11). It is therefore clear that complaints arose because, while they were offering voluntary sacrifices, they were not honoring God in them, since they offered what was unworthy, although these were in no way a matter of necessity. For if they had been commanded, they would seem to offer whatever they could by necessity; but when they offered these of their own free will, they ought to have offered such things as would show God’s service in themselves. But because their mind wandered through the desire for idols, they acted in these matters without due thought. Therefore they are reproached in a twofold way, because they dared to offer to God while acting wickedly, and they offered things that were unworthy; since wicked deeds are not redeemed by sacrifices, but by weeping and mercy. The Jews, though unjust and without mercy, thought God could be made favorable by offerings; just as even now certain people, despising righteousness, think they are to be praised for their offerings. How has the faithful city become a harlot, full of judgment! Righteousness rested in it, but now murderers. The Hebrew word JALIN (ילין), for which the Seventy translated slept, means both rested and will rest, that is, it signifies both the past and the future tense. Hence Aquila and Theodotion too speak as of the future. And he marvels in the prophetic spirit that the city which was once faithful, or the dwelling of the faithful, has suddenly become a harlot. This can indeed be understood also of the times of Isaiah, but it is referred more fully to the passion of Christ, when all turned aside and together became unprofitable (Ps 13 [14]:3). And although Zion is not found in the Hebrew, the Seventy nevertheless added it to make the sense plainer. Now Zion is the mountain on which the city of Jerusalem was founded; after it was taken by David it was called the city of David. Nor do I doubt that there were holy men in it when it had the tabernacle of God, and afterwards when the Temple was built; when Nathan and Gad prophesied, and Asaph and Jeduthun and Heman and the sons of Korah were set over the choirs (which are described more fully in the book of Days), so that religion might pass little by little from the sacrifices of victims to the praises of the Lord (1 Chr 25). The city of the faithful, then, which before was full of judgment, and righteousness rested in it, is now full of murderers, who killed the prophets and the Lord Savior himself. And the fornication of Jerusalem, how she spread her legs to everyone who passed by, Ezekiel sets out under the name of Oholibah, which means my tabernacle in her; which is now said in other words, righteousness rested in it. For righteousness, in the Hebrew is written SEDEC (צדק), which sounds rather like the righteous one than righteousness, so that we may understand that the Lord formerly dwelt in it, of whom it is said elsewhere: But what has the righteous one done? The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his seat is in heaven (Ps 10 [11]:5). All of which we can refer, according to the anagogy, to the soul of a man once holy, in which the righteousness of God formerly dwelt, if afterwards he has sinned, and in place of God as guest murderous demons have dwelt in it.
Discourses Against the Arians 3.26

Someone who looks at what is done divinely by the Word and denies the body, or looks at what is proper to the body and denies the Word's presence in the flesh or from what is human, entertains low thoughts concerning the Word … as a Jewish vintner, mixing water with the wine, shall account the cross an offense, or as a Gentile, will deem the preaching folly.
Commentary on Isaiah

Your silver is turned into dross. He speaks to the city of Zion, in which righteousness formerly rested: that its silver, namely the teaching of the Scriptures, of which we read in the Psalms, The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved in the earth, refined sevenfold (Ps 11 [12]:7), is turned into dross, which in Hebrew is called SIGIM (סיגים): namely the rust of metals, or the refuse and filth that are smelted out by fire; so that, since he had named silver, he keeps the metaphor. This can also be said: that the righteous and holy men who formerly lived in the city were afterwards turned into the filth of sins.

Your innkeepers mix wine with water. For which Symmachus translated, Your wine is mixed with water. And the sense is: the Law of God, pure and sincere, and (so to speak) resting on unmixed truth (Matt 15), has been violated by the traditions of the Pharisees; as the Lord teaches more fully in the Gospel, that they had abandoned the law of God and followed the commandments of men. And every teacher who turns the severity of the Scriptures, by which he could correct his hearers, into something pleasing, and speaks so as not to correct but to delight his hearers, violates the wine of the holy Scriptures and corrupts it with his own sense. The heretics too corrupt the truth of the Gospel by perverse understanding, and are the worst of innkeepers, making water out of wine, whereas on the contrary our Lord turned water into wine (John 2), and such wine that the steward of the feast marveled at it: such as the queen of Sheba too marveled at in Solomon's banquet, praising with her own voice his cupbearers and the servers of the wine (2 Chr 9). And Ecclesiastes too describes in mystical language the services of the wine and of his banquet (Eccl 2). Hence for wine Aquila translated συμπόσιον, that is, banquet, which among the Greeks is named ἀπὸ τοῦ πότου, from drinking, but among us more rightly from living together (convictus).
Commentary on Isaiah

Your princes are disobedient, companions of thieves. For disobedient, Aquila translated withdrawing, Symmachus turning aside. And by princes he means the Scribes and Pharisees, who, withdrawing from the Lord, or rather leaving the path of truth, walked on a perverse road and were companions of Judas, the betrayer and thief. This indeed we too must beware of, lest, by accepting gifts from men of the world who gather riches through robberies and the tears of the wretched, we be called not so much thieves ourselves as companions of thieves, and it be said to us: You saw a thief and ran with him, and you put your portion with adulterers (Ps 49 [50]:18).

All love gifts, they follow after rewards. In the catalogue of vices are numbered also those who love gifts. He did not say, those who accept them, for this often happens out of necessity; but those who count none their friends except those from whom they have received presents, and look not at the faces of their friends but at their hands, and judge those holy whose purses they drain; of whom Ecclesiastes too speaks: He who loves money will not be filled with money (Eccl 5:9). Such men follow after rewards, so that they praise those from whom they have received something, or certainly give nothing to anyone except one from whom they think they will receive in return. For rewards, Symmachus translated requitals, or vengeances, so that these too are at fault who render evil for evil, and tooth for tooth, eye for eye (Exod 21), and do not imitate that word of David: If I have repaid those who rendered evil to me (Ps 7:5); and of Jeremiah, who says of the righteous man: He will give his cheek to the one who strikes him, he will be filled with reproaches (Lam 3:30); so that he may fulfill the man of the Gospel, to whom it is said: Whoever strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also (Matt 5:39).
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore says the Lord of hosts, the mighty one of Israel. For the mighty one of Israel, which all translated alike, the Seventy alone, intending I know not what, put: Woe, you mighty of Israel; which we can expound thus, by saying that the princes too and the strong are rebuked, of whom it is written: The mighty shall mightily suffer torments (Wis 6:7); and: To whom more is given, more will be required of him (Luke 12:48). And we may turn this testimony to use, whenever there is need, against princes of the Church who destroy their own dignity by their deeds.

Ah, I will be comforted over my foes, and I will avenge myself on my enemies. Again in this place too the Seventy put what is not found in the Hebrew: For my fury has not ceased against my enemies. And he rebukes the Scribes and Pharisees, of whom he also speaks in the Gospel: Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees (Matt 23:13ff.). And in another place: An adulterous and perverse generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it but the sign of Jonah the prophet (Matt 12:39). And the most merciful father laments the offending princes, and calls them his foes and names them his enemies, because they perish, since they will not repent, since they did not receive him when he came. For drawing near to Jerusalem he wept and said: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you would not (Matt 23:37)! The consolation of God, then, is over his foes and enemies: that those who did not feel his benefits may be corrected by punishments.
HOMILIES ON 2 CORINTHIANS 5:3

"For we are not as the rest, which corrupt the word of God." `For even if we use great sounding words, yet we declared nothing to be our own that we achieved, but all Christ's. For we will not imitate the false apostles; the men who say that most is of themselves.' For this is "to corrupt," when one adulterates the wine; when one sells for money what he ought to give freely. For he seems to me to be here both taunting them in respect to money, and again hinting at the very thing I have said, as that they mingle their own things with God's; which is the charge Isaiah brings when he said, "Thy vintners mingle wine with water:" for even if this was said of wine, yet one would not err in expounding it of doctrine too. `But we,' saith he, `do not so: but such as we have been entrusted with, such do we offer you, pouring out the word undiluted.'
Commentary on Isaiah

And I will turn my hand upon you, and I will smelt away your dross to purity, and I will take away all your tin. For dross, which is Symmachus's translation, Aquila translated στέμφυλα, that is, grape-husks, Theodotion γιγαρτῶδες, that is, grape-stone; the Seventy alone, the unbelieving or the disobedient, rendering the sense rather than the words. For since he had said above, Your silver is turned into dross, he now keeps the metaphor: that he will turn upon her, that is, stretch out his hand to punish and to purge, and smelt away all the filth and vices of sins, so that, the tin being separated, pure silver may remain; which cannot be done without fire: by which he signifies that they are to suffer torments. We read also in Malachi of the Lord: He himself will go forth like the fire of a smelter, and like fullers' herb, and he will sit smelting and cleansing as silver and gold, and he will cleanse the sons of Levi (Mal 3:2, 3); so that, after they have been cleansed, it may be said of them: And they shall be offering victims to the Lord in righteousness. Ezekiel too says that the whole house of Israel is mixed with bronze and iron and lead and tin, and is afterwards to be purged, so that, after it has been purged, it may know that he is the Lord (Ezek 22:18). And in the Gospel too the same sense is shown under another metaphor: Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will purge his threshing floor, and will cleanse the wheat, and will gather the grain into barns; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire (Matt 3:12).
Commentary on Isaiah

And I will restore your judges as they were before, and your counselors as of old. In the faithful city of Zion, which afterwards became a harlot, murderers dwelt in place of the righteous one, or of righteousness. Therefore the Lord turns his hand, to smelt her to purity and take away all her tin, and to restore her judges as they were at the beginning, and her counselors as of old. The former judges were Moses and Joshua son of Nun and the others, from whom a book of holy Scripture also took its name; and afterwards David and other righteous kings. He will therefore restore the likeness of the Judges: either, after the Babylonian captivity, as the Jews would have it, Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah and the other princes who were set over the people up to Hyrcanus, whom Herod succeeded in the kingdom; or certainly, more truly and more rightly, the Apostles and those who believed through the Apostles and were appointed princes of the Churches; as we said at the beginning of this vision, that both the threat and the promise belong to the time of the Lord's passion, and to the faith which after his passion founded the Church.

After this you shall be called the city of the righteous one, a faithful city. These things the prophetic word plainly embraces concerning the Church, which is to believe in the Lord, from the Jews as well as from the nations. And the city of the righteous one, that is, of the Lord Savior, or she herself will be called righteous, of whom it was said: A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden (Matt 5:14). And by calling her faithful, or, according to the Seventy, metropolis, he shows that she is to be so named by those who are to believe in the Lord.
Commentary on Isaiah

Zion shall be redeemed in judgment, and they shall bring her back into righteousness, and he shall crush the wicked and the sinners together; and those who have forsaken the Lord shall be consumed; for they shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed, and you shall blush over the gardens which you had chosen. Not all will be redeemed, nor will all be saved, but the remnant, of whom it was spoken above too. And they will be brought back in righteousness when the wicked and the sinners have been crushed and those who forsook the Lord consumed. And when these have been saved, those who formerly sacrificed to idols will be confounded, and will blush in the gardens which they had chosen. And he signifies places of luxury, groves and woods.
Against the Pelagians 1.28

Moreover, who can agree with the thesis that you [the Pelagians] set down as your next heading: "In the day of judgment, no leniency shall be shown to the ungodly and to sinners, but they shall be consumed in eternal fires," for you prevent God from showing mercy, and you pass judgment on the sentence of the judge before judgment day, so that if he wanted to spare the unjust and the sinner, he could not, in view of your prescription? For, you say, it is written in Psalm 103, "Let sinners be consumed out of the earth, and the unjust, so that they be no more." And in Isaiah: "The unjust and the sinners shall burn together, and they who abandon God shall be consumed." And do you not know that a threat on the part of God at times hints at clemency? For he does not say that they shall be consumed in everlasting fires, but rather that they shall be consumed out of the earth and shall cease to be unjust. For it is one thing for them to avoid sin and injustice and quite another matter for them to perish forever and be consumed in eternal fires. Moreover, Isaiah, from whom you quote your testimony, says, "The unjust and the sinners shall burn together" (without adding the phrase "forever"), "and those who abandon God shall be consumed." This judgment refers, specifically, to heretics who have abandoned the right way of faith and will be consumed, if they are unwilling to return to God whom they have abandoned.
Commentary on Isaiah

For they shall be like a terebinth whose leaves fall off, and like a garden, or a paradise, without water. To this day the Jews, reading the holy Scriptures, are a terebinth, or an oak, as Symmachus translated. And according to the Gospel (Matt 21) they are the fig tree that withered, on which the Lord sought fruit and, not finding it, cursed it with everlasting barrenness. But even the very leaves and fruits of words have now ceased to be among them; the watered garden too, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, or the paradise of various trees, which is without spiritual grace, does not bear even herbs, of which the Apostle speaks: Let him who is weak eat herbs (Rom 14:2); and with its roots dried up, all its greenness has turned to dryness and squalor.
Commentary on Isaiah

And your strength shall be like the ash of tow. For ash, Symmachus translated ἀποτίναγμα: when tow is combed, and whatever filth it has is thrown away. So all the strength and pride of the sinners and wicked of Israel, who forsook the Lord and were therefore consumed, and sacrificed to idols, and will blush in the gardens which they chose, will be reduced to the refuse of tow, which is devoured by a light fire. For there follows: And its work, that is, the work of your strength, or of the idolatry in which you had gone astray, a tiny spark will consume.

And both shall be set on fire together, and there shall be none to quench it. Both, namely, the knowledge of the Jews and all the works they do; or else both the idol and Jerusalem, in which the idol was; and when the Lord sets it on fire, no one will be able to quench it. All of which we can also take of contrary doctrines: that both masters and disciples perish alike, and all their work is food for fire.

n: Jerusalem. Many particular prophecies are blended with the general one, which regards Christ. (Calmet)

Days. The whole time of the new law, from the coming of Christ till the end of the world, is called in the Scripture the last days; because no other age, or time shall come after it, but only eternity. (Challoner) --- It is therefore styled the last hour, 1 John ii. (Worthington) --- Mountains. This shews the perpetual visibility of the Church of Christ: for a mountain upon the top of mountains cannot be hid. (Challoner) --- This evidently regards the Church, Matthew v. (Worthington) --- The Jews can never shew the fulfillment of this prophecy in any material temple. Micheas (iv. 1.) copies this text.
Jerusalem. Our Saviour preached there, and in some sense the religion established by him, may be esteemed a reform, or accomplishment of the old law.
War. Ezechias enjoyed peace after the defeat of Sennacherib, as the whole world did at the birth of Christ. (Calmet) --- Claudentur belli portæ. (Virgil, Æneid i.)
Lord. Ezechias, or rather Christ and his Church, invite all to embrace the true faith. (Calmet)

Jacob. Thus the converts address God, (Haydock) or the prophet gives the reasons of the subversion of the ten tribes. --- Filled. Consecrated as priests. --- Children. Imitating idolatrous nations, (Calmet) and marrying with them, (Calmet; Septuagint; Theodoret) or even giving way to unnatural sins. (St. Jerome) (Menochius) --- The Jews were not utterly cast off till they had put Christ to death. His Church shall never perish. (Worthington)
Horses. Which the kings were forbidden to multiply, Deuteronomy xvii. 16. Great riches often precede the ruin of states.
Forgive. Septuagint, "I will not dismiss them." Hebrew, "and thou hast not pardoned them."
Rock. Screen thyself if thou canst. He alludes to the kingdom of Israel, which was ruined by idolatry, ver. 18, 20.

Basan. Israel; or Syria and the Ammonites, (Calmet) whom Nabuchodonosor subdued, five years after he had taken Jerusalem, (Josephus, [Jewish Antiquities?] x. 11.) as the Idumeans, (ver. 14.) Philistines, and Egyptians, (ver. 15.) and Tyrians, (ver. 16.) who felt also the indignation of the Lord, Jeremias xxv. 15.
Tharsis. In Cilicia, denoting large ships for merchandise. --- Fair. Hebrew, "desirable pictures." Septuagint, "ships." (Calmet)

Destroyed. This was verified by the establishment of Christianity. And by this and other texts of the like nature, the wild system of some modern sectaries is abundantly confuted, who charge the whole Christian Church with worshipping idols, for many ages. (Challoner) --- Yea, for above a thousand years, while she still professed the name of Christ. (Worthington)

Bats. The Egyptians adored all sorts of animals. (Herodotus ii. 65.) --- Ægyptus portenta colat. (Juvenal xv.) --- Omnigenumque Deum monstra. (Virgil, Æneid viii.) --- The mole was much esteemed by magicians, who promised any the art of divination and success, who should eat the heart of one still warm. (Pliny, [Natural History?] xxx. 3.) The Israelites were always ready to embrace such superstitious practices. (Calmet)

High. Adhere to Jesus Christ. (Origen) (Menochius) --- Septuagint omit this sentence, and St. Jerome thinks they did it perhaps for fear of shocking their brethren. In Jeremias xvii. --- It is supplied from Aquila's version, "how must he be esteemed?" (Calmet) --- Protestants, "for wherein is he to be accounted of?" Jesus will kill the wicked one with the spirit of his mouth, 2 Thessalonians ii. 8. (Haydock) --- No dependence must be had in man. The Israelites vainly trusted in Egypt. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

The word which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. In the former Vision too, which we have already expounded, where the Seventy translated, which he saw against Judea and against Jerusalem, there is written in the Hebrew AL JUDA UJERUSALEM (על יהודה וירושלם); and in this one, which is the second, the Hebrew likewise has it. And I wonder why the Seventy Translators said in that one, against Judea and Jerusalem, and in this one about Judea and about Jerusalem; unless perhaps, because there the nation is called sinful, a people full of sins, a most evil seed, sons of iniquity, and princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah, and a harlot city, and other things of that kind, they translated the sense rather than the word; and here, because prosperous things are promised at once, In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God on the summit of the mountains, they understood the prophecy not as against Judea and Jerusalem but as about Judea and Jerusalem: although in that one too we read prosperous things after the threat, I will restore your judges as they were before, and your counselors as of old: after this you shall be called the city of the righteous one, a faithful city; and in this one, after the prosperous things, there is a fierce threat: Behold, the ruler, the Lord of hosts, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty and the strong, all the strength of bread and all the strength of water, and the rest. Therefore, according to the Hebrew, both in that vision and in this word which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw, it is to be understood as about Judah and Jerusalem: not against Judea and Jerusalem, nor for Judah and Jerusalem, as Symmachus translated, but absolutely, about Judah and Jerusalem, in which both glad and sad things can be contained. And this must be considered, that there he sees a vision, here the Word, which was in the beginning with God; and that in that one, threatening the Jews, he comes to the salvation of the nations; in this one, beginning from the salvation of the nations, and Israel being punished, he gathers believers from both callings into the Church of Christ.
Catechetical Lecture 21:7
He calls the church a mountain when he says, "In the last days the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established."
Commentary on Isaiah

And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains. We read of the last days in Genesis too: that Jacob, calling his sons and saying, Come, that I may announce to you what is to come in the last days (Gen 49:1), afterwards said to Judah, from whose seed Christ was born: A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes for whom it is laid up; and he shall be the expectation of the nations. In these last days will be the last hour, of which John the Apostle speaks: My little children, it is the last hour (1 John 2:18); in which the stone cut from the mountain without hands grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth; by which the prince of Tyre is said in Ezekiel to have been wounded (Ezek 28:16 LXX). This mountain is in the house of the Lord, for which the Prophet sighs, saying: One thing have I asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life (Ps 26 [27]:4); and of which Paul writes to Timothy: But if I am delayed, that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth (1 Tim 3:15). This house is built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, who themselves too are mountains, as imitators of Christ (Eph 2). Of this house, Jerusalem, the Psalmist cries out, saying: Those who trust in the Lord are like mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever. Mountains are round about it, and the Lord is round about his people (Ps 124 [125]:1). Hence too Christ founds the Church upon one of the mountains, and says to him: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt 16:18). Something similar the holy man says to his soul, which longs and impatiently desires to see the house of God: Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me (Ps 41 [42]:6)? And again: These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me: for I shall pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession, the sound of those who feast (ibid., 5). The Seventy translated, The manifest mountain of the Lord, and the house of God upon the heads of the mountains. This testimony the prophet Micah too has set down in the same words: which I have expounded in its place (Mic 1).

And it shall be lifted up above the hills. He who was shown and prepared on the heads of the mountains, he shall be lifted up above the hills. Of these mountains and hills the bride too speaks in the Song of Songs: The voice of my kinsman: behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills; my kinsman is like a roe or a young hart on the mountains of Bethel (Song 2:8, 9).

And all nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go. For all nations shall serve him to whom it was said: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps 2:8); so that they may serve him, according to Zephaniah, under one yoke; of whom the same prophet testifies: From the borders of the rivers of Ethiopia they shall bring you victims (Zeph 3:10). And in Psalm 71 (72) we read: Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down (Ps 71 [72]:9). For at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth (Phil 2).
Commentary on Ezekiel

On my holy mountain, on the high mountain of Israel, says the Lord God, there all the house of Israel shall serve me: all, I say, in the land in which they shall please me; and there I will require your firstfruits and the beginning of your tithes in all your sanctifications. In an odor of sweetness I will receive you, when I have led you out from the peoples and gathered you from the lands into which you were scattered, and I shall be sanctified in you in the eyes of the nations. And you shall know that I am the Lord. Of this mountain, on which all the house of Israel is to serve God, Isaiah and Micah sang with one voice: In the last days the mountain of the house shall be manifest on the summit of the mountains and shall be raised above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways and we will walk in his paths; for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and again Isaiah: Go up onto a high mountain, he says, you who proclaim to Zion; lift up and exalt your voice, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem. This mountain, Zion, we understand either as the Church, which means 'watchtower' and is set on the height of holy doctrines, or as the Lord Savior himself, in whom the firstfruits and the tithes and all worship are turned into an odor of sweetness, so that all the nations round about, seeing that the people of the Lord has been saved, may glorify God, and those who have been saved may know that he is the Lord.
SERMON 62A.3

The central place they are all coming to is Christ; he is at the center, because he is equally related to all; anything placed in the center is common to all.…Approach the mountain, climb up the mountain, and you that climb it, do not go down it. There you will be safe, there you will be protected; Christ is your mountain of refuge. And where is Christ? At the right hand of the Father, since he has ascended into heaven.
SERMON 147A.4

It talks of a mountain, and the mountain is veiled to the party of Donatus. …The holy Daniel saw a vision and wrote down what he saw, and he said that he had seen a stone hewn out of a mountain without hands. It is Christ, coming from the nation of the Jews, which was also a mountain, you see, because it has the kingdom.…
What is the mountain over which the heretics stumbled? Listen to Daniel again: "And that stone grew and became a great mountain, such that it filled all the face of the earth." How right the psalm is to say to Christ the Lord as he rises again, "Be exalted over the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over the whole earth." What is your glory over the whole earth? Over the whole earth your church, over the whole earth your bride.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 33
Who is meant by "mountain of strength" but our Redeemer?
The First Apology, Chapter XXXIX

And when the Spirit of prophecy speaks as predicting things that are to come to pass, He speaks in this way: "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And He shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people; and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." And that it did so come to pass, we can convince you. For from Jerusalem there went out into the world, men, twelve in number, and these illiterate, of no ability in speaking: but by the power of God they proclaimed to every race of men that they were sent by Christ to teach to all the word of God; and we who formerly used to murder one another do not only now refrain from making war upon our enemies, but also, that we may not lie nor deceive our examiners, willingly die confessing Christ.
Commentary on Isaiah

And they shall say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. The nations and peoples, by no means content with their own salvation, will exhort one another and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob. We have said above what the prepared mountain of the Lord is, and what the house of the Lord on the top of the mountains. And the house of the Lord is called the house of the God of Jacob, so that we may receive the old Instrument, and not, after the manner of Manichaeus, seek another house outside the house of the God of Jacob. And when we are in the house of the God of Jacob, then he will teach us his ways, by which we may go to him, and we shall walk in his paths, which the others too have given. So too Jesus, going up into the mountain, taught his disciples the eight beatitudes and the other things which the word of the Gospel contains (Luke 6). First, then, the ways of the Lord must be learned, and afterwards we must walk in his paths.

For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. All the nations and many peoples will exhort one another for this reason and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and the rest that follows: For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem: by no means from Sinai, and from the desert, and from mount Horeb, but from mount Zion, on which Jerusalem was built, and from Jerusalem, in which is the Temple and the worship of God. We read that the Lord often taught in the Temple (Matt 13), and that it was not fitting for a Prophet to die outside Jerusalem; and above, the word and the law were named together. The princes are commanded to hear the word, the people to give ear to the law. For whoever has first kept the law afterwards comes to the speech of God. And indeed the Church, founded first in Jerusalem, sowed the Churches of the whole world. And this must be said, that whoever is in the watchtower and in the vision of peace, in him both the law and the word of the Lord are established. And he finely did not say: the word and the law of the Lord will be and remain in Zion and in Jerusalem, but will go forth, to signify that all nations are to be watered by the teaching of God from that fountain.
City of God 18.54

The first law, the Old Testament, had come out of Mount Sinai by the lips of Moses; but it was foretold of the law Christ came to give: "The law shall come forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." This explains why Christ ordered repentance to be preached in his name among all peoples but beginning in Jerusalem.
Homilies on the Gospels 2:15

It was opportune that the preaching of repentance and the forgiveness of sins through confession of Christ's name should have started from Jerusalem. Where the splendor of his teaching and virtues, where the triumph of his passion, where the joy of his resurrection and ascension were accomplished, there the first root of faith in him would be brought forth; [there] the first shoot of the burgeoning church, like that of some kind of great vine, would be planted. Just so, by an increase in the spreading of the word, [the church] would extend the branches of her teaching into the whole wide world.… It was opportune that the preaching of repentance and the forgiveness of sins, good news to be proclaimed to idolatrous nations and those defiled by various evil deeds, should take its start from Jerusalem, lest any of those defiled, thoroughly terrified by the magnitude of their offenses, should doubt the possibility of obtaining pardon if they performed fruits worthy of repentance, when it was a fact that pardon had been granted to those at Jerusalem who had blasphemed and crucified the Son of God.
AGAINST MARCION 4.1

Long ago did Isaiah declare that "out of Zion should go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem," some other law, that is, and another word. In short, he says, "He shall judge among the nations and shall rebuke many people," meaning not those of the Jewish people only, but also of the nations which are judged by the new law of the gospel and the new word of the apostles, and are among themselves rebuked of their old error as soon as they have believed. And as the result of this, "They beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears (which are a kind of hunting instrument) into pruning hooks." That is to say, minds that once were fierce and cruel are changed by the gospel and the word of the apostles into good dispositions productive of good fruit.
AGAINST MARCION 3.21

The gospel will be this "way" of the new law and the new word in Christ, no longer in Moses. "And he shall judge among the nations," even concerning their error. "And these shall rebuke a large nation," that of the Jews themselves and their proselytes. "And they shall beat their swords into plowshares"; in other words, they shall change into pursuits of moderation and peace the dispositions of injurious minds, hostile tongues and all kinds of evil and blasphemy.… You learn here that Christ is promised not as powerful in war but pursuing peace.
On the Incarnation of the Word 52:1

Who is the one who has done this, or who is the one who has joined together in peace people who once hated one another, except for the beloved Son of the Father, the Savior of all, even Jesus Christ, who because of his own love suffered all things for our salvation? For from ages past the peace he would initiate was promised.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he shall judge the nations, and rebuke many peoples. Therefore there is to be judgment among the nations too; nor are all unbelievers to be condemned by the same sentence, but according to the diversity of their merits they will suffer diverse things. And after he has judged the nations, then he will rebuke many peoples, or, as the Seventy translated, a great people. And note the order: the nations will be judged, because they are going to believe: For he who does not believe is already judged (John 3:18). But the great people, which is understood as Israel, will by no means be judged, but rebuked, because it did not receive the Son of God sent to it.
Commentary on Isaiah

And they shall forge their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles. Every zeal for war will be turned to peace, and instead of discord there will be concord in the whole world. Swords will be changed into ploughshares and spears into sickles, so that, putting aside the fury of war, they may serve agriculture and cut the richest harvests with sickles. This indeed can also be understood spiritually, when all the hardness of our heart is broken by the ploughshare of Christ, and the thorns of vices are rooted out, so that the seed of the word of God may grow into crops; and afterwards we shall eat the labors of our hands, when coming they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves (Ps 125 [126]:6).

Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be trained any more for battle. Let us turn over the ancient histories, and we shall find that up to the twenty-eighth year of Caesar Augustus (in whose forty-first year Christ was born in Judea) there was discord in the whole world, and the several nations burned with the zeal of fighting against their neighbors, so that they slew and were slain. But when the Lord Savior arose, when under Quirinius, governor of Syria, the first enrollment of the world was made, and by the peace of the Roman empire the way was prepared for the teaching of the Gospel, then all wars ceased, and they were by no means trained for battle throughout the towns and villages, but for the cultivation of the fields, the zeal for war against the barbarian nations being delegated only to the soldiers and the Roman legions: when that harmony of the Angels was fulfilled, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will (Luke 2:14); and in his days righteousness arose and abundance of peace.
Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter CXXXV

But as there the prophet says, 'And now, O house of Jacob, come and let us walk in the light of the Lord; for He has sent away His people, the house of Jacob, because their land was full, as at the first, of soothsayers and divinations;' even so it is necessary for us here to observe that there are two seeds of Judah, and two races, as there are two houses of Jacob: the one begotten by blood and flesh, the other by faith and the Spirit.
Commentary on Isaiah

House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord: for you have cast off your people, the house of Jacob. After the calling of the nations and the showing of the mountain of the Lord on the top of the mountains, the Prophet turns to his own people, that is, the people of the Jews, which is called the house of Jacob, and exhorts them that, being in the darkness of error, they should receive the light of truth and walk in the light of the Lord. And in a manner he sings that word of David: Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded (Ps 33 [34]:6). For everyone who does evil hates the light, and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved. But you, house of Jacob, house of my people, come with me, and let us walk together in the light of the Lord: let us receive the Gospel of Christ, let us be enlightened by him who says: I am the light of the world (John 8:12). And when he had said this to the people of the Jews, seeing their impenitent heart and their soul most hardened by unbelief, he makes an apostrophe to the Lord, and says: I exhort them to come to you and enjoy your light with me for this reason, that, in requital for their sins, you have forsaken your people, once the house of Jacob.
Commentary on Isaiah

Because they have been filled of old, and have had soothsayers, like the Philistines. For Philistines the Seventy always translated foreigners, a common noun for a proper one: this is today the nation of the Palestinians, as it were of the Philisthinians, because the Hebrew tongue does not have the letter P, but uses the Greek PHI in its place. Hence what is said in the Psalms, with the enumeration of the other nations, The foreigners have been made subject to me (Ps 59 [60]:10), signifies not all foreign nations but properly the Palestinians. And he gives the reasons why God has cast off his people, the house of Jacob: because they have been filled, he says, as they were at the beginning, with soothsayers and omens and all the filth of idolatry. We know from the writing of Moses that the omens and auguries which the nations had whom the Lord drove out before Israel, the Canaanites, Amorites and Hittites, were not to be heeded. The commentators of the Church expound this passage in one way and another. For some will have it to signify that, the people of the Jews having been cast off, the Roman army entered the land once of promise, and, the Jews being expelled, foreigners dwelt in Judea, settlers of diverse nations from the whole world, brought in by Titus and Vespasian and Hadrian and the other emperors. Others, however, think that this does not pertain to Roman times but to earlier ones, before they were laid waste by the Babylonians, because they are related to have lived under impious kings and were forsaken by the Lord.

And they have clung to strange boys. For which the Seventy translated: And many foreign sons were born to them. Symmachus: And with strange sons they applauded.
