If we understand this of the state of a soul which has sinned after the virtues, let us take her most beautiful son to be good works, which have fallen by the enemy's sword; and the strong too to have perished in battle, because the righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him in whatever day he has gone astray (Ezek 33:12). But if we follow the history, we shall be taught by these words that the prophet's discourse is not about women whose husbands fell in battle, but about the cities of Judea, which he called daughters of Zion, and whose warriors fell in the conflict. Lastly, the following verse speaks of the same Zion.
Commentary on Isaiah

And her gates shall lament and mourn, and the city itself, desolate, shall sit upon the ground. This we see with our eyes to this day. According to tropology the interpretation is easy: that whoever has given place to the devil and has not kept his heart with all watchfulness, his gates mourn; and, the bridegroom being absent, he is ever in mourning, and, falling from the heights, sits in the dust of the earth.

n: Seven. Many shall sue for a husband, men shall be so scarce. To continue unmarried was reproachful, Deuteronomy vii. 14. (Calmet) --- After the conversion of the Gentiles, pastors will be much wanted. (Worthington)
Bud. That is, Christ, (Challoner) who was faintly prefigured by Zorobabel, Zacharias iii. 8. Our Saviour was the fruit of the earth, and sovereign Lord. (Calmet)

Life. Only the faithful shall be saved. (Worthington) --- The Jews, after the captivity, shall be more obedient. But converts to the faith of Christ are styled saints, (Romans i. 7., &c.) such particularly as are predestined to glory, Romans viii. 30. (Calmet) --- Those who are called to life and the true faith, may forfeit this honour, by their own fault. (Menochius)
Burning. By baptism of water and fire, or of the Holy Ghost. (St. Jerome)
Protection. God will protect his Church, more than he did the Israelites by the pillar, Exodus xiv. 20. (St. Basil, &c.)

f: HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 3

The "seven women" suffer "reproach" and go about seeking to receive the one who is able to "take away their reproach". These same "seven women" make a promise, that they will "eat their own bread and be clothed with their own garments". They have no need of the "bread" of him who "takes away their reproach"; they do not lack the "garments of a man" whom they "take". They have better "garments" than a "man" can supply to them; they have more sumptuous foods than the human condition can bestow. It is therefore worth considering whose these "seven women" are and what their "reproach" is. The "seven women" are one; for they are the "Spirit of God". And this one is seven; for the "Spirit of God" is "the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord". This "wisdom" suffers "reproach" from the many wisdoms that rise up against it; this true "understanding" bears "reproach" from false understandings; this great "counsel" is reproached by many counsels that are not good; this "might" is reviled by a certain thing which, though it is not "might", promises that it is "might"; this "knowledge" suffers "reproach" from a certain "knowledge" of false name that filches its name; this "piety" is reproached by that which, though it calls itself "piety", is impiety and instructs the impious; this "fear" suffers "reproach" from that which is thought to be "fear"; for many promise a divine dread, but they do not fear "with knowledge". Let us therefore consider in what way these "seven" suffer "reproach". See the "wisdom of this world", see the "wisdom of the princes of this world", how they reproach the "wisdom" of my Christ, how they reproach the "wisdom" of the true Judaism, according to which we are circumcised spiritually, while those others are cut off. Understand, then, how the "wisdom of this world and of the princes of this world" reviles "wisdom"; and on this account a "man" is sought who may be with these "seven" spiritual "women", that he may "take away their reproach". Properly there is "one" "man" who may "take away their reproach". Who is this "man"? Jesus, who "came forth according to the flesh" "from the root of Jesse", "made of the seed of David according to the flesh, predestined the Son of God in power according to the spirit of justification". For "there came forth a rod from the root of Jesse". The "rod" is not "the firstborn of all creation", the "rod" is not "he who in the beginning was with God, God the Word", but "a rod from the root of Jesse", who "was born according to the flesh". "There came forth", therefore, "a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root". What is the "flower" and what is the "root"? For both are one in him who lies beneath; but the difference is one of dealings. For if you are a sinner, there is no "flower" for you, nor will you see the "flower which is from the root of Jesse"; for the "rod" will come even to you, just as the disciple speaks of the "rod" and the "flower". Of the "rod" indeed he says: "what do you wish? shall I come to you with a rod?", but of the "flower": "or in the love of God and the spirit of gentleness?". "There came forth", therefore, "from the root of Jesse a rod" for him who is punished with penalties, a "rod" for him who needs rebuke, a "rod" for him who has need to be reproved; but a "flower" for him who is already instructed and does not need harsh correction, or at least does not need punishments, but is now strong enough to begin to flower toward perfect fruit. For first the "flower" is shown, and then after the "flower" it becomes a "rod" unto fruit. "There came forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root. And the seven women shall rest, the Spirit of God, the spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him". For the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in Moses, the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in Joshua son of Nun, the "spirit of wisdom" did "not rest" in each of the prophets, in Isaiah, in Jeremiah.

But do not stone me as though I were blaspheming, while I desire to glorify my Lord Jesus Christ; rather, bearing with me, consider what is said, and you will see that in none of them did the "spirit rest", not because it came to none, but because it "rested" in none. It came "upon" Moses, and Moses does not believe after the "spirit of wisdom" that came to him. For he says: "Hear, you rebels: shall I bring forth water for you out of this rock?" It came "upon" all the just, it came also "upon" Isaiah. But what does he say? "Having unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips". The "spirit of wisdom" came after that "tongs" and fire, it came to him "having unclean lips", but it did "not rest". It used him indeed as a minister, but it did "not rest"; it is troubled, to whatever of men it comes. For every man sins, "there is no just man upon the earth who does good and does not sin"; "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day, but his months are numbered". Therefore it "rests upon" none. We can also prove from the Gospel that the "spirit came upon" many and "did not remain in" them. A little while ago it was read: "my spirit shall not remain in these men forever"; he does not say: it shall not be, but: "it shall not remain". John saw one alone in whom it "remained", and this was the sign: "upon whom you shall see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the Son of God". A certain one ministered to the Word of God when the "spirit descended"; a little after he "sins", a little after he speaks an "idle word". But I do not know whether he even remains without sin; do you think that, with the "spirit" present, it is granted to sin? "Upon" none, therefore, did "the Spirit of God rest", according to what is written: "there came forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower ascended from his root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of understanding, the spirit of counsel and might". On account of this he is the "angel of great counsel", on account of this he grew strong and, growing strong, ascended, and the powers marvel at him as he ascends and say of him: this is "the Lord strong and mighty in battle". To him, then, as he ascends into the heavenly places, or to his strength, I will say that: "the spirit of counsel and might rested upon him"; "the Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become for me salvation". "There rested", therefore, "upon him the Spirit of God, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of God filled him".

The "women", therefore, seeking whom they may "take, seven shall lay hold of one man". And this depends on what precedes, and one must first know when the "seven women receive one man". When the "strong ones" of Jerusalem "have been humbled", when the "cases of the ornament" of the daughters of Zion "have mourned", when she "has been left" "alone", when she "has been dashed to the ground", then "seven women shall lay hold of one man, saying: we will eat our own bread, and we will be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be invoked upon us", then "did they lay hold" and truly hold fast "seven women, one man", Jesus Christ our Lord, according to which he is understood to be "man", according to which he was born, according to which he took up a body. "Seven women shall lay hold of one man, saying: we will eat our own bread". Many "men" walk about and the "women lay hold" of none, no "man" pleases them; for it is not on account of a scarcity of men that they "lay hold of one man", but on account of the rarity of the "man" such as they wished, such as they sought; "one" "man" only they found, whom they "laid hold of", that they might "say" to him: "we will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments". There is a certain food of "wisdom", there is likewise a certain food both of "understanding" and of the other "spirits". What is this food? I am not afraid to say: there is another food beyond these; perhaps, as my food is the word of God, who says: "I am the living bread who came down from heaven" and "I give life to the world", so the food of "wisdom" is the Father himself, on account of this: "my food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to complete his work". Nor is it to be thought that "wisdom" and "understanding" and the rest of the "spirits" lack anything, because they have another food, since of the whole dispensation there is one food, the nature of God. "We will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments". There is a certain adornment of "wisdom", with which it is adorned; "wisdom" is adorned with speech. Each of these "women" has her adornments. "Only let your name be invoked upon us, take away our reproach". What is the "name of wisdom"? Jesus. What is: "let your name be invoked upon us"? I am "wisdom", I wish to be called by your name, that I, "wisdom", may be called Jesus, that "understanding" and "great counsel" and "might" and "knowledge" and "piety" and "the fear of God" may be named Jesus, that your "name" may become "all in all". "Let your name be invoked upon us, take away our reproach". Truly Jesus "took away the reproach". Therefore, rising up, let us pray to God, who sent this "man" and in whom "the spirit of the seven women rested", that this "man" may grant to us also the fellowship of these "women", and that, taking them up, we may become wise and understanding in God, and that the other virtues may adorn our soul in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages, Amen!".
Commentary on the Apocalypse of the Blessed John

"And He had in His right hand seven stars." He said that in His right hand He had seven stars, because the Holy Spirit of sevenfold agency was given into His power by the Father. As Peter exclaimed to the Jews: "Being at the right hand of God exalted, He hath shed forth this Spirit received from the Father, which ye both see and hear." Moreover, John the Baptist had also anticipated this, by saying to his disciples: "For God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto Him. The Father," says he, "loveth the Son, and hath given all things into His hands." Those seven stars are the seven churches, which he names in his addresses by name, old calls them to whom he wrote epistles. Not that they are themselves the only, or even the principal churches; but what he says to one, he says to all. For they are in no respect different, that on that ground any one should prefer them to the larger number of similar small ones. In the whole world Paul taught that all the churches are arranged by sevens, that they are called seven, and that the Catholic Church is one. And first of all, indeed, that he himself also might maintain the type of seven churches, he did not exceed that number. But he wrote to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Thessalonians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians; afterwards he wrote to individual persons, so as not to exceed the number of seven churches. And abridging in a short space his announcement, he thus says to Timothy: "That thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the Church of the living God." We read also that this typical number is announced by the Holy Spirit by the month of Isaiah: "Of seven women which took hold of one man." The one man is Christ, not born of seed; but the seven women are seven churches, receiving His bread, and clothed with his apparel, who ask that their reproach should be taken away, only that His name should be called upon them. The bread is the Holy Spirit, which nourishes to eternal life, promised to them, that is, by faith. And His garments wherewith they desire to be clothed are the glory of immortality, of which Paul the apostle says: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on mortality." Moreover, they ask that their reproach may be taken away-that is, that they may be cleansed from their sins: for the reproach is the original sin which is taken away in baptism, and they begin to be called Christian men, which is, "Let thy name be called upon us." Therefore in these seven churches, of one Catholic Church are believers, because it is one in seven by the quality of faith and election. Whether writing to them who labour in the world, and live of the frugality of their labours, and are patient, and when they see certain men in the Church wasters, and pernicious, they hear them, lest there should become dissension, he yet admonishes them by love, that in what respects their faith is deficient they should repent; or to those who dwell in cruel places among persecutors, that they should continue faithful; or to those who, under the pretext of mercy, do unlawful sins in the Church, and make them manifest to be done by others; or to those that are at ease in the Church; or to those who are negligent, and Christians only in name; or to those who are meekly instructed, that they may bravely persevere in faith; or to those who study the Scriptures, and labour to know the mysteries of their announcement, and are unwilling to do God's work that is mercy and love: to all he urges penitence, to all he declares judgment.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 47: HOW THE SEVEN WOMEN OF ISAIAH SIGNIFY THE SEVEN CHURCHES

HOW DO THE SEVEN WOMEN MENTIONED IN ISAIAH, “AND SEVEN WOMEN SHALL TAKE HOLD,” ETC. (Isa. 4:1), SIGNIFY THE SEVEN CATHOLIC CHURCHES? — “And seven women,” he says, “shall take hold of one man, saying, We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach.” It is absolutely clear that by the seven women the seven Churches are signified: for although the Church is one, it is called sevenfold, so that the one body may consist of a sevenfold number of members. For not only we, but also the citizens above are members of the Church, whose head is Christ (Eph. 5:23). Whether therefore the Churches are called one or seven does not conflict. It is called one because it has one head, which is Christ; it is called seven because, just as the members are diverse, so also the spiritual powers, among which we too are reckoned, have diverse functions, on account of which they are called “of the air.” They are diverse for this reason, that not each one can do all things, but all together are the body of Christ: for he is the head of the body, the Church (Col. 1:18), from whom the whole body exists, that is, from whom all things in heaven and on earth have their origin. In this Church which is on earth, mention is made of all the Churches: for when in it the mystery of the Creator is proclaimed, this teaching is also revealed to the heavenly beings. When it is made known to those below, it is necessary that those above also hear. Therefore the Apostle says, “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God who created all things, so that through the Church the diverse wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3:8). Through this Church, therefore, the heavenly beings are taught, because “Truth,” it says, “has sprung out of the earth” (Ps. 85:12). In order that mention of the higher ones might be made, seven Churches are here named in one people, and these seven Churches the prophet presents as suppliants to the Savior made man. For they understood that Christ was born for this purpose, that he might take away reproof, first indeed of those who were living under his Law, and then of the rest. They had also in memory that it was written, “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn ungodliness away from Jacob” (Isa. 59:20). These seven Churches therefore laid hold of one man, that is, of Christ born, saying, “We will eat our own bread, and wear our own apparel: only let your name be called upon us; take away our reproach.” (Isa. 4:1) What is it that they pray for? If they use their own bread and are clothed with their own garments, that is, if they live and are not naked, what do they lack? For if bread signifies life, and clothing signifies being clothed with God, for whoever is without God is called naked, therefore the Apostle says, “For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27); and again, “So that we may not be found naked when unclothed” (2 Cor. 5:3): what is it that they ask, that their reproach may be taken away, unless that this people is signified in the number of the seven Churches, which, living under the Law, was expecting Christ promised for the abolition of sins? Therefore they say, “We will eat our own bread,” that is, we will be fed by the words of the Law which hand on the one God: for “Not by bread alone does man live, but by every word of God” (Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4). “And we will wear our own apparel,” that is, we will be known by the name of our Creator: for each person is said to be clothed in that which he is and professes. Indeed, senators or officials are understood from their garments to be what they are. But because these things are not sufficient to win God’s favor, it was further ordained that through the mystery of the knowledge of the one God, man should become heir of the kingdom of heaven. For cleansed from sins by faith, and alienated from the second death (which, by the judgment pronounced on Adam, kept men in the underworld), held by none, he goes into the paradise of God the Father, of which the Lord said to the thief that he would be with him there (Luke 23:43). For although the aforesaid people, signified by the seven Churches, was under God’s law, and by devotion bound both for its own sin and for its ancestral sin, “For all,” he says, “have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23)—therefore the Churches mentioned above pray that their reproach may be taken away by the call of the name of Christ: for those who bear his sign, by which he conquered death, cannot be held by the enemy. And not only these Churches pray that the name of Christ be called upon them, but also the spiritual ones above, dwelling in the heavens. For although the spiritual and heavenly powers are such, yet they are subject to reproach if they are alienated from their Creator, and they will not be members of the body if, not recognizing their head, they wander. And the prophet bears witness in the following words to what we have explained, saying, “In that day God shall give light by counsel upon the earth.” And he added, “For the Lord shall wash away,” he says, “the filth of the sons and daughters, and shall purge the blood from their midst” (Isaiah 4:2, according to the LXX). What is more evident than that in that day, that is, when the promise of God was fulfilled and the mystery of faith was declared to men, they were enlightened, so that, purified through knowledge of the Creator, those who had been guilty of death might become heirs of eternal life? The prophet therefore spoke in a general way, so as to signify that all need the gift of God, so that both sinners and righteous may be known to have awaited the mercy of God: sinners on account of their own offenses, that they might be snatched from the jaws of death; and the righteous, absolved from their ancestral sin, with the sentence given in Adam wiped out, by which all were held by death, might enter the kingdom of God with the liberty received, now made not servants, but sons of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying: We will eat our own bread, and be covered with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us: take away our reproach. When the most beautiful men of the city of Jerusalem have fallen by the sword, and the strong have perished in battle, and her gates have lamented and mourned, and she herself has been made desolate through the very great scarcity of men, the warriors having been slain, seven women will take hold of one man, desiring to have seed in Zion and a household in Jerusalem, saying that they have food and clothing, only so that they may not be seen to be without a husband and lie under that curse which is written: Cursed is the barren woman, and she who does not make seed in Israel (Deut 7). Zechariah too agrees with this sense: In those days ten men out of all the tongues of the nations shall take hold of the fringe of a Jewish man, saying: We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you (Zech 8:23). The numbers seven and ten are familiar to the Jews on account of the sabbath and the ten precepts of the Law, and therefore they make frequent use of them; although, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, in which they interpret the word SABA (שבע) now as seven, now as many, now as oath, it may in this place signify not seven but many. This is according to the letter. But at the coming of the Lord and Savior, seven women, that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, of which the same Prophet is going to speak in what follows: There shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root; and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him (Isa 11:1, 2), will take hold of Jesus, whom they had long desired, because they had been able to find no other in whom they might rest in an everlasting abode. Hence John the Baptist too relates in the Gospel: And he who sent me said to me himself: He upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he it is (John 1:33). In Zechariah too we read of seven eyes upon one stone, and on one golden lampstand seven lamps and seven pipes, and two olive trees on either side of the lamp, founded with a firm root (Zech 3). And that the grace of the Holy Spirit possesses all things needs no exposition. But because among men it always suffered reproach, no one living as the gifts of the Holy Spirit demanded, therefore they desire the name of Jesus to be called upon them, so that what was imperfect in the Law may be completed in the Gospel.
Commentary on Zechariah

And in Isaiah we read: Seven women shall take hold of one man, saying: We will eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be called upon us, take away our reproach. Those, then, who there are called seven women, that is, Churches, whose number is contained also in the apostle Paul — for he writes to seven churches, to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to the Galatians, to the Ephesians, to the Philippians, to the Colossians, to the Thessalonians. And in the Apocalypse of John the Lord, girded with variety and with purest gold, walks in the midst of the seven lampstands, that is, of the churches of the Ephesians, the Smyrnaeans, the Pergamenes, the Thyatirans, the Sardians, the Philadelphians, the Laodiceans —, are now named ten in the prophet Zechariah, whom the Lord also sought, so that, if he had found them in Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, he might deliver them from destruction.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day the bud of the Lord shall be in magnificence and in glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted, and exultation for those who shall have been saved of Israel. And it shall be that everyone who is left in Zion, and remains in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, everyone who is written in life in Jerusalem. When the daughters of Zion have lost all adornment because of their pride, and her gates have lamented and mourned, and she herself has fallen desolate, and all her warriors have perished in battle, so much so that many women can scarcely have one husband, then the bud of the Christian name will spring up, and the earth will give its fruit; and there will be exultation for those who have been saved of Israel, of whom it was said above as well: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9).
Homilies on the Gospels 1:4

The Lord indeed gave of his generosity in that he arranged to liberate the human race from the crime of its transgression through his only-begotten Son. He gave of his generosity because with the grace of the Holy Spirit he consecrated for his entry the temple of a virginal womb. And our earth gave its fruit because the same virgin who had her body from the earth bore a son who was coequal to God the Father in his divinity but by the reality of [his] flesh consubstantial with her. Concerning this, Isaiah also, looking toward the time of human redemption, said, "On that day the branch of the Lord will be in magnificence and in glory, and the fruit of the earth will be sublime." The branch of the Lord was in magnificence and glory when the undying Son of God, appearing temporally in the flesh as a bright light, poured out upon the world the greatness of his heavenly virtues. The fruit of the earth became sublime when the mortal flesh that God received from our nature, already rendered immortal in virtue of the resurrection, was raised up to heaven.
Commentary on Isaiah

And note that not all Israel is saved, but the remnant of the people of Zion, and he who remains in Jerusalem: everyone who is written in life in Jerusalem, to whom the Lord too spoke: Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). It signifies the Apostles and those who believed through the Apostles.
The Instructor Book 3

The greatest cleansing is the spiritual washing that washes away the filth of the soul. The inspired word speaks of such a washing: "The Lord shall wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Israel and shall wash away the blood from their midst." This refers to the blood of immortality as well as the killing of the prophets. He means by this purification, seen from the added phrase, "by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning." The washing of the body, however, is physical and is accomplished only by water. In fact, it can even be done in fields far away from the baths.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 14

Then there follows: "when the days of their purification were fulfilled, according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem". On account of the purification, he says, "of them". Of whom, "of them"? If it had been written: on account of her purification, that is, of Mary, who had given birth, no question would arise, and we would boldly say that Mary, who was human, had need of purification after childbirth. But now, in that it says: "the days of their purification", it seems to signify not one, but another or several. Did Jesus, then, have need of purification and was he unclean, or defiled with some filth? Perhaps I seem to speak rashly, but I am moved by the authority of the Scriptures. See what is written in Job: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life should be of a single day". He did not say: "no one is clean from sin," but: "no one is clean from filth". For filth and sins do not signify the same thing; and that you may know that filth means one thing and sin another, Isaiah teaches most plainly, saying: "the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgment the filth and by the spirit of burning the blood". Every soul that has been clothed with a human body has its own "filth". And that you may know that Jesus too was made filthy by his own will, because for our salvation he had assumed a human body, listen to the prophet Zechariah saying: "Jesus was clothed with filthy garments".
Commentary on Isaiah

When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have washed the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning. Then the remnant of Israel will be saved, when in the baptism of the Savior their sins have been forgiven them, and that blood has been washed away which the erring people invoked upon itself: His blood be upon us, and upon our children (Matt 27:25). Hence we read above: When you stretch out your hands, I will not hear you: for your hands are full of blood (Isa 1:15, 16). And afterwards, calling them to penitence, he adds: Wash yourselves, be clean. And note that he washed the filth of the daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment, but the blood of Jerusalem by the spirit of burning. For what is light is washed; what is heavier is burned out. Of this spirit of judgment and spirit of burning John the Baptist spoke in the Gospel: I baptize you in water, but he who comes after me will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and in fire (Matt 3:11). From which we learn that man gives only water, but God gives the Holy Spirit, by whom both filth is washed away and the sins of blood are purged.
Commentary on Malachi

To those who sin gravely he is a refining and consuming fire; but to those who commit light sins, fullers' herb, so as to restore cleanness to those who have been washed, according to what is written in Isaiah: The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst, by the spirit of judgement and by the spirit of burning. Those who have filth need the spirit of judgement, that they may be washed; those who are full of blood need the spirit of burning, that the blood which has been smeared on them from without may be taken away.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord will create over every place of mount Zion, and where he has been called upon, a cloud by day, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night. For in Christ there is a new creation, of which we read elsewhere: The old things have passed away: behold, all things have been made new (2 Cor 5:17). For which the Seventy translated: And he will come, and it will be; every place of mount Zion, and all things that are round about it, a cloud will overshadow by day, and the light of flaming fire by night. And who will come, if not he of whom it is written: There will come out of Zion one who will deliver (Isa 59:20 LXX)? And of whom another prophet makes mention: Yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come, and will not delay (Hab 2:3). When he has come, the former happiness will be restored to the people, which they once had in the wilderness, when the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Exod 13), so that they may never be troubled either in prosperity or in adversity. This is said in the psalm as well: The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night (Ps 120 [121]:6). And smoke in this place signifies not error and ignorance but glory, according to what, in the opinion of some, we shall read in this same prophet (below, Isa 6): And the house was filled with smoke. And in Joel it is said of the grace of the Holy Spirit which descended upon the apostles: I will pour out of my spirit, and they shall prophesy (Joel 2). And: I will give wonders in the heaven above, and signs on the earth below, blood and fire and vapor of smoke (Acts 2:17). The same thing, I think, is signified also by that in the Psalms: Who touches the mountains, and they shall smoke (Ps 103 [104]:32).
Commentary on Isaiah

And over all the glory a protection. And there shall be a tabernacle for a shade by day from the heat, and for security, and for a hiding place from the whirlwind and from the rain. This place the Jews refer to Antichrist, who they judge is signified by the whirlwind and the storm, when the Lord is to defend them from a most powerful adversary. But let us refer everything to the first coming of Christ, of which we read in the psalms as well: He has protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle: upon a rock he has exalted me (Ps 26 [27]:5); upon which the Church, being founded, is shaken by no storm, overthrown by no whirlwind and winds. Very many of the Jews understand both these things and all those with which they are joined of the Babylonian captivity and the return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel and Ezra and Nehemiah.

n: My cousin. So the prophet calls Christ, as being of his family and kindred, by descending from the house of David. (Challoner) (Menochius) --- Hebrew and Septuagint, "beloved." Dod may also mean a near relation. (Calmet) --- Isaias being of the same tribe, sets before us the lamentations of Christ over Jerusalem, Luke xix. 41. (Worthington) --- The Hebrews had canticles of sorrow, as well as of joy. The prophet thus endeavours to impress more deeply on the minds of the people what he had been saying. The master of the vineyard is God himself, ver. 7. (Calmet) --- Hill. Literally, in the horn, the son of oil. (Challoner) --- The best vines grew among olive and fig trees. (Doubdan 21.) --- Septuagint, "in a horn, (mountain) in a fat soil." (Haydock)

Stones. They burn and starve in different seasons, Colossians xii. 3. --- Choicest. Hebrew sorek. (Haydock) --- There was a famous valley of this name, Judges xvi. 4. The angels guarded the vineyard, in which Abraham, Moses, &c., were found. --- Tower. To keep the wine, &c., Matthew xxi. 33. It denotes the temple, (Calmet) Scriptures, &c. (Menochius) --- Wild. Sour, Deuteronomy xxxii. 32.
Judge. God condescends to have his conduct scrutinized, chap. xli. 1.
Was it. "Why has it produced wild grapes, while I looked?" &c.
Down. By the Chaldeans, and after the death of Christ. (Calmet) --- When God withdraws his aid, man is unable to stand. Yet he falls by his own fault, which God only permits. (Worthington)
It. During the whole of the captivity, the land might keep its sabbaths, Leviticus xxvi. 34. (Calmet) --- The people shall be deprived of saving doctrine. (Menochius)

Israel. This comparison is very common, Psalm lxxix. 9., and Matthew xx. 1. (Calmet) --- The preceding parable is explained. (Menochius) --- Cry. For vengeance, Jeremias xii. 8., and Genesis iv. 10., and xviii. 20. (Calmet)
Even. Septuagint, "to take from your neighbour: shall," &c. (Haydock)
Things. Unjust practices. --- Inhabitant. What will your avarice avail, (Haydock) since you must abandon all? (Calmet)
Measure. Hebrew, "both." --- Thirty. Hebrew, "a chomer shall yield an epha."

To follow. Hebrew, "for shecar," (Calmet) palm wine, (Theodoret) or any inebriating liquor. (St. Jerome in chap. xxviii.) Our version is conformable to Aquila and Symmachus. (Haydock) --- Numbers vi. 3., and Ecclesiastes x. 16.
Work. Chastisement, ver. 19., and chap. xxviii. 21. (Calmet) --- They are admonished to observe the festivals of the Lord, and not to indulge in riotousness. (Worthington)
Hell. Or the grave, which never says enough, Proverbs xxx. 15. Isaias alludes to what should happen under Nabuchodonosor, as if it were past. (G.[Calmet?])
Justice. All will be taught to adore him. (Haydock)
Strangers. Ammonites, &c., (Calmet) shall occupy part of the land. (Haydock)
Cart. Fatiguing themselves with iniquity, (Wisdom v. 7.; Calmet) and delaying your conversion. (St. Isidore) (Menochius)
It. The Jews were often guilty of the like insolence, Jeremias xvii. 15.

Drink. Hebrew, "mix shecar." People generally mixed wine and water. They also strove who could drink most, and the Greeks had a feast for this purpose, (Calmet) which they styled Choas, for the measure which was to be swallowed down. (Aristophanes, Acharn. act. iv. 4. and 5. ultra) --- Cyrus the younger boasted to the Greek ambassadors, that "he could drink and bear more wine than his brother." (Plut.[Plutarch?] in Artax.)
Justice. Declaring the righteous guilty, ver. 20. (Haydock)
Still. After the ruin of Jerusalem, the people were led away. (Calmet) --- Grievous sins must be severely punished, as was that of the murderers of Christ. (Worthington)

Off. Like a king, leading all his subjects to battle. (Calmet) --- Whistle. He alludes to the custom of leading forth bees by music, chap. vii. 18. (St. Cyprian) --- Earth. The Chaldeans, (chap. xli. 9., and Jeremias vi. 22.) and not the Romans, as some would suppose. --- Swiftly. Like an eagle, Daniel vii. 4., and Jeremias xlviii. 40.

Hoofs. They were hardened, but not shod. (Xenophon) (Amos vi. 13.)

f: HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 10

And truly he was "a horn of salvation in the house of David", because this prophecy is sung in harmony: "For a vineyard was made on a horn". On what horn? On Christ Jesus, on him of whom it is now written: "he raised up a horn of salvation for us, in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets".
Discourses Against the Arians 4.24
And in Isaiah it says, "I will sing to my beloved a song of my beloved touching my vineyard. My beloved has a vineyard." Who is the "Beloved" other than the only-begotten Son?
Homilies on the Hexaemeron 5.6

He invites us to produce fruits in abundance, for fear lest our sterility should condemn us to the fire. He constantly compares our souls to vines. "My well beloved," says He, "hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill," and elsewhere, I have "planted a vineyard and hedged it round about." Evidently He calls human souls His vine, those souls whom He has surrounded with the authority of His precepts and a guard of angels. "The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him." And further: He has planted for us, so to say, props, in establishing in His Church apostles, prophets, teachers; and raising our thoughts by the example of the blessed in olden times, He has not allowed them to drag on the earth and be crushed under foot. He wishes that the claspings of love, like the tendrils of the vine, should attach us to our neighbours and make us rest on them, so that, in our continual aspirations towards heaven, we may imitate these vines, which raise themselves to the tops of the tallest trees. He also asks us to allow ourselves to be dug about; and that is what the soul does when it disembarrasses itself from the cares of the world, which are a weight on our hearts. He, then, who is freed from carnal affections and from the love of riches, and, far from being dazzled by them, disdains and despises this miserable vain glory, is, so to say, dug about and at length breathes, free from the useless weight of earthly thoughts.
The Six Days of Creation, 3.50

And through Isaiah the Lord himself spoke, saying: A vineyard has been made for my beloved in a fertile place. And I have enclosed it with a wall, and have dug around the vineyard of Sorech, and have built a tower in its midst. For it has surrounded her like a wall of celestial precepts, and the guardianship of angels. For the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear Him. He has placed her in the Church like a tower of the apostles and prophets and teachers, who are accustomed to defend the peace of the Church. He has dug around her, when he has relieved her of the burden of worldly anxieties. For nothing burdens the mind more than the solicitude and desire for wealth or power in this world.
Commentary on Isaiah

I will sing now to my beloved the song of my cousin concerning his vineyard. The prophet sings a lamentable song to the people of Israel, which he composed of whom it is written in the Gospel: But when he had seen it (doubtless Jerusalem) he wept over it, and said: If you too had known the things that are for your peace, for the days will come upon you, and your enemies will throw up ramparts around you, and will hem you in, and will lay you low, and your children (Luke 19:41ff.). And again: How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate (Matt 23:37, 38): to which this is like, which is now said in this song: I will abandon my vineyard. And that Christ is called the beloved and dearest one, whom Aquila interpreted πατράδελφον, uncle, or cousin, the title of the forty-fourth psalm teaches us: A song for the beloved. And the voice of God the Father in the Gospel: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17). And in the sixty-seventh psalm we read: The Lord will give the word to those who preach the good news with great power. The King of powers of the beloved (Ps 67 [68]:12, 13). This beloved, then, made a mournful song for his vineyard, which I will sing to my beloved and pitiable people. Or certainly it is to be understood thus: I will sing to Almighty God the Father the song of Christ, who is my cousin, that is, born of the same nation as I. And that the people of Israel is called the vineyard of God we read also at the end of this song: The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah his praiseworthy shoot. And in the seventy-ninth psalm (Verse 9): You have brought a vine out of Egypt, you have cast out the nations, and planted it. In the Gospel too, in almost the same words in which the Prophet now speaks, the Lord weaves a parable: There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard, and set a wall around it, and dug a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, etc. (Matt 21:33). And in Jeremiah we read: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true: how have you been turned into bitterness, a strange vine? (Jer 2:21). And so Jerusalem, as we have said, is lamented, and her ruin is sung in prophetic speech. But for the Church, and the people once of the nations, another song has been put forth, of which we read in the psalms: Sing to the Lord, all the earth; announce his salvation from day to day. Announce his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples (Ps 95 [96]:2, 3). And again: Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonders. The Lord has made known his salvation, in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness (Ps 97 [98]:1, 2).

My beloved had a vineyard on a horn, the son of oil. Theodotion and Aquila translated this according to the Hebrew; but Symmachus, in his manner, more plainly: My beloved had a vineyard on a horn in the midst of olive trees. The Seventy, moreover, interpreted the sense rather than the word: My beloved had a vineyard on a horn, in a fat place, or a fertile one, for πίων signifies both. And indeed nothing is fatter than the land of Promise, if you consider not the mountainous and desert parts but its whole breadth, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates toward the East, and on the northern side as far as Mount Taurus and Zephyrium of Cilicia, which overhangs the sea. And we often read that horn signifies kingdom and power, as in that saying in the Gospel: He has raised up a horn of our salvation in the house of David his servant (Luke 1:69). And: In you we will toss our enemies with the horn (Ps 43 [44]:6). And in Zechariah four horns denote four most powerful kingdoms (Zech 1). The Hebrews expound this place thus: A vineyard was planted for Christ on a horn, that is, in a strong and lofty place, which is called the son of oil, either because it stands in need of God's mercy and is sustained by his help, or because it has furnished the clear light of the knowledge of God to all nations.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he fenced it, and chose out the stones from it, and planted the vine Sorec, and built a tower in its midst, and set up a winepress in it. Through the metaphor of the vineyard, as we said before, he describes the people of the Jews, which he fenced with the help of the Angels. And he chose out the stones from it, either idols or all things that could hinder the worship of God. And he planted it with the vine Sorec, which Symmachus alone interpreted as choice, expressing, as it seems to me, not word for word but the sense contained in the word. For the Hebrews say that Sorec is a kind of excellent vine, because it produces abundant and lasting fruit. Lastly, Sorec is interpreted by some as καλλίκαρπος, which we can render as of most beautiful fruit. He also built a tower in its midst, that is, the temple in the midst of the city; and set up a winepress in it, by which some think the altar is signified. For just as all the grapes are carried to the winepress and trodden, so that wine may be pressed out of them, so the altar receives the fruits of all the people and devours the victims offered, according to what we read of Benjamin, in whose tribe the temple and the altar were: Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he will eat, and at evening he will give food (Gen 49:27). All that is said of the vineyard can also be referred to the state of the human soul, which, planted by God for good, has brought forth not grapes but wild grapes, and has afterwards been handed over to the beasts to be trampled, and has not received the divine rain of teachings, because it despised the former gifts.

And I waited for it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes. For wild grapes, as we have rendered it, in the Hebrew is written BUSIM (באשים), which Aquila interpreted σαπρίας, that is, most worthless fruits; Symmachus ἀτελῆ, that is, imperfect; the Seventy and Theodotion thorns, with which the Jews crowned the Lord. For while he waited for them to bring grapes to the winepresses at vintage time, for which the eighth, the eightieth and the eighty-third psalms have their titles, they, sinking themselves in the cares and vices of the world, which in the Gospel (Mark 4) are interpreted as thorns, offered the goads of blasphemies. But I think it better that Busim be understood as wild grapes rather than thorns, so that the likeness of the metaphor begun may be kept. Hence the Savior too says in the Gospel: Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? (Matt 7:16).
SERMON 376A.2

So let me warn you, holy seedlings, let me warn you, fresh plants in the field of the Lord, not to have it said of you what was said of the vineyard of the house of Israel: "I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns." Let the Lord find good bunches of grapes on you, seeing that he was himself a bunch of grapes trodden in the winepress for you. Produce grapes, live good lives.
Commentary on Isaiah

Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard: what is there that I ought to have done further for my vineyard and have not done for it? Or is it that I waited for it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes? I have done, he says, all that I ought: I planted the vineyard in a most fertile place, I set a wall around it, I chose out the stones, and I propped up its shoots with stakes and reeds; the vine itself too was not one of many, but choice and καλλίκαρπος. I built a very strong tower, in which to store the crops and from which to watch the beasts that lie in wait for the crops. I set up a winepress, so that the grapes might be pressed above all in that same place and pour out wine. Since, then, I have done the things I ought to have done, let the inhabitants of Jerusalem and of Judah answer me; nay rather, let them judge between me and my vineyard, what is there that I ought to have done and have not done? And as they keep silent, he answers himself: Unless perhaps I erred in this, that for my labor I waited for it to make grapes, not wild grapes, which an untilled and deserted vineyard is wont to bring forth. Something of the kind the Prophet Nathan, sent to David, says too (2 Sam 12), and he questions him through a parable, so that while judging of another he may pronounce sentence on himself. So here too the people is questioned as though about a vineyard, so that it may answer against itself. This place the Savior carries out more fully in the Gospel (Matt 21), and what is passed over here, he puts as a question to the Scribes and Pharisees. For in Isaiah nothing is said of the husbandmen, nor is it indicated what they are to suffer, but the discourse is only of the vineyard; there, however, as though the vineyard were one thing and the husbandmen another, he speaks of the people and of the teachers in such a way that he destroys the wicked wickedly and lets out the vineyard to other husbandmen, signifying the apostles and those who were to succeed the apostles. Nor is there a ταυτολογία, as many think, in his saying: Or is it that I waited for it to make grapes, and it made wild grapes? For above he speaks silently within himself, but here he asks others what he had been thinking.
Commentary on Isaiah

And now I will show you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it shall be for plunder; I will break down its wall, and it shall be for trampling. And I will make it desolate; it shall not be pruned, and it shall not be dug: and briers and thorns shall come up over it. I challenged you above, he says, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of the tribe of Judah, to judge between me and my vineyard, and I asked you to say what I ought to have done that I have not done. And since, according to the Gospel parable, you will not answer what I ask, I myself will answer for you, showing what I am going to do: Since I have done for my vineyard all that I ought, and instead of grapes it has brought forth wild grapes, I will take away all that I had given. I will take away the help of the angels, of whom it is written in the psalms: The Angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him, and will deliver them (Ps 33 [34]:8); and it will be plundered by its adversaries. I will destroy the walls, and it will lie subject to hostile nations, and it will be desolate and will not be pruned for ever, nor dug, so that it may be reduced to briers; and thorns will come up in it. These things are said, under the metaphor of the vineyard, of the desolation of Jerusalem and Judea, which most of the Jews think took place under the Babylonians: and we cannot deny that this was in part fulfilled. But since there follows, And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it, this cannot be understood of that captivity. For Jeremiah too prophesied among the people when the city had already been taken; and Ezekiel, Daniel too and the three boys, are related either to have prophesied or to have done wonderful signs even in the captivity; and afterwards Haggai and Zechariah foretold the future for the consolation of the people in servitude. And the help of God is taken away from those who are unworthy, so that, since they had not perceived God through his benefits, they may perceive him through punishments. Or else he threatens certain harsh and rough things for this reason, that, having turned to penitence, they may avoid the impending torments. The Hebrew word SAITH (שית) all have interpreted by a similar word as thorns. If, then, Saith in the present place is called thorns according to Aquila and Theodotion and the Seventy, let them answer how above they translated Busim not as wild grapes but as thorns.
Commentary on Isaiah

And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it. These are the clouds which the Lord brought out from the end of the earth, of which we read in the psalm as well: Your truth reaches to the clouds (Ps 35 [36]:6). These clouds, since under Elijah all were idolaters, did not rain upon the land of Israel for three years and six months (1 Kgs 18). This indeed we can understand not only of the prophets but of the apostles: that after the passion of the Lord the Jews had neither prophets nor apostles, lest instead of grapes they should bring forth thorns, but that they might pray, for their barrenness and dryness, to him who can supply the rains of the virtues. Hence in Leviticus too he says to them: I will make the heaven of iron for you, and the earth of bronze (Lev 26:19). And in Deuteronomy: The heaven over your head shall be of bronze, and the earth beneath you of iron (Deut 28:23, 24). And again: The Lord will give rain to your land. And: Ashes shall come down from heaven upon you, until it uproots you and destroys you; because land which receives the rain that often comes upon it, and produces not a crop but thorns and thistles, is reprobate and near to a curse, whose end is burning.
Commentary on Isaiah

But the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his delightful shoot. That is, of God; or, as the Seventy translated, a most beloved young planting. Israel and Judah differ from each other in this: that the whole people was at first called Israel, and afterwards, when David reigned over the tribe of Judah, and Rehoboam the son of Solomon over two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, those who were in Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, were called Israel; and those over whom men of David's line reigned were called Judah. And since calves were worshiped by Israel in Dan and in Bethel, Samaria was therefore taken first by the Assyrians; and a long time afterwards Judah was led away by the Chaldeans into Babylon, because they had sinned less. Hence in Ezekiel too, for purging the sins of both peoples, there are set on the left side for Israel, according to the Seventy, one hundred and ninety days, or, as is more truly contained in the Hebrew, three hundred and ninety, but for Judah forty days (Ezek 4, according to the Seventy and according to the Hebrew). I say this to show that, in comparison with Israel, that is, the ten tribes, Judah was lovable and beloved, in which were the priests and the Levites, and in which the worship of God was carried on at the time when the prophet Isaiah was speaking to the people. And beautifully Israel, that is, the whole people, is the house; but Judah, which sprang up afterwards when the tribes were separated, is called the delightful young plant. And this too is to be noted, that, according to prophetic custom, what was first said through a metaphor or through a parable is afterwards explained more plainly: that the vineyard and the young planting are Israel and Judah.

And I waited for it to do judgment, and behold, iniquity; and righteousness, and behold, a cry, or, as the Seventy translated, I waited for it to do judgment, and it did iniquity, and not righteousness, but a cry. We wish to convey to Latin ears what we have learned from the Hebrews. Judgment among them is called MESPHAT (משפט); iniquity, or scattering, as Aquila interpreted, MESPHAA (משפה). Again, righteousness is called SADACA (צדקה), and cry is called SAACA (צעקה). So, by either adding or changing one letter, he so tempered the likeness of the words as to set MESPHAA for MESPHAT and SAACA for SADACA, and to render an elegant structure and sound of words according to the Hebrew tongue. Now God waited for the people of the Jews to do judgment, that is, grapes; and it did iniquity, that is, wild grapes. And he waited for righteousness, that it should receive the bestower of such great gifts sent from the Father; and it made a cry, with which it shouted against the Lord, and cried out, saying: Away, away, crucify such a one (John 19:15). Hence the apostle Paul too writes: Let all anger and clamor and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice (Eph 4:31). Or else, since they had shed the blood of the righteous one, the blood of the Lord's passion cried out to the Lord; therefore they rendered a cry instead of righteousness, according to what we read in Genesis: The voice of the blood of your brother Abel cries to me (Gen 4:10).
The Six Days of Creation, 6.52

Attend to yourself, poor one; for your soul is precious: and if mortal flesh, a temporary soul: and if you lack money, grace does not lack: and if there is no spacious house, widespread possession, heaven is open, the earth is free. The elements have been given to all in common, the ornaments of the world are open equally to the rich and the poor. Are not the faces of the heavens, adorned with shining stars, more beautiful than the most precious gold-leaf ceilings of luxurious houses? Are the riches of the rich wider than the expanses of the earth? Whence it was said to those who join house to house and villa to villa: Will you alone dwell upon the earth? You have a larger house: the poor, in which you cry out and are heard. ... The house of God is common to the rich and the poor.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to you who join house to house, and link field to field, as far as the limit of the place: will you alone dwell upon the earth? For what we have said, as far as the limit of the place, the Seventy translated, that you may take something from your neighbor; Symmachus and Theodotion, until place fails, or there is none, so that, though the land fails, greed is by no means sated. This I think is said both generally against all for whom nothing is enough, and specially against the vineyard of the Lord, which instead of grapes made wild grapes, that is, instead of judgment iniquity, and instead of righteousness a cry. For what madness it is, when houses and fields ought to be had to keep off the rains and to sow crops, to desire to have those in all of which you cannot dwell and which you are not able to till, and to make another's need your pleasure! According to tropology some think this said against the heretics, who, moving their feet from the East, come into the plain of Shinar, which means shaking out of teeth, and build the city of confusion and the tower of pride, and hear in other words: Hear these things, leaders of the house of Jacob, and you remnant of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert all that is right, who build Zion in blood and Jerusalem in iniquity (Mic 3:9, 10). These join houses to houses, that is, doctrines to doctrines; to whom it is said through Micah, Do not build a mockery in the house (Mic 3), lest upon the foundation of Christ, which the apostle Paul laid (1 Cor 3), and on which they ought to have built gold, silver, precious stones, they on the contrary build wood, hay, stubble, whose end is burning. Of such houses the Savior speaks in the Gospel: Everyone who hears my words and does not do them shall be likened to a foolish man who built his house upon the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, the winds blew and beat upon that house, and it fell: and great was the ruin of that house (Matt 7:26, 27). And the heretics go on seeking to join new things to old, and to change the same for more recent ones, until both human sense and speech fail.
Commentary on Isaiah

These things of the Lord of hosts are in my ears: Unless many houses are made desolate, great and beautiful, without an inhabitant. For what we have rendered according to the Hebrew, These things of the Lord of hosts are in my ears, that is, the words which the Lord spoke still resound in my ears, the Seventy translated, These things have been heard in the ears of the Lord Sabaoth: not that the Prophet heard the words of the Lord, but that the things the Prophet was going to say were heard in the ears of the Lord; whereas it is more consistent to understand that the Prophet heard what the Lord spoke. And the Lord spoke this: that after the captivity great and most beautiful houses would be desolate, having no inhabitant.
Commentary on Isaiah

We ask, according to the anagogy, how the houses of the heretics are great and beautiful, which, when the time of judgment has come, have no inhabitant. For all the pomp and structure of words and the arguments of dialectic will be reduced to nothing. And since, according to the apostle Paul (1 Cor 3), we are not only God's building but also his husbandry, which the heretics imitate and are dug under and rooted up by Jeremiah: therefore where ten acres of vineyards, or where ten yoke of oxen are at work, they will make one bath, and thirty measures of seed will make an ephi (Jer 18), so that from the number ten, which in the holy Scriptures is mystical and perfect, and from thirty, at which Ezekiel prophesied (Ezek 1) and the Lord was baptized (Luke 3), they are reduced to an ephi, which, in comparison with a manifold number, is confined to unity. And that building and husbandry are referred to spiritual understanding the apostle Paul teaches in another place too (Eph 4), testifying that believers are founded and rooted in love. Hence Ecclesiastes too (Eccl 2) not only built himself houses but planted vineyards, and made gardens and orchards, and set out every fruit-bearing tree, and constructed pools to water the woodland. But the heretics, having only the image and shadow of the virtues and not the truth itself, without the fruit of works, promise the leaves of words. Of their trees the Lord says: Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Matt 15:13). For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and their offshoot from Gomorrah: their grape is a grape of gall, and theirs is a cluster of bitterness; their wine is the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps (Deut 32:32ff.).
Commentary on Isaiah

For ten acres of vineyards shall make one little flask, and thirty measures of seed shall make three measures. For little flask, which the Seventy alone translated, all the others interpreted bath, which in Hebrew is called BETH (בת). And for thirty measures, which we have set down for a cor, which in Hebrew is called OMER (תמר), the Seventy rendered six artabas, which is an Egyptian measure and makes twenty measures. In the excessive barrenness, then, which follows the captivity, ten acres of vineyards will make a bath, that is, three amphorae; and thirty measures of seed, that is, a cor, will make an ephi, which the Seventy interpreted as three measures, that is, three modii. Now bath is said of liquid kinds, and ephi or epha, of the same measure, of dry ones. As we read in Ezekiel according to the Hebrew: You shall have a just ephi, and a just bath. The ephi and the bath shall be equal and of one measure, so that the bath holds the tenth part of a cor, and the ephi the tenth part of a cor: their balance shall be equal according to the measure of the cor (Ezek 45:10, 11).
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, and to drink until evening, so as to be inflamed with wine. Harp and lyre, timbrel and pipe, and wine are in your feasts; and you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands. For drunkenness, as Aquila and Symmachus interpreted it, the Seventy set down the Hebrew word itself, SICERAM (שכר), which signifies every drink that can intoxicate and overturn the settled state of the mind. And, following the sequence of the explanation begun, he rebukes the husbandmen of the vineyard, who, with barrenness impending and the burning near at hand by which the briers and thorns are to be consumed, gave themselves over to luxury and pleasures, not only in eating and drinking but also in the delight of the ears and in the various kinds of the art of music. While they do these things, they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider what is to come. Let us turn this testimony against the princes of the Church, who rise in the morning to pursue strong drink, and to drink until evening; of whom it is said in another place: Woe to you, O city, whose king is a youth, and your princes eat in the morning (Eccl 10:16). Occupied with delights, they do not understand the Creator from the creatures, nor consider the works of his hands, of which we read: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the breath of his mouth (Ps 32 [33]:6). According to a higher understanding, every disturbance of the soul can be called drunkenness, which is conceived from the wine of the fury of dragons and from the incurable venom of asps, which some drink from youth to old age, that is, from morning until evening (Deut 32). Others are roused from the banquet at the third, sixth, or ninth, and the eleventh hour, and it is said to them: Awake, you who are drunk with wine. Upon this wine and upon such grapes and vineyards the Lord rains sulfur and fire from the Lord; and whoever drinks of their wine is inflamed and burned up. He seeks the harp and the psaltery, whose inventor is Jubal, born of the stock of Cain (Gen 4), and does not hear the Lord saying to Aaron: You and your sons shall not drink wine and strong drink when you enter into the tabernacle of testimony, or approach the altar (Lev 10:8). These harps and lyres and timbrel and pipes the Babylonian king had, at whose sounding together the peoples of all nations prostrated themselves on the ground and worshiped the golden statue (Dan 3). And that the first time of human wisdom, when we leave childhood and come to the age of reason, is understood as morning in the Scriptures, many testimonies can teach us; of which, by way of example, a few are to be set down: In the morning I sent the Prophets; and: In the morning you will hear my prayer. In the morning I will stand before you, and will see (Ps 5:4, 5); and: From the night my spirit will rise early (Isa 26:9 LXX); and: O God, my God, to you I watch from the dawn (Ps 62 [63]:1); and: In the mornings I put to death all the sinners of the land, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity (Ps 100 [101]:8); and in another place: Weeping will tarry until evening, and gladness until the morning, and other things like these. And we rise in the morning when we leave our vices behind in childhood, and can say: Remember not the sins of my youth and of my ignorance (Ps 24 [25]:7). And when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, the darkness is put to flight, and at once we put to death all the thoughts that provoke us to sins, and we destroy from the city of our mind those sinners of whom the Savior speaks: Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies (Matt 15:19), and the rest. But most unhappy are those who, occupied from morning until evening with drunkenness, gluttony and divers pleasures, do not understand the works of the Lord in themselves, nor consider why they were created.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore my people has been led away captive, because it had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished with hunger, and its multitude is dried up with thirst. That these things befell the people of the Jews according to the letter under Vespasian and Titus, the Roman emperors, both Greek and Latin history relates. And this indeed they suffer spiritually today too, enduring not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God; because they neither regarded the work of the Lord nor considered the works of his hands, nor had knowledge of him who has always spoken through the Prophets (Amos 8). Hence in the Psalms too it is said of them: They shall return at evening, and shall suffer hunger like dogs, and shall go round about the city (Ps 58 [59]:16). And that every word of teaching is called bread and water, that saying of the Gospel teaches: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that goes forth from the mouth of God (Luke 4:4); and: Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst for ever (John 4:13). And in the psalm it is said: He has brought me up beside the waters of refreshment (Ps 22 [23]:2). Hence the Lord too will not send away the hungry in the wilderness, lest they grow weary and collapse and be killed by hunger (Matt 15). And of the righteous man it is said: I have been young, and have grown old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread (Ps 36 [37]:25). Some wish to interpret what is said, My people has been led away captive, because it had no knowledge; and its nobles have perished with hunger, and its multitude is dried up with thirst, generally of the underworld and of Gehenna, in which everyone will be punished who has not had knowledge of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore the underworld has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit, and its strong ones and its people, and its exalted and glorious ones, shall go down into it. And man shall be bowed down, and the man of rank shall be humbled, and the eyes of the lofty shall be brought low. Those who rose in the morning to pursue strong drink, and continued in drunkenness until evening, and, occupied with pleasure and delights, would not regard the work of the Lord nor contemplate the works of his hands, were therefore led into captivity, because they had no knowledge of the Son of God, who himself says to them, You know neither me nor him who sent me (John 8:19); and in the captivity itself they perished with hunger and were dried up with thirst. Hence the underworld and death enlarged its soul and opened its mouth, and without any number or satiety devoured those who are to be punished for ever: so that the princes and the people, and the exalted and glorious ones of the land of Judah, went down into it, and all pride was humbled, and the eyes of the lofty were brought low, as they understood that they were mortal; and all that the Lord had announced through the Prophets as to come was fulfilled in fact. Now the underworld is said to have a soul, not because it is a living creature, according to the error of some, but because in words of human usage we express the condition of insensible things: that it is insatiable and is never filled by the multitude of the dead. Just as death too is said to be in the hand of the tongue (Prov 18), and Almighty God says that his soul hates the Sabbaths and New Moons of the Jews (Isa 1). Whatever we have said of the people of the Jews can be referred tropologically to those who, occupied with the delights of the world and not regarding the works of God, are led captive into sin and have no knowledge of God; and therefore they perish with hunger and thirst for good works and virtues, and will be dragged down into Gehenna, and there, consigned to eternal torments, they will see their power and pride changed into misery and humility.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord of hosts shall be exalted in judgment, and the holy God shall be sanctified in righteousness. When the people has been led away captive because it had no knowledge, and has perished with hunger and been dried up with thirst, and the underworld has enlarged its soul, and the strong and the exalted and glorious have gone down into the depth, and man has been bowed down and the man of rank humbled, and all have received according to their deserts: then the Lord will be exalted in judgment, whose judgment before seemed to be unjust, and the holy God will be sanctified by all in righteousness, so that what is said in the Gospel may be fulfilled: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name (Matt 6:9); and: Righteous Father, the world has not known you (John 17:25). Hence we must beware lest we anticipate the judgment of God, whose judgments are great and unspeakable, and of which the Apostle speaks: His judgments are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable (Rom 11:33), until he lights up the hidden things of darkness and lays open the thoughts of hearts (1 Cor 4:5), he who says in the Gospel: Judge not, that you be not judged (Matt 7:1). In agreement with this sentence the apostle Paul commanded: Who are you that judge another's servant? To his own Lord he stands or falls. But he will stand: for God is able to make him stand (Rom 14:4).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the lambs shall feed according to their order, and strangers shall eat the deserts turned into fruitfulness. For the lambs feeding according to their order, which is taken in the good sense, the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated, those that are plundered shall feed like bulls, understanding bulls in place of lambs, and again interpreting lambs in place of strangers. But when the Lord has been exalted in judgment, and the holy one sanctified in his righteousness, so that the wicked husbandmen perish wickedly and the lofty cedar is cut down by the axe of the Lord, then those who are of the number of the lambs, not of the goats, will feed in the meadows of the Church and will say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing (Ps 22 [23]:1); and what the Jews have deserted, turned into fruitfulness, the people of the nations will eat. This is according to tropology. But to complete the order of the history, the same thing is said in other words of which we read above: Strangers devour your land in your sight, and it is deserted and overthrown by foreign peoples (Isa 1:7). For a multitude of the nations, gathered from the whole world, dwells in Judea; and, the former peoples having been cast out, blindness has therefore come in part upon the house of Israel, that the fullness of the nations might come in (Rom 11). And beautifully, according to the Seventy, those were plundered and laid waste and led into captivity like bulls of whom the Lord had said, Fat bulls have beset me, so that lambs might occupy the places of the bulls.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to you who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with the rope of a cart. Who say: Let his work make haste and come quickly, that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, and we know it. For the rope of a cart the Seventy translated the strap of the yoke of a heifer, or of a cow. That sins are called bonds we read quite often; among them is this: Each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins (Prov 5:22). And the Lord, rebuking the offending people, which had joined sins to sins, made a scourge of cords, showing them how they had made the house of God a den of robbers (John 2), and had turned the seat of prayer into a house of trade (Matt 21). The guest too at the Lord's supper, not having a wedding garment, is bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness (Matt 22). And the Lord came to say to those who were in bonds, Come out (Isa 49:9); and to those who were in darkness, Be revealed (Ps 145 [146]:8). For he himself looses the fettered and enlightens the blind, whom Jeremiah calls the prisoners of the earth. Nor does he lament over those who have begun to sin and have at once ceased; for there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin at some time (Eccl 7:21); but over those who have drawn out their sins with a long cord. Hence we read in Numbers too (chapter 19) that the red heifer, whose ashes are the expiation of the people, is not sacrificed and offered at the altar of the Lord unless it has done no earthly works and has not drawn the yoke, nor been bound with the bonds of the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar. And in this same prophet, instead of the girdle of truth, the daughters of Zion are girded with a cord. Ahithophel too and Judas [one of whom betrayed David, the other the Lord], drawing their sins with a very long rope, perished by hanging, thinking that the evil of conscience would be ended by present death, and that there is nothing after death. And that according to the Hebrew and all the other translators they are called cords of vanity signifies this: that for those who commit it sin is easily woven, and is as empty and easy as the threads of spiders are woven; but when we wish to get out of it, we are tied with the most solid bonds. And the cart full and laden with sins they understand more easily who remember that it is written in Zechariah that impiety sits upon a talent of lead (Zech 5), and that the Egyptians, who were weighed down by the heavy burden of their sins, were sunk like lead in the Red Sea (Exod 15). And in another place the sinner says: My iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me (Ps 37 [38]:5). These things are said to the princes of the Jews, who were rebuked above for avarice and luxury: that, called by the Lord to penitence, and afterwards by his Apostles, they persevere to this day in blasphemies, and three times every day in all the synagogues, under the name of the Nazarenes, they anathematize the Christian name.
Homilies on the Gospels 2:1

Our Lord shows what reward awaits hypocritical workers when he made a scourge of cords and drove them all out of the temple. They are cast out as sharers of the inheritance of the saints if, after they are chosen to be among the saints, they either perform good acts deceitfully or evil acts openly. He also drives out the sheep and oxen when he shows the life and teaching of such persons deserve condemnation. The cords with which he expelled the wicked persons from the temple by scourging them are the progressive development of [their] evil actions, which provide material to the strict Judge for condemning those who are to be rejected.… The person who heaps sins upon sins, for which he will be condemned more severely, is like one lengthening the cords with which he can be bound and scourged, adding to them little by little.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the sense is: Woe to you who think that the day of judgment will not be, or that the captivity which the prophetic discourse foretells will not come; who say to the Prophet: How long will you threaten us with the wrath of God? We wish to know it; let it come now. And they say this in irony, because they think it will not come, but is feigned by the Prophet.
SCORPIACE 1

For, in like manner, they also who oppose martyrdoms, representing salvation to be destruction, transmute sweet into bitter, as well as light into darkness. Thus, by preferring this very wretched life to that most blessed one, they put bitter for sweet, as well as darkness for light.
Commentary on Isaiah
