Woe to you who call evil good, and good evil, putting darkness for light, and light for darkness, putting bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter. It is a crime of the same kind to call good, light and sweet by contrary names as to call evil, darkness and bitter by the names of virtues. This is against those who do not think it a sin if they disparage the good, and do not judge it an offense if they praise the evil. And the Jews put good as evil, and light as darkness, and sweet as bitter, when they took up Barabbas, the author of robbery and sedition, and crucified Jesus, who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to save what had perished. In Barabbas let us understand the devil, who, though he is night and darkness, transforms himself into an Angel of light (Matt 27). Hence the Apostle too says: What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor 6:14, 15). For neither is the lamp to be taken away and put under the bushel or under the bed, but upon the lampstand, that it may give light to all. Nor is a tree bearing evil fruits to be called by the name of a good tree (Matt 5). Hence in Genesis too it is related in mystical speech that God divided between the light and the darkness, which in the beginning were borne over the abyss (Gen 1). And that the Savior is called good, he himself says in the Gospel: The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep (John 10:11). He says too that he is the light: I am the light of the world (John 8:12); and daily, filled with the heavenly bread, we say: Taste and see how sweet the Lord is (Ps 33 [34]:9). On the contrary, when we say, Deliver us from evil (Matt 6:13), and, The world is set in the evil one (1 John 5:19), we desire to be delivered from the snares of the devil. And that he himself is signified by the names of darkness and bitterness we read quite often. But we can say this too, that all doctrines contrary to the truth are bitter, and the truth alone is sweet. Hence we must beware lest we follow falsehood instead of truth, darkness instead of light. For there are many ways that seem right to men, and their ends reach to the depth of the underworld. There is also the righteous man perishing in his righteousness, to whom it is said: Be not overly righteous (Eccl 7:17). For which reasons Israel promises that he will walk by the king's way and will turn aside neither to the left nor to the right (Deut 5). And to say what I feel: with difficulty can anyone be free of this curse, since we often flatter the wicked for their power and despise the good for their poverty. Hence Aquila interpreted more expressively: Woe to him who says to the evil man, You are good, and to the good man, You are evil (Prov 17:15). And with this sense agrees what Solomon says in Proverbs: He who judges the righteous unrighteous, and the unrighteous righteous, both are abominable with God. The Scribes and Pharisees too, receiving not the words of the Savior but the traditions of men and old wives' fables, made good evil and evil good.
Enchiridion 6:19

"Woe unto them that call evil good." For this text is to be understood to refer not to humans but to those things that make humans evil, and the prophet's accusation is rightly applied to one who calls adultery good. But if someone should call another good whom he believes chaste, not knowing that he is an adulterer, he is deceived not in his understanding of good and evil but through the secrets of human conduct. He is calling a person good whom he believes to possess that which indubitably is good. The adulterer he would call evil, the chaste person good, and he calls the person in question good simply through not knowing that he is an adulterer and not chaste.
The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter IV

That the Black One may find no means of entrance, let us flee from every vanity, let us utterly hate the works of the way of wickedness. Do not, by retiring apart, live a solitary life, as if you were already [fully] justified; but coming together in one place, make common inquiry concerning what tends to your general welfare. For the Scripture saith, "Woe to them who are wise to themselves, and prudent in their own sight!"
Against the Pelagians 2.7

Who is the greatest subverter of the people of God—he who, relying on the power of free choice, despises the help of the Creator and is satisfied with following his own will, or he who dreads to be judged by the details of the Lord's commandments?
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own sight. You who seem to yourselves, he says, to be wise, who follow the prudence not of God but of men: and though you do not receive the power of God and the wisdom of God, you think yourselves wise (1 Cor 1). Between wisdom and prudence the Stoics say there is this difference: that wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human, but prudence only of mortal things. And these things are said consistently against the Scribes and Pharisees, who, having the key of knowledge, neither enter in to Christ themselves nor allow others to enter (Luke 11).
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 7

Consider as your superiors one another, especially those who are not committed to your charge, your neighbors, because even those whom you see doing certain wicked things—you do not know what good things may lie hidden in them. Therefore let each one strive to be great, but yet in some way not know that he is, lest while he arrogantly attributes greatness to himself, he lose it. For hence it is said through the prophet: "Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent before yourselves." Hence Paul says: "Be not wise in your own eyes." Hence against the proud Saul it is said: "When you were little in your own eyes, you were made head among the tribes of Israel." As if it were openly said: When you saw yourself as little, I made you great above others. But because you now see yourself as great, you are esteemed little by me.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to you who are mighty to drink wine, and strong men to mix strong drink, that is, drunkenness. Of those to whom he had said above, Woe to you who rise early in the morning to pursue drunkenness, and to drink until evening, so as to be inflamed with wine, he speaks now too: who are mighty to drink wine, and strong men to mix strong drink (Deut 32). Drunk with the wine of the dragon and the incurable venom of asps, they slandered the power of the Lord. And being drunk themselves, they made the peoples drunk, so that, raving with a like fury, they cried out together against the Lord. According to tropology we have already said before that the priests who are to enter the Tabernacle of God ought not to drink wine and strong drink (Lev 10). To which we now add that it was commanded the Nazirites too, who sanctify themselves to the Lord, that they should neither drink nor eat wine and strong drink and anything that comes from grapes, not even a raisin, nor vinegar made from wine (Num 6). But in Proverbs too it is commanded: Let the mighty who are wrathful not drink wine, lest when they have drunk they forget wisdom. Between wine and strong drink, according to the anagogy, I judge the difference to be this: that wine is one disturbance out of many, for example, of lust, of avarice, of gluttony, and of envy; but strong drink, that is, drunkenness, contains in itself all the passions of the vices, which in the Latin tongue we can more rightly call disturbances, because they overturn the settled state of the mind and make the drunken not know what they do. Those, then, who are set over others ought above all to be free of vices, and most of all of anger, which is nearest to madness, lest the more they can, the more they harm those subject to them. He mixes strong drink who, though full of drunkenness, pretends, in order to deceive men, to have certain shadows and images of the virtues.
Commentary on Isaiah

You who justify the wicked for gifts, and take away from the righteous man his righteousness. This too is part of the vices of the vineyard which instead of grapes made wild grapes, and, when the Lord waited for it to do judgment, did iniquity, justifying the wicked for gifts, and considering not the cases but the presents, which blind even the eyes of the wise. Hence we must beware lest we be drunk with wine, in which is luxury (Deut 16:19; Eph 5), and the thighs of our shame be laid bare (Gen 9), and lest we flatter the wicked for gifts and despise the righteousness of the righteous man for his poverty. This is commanded in the Epistle of James as well: that we not become judges of iniquity by honoring the wicked rich and despising the holy poor.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and the heat of the flame burns it up, so their root shall be as ashes, and their bud shall go up as dust. For they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, and have blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. For the causes given above, of pride and drunkenness and avarice, because instead of grapes they brought forth thorns, and hay, wood, stubble, and briers that are to burn, therefore the root of their malice will be reduced to ashes, and every flower and beauty of riches and of the body will be compared to dust (1 Cor 3). For they did not only do these things, but by these steps they came to blasphemy, so that they did not receive the law of the Lord and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel; of which we read above: Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa 2:3). The root can be taken as evil thoughts, and the fruit and bud as evil works and words, so that what lies hidden in the root is shown in the bud; and both will be devoured by the Lord's burning. Hence the Apostle too (Heb 12:15) speaks of the root of the bitterness of evils springing up.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore the fury of the Lord is angered against his people, and he has stretched out his hand over it and struck it, and the mountains are troubled, and their carcasses have become like dung in the midst of the streets. For all this his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Because they cast away the law of the Lord of hosts, which the Lord promises through Jeremiah that he will give, saying: Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will strike a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not according to the pact which I made with your fathers in the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt (Jer 31:31, 32). And they blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel, saying: He has a demon, and is a Samaritan (John 8:48); and: Is not this the son of the carpenter? (Matt 13:55). Therefore the fury of the Lord is angered against his people, that fury which before had been angered against the princes and the mighty, who were wise in their own eyes and justified the wicked for gifts, and the tongue of fire had devoured them like stubble, and the heat of the flame had burned them up, so that the mighty might mightily suffer torments. And he stretched out his hand against it, which he calls his people because it was the portion of his inheritance and the cord of his possession (Deut 32). And he stretches out his hand to strike, and his fury is angered, of which we read in another place too: O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath (Ps 6:1). And Jeremiah: Correct us, he says, O Lord, but in judgment, and not in fury (Jer 10:24). And the Lord is said to rage, not because he is subject to human disturbances, but because we who offend do not fear the Lord unless we have heard him angry. Hence the Apostle too writes (Rom 2) that the goodness and patience of God call us to penitence, but we, according to our hardness and impenitent heart, treasure up wrath for ourselves in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God. And what the hand is that is stretched out or lifted up over the sinful people Job says more plainly: For the hand of the Lord has touched me (Job 19:21). Hence the devil too, knowing the mighty hand of the Lord and the arm that has been revealed to all the nations, says to the Lord: Put forth your hand and touch all that he has: and see if he will not bless you to your face (Job 2:5). And that what is to come is spoken of as past follows prophetic custom, in which the things foretold as to come are so certain that they are thought to be past. This is sung in the Psalms too: They gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink (Ps 68 [69]:22). And again: They divided my garments among them, and upon my vesture they cast lots (Ps 21 [22]:19). And as for what follows, And he struck it, that is, his people, and the mountains are troubled: some think the mountains are the contrary powers, or those spirits which are in the ministry of God and to whom sinners are handed over to be punished. But we think it is said hyperbolically: that because of the greatness of the impending evils even the mountains are moved, and all the streets of the cities are filled with the corpses of the dead. That this befell the Jews after the passion of the Lord under Vespasian and Hadrian no one doubts. And though these things have been done, his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out, or lifted high, which shows the bearing of one who is angry and strikes. And it is to be noted in all these things that he does not reproach them with idolatry, nor with other sins by which they offended God, but because they cast away the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the word of the Lord.
Epistle of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans

I Glorify God, even Jesus Christ, who has given you such wisdom. For I have observed that ye are perfected in an immoveable faith, as if ye were nailed to the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, both in the flesh and in the spirit, and are established in love through the blood of Christ, being fully persuaded with respect to our Lord, that He was truly of the seed of David according to the flesh, and the Son of God according to the will and power of God; that He was truly born of a virgin, was baptized by John, in order that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him; and was truly, under Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch, nailed [to the cross] for us in His flesh. Of this fruit we are by His divinely-blessed passion, that He might set up a standard for all ages, through His resurrection, to all His holy and faithful [followers], whether among Jews or Gentiles, in the one body of His Church.
AGAINST MARCION 4.15

He [God] says the following about the Gentiles, those he was about to call together from the ends of the earth: "Behold, they shall come swiftly with speed." He says "swiftly" because of the hastening toward end times. He says "with speed" because they will not be weighed down by the weights of the ancient law. He says "they shall be filled" because it is a promise made only to those who hunger and thirst.
Commentary on Isaiah

And he will lift up a signal among the nations far off, and will whistle to him from the ends of the earth; and behold, he will come swiftly in haste. There shall be none faint nor laboring among them; he shall not slumber nor sleep, nor shall the girdle of his loins be loosed, nor the latchet of his shoe be broken. His arrows are sharp, and all his bows bent; the hoofs of his horses are like flint, and his wheels like the rush of a tempest. His roaring is like a lion's; he shall roar like the lion's whelps, and gnash his teeth, and seize the prey, and embrace it, and there shall be none to rescue it. And he shall resound over it in that day like the sound of the sea: we shall look upon the land, and behold, the darkness of tribulation, and the light is darkened by its gloom. The Hebrews understand this place to be prophesied of the Babylonians and Nebuchadnezzar, that by the will of God he was brought into Judea and Jerusalem and overthrew the temple. But we, following the order and joining what follows to what precedes, say that the signal was lifted up among the nations far off, and that the Lord whistled for them or drew them from the ends of the earth, for this reason: because they cast away the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the holy word. For if the discourse were about the Babylonians, according to prophetic custom he would have said: I will call him who is from the North, because, relative to the position of Judea, the Assyrians and Chaldeans are in the northern region. Or certainly he would have described the Babylonians and Assyrians more openly. But now, by saying, He will lift up a signal among the nations far off, and will whistle to him from the ends of the earth, he signifies nations set far off and dwelling at the ends of the earth: doubtless the Romans and all the peoples of Italy, Gaul and Spain, who under Vespasian and Hadrian lay subject to the Roman empire. Hence Italy too, from the fact that Hesperus sets there, was once called Hesperia. And at his coming it was struck, and all the mountains of Judea were troubled, as Theodotion and Symmachus interpreted, or were moved, as Aquila set down, or were embittered, as the Seventy translated, so that by the onslaught of the enemies all the streets were filled with the corpses of the dead. The divine discourse, then, describes the swiftness of the army that comes, which came not by its own will but by the Lord's, nay rather was drawn and summoned by his whistle: that it did not faint nor grow weary on so long a march, and in its greed for plunder did not admit sleep to its eyes, and its shoes too were not worn out; the multitude of archers, the squadrons of horsemen, the heat of the chariots and four-horse teams; that like a lion it came not so much to fight as to plunder and devour; and the howling of the victorious army is compared to the waves of the sea. From this it is to be noted what the sound of the sea signifies wherever it is named in the Scriptures. When, then, the Roman army has come and seized the prey, and there has been no one to rescue it, the Prophet, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, joins himself to the people and says: We shall look upon the land, and behold, the darkness of tribulation. For we shall not dare to look upon heaven, whose dweller we have offended; and our light, which we always had in God, has been darkened by the gloom of tribulations. I have read in someone's Commentaries that what is said, He will lift up a signal among the nations far off, and will whistle to him from the ends of the earth, ought to be understood of the calling of the nations: that, when the signal of the Cross was lifted up and the burdens of sins laid down, they came swiftly and believed. But I do not know how what follows can agree with this sense.

n: Died. Either a natural (Calmet) or a civil death, by means of the leprosy. (Chaldean) (Tostat. 7.) --- This and the former chapters relate to the commencement of Joathan's reign, whether before or after the death of Ozias. (Calmet) --- Many think that this was the first prediction of Isaias. (Origen) (St. Jerome, ad Dam.) --- I saw. By a prophetic vision, as if I had been present at the dedication of the temple, 3 Kings viii. 10. (Calmet) --- Lord. Not the Father, as some have asserted, but the Son, John xii. 40. (St. Jerome, ad Dam.) (Calmet) --- Neither Moses nor any other saw the substance of God; but only a shadow. Yet Manasses hence took a pretext to have Isaias slain. (Origen) (St. Jerome, Trad.) (Paralipomenon) (Worthington)

The two Seraphims "burning." They are supposed to constitute the highest order of angels, Numbers xxi. 6. --- His. God's or their own face. Hebrew and Septuagint are ambiguous. Out of respect, (Calmet) they looked not at the divine majesty. (Menochius)
Glory. By no means of the Incarnation. The unity and Trinity are insinuated. (St. Jerome; St. Gregory, Mor. xxix. 16.)

Of him. Septuagint, "them," (Haydock) the Seraphim signifying that the veil was removed by the death of Christ, (Theodoret) or that the people should be led into captivity, as a Jew explained it to St. Jerome.

Peace. It is proper for sinners to do so, Ecclesiasticus xv. 9. The prophet was grieved that he was unworthy to join in the acclamation of the Seraphim, and had reason to fear death, Genesis xvi. 13., and Exodus xxxiii. 20. He finds himself less able to speak than before, like Moses, Exodus iv. 10., and vi. 12.
Coal. "Carbuncle," (Septuagint) the word of God, (St. Basil) spirit of prophecy, (St. Jerome, 142. ad Dam., &c.)
Sin. Impediment in speech. All defects were attributed to some sin, (John ix. 2.) as Job's friends maintained.
For us. Hence arises a proof of the plurality of persons. (Calmet) --- Send me. Thus Isaias was an evangelical and apostolical prophet. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

Blind. The prophets are said to do what they denounce. (St. Thomas Aquinas, 1. q. xxiv. 3.) (Sanctius) --- Septuagint, "heavy or gross is the heart," &c. The authors of the New Testament quote it thus less harshly. --- Them. Is God unwilling to heal? Why then does he send his prophet? (Calmet) --- He intimates that all the graces offered would be rendered useless by the hardened Jews. (St. Isidore. Pelus 2. ep. 270.) --- Hebrew may be, "surely they will not see," &c. (Calmet)
Desolate. By means of Nabuchodonosor, (St. Chrysostom) and the Romans, (Eusebius, &c.) or even till the end of the world, their obstinacy will continue.
Earth. After the captivity, the people shall be more docile. But this was more fully verified by the preaching of the gospel.

Tithing. The land shall produce its fruits, and people shall bring their tithes, Ezechiel xx. 40. There shall be some left; (chap. i. 9., and iv. 3.; Calmet) though only a tenth part will embrace Christianity. (St. Basil) --- Made. Septuagint, "ravaged." They shall be exposed to many persecutions under Epiphanes, and few shall escape the arms of the Romans, (Calmet) those particularly (Haydock) who shall be a holy seed. (Calmet) --- The apostles were of Jewish extraction, (Haydock) and spread the gospel throughout the world. (Menochius)

f: HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 1

So long as "King Uzziah" lived, the prophet Isaiah could not "see the vision". For "Uzziah" was a sinner, "doing what was wicked before the sight of the Lord", and acting against the will of the divine law. "He entered the temple" and the holy of holies, and for this reason he was covered with "leprosy on his forehead", so that, going outside the city, he was reckoned among the unclean. Such a ruler of the soul, therefore, must die, that we may be able "to see the vision" of God; for not in vain is it written: "and it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord". For each one of us "Uzziah" is alive, or Pharaoh, and we do not "groan" while doing the "works" of Egypt. But if he "dies", then we "groan", as it is written in Exodus. If "Uzziah" lives, we do not "see the glory of God"; but if he "dies", then we "see"—as soon as "Uzziah dies"—"the glory of God", provided only that the Word "reign" in us, the Word who said: "but I have been appointed king by him", and that wrath does not "reign". Indeed there is also a "king" of "sin"; the Apostle, knowing this, says: "let sin therefore not reign in your mortal body". Wretched is that man in whom "sin reigns", who hands himself over to such a "king", despising the kingdom of God and subjecting himself to pleasure. Therefore the lover of pleasure is not a lover of God, and according to the Apostle it is said of certain persons: "loving pleasure more than God". And indeed this very thing was said not of those who are entirely unbelievers, but of those who dwell within, "loving pleasure more than God, having a semblance of piety but denying its power". These things are said on account of the death of "King Uzziah", after whose demise the prophet says he "saw the vision". But what is the "vision"? "I saw the Lord seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". Not everyone who "sees the Lord" "sees" him "seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". I know that another prophet "saw the Lord" and "saw" him "seated upon a throne", but not "lofty" nor "exalted". Expounding the Scripture, Daniel says: "thrones were placed", and that "throne" was not "lofty". And: "I will come to sit in judgment over the people in the valley of Jehoshaphat". Therefore here he "sat in the valley", and "in the valley" when he is about "to judge", when he is about to condemn. But it is another thing "to see him seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". And in Micah "God goes forth and descends". And in order to see Sodom, "he descends": "Descending", he says, "I will see whether they have carried out to the full according to the cry of them that comes to me". God, therefore, is sometimes seen above, sometimes below, according to the dignity of the matters at hand. "I saw the Lord", then, Isaiah says, "seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". If I "see God" reigning over those who are here, I do not "see" him "upon a throne lofty and exalted"; if I "see" him "reigning" over the heavenly powers, I "see" him "upon a throne lofty and exalted". What do I mean by the heavenly powers? "Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers" are the heavenly powers. And if I "see" him, how he "reigns" over these in the Word, "I saw the Lord seated upon a throne lofty and exalted". "And the house was full of his glory". On high, where his "throne" is "exalted", "the house is also full of his glory". I do not think that this house which is on earth "is full of glory". "The Lord's is the earth and the fullness thereof". But the "fullness of the glory of God" you will not find in the present; yet if anyone builds a temple to God, the "glory of God" will be seen, and if he keeps what has been said, "the house" will be seen to be "full of the glory of God". But I do not know whether the "house" is filled with "glory" in this way. And in Leviticus, insofar as concerns the present, not yet—but, God granting, it will be read in the assembly that follows—it is said that the Lord commanded certain things to be done, that the "glory of the Lord" might be seen. Nor will the "glory of God" ever appear if these things are not done. And we shall come to know those things when they have been read.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 5

"It came to pass", he says, "in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". The "vision" is recorded; why is the time of the king signified? Give heed to when the "vision" arose: when "King Uzziah died", Isaiah "saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up". If any of us knows who "Uzziah" was and what he did, he can know what the prophet taught through the Spirit, what the divine word sets forth for us. I will go to the life of "King Uzziah" and inquire from the books of Kingdoms and from the history of Chronicles concerning "Uzziah", and there I see that it is necessary, if it is to come to pass that "I should see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne high and lifted up", that "King Uzziah" must "die" for me. This "Uzziah", descending from the seed of David and "reigning" over the people of Judah, as long indeed as "Zechariah, who had understanding" lived — for so it is written in the second book of Chronicles — "did what was right in the sight of the Lord". And not content with this, he made great lights for the Lord and set the temple of God in order, and many were his virtues in religion. But when "Zechariah who had understanding" died, then he did evil. Do you wish to know this evil that he did? He was a king, not a priest (one is the royal order, another the priestly order); he wished to "enter into the temple" and to perform the place of a priest and to do a work which had not been granted to him; he "entered in", forestalling the priests, and took the "vessel of libation". But there entered also the "chief of the priests" who was at that time, "and eighty priests with him"; "the chief of the priests said to him": are you not Uzziah, and not a priest? He violently persisted, "and leprosy went up upon his forehead"; he was cast out as dead, he "went out" of the temple, the Lord led him out. Therefore he became a "leper" because of his transgression of the law. Each one is under a kingdom, whether of "sin" or of righteousness. If "sin reigns" in me, I am one of the kings of Israel who "entered the temple" violently; if I am righteous according to the measure of my progress and do what is right and persevere before the sight of God, righteousness "reigns" in me. But as long as the "leper" lived, Isaiah had "unclean lips"; as long as the wicked man lived, Isaiah could not "see the Lord of Sabaoth" and had "unclean lips"; for he was under a wicked king. But when does he begin to "see the vision" of God? "In the year in which Uzziah died". Things similar to these you will be able to learn also from many scriptures, God granting it. In Exodus something of this kind is written: "and it came to pass after many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned, and their cry went up to God". As long as Pharaoh lived, the "children of Israel" did "not groan", and, placed under punishments, they did not even have the free faculty of "groaning"; for the king was alive, who commanded them to make "bricks and straw". As long as Pharaoh lived, they did "not groan to God"; when Pharaoh died, then they had the strength to lift up their faces wet with weeping. The wicked king lives in our breast as long as Pharaoh the devil lives. Then we labor at "bricks" and "straw", then we swallow our tears in silence and do the first works of iniquity; but when he has died, at the visitation of the Lord our God, then we "groan to the Lord". Therefore let us pray that the kingdom of "sin, which is in our mortal body", may die. For it says: "sin was dead, but I lived"; and again: "sin revived, but I died". When "Uzziah", who holds the kingdom of "sin", "dies", Pharaoh too "dies". When the most wicked "king dies", I lift my eyes to heaven and God hears my voice, as he did for Abraham and Isaac and Jacob; and "I see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting" and reigning "upon a high throne", whom the people did not see; for "Uzziah had not yet died". I wish to insert something similar concerning the good thing, which is contrary to this. This very "Uzziah", as long as "Zechariah who had understanding" lived, "did not sin in the sight of God"; when Zechariah died he turned aside from the Lord, at the time when he was ruling over the people and governing the city. And, reading these things by day and by night and hearing the Lord say: "you ought to have put the money on the table, and I at my coming would have exacted it with interest", let us not gather up "in a napkin the mina" entrusted to us, nor let us "put the money on the table", but let us lend it out to the peoples. And when we have entrusted the Lord's account to you, it will have to be seen how you will pay back what was entrusted "with interest". Amen!
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 88: WHY CHRIST APPEARED SEATED TO ISAIAH BUT STANDING TO STEPHEN

If grace is greater and understanding clearer in the New Testament than in the Old, why did the prophet Isaiah see the Lord of hosts, who is Christ, seated on the throne of majesty, according to the interpretation of John the Evangelist? For he said among other things: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his majesty and spoke of him” (Isaiah 6:1; John 12:41). But in the New Testament Stephen the first martyr says that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). What does it mean that here he appears as subject after his victories, and there as Lord before he had conquered? — As the occasion required, so the Lord showed himself. To the prophet he appeared as a king rebuking the people: and he showed himself as what he was, that is, seated. For the reason lay in the peace of his divinity. But the slander of the Jews caused him to appear to Stephen as standing. In Stephen the cause of the Savior was suffering violence. Therefore, with God the judge seated, he appeared standing, as one who was pleading a case: and because his cause is good, he was at the right hand of the judge. Everyone who pleads a case must stand.
Commentary on Isaiah

In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. That Isaiah prophesied under four kings, over Judah and Jerusalem, was shown by the title of the first vision; that is, under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. So when Uzziah was dead, under whom all the things we have expounded above were spoken, his son Jotham succeeded him, who reigned sixteen years, and did what was right in the sight of the Lord, and built the high gate of the temple. While he was ruling, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, so as to show the bearing of one who reigns.

And the things that were under him filled the Temple, or, as Theodotion and Symmachus translated: And the things that were under his feet filled the Temple. For which the Seventy translated: And the house was full of his glory. On this vision, about thirty years ago, when I was at Constantinople and was being trained in the study of the holy Scriptures under that most eloquent man Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of the same city, I know that I dictated a brief and hasty treatise, both to make trial of my little talent and to obey friends who bade me. To that little book, then, I send the reader, and I pray that he be content with the brief exposition of the present time. That Uzziah was struck with leprosy because he claimed for himself a priesthood not permitted to him, the sacred history relates; and when he was dead, the Lord is seen in the Temple which he had polluted (2 Chr 26). From this we perceive that while a leprous king reigns in us, we cannot see the Lord reigning in his majesty, nor know the mysteries of the holy Trinity. Hence also in Exodus, after Pharaoh was dead, who oppressed Israel with clay and straw and bricks, the people, who while he lived could not cry out, cried to the Lord. And Ezekiel, when Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, a most wicked prince, was dead, falls upon his face and cries with a loud voice to the Lord. And beautifully, according to the Hebrew, it is not the Lord himself who filled the Temple, whose throne is heaven and the earth the footstool of his feet, and of whom we read in another place: The Lord is in his holy Temple, the Lord's seat is in heaven (Ps 10 [11]:5); but the things that were under his feet filled the Temple (Isa 66). But who this Lord is who is seen, we learn more fully in the evangelist John and in the Acts of the Apostles. Of whom John says: These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory, and spoke of him (John 12:41), meaning without doubt Christ. Again Paul in the Acts of the Apostles, where at Rome he speaks to the Jews: Well, he says, did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: With the ear you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive; for the heart of this people has been made gross, and with their ears they have heard heavily; and they have shut their eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them (Acts 28:26-27). Now the Son was seen in the bearing of one who reigns, and the Holy Spirit spoke, on account of the fellowship of majesty and the unity of substance. Someone may ask how the Prophet now says that he has seen the Lord, and not simply the Lord but the Lord Sabaoth, as he himself testifies in what follows; when the evangelist John has said: No one has ever seen God (John 1:18). And God speaks to Moses: You cannot see my face; for man shall not see my face and live (Exod 33:20). To which we shall answer that not only the divinity of the Father, but not even that of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, since in the Trinity there is one nature, can the eyes of the flesh behold; but the eyes of the mind, of which the Savior himself says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matt 5:8). We read that the Lord was seen by Abraham in the figure of a man; and that he who was God wrestled with Jacob as a man. Hence that very place was called Phanuel, that is, the face of God: For I have seen, he says, the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved (Gen 32). Ezekiel too saw the Lord in the form of a man sitting upon the Cherubim; from his loins and downward there was as it were fire, and the upper parts had the appearance of electrum (Ezek 1). The nature of God, then, is not discerned, but he is seen by men as he wills.
Commentary on Isaiah

The sheer size of the volumes being woven in the explanation of the prophet Isaiah is enough for me, where to pass anything over is a loss to the understanding. Therefore in the individual books, which signify only their number and order, I have set brief little prefaces. And you, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, I beg to help me with your prayers in the exposition of a most difficult vision: in which God almighty is seen in his majesty; and two Seraphim standing round about him and crying: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory; and the threshold of the temple moved and shaken, and the Jewish house filled with the darkness of error. And the Prophet, in comparison with the divine glory, saying that he has unclean lips and dwells in the midst of a blaspheming people, who cried out with the concordant voice of impiety: Crucify, crucify such a one; and, We have no king but Caesar (John 19:6 and 15). And one of the Seraphim sent to Isaiah, who, having taken a coal from the altar with tongs, was to cleanse the prophet's lips, while the people remained unclean. This, then, is the opening of the third book on Isaiah.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 1:4

No one can deny that the prophet saw the Son in the glory of God the Father, as John said: "Isaiah said this because he saw his glory and spoke of him [Christ]." Look and see the great honor that is due to God, and see the authority he has over all creation. God is high and lifted up on a throne, crowned with the splendor of his reign.… In my view we should not think of the throne of God as lifted up in a physical way. That would be foolish and absurd. Rather, that the throne is said to be lifted up means that the reign of God transcends all things. That God is sitting refers to his immovability and that his blessings are everlasting and unchanging.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 4

It is impossible to find the beginning of God. The beginning of God's movement you can nowhere grasp—not you, I say, and not anyone else, nor any other of the things that have subsistence. The Savior alone and the Holy Spirit, who have always been with God, see His "face"; and perhaps also the "angels", who "continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven", see also the beginnings of His works. And so too before men "the Seraphim hide their feet"; for the "last things", such as they are, cannot be recounted. "Who has announced concerning the last things?" says the Scripture. The things that we see—granting even that we do see something—are the middle things. What existed before the world we do not know; yet certain things did exist before the world. What is to follow after the world we do not apprehend for certain; yet other things will be after the world. Those things, therefore, that are written—"in the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss; and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters"—these are apprehended; those "waters", over which the "Spirit of God" brooded, belonged to the world. But also the "darkness", which "was over the abyss", is not unbegotten; for both were created out of nothing. Hear God saying in Isaiah: "I am God, who framed light and made darkness". Hear wisdom proclaiming in Proverbs: "before all the abysses I was born". These were not unbegotten; but when or how they were born, I do not know. For by the "Seraphim" are "veiled" the first of God's works, that is, the "face of God"; and likewise also the "feet". The things that after the last age are to be for ages of ages, who can expound? It belongs to garrulous men to promise knowledge of these things—men who do not know that a human being can grasp only those things that are the middle things. And the things that after the world, up to the consummation, are to be in the judgment—concerning the punishments, concerning the recompense—of these too many things are hidden from us. This is because of what is written: "with two they veiled the face". But not only did they "veil", they also "covered over", that is, "veiled", so that neither might even a little of the first things be seen—I mean of the "face"—nor might even a little of the "last things" be recognized, that is, of His "feet". "And with two they were flying". The middle things are laid open for contemplation.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 1

"And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one, and six wings to the other". I see two "Seraphim", each of them having in itself "six wings". Then the arrangement of the "wings". "And with two wings indeed they covered the face"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they covered the feet"—not their own, but God's—"and with two wings they were flying". According to what is written, it seems contradictory: if they "stood", they could not "fly". But it is written: "they stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they covered the face and with two they covered the feet, and with two they were flying; and they cried one to another". Truly these "Seraphim", who are around God, who by knowledge alone say: "Holy, Holy, Holy!", on this account keep the mystery of the Trinity, because they too are holy; for among all the things that are, nothing is holier than these. And not lightly do they say "one to another": "Holy, Holy, Holy!", but they proclaim with a cry the confession that is salutary for all. What are these two "Seraphim"? My Lord Jesus and the Holy Spirit. And do not think that the nature of the Trinity is divided, if the functions of the names are preserved. "They covered the face" of God; for the beginning of God is unknown. But also the "feet"; for what last thing is comprehended in our God? Only the middle things are seen; what was before these, I do not know. From the things that are, I understand God; what will come after these, insofar as they are to come, I do not know. "Who has declared it to him?" said Ecclesiastes. "Announce to me the first things and the last things that shall be, and I will say that you are gods", said Isaiah. From which, if anyone should tell the "past things" and be able to tell the "last things", he is "God"; who, then, can tell them except the "Seraphim"? Who can say: "Holy, Holy, Holy!" except the "Seraphim"? But they laid bare which part of God, so to speak—his middle—and "they cried one to the other", standing beside God "and saying": "Holy, Holy, Holy!". They "stand", therefore, and are moved; they "stand" with God, they are moved in making God known; for understand that "they cover the face, they cover the feet"—they do not move the things that are covered, they do not "cover" the things with which "they fly". And they say: "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory". The coming of my Lord Jesus Christ is announced; and so now "the whole earth is full of his glory". Or else it is not yet "full", but it is to come to pass that it be filled, when that prayer shall have been fulfilled by which the Lord himself commanded us to "pray" to the "Father", saying: "when you pray, say: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name! Thy kingdom come! Thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth!". As yet the "will" of the "Father" is "in heaven"; "on earth" his "will" is not yet fulfilled; and Jesus himself, according to the dispensation of the flesh which he had put on, says: "he gave me all power, as in heaven so on earth"—not that he did not have "power on earth", he who had it "in heaven", and that he received something of the world, he who "had come into his own", but that God might so be believed "on earth" as he was believed "in heaven"; therefore the man Christ received "power" which before he did not have, and up to the present he does not yet have "power" over all "on earth". For over those who sin he does not yet reign; but when the "power" over these too has been given to him, when "all things have been made subject" to him, then the "power" will be complete and he will go about "subjecting all things to himself". But some do not yet wish to be "made subject" to him, but as yet are "subjected" to his enemies. Let us, moreover, say: "shall not my soul be made subject to God? for from him is my salvation".
Commentary on Isaiah

Seraphim stood above it; six wings to the one, and six wings to the other: with two they covered his face, and with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to another, and said: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. What we, following the other Translators and the Hebrew truth, in which is written MEMMALLO ממעללו, that is, ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ, which in Latin is said above it, have rendered, the Seventy translated round about him, so that the Seraphim are described as standing not above the Temple but round about the Lord. Again, where we said that one of the Seraphim covered his face and feet, by which is understood God's: in the Hebrew is written PHANAU פניו and REGLAU (רגליו), which can be interpreted both as his and as its own: so that, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew speech, the Seraphim may be said to cover both the face and feet of God and their own face and feet. In the seventy-ninth psalm we read: You who sit upon the Cherubim, shine forth (Ps 79 [80]:3): who in our language are interpreted multitude of knowledge. Hence the Lord is plainly shown to sit upon the Cherubim in the manner of a charioteer. But the Seraphim, apart from this place, I do not know that I have read anywhere else in the canonical Scriptures, who are said to stand above the Temple, or round about the Lord. Therefore those err who are accustomed to say in their prayers: You who sit upon the Cherubim and Seraphim, which Scripture has not taught. Now Seraphim is interpreted ἐμπρησταὶ, which we can say as kindling or burning, according to what we read elsewhere: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire (Ps 103 [104]:5). Hence also the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews, which Latin custom does not receive: Are they not all, he says, ministering spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb 1:14)? Daniel too, when he had described the Lord in the bearing of one who reigns, added: Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him. (Dan 7:10). In the Cherubim, then, the Lord is shown; in the Seraphim he is in part shown, in part hidden. For they cover his face and feet, because we can know neither the things past before the world nor the things to come after the world; but we contemplate only the middle things, which were made in the six days. Nor is it strange to believe this of the Seraphim, since the apostles too open the Savior to believers and hide him from unbelievers; and there was a veil before the Ark of the Testament (Exod 40). They are said also to have wings, on account of their swiftness and their running to and fro in all things; or because they always dwell in higher places. For neither does that which is said of the winds, Who walks upon the wings of the winds (Ps 103 [104]:4), testify that the winds truly have wings, after the fables of the poets and the licence of painters; but rather their swift running to and fro in all things. And each has six wings, because we know only of the making of the world and of the present age.
Commentary on Isaiah

Impiously, therefore, a certain one understands the two Seraphim as the Son and the Holy Spirit: since, according to the evangelist John and the apostle Paul, we teach that the Son of God was seen in the majesty of one who reigns, and that the Holy Spirit spoke. Some of the Latins understand the two Seraphim as the old and the new Instrument, which speak only of the present age. Hence they are said to have six wings, and to cover the face and feet of God, and to bring forth in rivalry the testimony of the truth, and in all that they cry to show forth the mysteries of the Trinity. And to marvel together that the Lord Sabaoth, being set in the form of God the Father, took the form of a servant and humbled himself even unto death, and the death of the cross (Phil 2), and that no longer, as before, do heavenly things alone know him, but earthly things also.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 1:3

My Hebrew master used to say that the two seraphim, which are described in Isaiah as having six wings each and as crying one to another and saying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts," were to be understood to mean the only-begotten Son of God and the Holy Spirit.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 4:3

My Hebrew teacher also used to teach as follows, that since the beginning or the end of all things could not be comprehended by any except our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, this was the reason why Isaiah spoke of there being in the vision that appeared to him two seraphim only, who with two wings cover the face of God, with two cover his feet and with two fly, crying one to another and saying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of your glory." For because the two seraphim alone have their wings over the face of God and over his feet, we may venture to declare that neither the armies of the holy angels, nor the holy thrones, nor the dominions, nor principalities nor powers can wholly know the beginnings of all things and the ends of the universe.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 4

"And they cried out one to another", not "one" to many, but "one to another". For to hear the holiness of God, which is announced by the Savior, according to the dignity of the matter no one can except the Holy Spirit; just as, in turn, to indwell the sanctity of God, which is announced by the Holy Spirit, no one can except the Savior alone. On this account "they cried out one to another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy!" It does not suffice for them to cry 'Holy!' once, nor twice, but they take up the perfect number of the Trinity, that they may manifest the multitude of the holiness of God, which is the repeated commonalty of a threefold holiness; to the holiness of the Father is joined the holiness of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. "For both He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one". He who "sanctifies" is the Savior, according to this—that as a man He receives holiness from God the Father. And so they say: "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth!". And "Sabaoth" is interpreted, as Aquila has handed down, the Lord of armies.

"The whole earth is full of His glory". Once the "house" was full of "glory", but now to those who are upon the "earth" it is prophesied by the Seraphim that it shall come to pass that Christ will fill "the whole earth" with the "glory" of God. For in all who by their manner of life glorify God, there is "His glory", and thus "the whole earth is full of the glory" of God. Once "the whole earth was" not "full of the glory" of God, but one corner of the earth, when it was said: "God is known in Judea, in Israel His name is great". Glory be to God, "who sent His Son", that "the whole earth might become full of His glory". But what does it profit you if the "earth" is "full" of the "glory" of God because of the churches of the blessed who are everywhere, but you yourself are not a partaker of the "glory" of the "fullness of God"? You too, therefore, labor and strive in all things, seeking the "glory" of God, that it may dwell and find a place also in you, and that you too may become, together with "the whole earth" in which is the "glory" of God, "full of His glory". How does the fullness of the "glory" of God come about through each one of us? If the things I do, the things I speak, are done unto the "glory" of God, then my word and my act become "full" of the "glory" of God. If both my going out and my coming in are unto the "glory" of God, if my food, if my drink, if "all" that I do "is done unto the glory of God", then I too am a partaker of this saying: "the earth is full of His glory".
Catechetical Lecture 23:6

We make mention also of the seraphim, whom Isaiah in the Holy Spirit saw standing around the throne of God, and with two of their wings veiling their face, and with two their feet, while with two they flew, crying, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts." For the reason of our reciting this confession of God, delivered down to us from the seraphim, is this, that so we may be partakers with the hosts of the world above in their hymn of praise.
On the Holy Spirit 3.16.110

Cherubim and seraphim with unwearied voices praise him and say, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts." They say it not once, lest you should believe that there is but one; not twice, lest you should exclude the Spirit; they say not holies [in the plural], lest you should imagine that there is plurality, but they repeat three times and say the same word, that even in a hymn you may understand the distinction of persons in the Trinity and the oneness of the Godhead, and while they say this they proclaim God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And in that they cry one to another, or, according to the Hebrews, this one to that one, that is, one to one, they exhort one another to the praises of the Lord, and say: Holy, Holy, Holy, the Lord of hosts, so as to show the mystery of the Trinity in one Godhead; and to testify that no longer the Temple of the Jews, as before, but the whole earth is full of the glory of him who for our salvation deigned to take a human body and to come down to the earth. Indeed, when Moses too was praying the Lord, after the calf had been worshipped, to spare the sinful people, the Lord answered: I will be propitious to them. But as I live, and as my name lives: for the whole earth shall be filled with my glory (Num 14:20-21). And the seventy-first psalm sings: The whole earth shall be filled with his glory (Ps 71 [72]:19). Hence also the Angels cried to the shepherds: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will (Luke 2:14).
SERMON 211A.2

What are we going to do there? Tell me. Sleep? Yes, here people who have nothing to do just sleep. But there is no sleep there, because there is no weariness. So we aren't going to perform works of necessity, aren't going to sleep—what are we going to do? None of us must be afraid of boredom; none of us must imagine it's going to be so boring there. Do you find it boring now to be well? You can get tired of anything and everything in this age; can you get tired of being well? If you don't get tired of good health, will you get tired of immortality? So what activity are we going to engage in? "Amen" and "Alleluia." Here, you see, we do one thing and another, there one thing, I don't say day and night but day without end; what the powers of heaven, the seraphim, say now without ever getting bored: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts."
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 1:4

The mouths of the seraphim are filled with blessings. They offer a doxology in turn, not in my opinion because they are tired but because they show respect to one another, both receiving and giving the doxology. They say "holy" three times and then conclude with "Lord of hosts." This demonstrates that the Holy Trinity exists in one divine essence. All hold and confess that the Father exists, along with the Son and the Spirit. Nothing divides those who are named nor separates them into different natures. Just the opposite is true. We recognize one Godhead in three persons.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 1:4

In announcing that the whole earth is full of his glory, the seraphim are predicting the mystery of the economy that will be brought to pass through Christ. Prior to the Word's becoming flesh the world was ruled by the devil, the evil one, the serpent, the apostate. The creature, rather than the Creator, was worshiped. But when the only-begotten Word of God became human, the entire earth was filled with his glory.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 1

"And with two they were flying, and they said one to another: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory. And the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried", by the "voice" of Jesus Christ and the "voice" of the Holy Spirit. If any one of us hears the "voice" of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit "crying out", the "lintel is lifted up" and becomes higher than at that time when "it was lifted up" and when it was said: "lift up the gates, your princes, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the king of glory shall enter in". "And the house was filled with smoke". From the remission of the fire the whole "house was filled". And "smoke" is the vapor of fire.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 4

When therefore I have done all these things, "the lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out". It is a blessed thing, then, for each one of us so to labor that he may become a partaker of the door and of the "lintel" of the door, which is according to the understanding of Christ God. For it is not, I think, unseemly to say that the flesh is called the door and the Word the "lintel". "The lintel was lifted up by the voice with which they cried out, and the house was filled with smoke", with that good "smoke" from the "glory" of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the lintels of the hinges were moved at the voice of him who cried, and the house was filled with smoke. When the Seraphim cried and proclaimed the mystery of the Trinity in all the earth, when the whole earth came to know the passion of the Lord and Savior, at once the threshold of the Temple was moved, or taken away, and all its hinges fell down, the Savior's threat being fulfilled, when he said: Your house shall be left to you desolate (Matt 23:38). And how beautiful is the order of the words! After the earth was filled with the glory of the Lord Sabaoth, the Temple of the Jews was filled with the darkness of ignorance, and with gloom, and with smoke, which is harmful to the eyes. Or certainly by the smoke of the Temple a burning is signified. For first the Gospel of the Savior was preached in the whole world, and forty-two years after the Lord's passion Jerusalem was taken and the Temple burned. The Jews think that the Temple filled with smoke signifies thymiama, that is, incense, and through this the coming of the divine majesty.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 4

"And I said: O wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction!". Before you "see the vision", do you not confess yourself to be "wretched", O Isaiah? He does not say: so long as "Uzziah" lived did it never come into my mind that I was "wretched"; for I begin to know that I am "wretched" when I "see the vision", when "Uzziah the leprous king" is "dying" for me, and I say: "O wretched me!"? Now I too begin to confess to the Lord and to say of my very self: "O wretched me!", as Isaiah says: "O wretched me!". And close to this the Apostle too says: "wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?". It is a blessed thing, then, that I should confess myself "wretched". If I humble myself and, repenting, weep over my sins, God will hear me and give me a deliverer, and I say: "thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!". In truth let us say from the heart: "wretched me". Let each one call to mind the causes of his miseries and his offenses, and let us say, rising to prayer, mindful indeed as though confessing, but forgetful as though no longer committing them, and let us say: "wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction!". He is not "pricked with compunction" before he "saw the vision", before "Uzziah died"; when he begins to do penance, at once he says: "for I am pricked with compunction". If anyone is without feeling "in respect of the inner man", though he be a sinner, he is not "pricked with compunction"; but just as, though you apply a goad to the outer members, the dead body does not feel it, in the same way also, even if you apply the divine words to a sinner who has been put to death through sin and does not do penance, he is neither sorrowful nor repentant, nor has he "the sorrow that works confession, the sorrow that is according to God". But if anyone wishes to be saved and hears the words of one reproving and correcting him, at once he says: "O wretched me". Nor does it suffice to say: "wretched me"; there must be added to it: "because I am pricked with compunction". And would that he might be "pricked with compunction" yet more! For the more we are "pricked with compunction", the more the bonds of our sins are loosed from us. On this account that Ahab gained no great profit, because he was not much "pricked with compunction", but he was indeed "pricked with compunction", yet only once. For which reason it was said: "have you seen how Ahab has been pricked with compunction!" But if anyone be such that he does not cease to be "pricked with compunction", he says likewise as the Apostle: "I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God", and: "to me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given", and: "faithful is God, for Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first". Do you see that he was much "pricked with compunction", not once but always—that in writing and speaking and acting he was "pricked with compunction"? As also Isaiah in the present passage, who says: "O wretched me, for I am pricked with compunction, because, since I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell also in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". Note also another thing: that the sins of Isaiah were not also in deeds, but only in words; for which reason he says: "because, since I am a man and have unclean lips". But there was also "a people having unclean lips"; it did not befit him to accuse the "people" and to say that there were more sins in it than of "unclean lips".
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 1

"And I said: O wretched me, for I am pierced with remorse, since, although I am a man and have unclean lips". I cannot suppose that Isaiah humbled himself; rather, the Scripture says and gives testimony that his "lips are cleansed" by "one of the Seraphim", who "was sent" to "take away his sins". And "one" of the "Seraphim" is my Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent by the Father to "take away" our "sins", and he says: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities and have cleansed away your sins". And do not think it an affront to his nature, if the Son is sent by the Father. Indeed, that you may recognize the unity of the deity in the Trinity, Christ alone in the present reading now forgives "sins", and yet it is certain that "sins" are forgiven by the Trinity. For he who has believed in one, believes in all. Let there be brought to me, then, from the heavenly altar the "tongs", that it may touch my lips. If the "tongs" of the Lord touch "my lips", it "cleanses" them. And if it "cleanses" them and "cuts away" their vices, as we said just now, I shall open my mouth to the Word of God, and no longer shall an "unclean" word go forth from my mouth, "since, although I am a man and have unclean lips, I also dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". The "Seraphim" that was sent cleansed the "lips" of the prophet, but did not "cleanse the lips of the people". For he himself confessed that "he had unclean lips and dwelt in the midst of a people that has unclean lips". But this "Seraphim" that "was sent" did not judge any of the "people" worthy to have "their lips" too "cleansed", and therefore they still act impiously, therefore they still repudiate my Lord Jesus Christ, still curse him with "unclean lips". But I pray that the "Seraphim" may come and "cleanse" my "lips".
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 1

"And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". Why should we not set forth in the present a certain tradition of the Jews, plausible indeed yet not true, and why should we not find its solution? They say that Isaiah was for this reason sawn asunder by the people, as one transgressing the law and proclaiming things beyond the Scriptures. For the Scripture says: "no one shall see my face and live", but this man says: "I saw the Lord of Sabaoth". Moses, they say, did not "see", and you have "seen"? And for this reason they sawed him and condemned him as impious; for they did not know that "with two wings the Seraphim covered the face of God". "I saw the Lord". If Isaiah "saw the face", Moses also "saw". Moses "saw the back parts", as it is written; nevertheless he "saw the Lord", even though he did not "see" his "face". And so this man too "saw", although he did not "see" the "face". Wrongly, therefore, did they condemn the prophet. "And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth; and one of the Seraphim was sent to me". There is not one single coming of my Lord Jesus Christ by which he descended to the earth; he came both to Isaiah and to Moses, and to the "people" he came, and to each one of the prophets he came; and do not you fear: even though he has now been received up, he will come again. But that he came also before his coming in the flesh, receive as witness the one who declares and says: "Jerusalem! Jerusalem! you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often have I wished to gather your children!". "How often have I wished". He does not say: I did not see you except at this coming, but he says: "how often have I wished". And turning himself through each of the prophets, saying, I was Christ, who spoke through the prophets: do not you fear; and now Jesus Christ is sent. He does not lie. "I am with you", he says, "all the days until the consummation of the age". He does not lie. "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them". Since, therefore, Jesus Christ is at hand and stands beside us, and the high priest is ready and girded to offer to the Father our supplications, let us rise and through him offer sacrifices to the Father. For "he" is "the propitiation for our sins", "to whom is the glory and the dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 5

"And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, that I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up; and the house was full of his glory. And the Seraphim stood round about him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and with two they veiled his face, and with two they veiled his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Sabaoth, the whole earth is full of his glory", and the rest. But in order that we too may see the "vision" which Isaiah "saw", let us call upon Jesus, who has bestowed eyes upon those who do not see. For even now he can come and bring it about that we may behold with opened eyes the things that have been spoken in the reading of the sacrament; let us promise him that from now on we will no longer make "the body of Christ the body of a harlot", nor do works worthy of mourning. Let each one of us speak these things in his heart to God, and let us pray that his coming may take place even now; for if Jesus does not come, we cannot see these things. I pray that "a Seraph may be sent to me too", and that, "taking a coal with the tongs, he may cleanse my lips"; and why do I say "lips"? Isaiah was holy, and therefore only his "lips" were "cleansed", because he had offended only with his "lips", that is, in speech. But I am not such that I can say: "I have unclean lips"; I fear that I have an "unclean" heart, "unclean" eyes, "unclean" ears, an "unclean" mouth. As long as I sin in all these, I am wholly "unclean". If "I have looked upon a woman to lust after her, I have committed adultery with her in my heart". Behold, "unclean" eyes. If "out of my breast there go forth evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, false testimonies", behold, an "unclean" heart. "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring the gospel of peace, who bring the gospel of good things!". But I fear that, running toward evil, I have "unclean feet". "I stretch out" my "hands" to God, and perhaps "turning away his face" he says: "if you stretch out your hands, I will turn my face away from you". Who, then, cleanses me? Who "washes my feet"? Come, Jesus; I have filthy "feet"; for my sake become a servant, "pour your water into your basin", come, "wash my feet". I know that what I say is rash, but I fear the threat of him who says: "if I do not wash your feet, you will have no part with me". Therefore "wash my feet", that "I may have part with you". But why do I say: "wash my feet"? Peter can say this, who had need only that "his feet be washed"; for he was wholly clean. But I, since I have been washed once, need that baptism of which the Lord says: "I have another baptism to be baptized with". Why have we said these things? I am preparing both myself and my hearers for greater mysteries, if indeed the word of God comes, if it descends to us; for I fear that it may flee from me, that it may even disdain to bless me. The word once fled from the people because of "Achar", one sinner; the word fled, I say, from the people because of one sinner, "Achar the son of Zimri, the son of Zerah", from the "tribe of Judah", who was disobedient to God and therefore was "made anathema". And since now there is a multitude of people because of the preparation-day, and especially on the Lord's day, which is the commemoration of Christ's passion — for the resurrection of the Lord is not celebrated once a year, but always after every eighth day — pray to almighty God, that his word may come to us. Even if you are sinners, pray; God hears sinners. But if you fear that which is said in the Gospel: "we know that God does not hear sinners", do not be afraid, do not believe it: he who said this was "blind". Rather believe him who speaks and does not lie: "even if your sins be as scarlet, I will whiten them as wool; and if you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth". If you are "willing" even now to "hear", let us pray in common to the Lord, that at least now, at the coming of the Word, we may be able to give heed to the prophetic sayings.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 71: ON WHETHER GOD CAN BE SEEN

JACOB IS CALLED “THE MAN WHO SEES GOD,” AND MOSES SAW GOD FACE TO FACE; LIKEWISE ISAIAH SAYS, “I HAVE SEEN THE LORD OF HOSTS WITH MY EYES.” BUT ON THE OTHER HAND JOHN THE EVANGELIST SAYS, “NO ONE HAS EVER SEEN GOD” (Gen. 32:28; Exod. 33:11; Isa. 6:5; 1 John 4:12); THIS, AS FAR AS IT APPEARS, IS CONTRADICTORY. — As far as true faith is concerned, absolutely no one has ever seen God, neither the Father nor the Son. For what is called “seeing” refers to understanding; for sight is as in an image. Just as when we do not know emperors personally, we see them in likeness, not in reality; so too God was seen so that it might be understood that the one who appeared was God, by reason, not by substance; because in His own nature God cannot be seen. And to reveal more truly the hidden things of the question set before us, let us strive to explain the Evangelist’s meaning. For John wished to disclose something hidden, which he knew apply to saving teaching: therefore he says, “No one has ever seen God, except the only‑begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father, He has made Him known.” Let us observe the Evangelist’s meaning: in order to show that it is true that no one has ever seen God, he teaches that the Son has revealed this; and it is utterly impossible for Him to be mistaken, because He is in the bosom of the Father. But what is the bosom of the Father, if not the affection of the true Father in love, through the unity of nature in the Son? Wherefore no one has seen God except the only Son: this John the Apostle heard the Son of God saying among other things, “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except Him who is from God; He has seen the Father.” (Jn. 6:46) Therefore, in order to advance the condemnation of the Jews, who were unwilling to hear or believe that Christ is the Son of God, the Evangelist shows that this is the Christ who had appeared to the Fathers as God; but that the One who is the Father is never seen except by the Son. For when He denies that God the Father has been seen, and yet confesses that God appeared to the Fathers, He wishes to make it clear that He, the Son of God, is the One who has always been seen by the Fathers as God. Therefore, among other things, He says to the Jews about the Father, “You have never at any time heard His voice, nor seen His form” (John 5:37). Behold, it is not contradictory that God is both seen and unseen.
Against the Pelagians 2.24

According to the Hebrew, Isaiah cries out in anguish and says, "Woe is me because I have held my peace, because I am a man of unclean lips and I dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the Lord of hosts!" Because of his virtues, he deserved to enjoy the sight of God, and, because of his awareness of his sins, he confessed that his lips were unclean. Not because he had said anything that was contrary to the will of God, but because he had held his peace, deterred either by fear or modesty, and because he had not exercised the prerogative of a prophet, of condemning a sinful nation. When we, who flatter the rich and accept sinful persons, rebuke sinners, is it for the sake of base gain? Unless, perhaps, we speak with complete frankness to those whose wealth we stand in need of. We may act otherwise; we may refrain from every type of sin, but, if we keep silent about the truth, we are certainly committing a sin.
Commentary on Isaiah

And I said: Woe is me, because I was silent, because I am a man polluted in lips, and I shall dwell in the midst of a people having polluted lips, and I have seen with my eyes the king, the Lord of hosts. Abraham too, after he saw the Lord and heard his voice, says that he is earth and ashes (Gen 18); and Isaiah, according to the Seventy Translators, testifies that he is pierced with compunction, not for other crimes, but because he had unclean lips. Happy the conscience that has sinned only in speech, and that not by its own fault, but by fellowship with a people having polluted lips, with whom he was very often compelled to speak. From this it is shown that it is harmful to live with sinners: For he who touches pitch shall be defiled by it (Sir 13:1). But since in the Hebrew we read: Woe is me, because I was silent, the Prophet bewails himself because he was not worthy to praise the Lord Sabaoth with the Seraphim, whom we understand as the Angelic powers. And he did not dare to praise the Lord because he had unclean lips. And he had unclean lips for this reason, because he lived among a sinful people. Or certainly it is to be understood thus: Because I was silent, and did not boldly rebuke Uzziah the impious king, therefore my lips are unclean, and I do not dare to sing the praises of the Lord with the Angels, lest it be said to me: Why do you declare my righteousnesses, and take my covenant in your mouth (Ps 49 [50]:16)? For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Sir 15:9). And we say this, not as teaching that Isaiah was such a man, but that he himself, out of humility, and only because of unclean lips, confesses himself unworthy of the praise of God.
Dialogues, Book 3, Chapter 15

Purity of heart and simplicity, Peter, is of great force with almighty God, who is in purity most singular, and of nature most simple. For those servants of his, which do retire themselves from worldly affairs, avoid idle words, labour not to lose their devotion, nor to defile their soul with talking, do especially obtain to be heard of him, to whom, after a certain manner, and as they may, they be like in purity and simplicity of heart. But we that live in the world, and speak oftentimes idle words, and that which is worse, sometime those that be hurtful: our words and prayers are so much the farther off from God, as they be near unto the world: for we are drawn too much down towards the earth, by continual talking of secular business: which thing the prophet Esaye did very well reprehend in himself, after he had beheld the King and Lord of armies, and was penitent, crying out: Woe be to me for being silent, because I am a man that have defiled lips: and he sheweth straight after the reason why his lips were defiled, when he saith: I dwell in the midst of a people that hath defiled lips. For sorry he was that his lips were defiled, yet concealeth not from whence he had them, when he saith, that he dwelt in the midst of a people that had defiled lips. For very hard it is that the tongues of secular men should not defile their souls, with whom they talk; for when we do sometime condescend to speak with them of certain things, by little and little we get such a custom, that we hear that spoken with pleasure which is not meet to be heard at all, so that afterward we are loath to give that over, to which at the first, to gratify others, we were brought against our wills. And by this means we fall from idle words to hurtful speeches, and from talk of small moment to words of great importance: and so it cometh to pass that our tongue is so much the less respected of God when we pray, by how much we are more defiled with foolish speech, because, as it is written: He that turneth away his ear that he hear not the law, his prayer shall be execrable. What marvel, then, is it, if, when we pray, God doth slowly hear us, when as we hear God's commandments, either slowly or not at all?
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 4

"And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". If ever we have thought about God while we are still sinners, we too say what the prophet now says: "and one of the Seraphim was sent to me". How good is God! Because, He says, I hear Isaiah confessing—for he said: "O wretched me!"—because I hear him repenting—for he says: "I am pricked with compunction"—because he has declared his own offenses, saying: "since I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", I too, "while he is yet speaking, say: behold, I am present". "And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal". A "coal" is brought to the prophet, that through the burning of fire his "lips" might be purged, which had at some time sinned. Who is this "one of the Seraphim"? My Lord Jesus Christ: He, according to the dispensation of the flesh, was sent, having in His hand a "coal" and saying: "I came to send fire upon the earth, and would that it were already kindled!"

"And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal, which he had taken with tongs from the altar". Not by just any "fire" simply and by chance is the prophet purged, but by that which is "from the altar" of God.
