If you have not been purged by the "fire" of the "altar", there remains for you that fire of which it was said: "depart from me into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels". Not such is the "fire" that is "from the altar". All are to be delivered to the "fire", but not all to one "fire": some the "fire" "from the altar" awaits, others "that" which "is prepared for the devil and his angels".
Commentary on Isaiah

And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand a pebble, which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and he touched my mouth, and said: Behold, I have touched your lips with this, and your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed. One of the Seraphim, which is interpreted kindling, flew, or was sent, to cleanse the Prophet's unclean lips, and to purge them with the live coal, or pebble, which he had taken from the altar. Many, however, think that there are two Seraphim, because one cried to another, although among many too individuals can cry to individuals; and the edition of the Seventy rather signifies very many, who translated, Seraphim stood round about him. For if it were said of two, they would have said not round about, but on either side. And this fits the multitude of Angels, which is made ready for the ministry of God. And they are called Seraphim in the plural number, and Seraph in the singular: just as Cherubim and Cherub. And that an altar, under which are the souls of the martyrs, is seen in heaven, John too speaks in the Apocalypse (Rev 6); and this pebble, which by the Seventy alone was translated ἄνθραξ, that is, carbuncle, may signify not a coal or a live ember, as most think, but ἄνθρακα, that is, the carbuncle stone, which is called fiery because of the likeness of its flame-like color. From this we understand that the altar of God is full of carbuncles, that is, of fiery pebbles and live coals, which purge sins. Hence we read it written of God: Coals were kindled by him (Ps 17 [18]:9). And of the Lord himself it is said that he is a consuming fire. And the Savior in the Gospel: I came to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 12:49): that he might baptize in the Holy Spirit and in fire. For the fire will prove of what sort each one's work is (1 Cor 3). And he who is to be saved will be saved thus, as if he had passed through fire. And this is to be noted, that to Jeremiah, to whom it was said: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and in your mother's womb I sanctified you (Jer 1:5), because he did not have unclean lips but had only said: I do not know how to speak, for I am a youth, the Lord himself stretched out his hand and touched his mouth and said: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth. But to Isaiah, who had said: I am a man polluted in lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having polluted lips, the hand of God is not stretched out, but a Seraph is sent by God, or flies of his own will, because he has been bound over to this office. And in his hand he holds the pebble, which, according to the Seventy and Theodotion, he took with tongs (in the singular), according to Aquila and Symmachus, who followed the Hebrew, with tongs (in the plural), that is, MALCAIM (מלקחים), so as to touch his mouth and purge his former offenses. And the hand is sent both by God and by the Seraph, so that the Prophet, seeing a member of his own body, may not be terrified by an outward touch. Some of our people think that the tongs, by which the pebble is grasped, are the two Testaments, which are joined to one another by the union of the Holy Spirit. And since the Lord is introduced sitting, and sitting in the Temple, and the house was filled with smoke, of thymiama, as the Jews think, consequently tongs too are set down, which we also read of in the priestly ministry (Exod 37).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 1:4

Let our lips be touched by the divine coal, which burns away out sins and consumes the filth of our transgressions. Moreover, it makes us zealous by the Spirit. By saying "taken from the altar with tongs," Isaiah means that we receive faith in and knowledge of Christ from the teachings or announcements in the law and the prophets, in which the word of the holy apostles confirms the truth. By quoting from the law and the prophets, the apostles convince their hearers and "touch their lips with the burning coal" in order to lead them to confess faith in Christ.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 34

But Dionysius the Areopagite, that ancient and venerable Father, is said to declare that from the lesser hosts of angels some are sent forth to fulfill their ministry either visibly or invisibly, namely because angels or archangels come for human consolation. For those higher hosts never withdraw from the inner places, since those who are preeminent have no function of external ministry. This seems to be contradicted by what Isaiah says: "And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth." But in this statement of the prophet, he wants it understood that the spirits who are sent receive the name of those whose office they perform. For the angel who carries a coal from the altar to burn up the sins of speech is called a Seraphim, which means burning. This interpretation is also believed to be supported not unsuitably by what is said through Daniel: "Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him." For ministering is one thing, and standing before is another, because those minister to God who also go out to us announcing; but those stand before who so enjoy inward contemplation that they are not at all sent forth to accomplish external works.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 9

We read also in Isaiah that the prophet is purged by fire through "one of the seraphim, which was sent to him, when it took with tongs one coal from those which were upon the altar, and touched the lips of the prophet and said": "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". To me these things seem to be mystical and to indicate this, that to each one, according to that in which he sins, if he is worthy to be purified, coals are applied to his members. For since the prophet here says: "I have unclean lips, and I dwell also in the midst of a people having unclean lips", therefore the "coal taken up with the tongs" by the seraph purges his lips, in which alone he professes himself not to be clean. From which it is shown that only as far as the word was his sin found, but that in deed or work he had sinned in nothing; otherwise he would have said that I have an unclean body, or I have unclean eyes, if he had sinned in desiring the things of others, and he would have said: I have unclean hands, if he had polluted them with wicked works. But now, since perhaps in speech alone he was conscious to himself of that fault of which the Lord says: "that even for an idle word you shall render account in the day of judgment", because it is difficult even for the perfect to avoid the fault of speech, therefore the prophet too needed only the purging of the lips.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 4

Let the reproving word, therefore, touch the "lips" of our mind and soul, that we too may say: "and it touched my mouth". If I shall have cleansed "my mouth", so that I speak nothing idle, nothing foolish, nothing base, nothing scurrilous—to name them all at once—nothing of those things that are forbidden, then I can say: "it touched my mouth". But so long as I "have unclean lips" and carry on unclean affairs, because of the words of sin "the fire from the altar does not touch me", nor "is one of the Seraphim sent to me".

"And He said: behold, this has touched your lips, and it has taken away your iniquities, and has purged your sins round about". Let the divine word bite us, let it burn up our souls, and let us say as we hear: "was not our heart burning within us?", that "our iniquities and sins may be taken away", and that, made clean, with clean mouth and clean heart and a whole clean conscience, we may give thanks to almighty God in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen!"
On the Holy Spirit 1.10.112

Tell me, then, whoever you are who deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit could not be liable to sin, who rather forgives sin. Does an angel forgive? Does an archangel? Certainly not, but the Father alone, the Son alone and the Holy Spirit alone [can forgive sins]. Now one is obviously able to avoid that which he has power to forgive.But perhaps someone will say that the seraph said to Isaiah, "Behold, this has touched your lips and shall take away your iniquities and purge away your sins." Shall take away, he says, and shall purge, not I will take away, but that fire from the altar of God, that is, the grace of the Spirit. For what else can we piously understand to be on the altar of God but the grace of the Spirit? Certainly not the wood of the forests or the soot and coals. Or what is so in accordance with piety as to understand according to the mystery that it was revealed by the mouth of Isaiah that everyone should be cleansed by the passion of Christ, who as a coal according to the flesh burnt up our sins, as you read in Zechariah: "Is not this a brand snatched from the fire? Now Joshua was clothed in filthy garments."
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 34

But Dionysius the Areopagite, that ancient and venerable Father, is said to declare that from the lesser hosts of angels some are sent forth to fulfill their ministry either visibly or invisibly, namely because angels or archangels come for human consolation. For those higher hosts never withdraw from the inner places, since those who are preeminent have no function of external ministry. This seems to be contradicted by what Isaiah says: "And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth." But in this statement of the prophet, he wants it understood that the spirits who are sent receive the name of those whose office they perform. For the angel who carries a coal from the altar to burn up the sins of speech is called a Seraphim, which means burning.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 6

Isaiah, "seeing the Lord of Sabaoth seated upon a lofty and lifted-up throne", and "seeing" also "the Seraphim standing about him", and receiving the remission of sins through that fire which, brought "from the altar", "cleansed" his "lips" by its touch, says that "he heard the voice of the Lord" — not commanding, but rousing and "saying": "whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?" Then he says that "he answered" the Lord: "behold, it is I, send me". But when I take my place here and search into what is written, I find that Moses did one thing and Isaiah another. For Moses, chosen for the leading-out of the people from the land of Egypt, says: "provide another whom you may send", and he seems to contradict God; but Isaiah, not chosen, but "hearing": "whom shall I send, and who will go?", says: "behold, it is I, send me". It is worthwhile, therefore, for one "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" to inquire which of the two did better: Moses, who, after he was chosen, refused, or Isaiah, who, without even being chosen, offered himself to be "sent to the people". For I do not know whether anyone, attending to that contrariety of the affairs which appears in each, can say that Moses did the very same thing as Isaiah. So then I boldly make a comparison of these two holy and blessed men, and I decide and declare that Moses acted more modestly than Isaiah. For Moses was considering the magnitude of presiding over the people so as to lead them out of the land of Egypt, of contending against the "incantations" and sorceries of the Egyptians; on this account he says: "provide another whom you may send". But this man, not waiting to hear what would be enjoined upon him to say — even if he had been chosen — says: "behold, it is I, send me". Hence, because, being ignorant of what would be enjoined upon him, he says: "behold, it is I, send me", he is commanded to say those very things which were unwished-for by the one who was to say them. Or was it not undesirable, having been immediately bidden to prophesy, to begin from curses, saying: "with the ear you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will perceive and not see; for the heart of this people has been thickened" and the rest? Perhaps, then — if indeed it is expedient to say it boldly — he received as the wage of his rashness and boldness that he was commanded to say the very things which he was unwilling to prophesy. But since we have compared Isaiah and Moses, let us set up also another comparison closely akin, Isaiah and Jonah. The latter is sent "to preach" the overthrow of the Ninevites after "three days", and it irks him, unwilling to set out, to be the cause of evils for the city. But this man, not waiting for what would be commanded him to say, says: "behold, it is I, send me". It is good not to leap forward toward those dignities and offices of rule and ministries of the Church which are from God; would that we imitated Moses and said with him: "provide another whom you may send". For he who wishes to be saved comes to the rule of the Church not to lordship — even though he presides — but to servitude, if one must speak also from the Gospel: "the princes of the nations indeed lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called magistrates; but it shall not be so among you". For neither do "the princes lord it over you", but "whoever of you wishes to be greater shall be least of all"; "whoever wishes to be first shall be last of all". He, therefore, who is called to the episcopate is called not to lordship, but to the servitude of the whole Church. If you wish to believe from the scriptures that in the Church he who presides is the servant of all, let the Savior and Lord himself persuade you: such and so great a one became "in the midst of the disciples not as one reclining, but as one serving". For "taking a towel", after "he had laid aside his garments, he girded himself and, pouring water into a basin, began to wash the feet of the disciples and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded". And teaching that rulers ought to be such as servants, he says: "you call me master and lord, and you say well; for so I am. If then I, the Lord and master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet". The ruler of the Church, therefore, is called to servitude, so that from this servitude he may be able to go to the heavenly throne, as it is written: "you shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel". But hear also Paul, so illustrious a man, saying that he was the servant of all believers. "For I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God". Further, if this seems to prove not his servitude but only his humility, hear him saying: "we became little ones in your midst, as if a nurse should cherish her own children, though we could be burdensome as Apostles of Christ". It is expedient, therefore, that we be imitators of the humble words and deeds of the Lord himself and of his "Apostles", and do what was done by Moses, so that, even if someone is called to rule, he may say: "provide another whom you may send". "He says to God": "I have not been worthy since yesterday and the day before; I am of feeble voice and slow of tongue". And because "he said to God" humbly: "I am of feeble voice and slow of tongue", he hears from God: "who gave a mouth to man, and who made the deaf and dumb, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?" Believe God and consecrate yourself to him. Although you are "of thin voice" and "slow tongue", hand yourself over to the word of God; you will say afterward: "I opened my mouth and drew in the Spirit". These things, indeed, on account of what Isaiah says: "behold, it is I, send me".

But let us in part take his side as well. For he willed, once he had received grace from God, not to receive it in vain, but to use it for what was needful. "Seeing the Seraphim", "seeing the Lord of Sabaoth seated upon a lofty and lifted-up throne, he said": "O wretched me, for I am pricked to the heart, because, being a man and having unclean lips, and dwelling also in the midst of a people having unclean lips, I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth". Saying this and making himself "wretched", he merits help, God taking up his humility. What is this help? "There was sent", he says, "to me one of the Seraphim, and he had in the tongs a coal which he had brought from the altar, and he touched my lips and said: behold, I have taken away your iniquities and have purged round about your sins". He obtained the benefit, being made clean and receiving the remission of sins. When he had heard: "whom shall I send to this people, and who will go for us?", it was not on account of his former conscience that he dared to say: "behold, it is I, send me", but because he had heard: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities". Therefore, since the saints are pricked to the heart and the inquiry is made between Moses and Isaiah, let us make satisfaction on behalf of Moses and also on behalf of Isaiah, giving to each of them from the scriptures his own portion. Moses did not receive the remission of sins, so as to say, as if already conscious of having been cleansed: "send me". On which account he says: "provide another whom you may send", for he had in his conscience the slaying of the Egyptian; and perhaps, being a man, he knew that he had also certain other sins, and therefore he refuses. But this man asks for the ministry not as one just by nature, but as one who has obtained grace. If Moses too had received a like grace and had heard: "behold, I have taken away your iniquities" and this: "I have cleansed round about your sins", perhaps he would never have said: "provide another whom you may send". There is, therefore, some reason both in Moses refusing and in Isaiah saying: "behold, it is I, send me".
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 9

"And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said: behold, here I am; send me. And he said: go and say to this people: with hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand" and the rest. Concerning this discourse of the prophet Isaiah which has now been read, let us pray to God that he may grant us grace and that we may be able to expound things worthy of the prophetic spirit. "And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: whom shall I send?" After the prophet's "lips" had been cleansed, being prepared he took up the ministry of God and says: "behold, here I am, send me". But that he might be the more prepared for this, he remembered the voice of Moses. For Moses too, using the same words: "send me", was made "ruler of the people" and judge and was called "the servant of God".
Commentary on Isaiah

And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And I said: Here am I, send me. In place of what both we and all the other translators rendered for us, which in Hebrew is said LANU (לנו), the Seventy, wishing I know not what, set down to this people, which is not found in the Hebrew at all. Now when for us is said in the person of God, it is to be taken in the sense in which we also read in Genesis: Let us make man to our image and likeness (Gen 1:26), so as to indicate the mystery of the Trinity. For just as we read in the Gospel, where the Lord says: I and the Father are one (John 10:30); and one we refer to the nature, are to the distinction of persons: so, when the Lord commands, the Trinity gives the order. And the Lord does not say whom he orders to go, but sets the choice before those who hear, so that the will may obtain the reward. And the Prophet promises that he will go not out of the rashness and arrogance of his own conscience, but out of confidence: since his lips have been cleansed, and his iniquity taken away, and his sin cleansed. So Moses too, to whom the Lord had said: Come, I will send you to Pharaoh king of Egypt (Exod 3:10), and he said: I beseech you, Lord, I am not worthy; provide another whom you may send, or as is read in the Hebrew, Send whom you are going to send (Exod 4:13), answered not out of contempt but out of humility, because he who had been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians had heard nothing about his lips being cleansed. And Isaiah, not by his own merit but by the grace of the Lord, by which he was cleansed, offers himself for the ministry. Others, however, think that Isaiah offered himself for this reason, because he supposed that prosperous things were to be announced to the people: but because he heard: Go, say to this people: With your ears you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not know (Isa 6:9), for that reason, in what follows, when the voice of the Lord says to him: Cry, he does not cry at once, but asks, what shall I cry? And Jeremiah, to whom it had been said: Take the cup, and you shall give drink to all the nations to whom I shall send you (Jer 25:15), gladly accepting the cup of punishments to pledge it to the hostile nations, that they might drink and vomit and fall, after he heard, go, and first you shall give drink to Jerusalem, answered: You have deceived me, Lord, and I have been deceived (Jer 20:7). This is an observation of the Hebrews. For our part, however, we say that it was not of rashness but of obedience that he offered himself to the Lord to be sent.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 6

But let us look also at those things which the Lord commanded to be "said to the people": "go, and say to the people: with the ear you will hear and not understand, and seeing you will perceive and not see. For the heart of this people has been thickened, and with their ears they have heard heavily and have closed their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart and turn back, and I heal them". Knowing that the hearing of words is twofold and recognizing a double constitution — that is, one of them bodily, the other spiritual — he says to "the people", prophesying about those things which were to be at the coming of Christ, that there would be a time when "they would hear and not understand" them, seeing that, when "they heard" my Lord Jesus Christ, they "heard" only the voice of the sayings, not the sense. And this is manifest from the fact that "he spoke in parables" "outside" to "the people", but "to the disciples in secret he unfolded" them. And he prophesies what came to pass: "with the ear you will hear and not understand". Further, that this was "prophesied" "to the people" about the coming of the Lord, the Savior himself says: "well did Isaiah prophesy about you, saying: "with the ear you will hear and not understand"". Let us grant, then, that "the people", listening to the words of the Lord, could not know what was said. But let us see what this is, which follows: "and seeing you will see and not know". Not everyone who "saw" those things which the Savior did was straightway, by "seeing", able to "understand" why they were done. Let us take, for example, "he washed the feet of the disciples", and they indeed "saw" well how the master "washed the feet" of "the disciples"; but others too who were present "saw" — yet only what was being done, not also why it was being done. For there was a likeness in the washing of "the feet" with which the Word of God "washed the feet of the disciples"; therefore the Savior says to Peter, who refused and said: "you shall not wash my feet", what does he say? "What I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward". What, then, do "you do" now? says Peter; I see you "washing" our "feet", and the "basin" set, you "girded with a towel" and serving us and "wiping" our "feet". But because this was not the whole business — for indeed the Savior, stripped, "pours" spiritual "water into a basin" according to the scriptures and "washes the feet of the disciples", so that, when they have been made "clean", they may ascend to him who says: "I am the way", and not be full of the "dust" which he willed to be "shaken off" upon the unworthy and upon those who did not receive peace nor were worthy of the things which were spoken — and because this was what was signified, therefore he says: "what I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward". And this was what was said in the rest: "you call me master and Lord, and you say well; for so I am. If then I, the Lord and master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet". Does he then say this, that the bishop, "pouring water into a basin and having laid aside his garments and being girded with a towel", should "wash" my "feet" as I stretch them out, seeing that "you", he says, "ought to wash one another's feet"? If this is what is meant, none of us will keep the commandment; for no deacon or presbyter or bishop, "taking a towel", has "washed the feet" of any and all who come. But if you understand what is written, those who are truly blessed bishops, serving the Church, "pour water" from the scriptures into the "basin" of the soul, which is according to the scriptures, and attempt to "wash" and cleanse away and cast off the filth of "the feet of the disciples". And thus the bishops keep the commandment, imitating Jesus, and thus also the presbyters. Would that I too might now receive "water" which could "wash the feet" of your soul, so that each one of you, when he has been "washed", may say: "I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?". For the bride says this in the Song of Songs, showing not bodily "feet washed", but "feet that do not stumble", of which Solomon says: "let your foot not stumble", and of which it is also written in the Psalms: "but my feet were almost moved". And moreover, those women who are appointed "widows" in the churches — "if", he says, "she has washed the feet of the saints". But if you wish to hear more plainly how the "widow washes the feet of the saints", hear Paul in another place appointing rules for "widows" and saying: "teaching well, that they may make the young women chaste", "washing the filth of "the feet" of the young women". And these "widows" are worthy of ecclesiastical honor, whoever they be that "wash the feet of the saints" with the word of spiritual teaching — "the saints", however, not males, but women; for I do not permit a woman to teach nor to rule over a man. He wishes women to be "teaching well, that" they may urge to chastity not young men, but "young women" — for it is unseemly that a woman become the teacher of a man — but that they urge "young women" to chastity and to "love their husbands and their children". Let us learn, therefore, to "wash the feet of the disciples". These things have been said on account of this: "seeing you will see and not know". For if anything was done by the Savior, by those indeed who "did not understand" it "was seen" with respect to the body, it was not "seen" with respect to knowledge; but by those who "understood" it "was seen" indeed with respect to the eyes, and it "was seen" also with respect to the understanding — so that this which was said, "seeing you will see and not know", was fulfilled not upon those who blessedly "see", but upon sinners. And we pray that, "seeing" all the things of the Gospels, we may "see" in a double manner how they were done with respect to the body, when our Savior descended to the earth; for indeed each thing that was done in the body was a likeness and a type of things to come. As, for instance, some man "blind from birth" recovered his sight; but truly this "man blind from birth" was the people of the Gentiles, to whom the Savior restored sight, "anointing" his "eyes" with his own "saliva", and sending him "to Siloam, which is interpreted sent". For he was sending those whom he "anointed" with the Spirit, that they might believe, "to Siloam", that is, to the Apostles and teachers, on which account it is written of "Siloam" that "it is interpreted sent". And as often as we begin to be visited by Jesus, so that we may receive the eyes of the soul, we are sent "to Siloam", that is, "sent". And so let each one of us, when he reads those things which were done in the Gospels, pray that this too be not fulfilled in himself: "seeing you will see and not know".

But if, as the simpler suppose, those things which were done were done not "on account of us", but merely done, and were not examples of another reality, let them explain how this which was said, "seeing you will see and not know", has any sense. For if those things which "were seen" did not have some sacred meaning, such that with the carnal eyes they were also spiritually beheld, he would never have said: "seeing you will see and not know". And for the proof of these things let us bring forward the testimony of another passage from the Gospel, which, according to those who follow the letter only, is a falsehood. Our Savior and Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel according to John: "if you believe, not only will you do the things which I do, but you will do even greater than these". Let us see, then, whether the disciples "did" any "greater" things. What is "greater" than to "raise the dead"? Who — I do not say of us, but of the Apostles — "raised the dead"? The history relates that Paul "raised Eutychus from the dead", and Peter "Tabitha, which is interpreted Dorcas". But these things, and others of this kind, you can find; yet where are the "greater" things? But the Savior also made "the blind" see again, and, what is "greater", those who had been born so: let them show whom they have beheld "blind" from the womb cured by the hands of the Apostles. And countless other things one can find from the Gospels, who seeks them, since neither did the Apostles "do greater things than these" nor did their successors. But the word of Scripture spoke some such thing as this: "than these things which I have done", the bodily ones, "you will do greater". "I made men rise from the dead" bodily, you "will make them rise from the dead" spiritually. I poured this perceptible light upon "the blind", you will give spiritual light to those who do not see. And down to this present day I see these signs, "greater" than the bodily ones which Jesus "did", being done through the most faithful disciples of Jesus. Do not "the blind" now "see" and "the lame walk" and "the lepers are cleansed" and the rest come to pass, if he who yesterday was "blinded", approaching an idol as though to God, today calls upon the living God, abandoning his former ways? Does not he who yesterday was "lame" on account of sin, now, through the teaching of the disciples, taught the true way, walk with steady foot; and he who yesterday "had a withered hand", idle for doing good, today, receiving back his "hand", has it living? If you see someone polluted and having leprosy in his soul suddenly repent, pricked to the heart by the word of teaching, let it not irk you to say that it is "greater" that this man be spiritually "a leper" cleansed than that some other be carnally purged. And these things indeed the discourse has poured forth abundantly, desiring to show what this is which was said: "and seeing you will see and not know".
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 9

Now I heard a certain Hebrew expounding this passage and saying that the prophet indeed willingly and readily took up the prophecy to the people, not knowing what he would have to say to them; but then, hearing the sad things that had to be announced to the people—that is: "with hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand" and the rest—in what follows he becomes more reluctant; and when the voice of God says to him: "cry out", he answers him and says: "what shall I cry?". But I think these things are prophesied concerning the Savior, because it was to come to pass that "hearing they should not hear and seeing they should not see". Moreover, what is said will become plainer if we consider a little the passage: "perceiving you shall look and you shall not see". It is of this kind. The Jews indeed at that time "saw" the blind receiving their sight, but the reason of the sight they did not know; they "heard" the "parables" which the Savior "unfolded to his disciples in secret", but they themselves "did not hear", not knowing the things that were said; on account of this, bearing witness against them, he said: "he who has ears to hear, let him hear!". For they were not deprived of these "ears", so that they "should not hear", but their inner "ears" were dulled for hearing. On account of this he preaches to them and through the prophet foretells the things to come, saying: "with hearing you shall hear and you shall not understand, and perceiving you shall look and you shall not see. For the heart of this people has been made fat".
Commentary on Isaiah

And he said: Go, and you shall say to this people: Hear with hearing, and do not understand, and see with sight, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make its ears heavy, and shut its eyes, lest perhaps it see with its eyes, and hear with its ears, and understand with its heart, and be converted, and be healed. The Seventy translated this place as the evangelist Luke set it down in the Acts of the Apostles: And when they did not agree among themselves, without doubt the Jews, they departed, Paul having said one word: Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: go to this people and say: With the ear you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive; for the heart of this people has been made gross, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have shut their eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them (Acts 28:25ff.). And at what time this prophecy was fulfilled, the Apostle Paul himself says in what follows: Let it be known to you, therefore, that this salvation of God has been sent to the nations, and they will hear (Acts 28:28). Hence too we read in the same Acts of the Apostles that Paul and Barnabas, when the Jews would not believe, said: It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you have thrust it away and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46-47). For thus the Lord has commanded us: I have set you for a light to the nations, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth (Isa 49:6). So according to the Seventy the interpretation is easy: that Isaiah the prophet, at the Lord's command, foretells what the people is going to do. In the Hebrew there is a difficulty: how God himself commands the people to hear with hearing and not understand, and seeing to see and not recognize, and afterward the prophet is introduced speaking, and he entreats the Lord and says: Blind the heart of this people, and make its ears heavy, and shut its eyes, lest perhaps it see with its eyes, and hear with its ears, and understand with its heart, and be converted, and be healed (Isa 6:10). And first we must resolve the question that can be put to us: why did the apostle Paul, disputing with Hebrews, speak not according to the Hebrew, which he knew to be correct, but according to the Seventy? The ancient expositors of the Church relate that the evangelist Luke was most learned in the art of medicine, and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew. Hence his speech too, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, that is, in both volumes, is more polished and has the scent of secular eloquence, and he uses Greek testimonies more than Hebrew. But Matthew and John, of whom the one wove his Gospel in the Hebrew tongue, the other in Greek, bring forward testimonies from the Hebrew, such as this: Out of Egypt I have called my son (Hos 11:1). And: For he shall be called a Nazarene (Matt 2:23). And: Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly (John 7:38). And: They shall look on him whom they pierced (Zech 12:10; John 19:37), and other things like these. The Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews too is gainsaid for this reason, that in writing to Hebrews he uses testimonies that are not found in the Hebrew volumes. But if anyone should say that the Hebrew books were afterward falsified by the Jews, let him hear what Origen answers to this little question in the eighth volume of his Explanations of Isaiah: that the Lord and the Apostles, who rebuke the other crimes in the Scribes and Pharisees, would never have kept silent about this crime, which was the greatest. But if they should say that the Hebrew books were falsified after the coming of the Lord and Savior and the preaching of the Apostles, I shall not be able to hold back my laughter, that the Savior and the Evangelists and the Apostles should have brought forward testimonies in such a way as the Jews were afterward going to falsify them. But of the present place this must be said: that we take refuge in the translation of the Seventy in vain, lest what is said according to the Hebrew should seem blasphemous: Hear with hearing, and do not understand: and see the vision, and do not know, since we find testimonies of this kind in the Seventy Translators too, such as that in Exodus which is said to Pharaoh: For this reason I have raised you up, to show my power in you (Exod 9:16). But if he himself raised him up and hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he should not believe; and of others it is said: God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear (Rom 11:8); and in the Psalms: Let their table become a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block, and a recompense: let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bend their backs always (Ps 68 [69]:23-24): then those who do not see are not at fault, but he who gave them eyes for not seeing. So even apart from this testimony which we are now trying to expound, the same question remains in the Churches, and either the others will be resolved along with this one, or this one too will be insoluble along with the others. The blessed apostle Paul explains this place more fully to the Romans, and we should be doing something superfluous if we wished to comprise in a brief discourse what he pursued through almost the whole epistle. For he says, after many things: God has shut up all things in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all (Rom 11:32). And marveling at the mysteries of the Lord he added: O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways. And again, disputing about the unbelief of the Jews, he says: Have they so sinned that they should fall? God forbid; but by their offense salvation came to the Gentiles, to provoke them to emulation (Rom 11:11). And a little after: For if their casting away is the reconciliation of the world, what will their taking up be? Is it not life from the dead? And again: For I would not have you ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in yourselves, that blindness has come in part upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, and then all Israel should be saved. And a little after (Rom 11:25): As concerning the Gospel they are enemies for your sakes, but as concerning the election they are beloved for the sake of the fathers: for the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance. For as you, he says, once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy because of their unbelief: so these too have now not believed in your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. For God has shut up all things under sin, that he may have mercy on all. It is therefore not the cruelty of God but his mercy that one nation should perish so that all may be saved; that a part of the Jews should not see, so that the whole world may behold. Hence the Lord himself too in the Gospel turns the mystery of the man blind from birth, who had received his eyes, to Tropology, and says: For judgment I came into this world, that those who see may not see, and those who do not see may see (John 9:39). And in another place Simeon speaks: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising again of many (Luke 2:34). So while they do not see, we see; while they fall, we rise again. Understanding this, the Prophet in a certain manner says in other words: O Lord, you command me to speak to the people of the Jews, that they may hear and not understand the Savior, and see him and not recognize him. If you will that your command be fulfilled and the whole world be saved, which I too desire to come about, then blind the heart of this people and make its ears heavy and shut its eyes, that they may not understand, may not hear, may not see. For if they see, and are converted, and understand, and are healed, the whole world will not receive healing. From this we perceive that, however grave the sin, if anyone is converted he can be healed. And at the same time this too is to be understood: that for the greatness of their crime they were judged unworthy even of repentance, as the Lord himself says to Jerusalem: How often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not (Matt 23:37).
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 6

But what is the cause that the one hearing "does not understand and the one seeing does not see"? "The heart of this people", he says, "has been thickened". Since indeed this too must be understood, whence it comes, bodily and spiritual fatness are not the same, nor are bodily and spiritual thinness the same. For that which is bodily thick comes to be in the flesh, and a "fleshly heart" does me no harm if "it be thickened", nor does it profit if by illness or by whatever cause it be made thin. And I suppose that the fleshly "heart" of those who are held by fear becomes such. For as they waste away entirely from sickness, so they say that the thickness too, and whatever is fat about their "heart", is thinned out. What harm, then, does it do me if my bodily "heart" "be thickened"? And suppose too my "heart" be made thin — what profit do I have from that? But by a shared term with the bodily "heart", the ruling part of our soul is named, as is manifest from what is said in the Gospel: "blessed are the clean of heart"; for those are not "clean of heart" who have not within them blood or any bodily matter. But it was said: "blessed are the clean of heart" in the sense of "blessed" are those who have "a clean heart", the ruling part of the soul being named instead of "heart". Since, therefore, the ruling part of our soul, which is said to be in the bodily "heart", is either "clean" or unclean — and our "heart" is unclean indeed when "the worst thoughts go forth from" it, "murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, blasphemies", but "clean" when there are holy thoughts and divine understandings and a pure mind — on this account it must be judged that it is said to be made thin by the "thin" and holy Spirit of him who is saved, but "thickened" by malice and choked in him who sins. For it is said of the "Holy Spirit", who is according to "wisdom", that he is "only-begotten, manifold, thin, mobile", and that the just man receives this "subtle spirit"; for this "spirit" differs from "all intellectual, clean, subtle spirits". The ruling part of the heart, therefore, is "thin" indeed insofar as it is spiritual, but fat insofar as it is concreted from the vice of bodily matter, full of bodily thoughts, which are under reproach. Thus it is said: "the heart of this people has been thickened". Understand: from this "the heart has been thickened", that there is nothing in it besides human and fleshly cares; for just as the matter of the body is fat, in the same way also are bodily understandings and thoughts. Wherefore, since two things are set before us — that the "heart is thickened" from worldly cares and made thin from spiritual solicitude, when one thinks of the things which are the Lord's, casting off the fatness from the "heart" and knowing that, if his "heart be thickened", he will neither receive the words of God nor see the sacrament of salvation — let us lay aside the thickness and take up that thinness which has been spoken of, so that we too may say, as the prophet: "my soul has thirsted for you; how manifoldly does my flesh thirst for you, in a land desert and pathless and waterless, so in the holy place have I appeared to you" — not as though I were "holy" by nature, but if the prudence "of the flesh" wastes away, and if the prudence "of the flesh" has been wasted, then "in the holy place I shall appear to you". These things in explanation of that which was said: "for the heart of this people has been thickened".

There follows: "and with their ears they have heard heavily". It does me no harm if I "hear heavily" bodily, nor does this become for me a cause that I should not hear the words of God. For just as bodily blindness does me no harm, if my soul has not been blinded, so neither does lightness nor heaviness of bodily hearing hinder me. But there is a certain heaviness of hearing which harms the soul of man. What is this heaviness which is in the hearing of the soul? Sin, according to the scriptures, is "heavy". On which account someone, perceiving his sins, says: "like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me". And because "iniquity" is heavy, on this account "it sits upon a talent of lead", as is written in Zechariah. But the Egyptians "were sunk like lead in the mighty water" not because they had "heavy" bodies, but because their souls "had been made heavy" by the "talent of lead upon which iniquity was sitting" — on this account "they were sunk like lead in the mighty water". The heaviness of "the ears", therefore, comes from sin, and the lightness from righteousness. What is it that makes the hearing "hear" not "heavily", but lightly? The "wings" of the Word, the "wings" of virtue; for indeed the "wings" of the Word bestow much lightness. "Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I shall find rest?" This the prophet says, praying not that he may receive the bodily "wings of a dove", but the "wings of the dove" of the Holy Spirit. And again Solomon says of the rich man: "but he equips for himself wings like an eagle, and he turns back into the house of him who presides over him". If, therefore, we take "wings", we shall hear lightly; but if we sin and are negligent about our wings and our "wings" fall away, we shall be "made heavy" and "shall hear heavily". "With their ears", therefore, the sinners "have heard heavily". All the Jews indeed who then "heard" the Savior "heard" him "heavily", and therefore did not believe. And down to this day, as many as, "hearing" the scriptures, have not "heard" the spiritual word, which is light, but the "letter", which is "heavy" and "kills", "hear heavily". And thus Scripture is heard in a twofold manner: by him who does not understand what is said, it is "heard heavily"; but by him who understands it, it is not only not "heard heavily", but rather keenly, whence one becomes an understanding hearer.

And yet another thing is prophesied about the people of the Jews and about all of us, if we sin. "And they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart". Of those who do not "see", some are "blind" and on account of blindness do not "see"; some are "in darkness" and therefore do not "see"; but others are neither "in darkness" nor blind, but because they "close their eyes" they do not "see". And the divine Scripture knows these differences, which belong to the ruling part of our heart; for the Savior says "to those who are in bonds: come forth, and to those in darkness, that it may be revealed to them", and "to those sitting in the region and shadow of death: a light has arisen for them". These did not "see" for the reason that they were "in darkness", until "a light should arise for them". "Deaf ones, hear, and blind ones, look". These formerly did not "see" for the reason that they were "blind" by nature. But those who are outside these, and who, in comparison with "the blind" and those who are "in darkness", are much worse, are those who do not "see" for the reason that they have willingly "closed their eyes". And that this is so, as we have asserted, the Savior will be a witness to me, saying: "if you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say that you see; your sin remains". And he says well: "you say that you see"; for truly "they say that they see" and have the possibility of "seeing", but, "closing their eyes", they do not "see". And if ever you see a soul ingenious for understanding, and swift and eager, that does not meditate on the words of God, know that it is not on account of blindness that it does not "see" those things which are contained in the scriptures, not because it is "in darkness", but because it "closes its eyes". If, therefore, you have heard Scripture saying to those who "close their eyes": "open your eyes and see rightly", "open your eyes from that which you had closed", then you will be able to "see rightly" and to consider the light of truth. And it accuses indeed those about whom the inquiry is made, why they "close their eyes, lest they see"; yet it does not also say this, that it is never expedient to "close" the "eyes" of the soul. For it is expedient, as Isaiah makes plain, saying in what follows: "who will announce to you the eternal place? He who walks in righteousness and speaks the true and right way, stopping his ears, that he may not hear the judgment of blood, closing his eyes, that he may not see iniquity". If it is going to happen that, opening the "eyes" of my soul, I "hear" and perceive base speech, it is better to "close" the entrances than to "hear" and understand things that harm. When, then, do I "close"? When evil things are spoken, so that I may not even understand them. When the words of God are to be seen, then "we turn back and" God "heals" us, sending the word which "heals" those who wish to be cured in Christ Jesus, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 9

Let us examine what this means, which is said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat". Everyone who is occupied in the cares of the present life has "a heart made fat"; for those who dwell among worldly things the "heart is made fat" no otherwise than as if they were being choked by thorns. For this reason the "heart" grows fat and cannot receive the notions of the more subtle spirit. Let us therefore flee from such cares, so that our heart, made thin, may become acceptable to God. Let us flee earthly business; for these are the things by which the "heart is made fat". On account of this the discourse of Moses was subtle (as is written of him in Exodus), because he said that whoever, on account of such subtlety, shall be "pure in heart, they shall see God". For by such eyes God is seen. There are three things that are said: "for the heart of this people has been made fat" and "with their ears they have heard heavily" and "they have closed their eyes". But the things said in this passage can also be understood otherwise, more plainly. For many people think, when they look upon the creatures and contemplate this world, that they see them. And why do I speak of people? Behold, the birds and the four-footed beasts see the sun and the moon and the whole heaven together with the choir of stars, but they do not understand their reasons; only the just and holy, comprehending them through the reason of the wisdom of God, look upon them. Therefore in the eighth Psalm David says: "for I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded". For does the prophet not now "see the heaven and the moon"? But this, that he says: "I shall see", if we consider it, we shall be able to understand.
Commentary on Matthew

For the heart of this people has grown fat, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes, and the rest. He gives the reasons why seeing they do not see and hearing they do not hear: because it has grown fat, he says, the heart of this people, and with their ears they have heard heavily; and lest perhaps we should think that fatness of heart and heaviness of ears belong to nature, not to the will, he adds the fault of free choice and says: They have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and be converted, and I should heal them. In parables, therefore, and in an enigma do they hear who, with their eyes closed, do not wish to see the truth.
Commentary on Isaiah

And I said: How long, Lord? And he said: Until the cities are made desolate without inhabitant, and the houses without men, and the land is left deserted. And the Lord will remove men far away, and she that had been forsaken in the midst of the land shall be multiplied. And yet in it there shall be a tithing, and again it shall be for a plundering, like a terebinth, and like an oak that has cast its fruits: the seed that shall have stood in it shall be holy. The Lord says: Go, and tell this people that it hears and does not hear, sees and does not see. And for this reason it neither hears nor sees: because it is not going to understand the words of the Lord nor to recognize his works, and because it has grown fat and broad and has forgotten its Creator (Deut 32). The Prophet answers, and asks anxiously about his people: How long, Lord, will this sentence remain, that hearing it should not hear, and seeing should not see? To whom the Lord answered: So long will it not hear and not see, and have its heart blinded, until the cities of Judea, when Vespasian and Titus make war, are utterly overthrown, so much so that not even their former name remains, and the houses, if any remain, are without inhabitant, and the land is reduced to a wilderness; and the Jewish people is scattered over the whole world, either by flight or by captivity; and the people of the Jews is multiplied no longer in Judea, as before, but among all the nations.
Commentary on Isaiah

And though I say that it is multiplied, so great will be the misfortune of the remnant of the people that, in comparison with its former multitude, scarcely a tenth part remains. And when there is a wilderness in the land itself also (for this place can be understood in two ways: that scarcely a tenth part remains even in the whole world, and that in Judea itself scarcely a small part of the people is preserved), again those very remnants will be for a plundering, when, after about fifty years, Hadrian comes and has utterly plundered the land of Judea, so much so that it is compared to a terebinth and to an oak that has lost its acorns. Finally, after the last devastation, public laws were even posted, and the Jews were forbidden to enter the land from which they had been cast out. But if anyone believes in Christ, and that is fulfilled which we read above: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9): when, according to the Apostle (Rom 9), the remnant will be saved; this seed will be holy, and from the shoot of the Apostles all the Churches will sprout. What we have said, the seed that shall have stood in it shall be holy, or according to Aquila, its shoot shall be a holy seed, is not found in the Seventy Translators, but was added by Origen from the Hebrew and the edition of Theodotion; it is carried in the copies of the Church, so that after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel may be saved; and that in this too the word of the Lord may be fulfilled, who says: I will kill, and I will make alive, and I will strike, and I will heal (Deut 32:39).

h.p: < Previous Chapter ----- Next Chapter > Isaias vii. Notes & Commenatry:
n: Achaz. This must be seventeen years later than the former prediction, 4 Kings xv. 37. The kings of Syria and Israel jointly attacked Juda, but were forced to raise the siege of Jerusalem. The next year they came separately, and committed the following ravages. The news of their junction threw all into confusion, ver. 2. Isaias was then sent to inform the king, that the designs of his enemies should not take effect. Yet the two kings obtained each a victory. But they could not dethrone Achaz, as they intended. (Calmet) --- Paine traduces this prophecy as a lie, asserting that they succeeded. What! did they make Tabeel king? ver. 6. The Israelites would not even keep the captives who had been taken, 2 Chronicles xxviii. 15. (Watson, let. 5.) --- Achaz had been made captive before. But now the Lord defeated the projects of his enemies, as he will the conspiracy of heretics against his Church. (Worthington)

Jasub. This name was mysterious: Shear-Jashub means "the rest shall return" from Babylon, or be converted under Ezechias, chap. x. 22. (Calmet) --- Protestants, Go "thou, and Shear-Jashub, thy son, at the end of the conduit," &c. (Haydock)

Tails. So he styles the two kings in derision. The distrust of Achaz was punished by the loss of many of his subjects, but he was not dethroned, having engaged the Egyptians and Assyrians to attack his enemies, ver. 17.
Tabeel. Chaldean, "whom we shall think proper." He will not so much as name him.

Rasin. Both the king and his capital shall be ruined. --- And five. Capellus (p. 497.) would read six and five; or, in eleven years time. But (Calmet) Ephraim was led captive twenty-one years after, and the Cutheans took their place when sixty-five years had elapsed. (The year of the world 3327., Usher) --- Most people date from the prophecy of Amos to the ruin of Samaria, just sixty-five years. The former solution seems preferable. (Calmet)
Continue. Septuagint, "and will not understand, even the Lord," &c. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "and since you do not believe," (Calmet) or "because you are not confirmed" by a miracle. (Grotius)
Above. Require it to thunder, (1 Kings xii. 17.) or the earth to open, Numbers xvi. 28. (Calmet)
Lord. He was afraid of being forced to relinquish his evil ways. (St. Jerome) --- Though an idolater, he knew he ought not to tempt God.

Virgin, halma, (Haydock) one secluded from the company of men. Alma in Latin signifies "a holy person," and in Punic "a virgin." The term is never applied to any but "a young virgin." If it meant a young woman, what sort of a sign would this be? (St. Jerome) --- It was indeed above the sagacity of man to declare that the child to be born would be a boy, and live till the kings should be destroyed. But the prophet undoubtedly speaks of Jesus Christ, the wonderful, &c., (chap. ix. 5.) as well as of a boy, who should prefigure him, and be an earnest of the speedy destruction of the two kings. He was to be born of Isaias, (chap. viii. 4.) and of all the qualities belonging to the true Emmanuel, only that regards him, which intimates that the country should be delivered before he should come to years of discretion, ver. 16. (Calmet, Diss.) (Bossuet) --- The Fathers generally apply all to Christ. --- Called. Or shall be in effect, chap. i. 26. (Calmet) --- The king hardly trusted in God's mercies, whereupon the incarnation of Christ, &c., is foretold. (Worthington)
Honey. Like other infants. (Calmet) --- The new baptized received some to remind them of innocence. (Tertullian, cor. 3.) --- Christ shall be true man. (Menochius)

Good. Being arrived at the age of discretion, Achaz engaged the Assyrians to invade Damascus. Its citizens and four tribes were carried into captivity the year following. Phacee only survived another year, the year of the world 3265. This was a pledge, that what regarded the son of the virgin would also be accomplished. (Calmet) --- Land of the enemy. (Calmet) (4 Kings xvi.) (Menochius)

Assyrians. His aid shall prove the greatest scourge, (2 Paralipomenon xxviii. 20.) while the Idumeans and Philistines shall also ravage the country. (2 Paralipomenon xxviii. 17.) Achaz has vainly trusted in man.
Of Egypt. The Idumeans, &c., dwell on the borders, chap. v. 26. Yet many explain this of the victories of Nabuchodonosor and Nechas.

Razor. Or cut off with scissors all the hair, as was done with lepers, (Leviticus xiv. 9.) and Levites, Numbers viii. 7. The country shall be pillaged, and all shall be in mourning. (Calmet) --- The men shall be despised as no better than women and cowards. (St. Jerome) (Theodoret) --- Hired. With large sums. (Calmet)
Land. Pastures shall be so large, (Menochius) though uncultivated, the greatest part of the inhabitants being removed.
Pieces. Sicles. This was the price of the best vineyards, Canticle of Canticles viii. 2. (Calmet) --- Now people may hunt in them. (Haydock) --- The subjects of Achaz were much reduced. (Calmet)
Thither. The hedges shall be rooted up (Haydock) or neglected, so that cattle may graze. (Menochius) --- Two sorts of mountains are specified; some for vineyards, and others for pasture. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah: Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, the king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight against it, and they could not subdue it. And they told the house of David, saying: Syria has come to an agreement with Ephraim; and his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the woods are moved before the wind. Uzziah, who is also Azariah, king of Judah, reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years (2 Kgs 15). At the very end of his time Isaiah saw the things which the preceding discourse has set out. When he was dead and Jotham his son, a most righteous king, was reigning in his place, the prophet at once saw the Lord and Savior reigning in his majesty, and announcing the blindness of the Jewish people, and the overthrow of Jerusalem and of the other cities under Vespasian and Hadrian; and how in the Apostles a remnant was to be saved. As third king, the son of Jotham, Ahaz succeeds, a most impious man (2 Kgs 16; 2 Chr 28), who shut the doors of the temple, and in the valley of Ben-hinnom worshipped the Baals, and consecrated his son to idols; so that he even took away the bronze altar that Solomon had made, and placed in the Temple of God an altar of the idols, whose pattern he had received from Damascus. Justly, therefore, was he forsaken by the help of the Lord, and Rezin the king of Syria, that is, Aram, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel in Samaria, rose up together against him, and came to Jerusalem to storm it (ibid.). We read in the book of Chronicles that Rezin the king of Damascus, having conquered Ahaz, carried many from Judea off to Damascus; and that Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of the ten tribes, which were called Israel, who reigned in Samaria, struck down in one day a hundred and twenty thousand fighting men of Judah, and led captive into Samaria two hundred thousand women, boys and girls, with boundless plunder. Of that contest the prophet has now kept silent, but relates the second battle, when, having had proof of their strength and victory, and lured by the greatness of the plunder, they come again to Judea and desire to subdue Jerusalem, and could not, because the Lord helped it, so that, on the occasion of the mercy by which he was freeing the besieged people, he might announce that his Son would be born of a Virgin. When the house of David, that is, the royal house, heard that Syria and Ephraim, that is, Rezin and Pekah, were coming with joined army, it was terrified and greatly afraid, and both king and people trembled so that you would think the leaves of trees were being tossed by the blasts of the winds. According to the anagogy the interpretation is easy: that while Ahaz the impious king is reigning, the king of Aram, which is interpreted lofty and sublime, so as to indicate the arrogance of secular wisdom, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, who himself too, according to the prophet Hosea, was of the tribe of Ephraim, from which Jeroboam the son of Nebat had set up the golden calves in Bethel and Dan (1 Kgs 12) and had separated the people of God from David, are referred to the heretics, who agree together to storm the Church. And when the house of David hears this, David whom we read in Ezekiel is to be raised up as the good shepherd (Ezek 34), and his people believing simply in the Lord, it trembles greatly. And it trembles for this reason, because it is compared not to fruit-bearing trees but to an unfruitful forest. And that these same heretics and the gentiles fight against the house of David with the swords of arguments and of the dialectical art, no one doubts: so that those who are at variance among themselves agree in attacking the Church; according to that instance in which Herod and Pilate, who were at discord with each other, were bound together in friendship at the Lord's passion.
Commentary on Isaiah

This much we have said according to the history. But according to the tropology we have begun, we must consider that Isaiah is ordered to meet the impious king, going out from his own place, not at the beginning of the conduit, but at the outermost bounds of the upper pool, which was in the fuller's field, where filth and stains were washed away. For although Ahaz was reigning over Judah, yet because he was impious he lingered at the outermost bounds of the upper pool. So God has mercy not so much on the king, whom he judged unworthy of salvation, as on his people. And by the two tails of smoking brands, as we said before, he means secular wisdom and heretical speech, whose end is burning. They took counsel in vain to go up against Judah, and to seize it as though negligent and sleeping, and to join it to their own errors, and to set over it as king the son of Tabeel, that is, of the good God. For each adversary judges that the truth is with himself, that the best doctrine is with himself. Indeed Marcion the heretic thinks that Christ is the son of the good God, that is, of another, and not of the just God whose the Prophets are, whom he calls bloodthirsty, cruel, and a judge. While they say these things, the Lord threatens that their counsel shall not stand, but that for the meantime, now, as long as this world stands, the things also that are of the world hold sway within their own bounds and in their own cities. But when the time of the consummation has come, that is, the sixty-five years, and both the things of the world, which were made in six days, and all that pertains to the five senses have received their end, then all things are to be dissolved, which the gentiles and the heretics do not believe will come, and on account of their unbelief they do not understand the things that are said.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord said to Isaiah: Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Jasub your son who is left, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field. And you shall say to him: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and let not your heart be afraid of the two tails of these smoking firebrands, in the wrath of the fury of Rezin and of Syria and of the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah have taken most evil counsel against you, saying: Let us go up to Judah, and rouse it up, and tear it away to ourselves, and set a king in the midst of it, the son of Tabeel. Thus says the Lord God: It shall not stand, and this shall not be; but the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin, and yet sixty-five years, and Ephraim shall cease to be a people. And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria the son of Remaliah. If you do not believe, you shall not remain. Jasub the son of Isaiah, which is interpreted left over and returning, as a type of the people of Judah, which was to be freed from the hands of two kings, is ordered to go out with his father and to meet Ahaz king of Judah at the place of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field, where we shall read later that under Hezekiah king of Judah Rabshakeh stood and, at the command of Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, blasphemed the people of God. To which place there went out, sent by Hezekiah, the princes of the city whom we read of in the volume of Kings.
Commentary on Nahum

And let it not disturb anyone that we take the pool in the bad sense, when that pool to which Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, is commanded to go up is taken in the good sense. For there it is said with an addition: The pool of the aqueduct, and the pool of the fuller, which is accustomed to wash away filth and to cleanse the stains of garments. And because it is set on high, the prophet is therefore commanded to go up to it and, in meeting the king, to promise victory over the two burnt firebrands.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Ahaz (2 Kgs 18), though an impious king, is commanded, on account of the mercy of the Lord, to keep silence and not to be terrified, nor let his heart be afraid, thinking that he will suffer things like those he had endured before. And he calls Rezin king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Samaria two tails of firebrands, that is, of smoking brands, because in them the kingdom of Syria, that is, of Damascus, was ended, and the kingdom of Samaria, that is, of the ten tribes, which by another name were called Ephraim. For it is written (2 Kgs 16) that Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, under king Ahaz, went up against Damascus and laid it waste, and carried its inhabitants off to Kir, and killed Rezin; and that Hoshea the son of Elah laid an ambush for Pekah the son of Remaliah, and struck him and killed him, and reigned in his place in Israel nine years; and that Shalmaneser king of Assyria came and besieged Samaria, which is now called Sebaste, for three years, and in the ninth year of the reign of Hoshea took it, and sent Hoshea bound into prison, and carried Israel off to the Assyrians, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river Gozan, in the cities, or, as the Seventy translated, in the mountains of the Medes (2 Kgs 17).
Commentary on Isaiah

For although these two most evil kings took counsel to go up to Judah, whose region is set in the mountains, and to rouse it up while it was at rest and in a manner sleeping, and to subjugate it to their own rule, and to set over it as king the son of Tabeel, which is interpreted good God, so as to indicate either a man of this name or an idol; nevertheless thus says the Lord God: This counsel shall not stand, but for the meantime only Damascus shall be the head of the cities of Syria, and in Damascus itself, the metropolis, Rezin shall rule. Further, in Ephraim, on account of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who first reigned from Ephraim, Samaria shall be the head, that is, the royal house in the city of Samaria, and the head of Samaria shall be the son of Remaliah, that is, Pekah; but the kingdom of the ten tribes, that is, of the people of Ephraim, will cease to exist after sixty-five years. Which, unless we attend more carefully, cannot stand. For in the twelfth year of Ahaz the son of Jotham in the tribe of Judah, Hoshea reigned over Samaria, and in the ninth year of his rule he was taken (2 Kgs 17). And Ahaz reigned over Judah sixteen years (2 Kgs 16), and in the seventh year of Hoshea's rule after Ahaz's death Hoshea was taken, and Samaria destroyed, and the whole people carried over into Media: so that if we choose to put sixteen years of Ahaz and seven of Hoshea, the result is twenty-three years, or at most twenty-four; and where will the sixty-five years be, within which the kingdom of Israel is said to be ended? The Hebrews therefore set out this place thus: that Amos, who began to prophesy under Uzziah, when Isaiah too had the beginning of his prophecy, was the first to prophesy against Israel, saying: But Israel shall be led captive out of his land (Amos 7:11, 17). And that the title of his prophecy is against Samaria; and that he began to prophesy in the days of Uzziah king of Judah two years before the earthquake, which they hold to have occurred at the time when Uzziah, entering the Temple of God, claimed the priesthood for himself, and the earth was struck, and the ashes of the altar were poured out, and the king himself was struck with leprosy (2 Chr 26). And they hold that it was the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah when these things happened, whose remaining years are twenty-seven. For Uzziah reigned fifty-two years (2 Kgs 15); after him reigned Jotham his son for sixteen years, and his son Ahaz for another sixteen years; after whom reigned Hezekiah, in the sixth year of whose rule Samaria was taken; and thus sixty-five years are made up together (2 Kgs 16).
Commentary on Isaiah

When the Lord foretold these things through the prophet, both Ahaz and the people did not believe that they would come to pass. Hence it is added: If you do not believe, you shall not remain, as Symmachus translated, that is, you too shall not remain in your kingdom, but shall be led into captivity, suffering the penalties of those whose unbelief you have imitated. Or certainly, according to the Seventy, you shall not understand. And the sense is: because you do not believe the things that the Lord says are to come, you will not have understanding.
REPLY TO FAUSTUS THE MANICHAEAN 22:53

The commandments are those concerning righteousness, and the righteousness is that which is by faith, surrounded with the uncertainty of temptations; so that understanding is the reward of a pious belief of what is not yet understood. The meaning I have given to these words, "Thou hast desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord shall give it thee," I find also in the passage, "Unless ye believe, ye shall not understand;" showing that as righteousness is by faith, understanding comes by wisdom. Accordingly, in the case of those who eagerly demand evident truth, we must not condemn the desire, but regulate it, so that beginning with faith it may proceed to the desired end through good works. The life of virtue is one of toil; the end desired is unclouded wisdom.
SERMON 68 (118).1
If you are not able to understand, believe, that you may understand. Faith goes before; understanding follows after; since the prophet says, "Unless you believe, you shall not understand.
SERMON 76:1

The mysteries and secrets of the kingdom of God first seek for believing people, that they may make them understanding. For faith is understanding's step, and understanding faith's attainment. This the prophet expressly says to all who prematurely and in undue order look for understanding and neglect faith.
LETTER 120

So, then, in some points that bear on the doctrine of salvation, which we are not yet able to grasp by reason—but we shall be able to sometime—let faith precede reason, and let the heart be cleansed by faith so as to receive and bear the great light of reason; this is indeed reasonable. Therefore the prophet said with reason: "If you will not believe, you will not understand"; thereby he undoubtedly made a distinction between these two things and advised us to believe first so as to be able to understand whatever we believe. It is, then, a reasonable requirement that faith precede reason, for, if this requirement is not reasonable, then it is contrary to reason, which God forbid. But, if it is reasonable that faith precede a certain great reason that cannot yet be grasped, there is no doubt that, however slight the reason which proves this, it does precede faith.
Against Heresies (Book III, Chapter 21), Section 4

For the one and the same Spirit of God, who proclaimed by the prophets what and of what sort the advent of the Lord should be, did by these elders give a just interpretation of what had been truly prophesied; and He did Himself, by the apostles, announce that the fulness of the times of the adoption had arrived, that the kingdom of heaven had drawn nigh, and that He was dwelling within those that believe on Him who was born Emmanuel of the Virgin. To this effect they testify, [saying,] that before Joseph had come together with Mary, while she therefore remained in virginity, "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost;" [Matthew 1:18] and that the angel Gabriel said unto her, "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God;" [Luke 1:35] and that the angel said to Joseph in a dream, "Now this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, Behold, a virgin shall be with child." [Matthew 1:23] But the elders have thus interpreted what Esaias said: "And the Lord, moreover, said unto Ahaz, Ask for thyself a sign from the Lord thy God out of the depth below, or from the height above. And Ahaz said, I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord. And he said, It is not a small thing for you to weary men; and how does the Lord weary them? Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son; and ye shall call His name Emmanuel. Butter and honey shall He eat: before He knows or chooses out things that are evil, He shall exchange them for what is good; for before the child knows good or evil, He shall not consent to evil, that He may choose that which is good." [Isaiah 7:10-17] Carefully, then, has the Holy Ghost pointed out, by what has been said, His birth from a virgin, and His essence, that He is God (for the name Emmanuel indicates this). And He shows that He is a man, when He says, "Butter and honey shall He eat;" and in that He terms Him a child also, [in saying,] "before He knows good and evil;" for these are all the tokens of a human infant. But that He "will not consent to evil, that He may choose that which is good,"— this is proper to God; that by the fact, that He shall eat butter and honey, we should not understand that He is a mere man only, nor, on the other hand, from the name Emmanuel, should suspect Him to be God without flesh.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell, or in the height above. He who had before spoken to Ahaz through the prophet: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and the rest, since Ahaz did not believe and therefore did not understand, himself speaks to Ahaz: that, terrified at least by the authority of the Lord, he may accept what is said. Because it seems difficult to you, he says, that most powerful kingdoms are to be ended in a short time, and that you with your people should be freed from great danger, ask for yourself a sign, not at all from the idols in whose error you are held, but from the Lord your God, who promises you help; and the very sign is of your own choosing, whence you would demand it, whether from the depth or from the height. Whereas the Seventy alone said this, the others, according to the Hebrew, translated more expressively, from the depth of hell. So just as the depth signifies hell, so by the height we ought to understand above the heavens: so that when you have received a sign from hell or from the height, you may believe that the things I have said will come.
