And that the Lord of hosts dwells on Mount Zion, the same Apostle writes: You have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22). Hence I wonder at a certain one of our people who understands these children as the two sons of Isaiah, whom he begot from the conception of the prophetess his wife, namely Jasub and Emmanuel: of whom the former went before as a sign of the rejection of the former people, the latter of the taking up of the nations. Whoever accepts this will consequently also affirm that the prophet Hosea truly had a harlot for a wife.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 7

"And if they say to you: seek out ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things, who cry out from the belly — does not a nation seek to its own God? Why do they seek the dead among the living?" Attend, for these things are spoken obscurely, and the meaning must, by God himself granting and revealing it, cohere with what went before. He teaches us therefore not to be disciples of any discourses save the heavenly and the good. For there are certain men "who speak" and who promise true teaching, who "speak" not heavenly but earthly things. "He who is of the earth speaks of the earth; he who comes from heaven is above all; what he has seen and heard, that he testifies." If anyone, he says, to the "children" who believe in me "shall say: seek out ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things, who cry out from the belly" — as if to say "seek out" demons (for from the single kind of the "ventriloquist" demon he named, τροπικῶς [figuratively], all demons) — "if they say to you: seek out ventriloquists," that is, "seek" from demons either divination or truth or sacred contemplation, answer them these things which I say. What are the things he teaches them? He says in what follows. And there are certain men who send you — and rather the catechumens, so far as in them lies — to the "ventriloquists." For those who wish you to go to idols, of which it is written "all the gods of the nations are demons," wish you to go not only to "ventriloquists" but to every kind of demon. Yet may "our God, who does what he wills in heaven and on earth," tear us away from demons and make us his own household through our Savior Jesus Christ. See, then, lest at any time the soul of one of you be deceived and still waver and doubt, when it hears that such and such a man in that idol had a demon cure that ailment, or that it divined this thing and that; all these are idols of demons and of men not knowing the truth. Ascend in mind to him who is the "creator of all," and compare this true piety with every piety that is announced to be piety and is not piety, and see that you are blessed. For "who is like you, O people saved by the Lord?" And "blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord its God, the people whom he has chosen for his inheritance." For the nation of the Jews was once a "blessed nation," but it lost its blessedness and was cast out from its place, because him who was sent and had the testimony of the Father — not only through the law and the prophets, but also through "signs and wonders" — it plotted against and slew. The blessedness therefore has passed over to us, the disciples of Jesus Christ, and we believe in him, living unshaken and steadfastly according to that which we have been taught.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 7

"And if they say to you: seek out ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things." He named them "empty-speakers." Every discourse that is spoken is either empty or full of truth. Every discourse is empty which is false, but that is full of truth which has the knowledge of the God of the universe and teaches us to believe God, who promises the kingdom of heaven to his saints. See, then, what they say who were not "empty-speakers" nor ever appeared empty in the sight of the Lord God: "We have all received of his fullness." Those who are "empty-speakers" do not have "all of the fullness," but they are "all" empty of truth, empty of virtue, empty of Christ. "If they say to you: seek out those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things, who cry out from the belly." I wish to state also the reason why the discourse has now taken up this chief one of the "ventriloquist" demons, so as to say: "If they say to you: seek out ventriloquists." You will find that all who make promises and do not have the truth are serving their own belly and in a way do everything for the sake of its pleasure and its abundance — and not only the Gentiles, but also those who, while promising the religion in Christ, are heretics; and not only those, but even among us who are of the Church you will find someone who does everything for the filling of the belly, that he may be honored and receive the gifts which are brought into the church. Such a man speaks "from the belly," and the "fountain" of his discourses is situated in the "belly"; for the "fountain" of his discourses does not "flow" from the heart, does not "flow" from good thoughts, nor from the Holy Spirit. If therefore anyone at any time promises to teach, observe whether his discourses have their beginning "from the belly" or not. But the objection which can be raised against me, I will myself bring forward, lest perhaps someone among you, hearing it from someone, should think either that the Scripture is contrary to itself or that we did not examine how one ought to approve this discourse accusatory against those "who cry out from the belly." What then is the objection? "If anyone," he says, "believes in me, rivers shall flow from his belly, a fountain of water leaping up unto life eternal." Let someone therefore of those who raise the objection say: if the Savior promises "from the belly a fountain of water leaping up unto life eternal," it issues from the just man, and the just man "cries out from the belly," if indeed the "fountain of water" which the Savior promises is in "his belly." But it must be said that perhaps we have two "bellies," and one is bodily, the other spiritual — just as the other parts which seem to be named in the body, such as the eyes, are indeed some of the body, some of the soul. For if it is said of the "eyes": "The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes," I do not think this is to be referred to the bodily "eyes." And if it is said: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear," this is not to be thought to be said of the "ears" of the body, but of the soul, which those who are pure possess, in the hearing of the soul. But also, if it is said in a promise: "Your foot shall not stumble," this is not to be judged to be said of the "foot" of the body; for there is a certain "foot" of the heart entering into him who said: "I am the way." So therefore, like the bodily "belly," there is a "belly" of the soul, of which the just man speaks: "From fear of you, O Lord, we conceived in the belly and were in labor and brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which you have made upon the earth." But whosoever have a "belly" full of empty discourses "which are of the earth," they have a "belly" subsisting "of the earth," of which it is written: "But God will destroy both this and these." The saints therefore have a "belly" in which "from the fear of the Lord they have also conceived," and their "belly" is "full of fountains of water leaping up unto life eternal." Of this "belly" that one says: "And my belly is like new wine without vent, bound up." For he said these things not of the bodily "belly"; for his bodily "belly" was not "full" of divine things and of things near to them, "of wine bound up in a wineskin." Let these things stand for the resolution of the objection.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 7

Now let us return to what we had begun. "If" therefore "they say to you: seek out ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things, who cry out from the belly" — "does not a nation seek to its own God?" — answer them these things; but it is said elliptically, ‘answer them these things: "does not a nation seek to its own God?"’ Every "nation," if it "seeks," refers to its own "God" what it has "sought": answer them these things. But you, O Israelites, having the true "God, who is over all," when you "seek," do not "seek out ventriloquists" nor "those who cry out from the earth" nor "empty-speakers," but your own "God." "Why do they seek the dead among the living?" For "dead" are the demons, deprived of the true "life," which says: "I am the life." Do not therefore inquire of the "dead" concerning living matters, for you have received the "law."
Commentary on Isaiah

And when they say to you, Seek from the Pythons and from the diviners, who hiss in their incantations: does not a people inquire of its God? on behalf of the living, of the dead? To the law rather and to the testimony. But if they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them. And it shall pass through it: it shall fall and shall hunger: and when it hungers, it shall be angry, and shall curse its king and its God. And it shall look up above, and shall gaze at the earth, and behold, tribulation and darkness, dissolution, distress, and pursuing gloom: and it shall not be able to fly away from its distress. If it is the voice of the prophet Isaiah, as the Jews judge: Behold, I and my children, whom the Lord has given me for a sign and for a portent of Israel, then these things that follow too must be believed to be said by him to his disciples. When, he says, the nations and peoples say to you, those of whom it was read above: Be weak, O peoples, and be conquered, why do you want to listen to prophets, why are you deceived by the words of Isaiah and think that he knows the things to come? Seek rather from the Pythons and from the diviners, who hiss in their incantations. In place of which the Seventy translated: Who speak from the earth, who cry out from the belly. For everyone who is of the earth speaks of the earth (John 3:31). And he whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in his shame (Phil 3:19), must be believed to cry out from the belly. Do you answer them and say: Does not a people inquire of its God? on behalf of the living, of the dead? If you, he says, in keeping with the variety of your idols (for you have not one god but many), consult those whom you judge to be gods, and inquire of the dead, or of the images of dead men, about the living: how much more ought we to hear our God through the prophets?
Commentary on Isaiah

But, as we said above, if it is the person of Christ saying: Behold, I and my children, whom God has given me, then he himself also speaks these things to the Apostles and to the believers from the nations who have received his Gospel. If, he says, your fathers whom you have left say: seek the ventriloquists, whom we understand as pythons (such as the slave girl we read of in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 16), who was a source of gain to her masters), and those who speak from the earth, which the magi promise to do in the calling up of souls, and the other kinds of evil arts: you ought to know this, that each nation consults its own gods and questions the dead about the welfare of the living.
Commentary on Isaiah

But the Nazaraeans set out this place thus: When the Scribes and Pharisees tell you to listen to them, who do everything for the sake of the belly, and in the manner of magi hiss in their incantations so as to deceive you, you ought to answer them this: It is no wonder if you follow your traditions, since each nation consults its own idols. So we too ought not to consult you, the dead, about the living: rather God has given us the law and the testimonies of the Scriptures; and if you will not follow them, you will not have light, but gloom will always oppress you, which will pass through your land and doctrine: so that when those deceived by you see themselves in error and suffering a famine of truth, then they will be saddened, or angry, and will curse you, whom they used to think of as their gods and kings. And in vain will they look back to heaven and earth, since they are always in darkness and cannot fly away from your snares.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 7

O you, who could not be persuaded to "seek" those things from the "ventriloquists" and "from those who cry out from the earth" empty discourses — attend to the word of truth and the "law," receiving it "for a help to your law." In your "law" it is written: "you shall not" follow "idols"; acting according to the "law," do not attend to "ventriloquists," nor to "those who cry out from the earth." "For he gave the law for a help, that they may say: not like this word, for which no gifts are to be given." For he who has taken up the "law" and has come to know that "the law is for a help" and above all "spiritual" — the law which forbids "ventriloquists" and auguries — he, when he has understood the "law," ought in wonder to say that there is no word in the world, among Greeks or Barbarians, such as is the word of the "law"; for from every word, from all teaching which promises truth, the "law" differs — the law which was given to us by God. "For he gave the law for a help, that they may say: not like this word." What is it that "is not like this word"? There are many words, but "not like this word." For there is no word after the "word" of Moses, after the "word" of the prophets, and much more after the "word" of Jesus Christ and his Apostles. See whether the mind of God has not "cried out" in what has been said: "For he gave the law for a help, that they may say" — those who have received the "law for a help" — "it is not like this word," such as Moses spoke in "the law enacted through angels in the hand of a mediator." But far more worthily can the Church say this: "It is not like this word," which "was made flesh," which "dwelt among us," whose "glory we beheld," not veiled "as Moses" was with a veil, but "glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." "It is not like this word," which the Church has received, in which it believes, "through which also it shall be saved," the "word" which "in the beginning was with God, God," the "word" "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
Commentary on Isaiah

So he teaches the disciples, and adds: to the law rather and to the testimony. If, he says, you are in doubt about anything, know that it is written: The nations which the Lord your God will destroy before your face listen to dreams and to diviners; but to you the Lord your God has not so delivered: The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet from your brothers, like me; him you shall hear (Deut 18:15). Hence, if you wish to know things that are doubtful, give yourselves rather to the law and to the testimonies of the Scriptures. But if your congregation will not seek the word of the Lord, it will not have the light of truth, but will move about in error and darkness.
Commentary on Isaiah

But to you God has given the law as a help, so that you can say: the divination of the heathen, who often deceive their worshippers, is not such as ours, which is brought forth from the law without any payment. Hence the Seventy translated: Not as this word, for which there is no giving of gifts. For freely, he says, you have received, freely give (Matt 10:8).
Commentary on Isaiah

The light will pass through it, that is, through your congregation, or land, and you will fall, and you will hunger, and when you hunger you will be angry, according to what is written: And if they are not filled, they will murmur (Ps 58 [59]:16): and you will curse God your king, and in your necessities you will look up above to heaven and down to the earth: and behold, tribulation and darkness, dissolution of the knees, and distress of mind, and gloom of the eyes, and you will not be able to be rescued from the distress. This according to the Hebrews.
Commentary on Isaiah

But upon the unbelievers will come a most grievous famine, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God (Amos 8). And when you hunger you will be saddened, and will curse your prince and your fathers' traditions, that is, the devil and your ancient errors. And he says this to those who have suffered famine of the truth, and will look up above to heaven and down to the earth, and will be in distress, in darkness, and in tribulation: so that they may not see until the time when they too are converted to the Lord. These places call for a broad explanation, but we spare the size of the books, to remove the reader's weariness. These things we have touched on in part according to the translation of the Seventy, which in very many places is out of tune with the Hebrew.

n: Loaded. Theglathphalassar took away whole tribes, (2 Paralipomenon v. 26.) the year after this. Yet these people were the first enlightened with the rays of the gospel, (Matthew iv. 13.) though so much despised, John vii. 52. (Calmet) --- Here Christ preached first. But after his passion, few Jews believed in him. (Worthington)
Risen. The kingdom of Juda hoped for redress, when they saw the people of Israel humbled, (Haydock) or rather after the defeat of Sennacherib. (Calmet)

And hast. Parkhurst says it should be, "(whom) thou hast not brought up (the Gentiles) with joy they," &c. (Symmachus) (Haydock) --- The numerous forces of the Assyrians could not save them from the angel. Under Ezechias the people increased. Was not his reign a figure of the Church persecuted and increasing: but on that account, in danger from a relaxation of discipline? (Luke v. 7.) --- Spoils. They shall return thanks to God for the unexpected liberation.

Oppressor. Who levied taxes for Assyria, 4 Kings xviii. 7. Sennacherib made war, because Ezechias refused to pay them any longer, and his troops fell upon each other, (Calmet) as the Madianites had done, Judges vii. (Haydock)
Fire. Being cut and useless. See Diss. on the defeat of Sennacherib. (Calmet)

Child. The Messias, whom the son of Isaias prefigured. --- Shoulder. Where the badges of royalty were worn. (Calmet) --- Christ bore his cross. (Tertullian, &c.) --- Wonderful. In his birth, &c. --- Counsellor. From whom all good advice proceeds. Grotius falsely translates, "the consulter of the strong God," meaning Ezechias. Though he deemed the Socinians unworthy of the Christian name, (Ep. ad Valleum.) he too often sides with them. Johets always means one who "gives counsel," chap. xl. 13. Ezechias was at this time ten years old, and he did not always take advice, nor was his reign peaceful, &c. --- God. The three Greek versions maliciously render El "the strong," though it be uncertain that it ever has that meaning, as it certainly has not when joined with gibbor, "mighty." Why should two terms of the same import be used? The Septuagint copies vary much. Some read only, "he shall be called the angel of the great council, for I will bring peace upon the princes and his health." St. Jerome thinks they were afraid to style the child God. But this reason falls to the ground, as other copies have, (Calmet) after council, "Wonderful, Counsellor, God, the Mighty, the Potent, exousiaszes, the Prince of Peace, the Father of the world to come, for, &c., (7.) His." Grabe (de Vitiis lxx. p. 29.) asserts that the former is the genuine version, and that the inserted titles are a secondary one; so that there must have been two version before the days of Aquila, as the text is thus quoted at large by Clement and St. Iræneus, the year of the Lord 180; Kennicott adds also by St. Ignatius, the year of the Lord 110. (Haydock) --- The omnipotent God became a little child, and without violence subdued the world, which he still governs. (Worthington)
Peace. Christ gives it, and propagates his Church, Hebrews xii. 2.
Word. Septuagint, "death." This also agrees with the Hebrew term, and with the context.
Cedars. They speak in a proverbial way, that they will shortly repair the injuries done by the Assyrians depending on king Osee.
Him. Israel. Salmanasar came to ruin the kingdom. (Calmet)
Still. God punishes the impenitent throughout eternity, ver. 12., and chap. x. 4. (Worthington)
Him. Hebrew, "the branch and the rush." (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "the great and the small."
Headlong. If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the ditch, Matthew xv. 14. (Haydock)
Folly. Sin. They are all guilty. He will shew no compassion.
High. All shall witness the fall of Israel, (Calmet) like a forest on fire. (Haydock)

Brother. Civil wars shall rage, 4 Kings xv. Josephus (Jewish Wars vii.) perhaps alluded to this passage, when he said, that an ancient prophecy announced ruin to the Jews, when they should turn their arms against each other. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened: and at the last the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, of Galilee of the nations, was made heavy. The people that walked in darkness has seen a great light: to those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen upon them. LXX: Drink this first, act quickly, region of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, and the rest of you who are by the sea beyond the Jordan, of Galilee of the nations. The people that walked in darkness has seen a great light: you who dwell in the region and shadow of death, light shall rise upon you. We have set down the double edition because the testimony is well known and was used by the Evangelist Matthew: so that either the difference of the translation or the likeness may be recognized. And first it must be noted that the Evangelist Matthew set down this testimony not according to the Seventy but according to the Hebrews. For the Gospel word says: Now when Jesus heard that John had been delivered up, he withdrew into Galilee, and leaving Nazareth he came and dwelt in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali: that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people that sat in darkness has seen a great light; to those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen upon them. From that time Jesus began to preach and to say: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near (Matt 4:13ff.). And John the Evangelist relates that Jesus, invited with his disciples to a wedding at Cana of Galilee, did his first sign there, turning water into wine: This beginning of signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee: and he manifested his glory: and his disciples believed in him (John 2:11). Hence too it is said in the Seventy: Drink this first, act quickly: because the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali first saw the miracles of Christ: so that the land which had first seen the Lord doing signs might first drink the draught of faith. And according to the Hebrew it is said to have been lightened at the first time of the burden of sins: because the Savior first preached the Gospel in the regions of the two tribes. Hence too it is said in the sixty-seventh Psalm: Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel. There is Benjamin the younger (Ps 67 [68]:27-28; Acts 9); Paul the apostle, in ecstasy of mind, who also said elsewhere: whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God (2 Cor 5:13): The princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali, their leaders; because in these tribes were the little villages from which our leaders the Apostles believed. And they believed, according to Symmachus, swiftly, so that, hearing: Come, and I will make you fishers of men (Matt 4:19), they at once left both their father and their boat. But at the last time their faith was made heavy, since very many of the Jews remained in error. And here he calls the sea the lake of Gennesaret, which is formed by the inflowing Jordan; on whose shore Capernaum and Tiberias and Bethsaida and Chorazin are situated: in which region above all the Lord stayed; so that the people which either sat or walked in darkness saw a light, by no means a small one, like that of the other prophets, but a great one, like that of him who says in the Gospel: I am the light of the world (John 8:12). And those who dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen upon them. Between death and the shadow of death I think the difference is this: that death belongs to those who have gone down to the underworld with dead works: For the soul that sins, it shall die (Ezek 18:20); but the shadow of death belongs to those who, while they sin, have not yet departed from this life: for they can, if they will, do penance. For Galilee of the nations Aquila translated θῖνας of the nations, Symmachus borders of the nations; and by θῖνας we understand mounds of sand, which are either on the shores or on the banks. The Hebrews who believe in Christ set out this place thus: At the first time these two tribes, Zebulun and Naphtali, were captured by the Assyrians and led into the enemy's land; and Galilee was deserted (2 Kgs 15), which the prophet now says was lightened, because it bore the sins of the people. But afterward not only the two tribes, but also the rest, who dwelt beyond the Jordan and in Samaria, were led into captivity (2 Kgs 17 and 18). And this, they say, is what the Scripture now says: that the region whose people was the first to be led into captivity and began to serve the Babylonians, and which before was moving in the darkness of error, itself first saw the light of Christ preaching, and from it the Gospel was sown into all the nations. The Nazaraeans, whose opinion I set down above, try to explain this place thus: When Christ came and his preaching flashed forth, the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was the first to be freed from the errors of the Scribes and Pharisees, and shook off from its neck the most heavy yoke of the Jewish traditions. But afterward, through the Gospel of the Apostle Paul, who was the last of all the Apostles, the preaching was made heavy, that is, multiplied; and the Gospel of Christ shone into the borders of the nations and the way of the whole sea. Finally, the whole world, which before walked or sat in darkness and was held by the chains of idolatry and of death, beheld the clear light of the Gospel.
Commentary on Matthew

Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, and the rest. These were the first to hear the Lord preaching, so that where Israel's first captivity at the hands of the Assyrians had been, there the proclamation of the Redeemer should arise.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 13:134

Now the expression darkness will likewise be used to refer to two corresponding concepts. The statement "And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night" is an example of the more common meaning. An example of the spiritual meaning occurs in the statement "The people who sat in darkness … and in the shadow of death, light has dawned on them."
On Paradise 5.29

Therefore, he had the pledge of immortality: but being placed in the shadow of life, he could not see and grasp the hidden life with Christ in God by some common touch and sight. And if not yet a sinner, certainly not of an incorruptible and inviolable nature; for he who has fallen into sin is not yet a sinner. Indeed, he was in the shadow of life; but those who are sinners are in the shadow of death. For the people of sinners, as Isaiah teaches (Isaiah 9:2), sat in the shadow of death, until the light arose through the grace of God, not through their own merit. Therefore, there is no distinction between the breath of God and the food of the tree of life. No man can claim to possess more than what has been bestowed upon him by divine generosity.
Commentary on Isaiah

You have multiplied the nation, you have not magnified the joy: they shall rejoice before you, as they rejoice in the harvest, as victors exult when the prey is taken, when they divide the spoils. For the yoke of its burden, and the rod of its shoulder, and the scepter of its oppressor you have overcome, as in the day of Midian. For every violent plundering is with tumult: and the garment mixed with blood shall be for burning and food for the fire. LXX: The greatest part of the people you have led down in your joy: and they shall rejoice in your sight, as they are wont to rejoice in the harvest, and as those who divide the spoils: because the yoke that was set upon them has been taken away, and the rod from their neck. For the rod of the oppressors shall be scattered, as in the day of Midian. For every robe gathered by deceit, and the garment of exchange, they shall restore: and they shall wish that they had been burned with fire. In obscure places we set down both editions, so that the diligent reader may recognize how far the common translation differs from the other editions and from the Hebrew truth. An apostrophe is made to the light itself, which appeared to the people set in darkness, that is, to the Lord and Savior. And it is said to him: You have multiplied the nation, that is, you have filled all the nations with the knowledge of you; but you have not magnified the joy. In accordance with which the Apostle says that he has unceasing sorrow for his brothers who are Israelites (Rom 9). And Jonah is saddened that the Ninevites were saved in such a way that the gourd, or CICEION (קיקיון), withered (Jonah 4). And the Lord himself says in the Gospel: I did not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt 15:24). And in the passion: Father, if it be possible, he says, let this cup pass from me (Matt 26:39). This place has this sense: If it can be that the multitude of the nations believe without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the passion. But if they are to be blinded so that all nations may see, Father, let your will be done. So when Christ has come, and the nation of Christians has been gathered from all nations, then the Apostles will rejoice as reapers rejoice in the harvest, of whom the Lord spoke: The harvest indeed is great, but the laborers are few (Matt 9:37). And as victors exult who divide the captured prey. For when the strong man has been captured and bound, all his house is plundered and the spoils are divided (Matt 12).
Commentary on Isaiah

The Seventy signify that not all but a certain part of the people believed: although for what they said, you have led down in joy, others have interpreted you have magnified. And while in the rest they hold the same sense, they add that he, that is, the devil, will restore the robe gathered by deceit and the exchanged garment: namely, that he is going to restore with their former ornaments all the souls which he had stripped of God's help; and not he alone, but also his satellites, the demons: who, if the choice were given them, would rather choose to perish in flames than to lose their prey.
Commentary on Isaiah

But you, O Lord and Savior, have pulled from their shoulders the yoke of his burden, that is, of the devil, who before exulted in the world, who ruled over all nations, who pressed down the necks of all with the most heavy yoke of slavery; and the rod with which he struck all men and compelled them to render him their sins as a kind of tribute; and you have made those freed serve you, without any army and without shedding of blood, by a hidden hand: as once under Gideon you gave the people of Israel victory over the Midianites (Judg 7).
Commentary on Isaiah

For just as a garment that has been bloodied with human blood cannot be washed, but, stained with blood, is burned with fire, so that the stains of the foul gore perish along with the garment: so the violent plundering of the devil, and the tumult and crowds by which he had subjected the human race to himself, have been assigned to the fires of Gehenna.
The First Apology, Chapter XXXV

"Unto us a child is born, and unto us a young man is given, and the government shall be upon His shoulders;" which is significant of the power of the cross, for to it, when He was crucified, He applied His shoulders, as shall be more clearly made out in the ensuing discourse.
Dialogue with Trypho, Chapter LXXVI

And when Isaiah calls Him the Angel of mighty counsel, did he not foretell Him to be the Teacher of those truths which He did teach when He came [to earth]? For He alone taught openly those mighty counsels which the Father designed both for all those who have been and shall be well-pleasing to Him, and also for those who have rebelled against His will, whether men or angels.
AGAINST MARCION 3.19

Likewise Isaiah also says, "For unto us a child is born." But what is there unusual in this, unless he speaks of the Son of God? "To us is given he whose government is upon his shoulder." Now, what king is there who bears the ensign of his dominion upon his shoulder, and not rather upon his head as a diadem, or in his hand as a scepter, or else as a mark in some royal apparel? But the one new King of the new ages, Jesus Christ, carried on his shoulder both the power and the excellence of his new glory, even his cross; so that, according to our former prophecy, he might thenceforth reign from the tree as Lord.
AGAINST EUNOMIUS 11:3

For we too say plainly, that the prophet, wishing to make manifest to men the mystery concerning Christ, called the Self-Existent "Angel," that the meaning of the words might not be referred to the Father, as it would have been if the title of "Existent" alone had been found throughout the discourse. But just as our word is the revealer and messenger (or "angel") of the movements of the mind, even so we affirm that the true Word that was in the beginning, when He announces the will of His own Father, is styled "Angel" (or "Messenger"), a title given to Him on account of the operation of conveying the message. And as the sublime John, having previously called Him "Word," so introduces the further truth that the Word was God, that our thoughts might not at once turn to the Father, as they would have done if the title of God had been put first, so too does the mighty Moses, after first calling Him "Angel," teach us in the words that follow that He is none other than the Self-Existent Himself, that the mystery concerning the Christ might be foreshown, by the Scripture assuring us by the name "Angel," that the Word is the interpreter of the Father's will, and, by the title of the "Self-Existent," of the closeness of relation subsisting between the Son and the Father. And if he should bring forward Isaiah also as calling Him "the Angel of mighty counsel," not even so will he overthrow our argument. For there, in clear and uncontrovertible terms, there is indicated by the prophecy the dispensation of His Humanity; for "unto us," he says, "a Child is born, unto us a Son is given, and the government shall be upon His shoulder, and His name is called the Angel of mighty counsel." And it is with an eye to this, I suppose, that David describes the establishment of His kingdom, not as though He were not a King, but in the view that the humiliation to the estate of a servant to which the Lord submitted by way of dispensation, was taken up and absorbed into the majesty of His Kingdom. For he says, "I was established King by Him on His holy hill of Sion, declaring the ordinance of the Lord." Accordingly, He Who through Himself reveals the goodness of the Father is called "Angel" and "Word," "Seal" and "Image," and all similar titles with the same intention. For as the "Angel" (or "Messenger") gives information from some one, even so the Word reveals the thought within, the Seal shows by Its own stamp the original mould, and the Image by Itself interprets the beauty of that whereof It is the image, so that in their signification all these terms are equivalent to one another. For this reason the title "Angel" is placed before that of the "Self-Existent," the Son being termed "Angel" as the exponent of His Father's will, and the "Existent" as having no name that could possibly give a knowledge of His essence, but transcending all the power of names to express.
On the Death of Satyrus 1.12

So we have in another place: "A child is born to us, and a son is given to us." In the term child there is an indication of age; in the term son a reference to the fullness of Godhead. He was made of his mother and born of the Father, but as the same person he was born and given. Do not think of two but of one. For the Son of God is one person, born of the Father and sprung from the virgin. The names differ in order but unite in one, just as the scriptural lesson just read teaches: "Man was made in her, and the Highest himself has founded her." He was man indeed in body, but the Highest in power. And while he is God and man through diversity of nature, he is the same person, not two persons, though being God and man. He has, therefore, something peculiar to his own nature and something in common with us, but in both cases he is one and in both he is perfect.
On the Holy Spirit 3.2.9

And not only did the Father send the Son but also gave him, as the Son himself gave himself. For we read, "Grace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins." If they think that the Son was subjected to God because he was sent, they cannot deny that it was of grace that he was given. But he was given by the Father, as Isaiah said: "Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given." But he was given by the Spirit and was sent by the Spirit. For since the prophet has not defined by whom he was given, he shows that he was given by the grace of the Trinity; and inasmuch as the Son himself gave himself, he could not be subject to himself according to his Godhead. Therefore that he was given could not be a sign of subjection in the Godhead.
On the Blessings of the Patriarchs 6.31

Therefore, in order to call the Gentiles to the grace of his resurrection (for it is indeed a rich and fertile land that produces eternal fruits, fruits a hundred and sixty times over), he subjected his shoulder to work, subjecting himself to the cross, in order to carry our sins. And so the Prophet says: His authority is on his shoulder (Isaiah 9:6), that is, the power of divinity over the bodily passion, or the cross surpassing the body. Therefore, he placed his shoulder on the plow, enduring all insults, subjected to labor in such a way that he was wounded because of our iniquities, and weakened because of our sins.
Exposition of the Christian Faith 3.7.52-53

Christ, then, is the beginning of our virtue. He is the beginning of purity, who taught maidens not to look for the embraces of humanity but to yield the purity of their bodies and minds to the service of the Holy Spirit rather than to a husband. Christ is the beginning of frugality, for he became poor, though he was rich. Christ is the beginning of patience, for when he was reviled, he reviled not again. When he was struck, he did not strike back. Christ is the beginning of humility, for he took the form of a servant, though in the majesty of his power he was equal with God the Father. From him each various virtue has taken its origin.For this cause, then, that we might learn these different virtues, "a son was given us, whose beginning was upon his shoulder." That "beginning" is the Lord's cross—the beginning of strong courage, wherewith a way has been opened for the holy martyrs to enter the sufferings of the holy war.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 81

"'Messenger' of great counsel," the Son of God is called, because of the other things which He taught, and principally because He announced the Father to men, as also now He saith, "I have manifested Thy Name unto the men." For after having said, "I have finished Thy work," He next explaineth it in detail, telling what sort of work. Now the Name indeed was well known. For Esaias said, "Ye shall swear by the true God." But what I have often told you I tell you now, that though it was known, yet it was so only to Jews, and not to all of these: but now He speaketh concerning the Gentiles. Nor doth He declare this merely, but also that they knew Him as the Father. For it is not the same thing to learn that He is Creator, and that He hath a Son.
Commentary on Isaiah

For a little child is born to us, a son is given to us: and the government is upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and of peace there shall be no end: upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to establish it and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from henceforth and for ever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this. LXX: For a little child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose government is upon his shoulder: and his name is called messenger of great counsel. For I will bring peace upon the princes, and his health: great is his government, and of peace there is no bound, upon the throne of David and his kingdom: to set it right and to help in judgment and righteousness: from this time now and for ever. The zeal of the Lord Sabaoth will do these things. Therefore the devil, and all his violent plundering, by which he had oppressed the human race and mingled blood with blood, will be for burning and food of the eternal fire: because a child is born to us of a Virgin, of whom it was said above: Before the child knows to refuse evil and to choose good (Isa 7:16); and afterward, in the begetting by the Prophetess: Before the child knows how to call his father and his mother (Isa 8:4). This child, then, who was born of the Virgin, is called Emmanuel, that is, God with us; and, begotten of the Prophetess, that is, of the Holy Spirit, he was named Make haste, strip the spoils, hasten to take the prey: now he is called by many names. And although from what he had said above, Emmanuel, that is, God with us, he showed that he is God; yet now he says that his government was set upon his shoulder, either because he himself carried his cross, or, by the shoulder, showing the strength of his arm, as the same Isaiah says: The Lord God has revealed his holy arm to all the nations (Isa 52:10). And again: Lord, who has believed our report: and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed (Isa 53:1)? So after two names he will be called by six other names: Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of peace. For not, as most think, are the names to be joined in pairs, so that we read Wonderful counselor, and again, Mighty God; but Wonderful is to be read separately, which in Hebrew is said PHELE (פלא); and Counselor apart, who in their tongue is called IOES (יועץ); and God separately, who in Hebrew is said EL (אל). Indeed, in what follows, where we read: For you are God, and we did not know; and again: I am God, and there is no other besides me (Isa 45:5), and many things like these: in place of what is said in Latin, God, in the Hebrew EL is written. And what follows, Mighty, is called in Hebrew GIBBOR (גבור). Hence too in the place where the same prophet records: They shall trust upon God, the holy one of Israel, in truth: and what is left of Jacob upon the mighty God (Isa 10), for mighty God the Hebrew has written EL GIBBOR. And the Father of the age to come and of the resurrection, which is fulfilled in our calling; and the prince of peace, who said to the Apostles: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you (John 14:27): no one will doubt this who has read, according to the apostle Paul, that the Savior is our peace. Terrified by this majesty of names, I think, the Seventy did not dare to say of a child that he was openly to be called God, and the rest; but in place of these six names they set what is not found in the Hebrew, Angel of great counsel, and I will bring peace upon the princes, and his health. Which seems to me to have this sense: He is the Angel of great counsel who announced to us that Israel was to be cast off for a time and the nations to be saved; and he gave peace to his princes, the Apostles and apostolic men, and left the health of his teachings to believers.
SERMON 187:4

We read, "A child is born to us," because we see him in the nature of a servant, which he had because the Virgin conceived and brought forth a son. However, because it was the Word of God who became flesh in order to dwell among us, and because he remains what he was (that is, really God hidden in the flesh), we use the words of the angel Gabriel and call "his name Emmanuel." SERMON 7:3

The fact that the one who talked to Moses is called both the angel of the Lord and the Lord raises a big problem, which calls not for hasty assertion but for careful investigation. There are two opinions that can be put forward about it, of which either may be true, since they both fit the faith. When I say that either may be true, I mean whichever of them was intended by the writer. When we are searching the Scriptures, we may of course understand them in a way in which the writer perhaps did not; but what we should never do is understand them in a way which does not square with the rule of faith, with the rule of truth, with the rule of piety. So I am offering you both opinions. There may be yet a third that escapes me. Anyway, of these two propositions, choose whichever you like. Some people say that the reason why he is called both the angel of the Lord and the Lord is that he was in fact Christ, of whom the prophet says plainly that he is "the angel of great counsel." "Angel" is a word signifying function, not nature. "Angel" is Greek for the Latin nuntius. So "Messenger" is the name of an action: you are called a messenger for doing something, namely, for bringing some message. Now who would deny that Christ brought us a message about the kingdom of heaven? And then an angel, that is to say, a messenger, is sent by the one who wants to give a message by him. And who would deny that Christ was sent? So often did he say, "I did not come to do my own will but the will of him who sent me," that he of all people is the one who was sent. After all, that pool at Siloam "means Sent." That is why he told the man whose eyes he anointed with mud to wash his face there. No one's eyes are opened except those of the person who is cleansed by Christ. So then, the angel and the Lord are one and the same.
Homilies on the Gospels 2:9

Surely the entire divinely arranged plan of our Redeemer's [coming] in the flesh is the reconciliation of the world—it was for this purpose that he became incarnate, for this he suffered, for this he was raised from the dead—that he might lead us, who had incurred God's anger by sinning, back to God's peace by his act of reconciliation. Hence he was rightly given the name "Father of the world to come" and "Prince of peace" by the prophet; and the apostle, writing about him to those from among the nations who had believed, said, "And coming, he brought the good news of peace to you who were from far off and peace to those who were near, since through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father."
Homilies on the Gospels 1:23

Clothed in flesh, [Christ] descended into the water as "an angel of great counsel," that is, as a herald of the Father's will to Jewish people. By his deeds and his teaching he moved sinners, so that he would be killed—he who, by his bodily death, was able not only to heal those who were ailing spiritually but also to bring the dead back to life. The movement of the water, then, suggests the Lord's passion, which occurred by the Jewish nation being moved and stirred up.
Homilies on the Gospels 1:6

"Which will be to all people," not to all the people of the Jews, nor to all the people of the nations, but to all the people who, either from the Jews or from the nations of the whole world, are brought together in one flock to one confession of Christ. From one and the same partaking of the mysteries of Christ they are called "Christian." …The light of life rose for those of us dwelling in the region of the shadow of death.

And what follows: His dominion shall be multiplied, and of peace there shall be no end, in place of which the Seventy translated: Great is his government: we ought to know that the Hebrew word MESRA (משרה), both here and above, the Seventy interpreted ἀρχὴν, that is, government. In place of which we rendered government above, here dominion. But Aquila, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, interpreted μέτρον, that is, measure, which is called by the same name in Hebrew and in Latin. Nor can anyone doubt about the manifold dominion of the Savior and his peace, which has no end, who has read in the Psalms: Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession (Ps 2:8); and again: And abundance of peace, until the moon be taken away (Ps 71 [72]:7), that is, until the consummation of the age. And the zeal, that is, the jealousy, of the Lord of hosts did this for this reason, because they provoked him to jealousy with those who were not gods, and he provoked them to jealousy with a nation that was not a nation (Deut 32). The prophecy of Emmanuel and of the child to be born of a Virgin, begun at the place where it is said to Ahaz: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, is ended with this little verse, in which is added: The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this (Isa 7:11). Now let us pass on to the rest.

When Israel had been saved through the apostles, all the world flocked to the threshold of truth and of the peacemaker Solomon, of whom it was said, "His dominion will be increased and there will be no end of peace." And, indeed, just as in his divinity the Mediator between God and human beings foresaw the mother of whom he willed to be born when he should so will, so also in his humanity he chose the time that he wished for his nativity. The very author of peace and the Maker of time sent before him a time of peace, and thus when he appeared in the flesh he opened an approach to light and proclaimed the joys of eternal peace first to the house of Jacob (that is, the Israelite people), and then to all the nations which came streaming to him. And we must not pass over the fact that the serenity of that earthly peace, at the time when the heavenly king was born, not only offered testimony to his grace but also provided a service, since it bestowed on the preachers of his word the capability of traveling over the world and spreading abroad the grace of the gospel wherever they wished.
Homilies on the Gospels 2:24

All these things, as the apostle teaches, "were done as an example for us" and were written down for us, and so we must scrutinize them carefully for their spiritual meaning. The temple that he built is his catholic church, which he gathers into the one structure of his faith and charity from all the believers throughout the world, as it were from living stones.

This voice of repentance is that of the Jewish people and of all who found in Christ access to the salvation for which they were searching. Thus, having received the pledge of the Spirit, may I remain confident that you will forevermore preserve from destruction the generation of works which were begotten by my heart after the washing of my body and that you will never remove my name from the heavenly home which you deigned to grant to my fathers who, through the law, faithfully and devoutly awaited your coming.
Commentary on Ezra and Nehemiah 1:14-30

What does the spiritual house or temple that King Solomon made for the Lord in Jerusalem signify? Solomon himself, whose name means "peaceful," is a fitting symbol of the one about whom the prophet sang, "His government will be increased, and there will be no end to peace." [This is] the same one concerning whom the apostle also wrote to the church of the Gentiles, "and he came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near, for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father."That it took Solomon seven years to build the temple, which he completed and dedicated in the eighth year, was a sign that for seven years, or the entire span of the present age, the Lord would build the church as a heavenly dwelling for the gathered faithful. In this verse, Solomon signifies the everlasting light by "length of days," the survival of death by "years of life" and the state of happiness to be discovered by "growth in peace." Isaiah refers to the same reality when he says, "His government will be increased, and there will be no end to peace." For when the people of God are obedient to God's law, both historically and at the present time, they are enabled to live for a long time in the repose of peace.
Commentary on Proverbs 1:1
