For it is through this that the church is strengthened and the kingdom of Christ is extended both within each of the faithful and throughout the entire world.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 37: WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT DEATH WAS SENT INTO JACOB AND CAME INTO ISRAEL?

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT DEATH WAS SENT INTO JACOB AND CAME INTO ISRAEL, WHEN JACOB HIMSELF IS CALLED ISRAEL? — He gave two names to one people, so that from the names their merits might be understood. For the one who was surnamed Israel was previously called Jacob. Wrestling with the Savior, he realized that the one whom he saw in bodily form was God; and therefore he was called "the man seeing God" (Gen. 32:24–28). Therefore the people whom he calls Jacob, in this passage and for this reason, signifies the carnal people, in the way that names are given by parents to their offspring. But these, that is, the Jews, because of their evil deeds were not called Israelites, since they sacrificed to calves and lights in Samaria, by the zeal and command of King Jeroboam. The people, however, who in Jerusalem offered sacrifices in the temple of the Lord through the priests of God, were called Israel. Samaria therefore, because of its wickedness, was handed over to captivity and death; but Jerusalem was spared, because it had kings who loved God. Yet when Jerusalem itself followed the wickedness of Samaria, the sentence that was given against Samaria also encompassed it. Therefore it is said, "God sent death into Jacob," (Isa. 9:8) that is, into the people of Samaria, who lived carnally, as we said above; "and it came into Israel," that is, into the people of Jerusalem, because it followed idolatry, imitating Samaria, so that in like manner it might be led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, just as Samaria was by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians. This is plain: the sentence pronounced against the wicked also finds the good, once they cease to be righteous. For death, once sent into Jacob, as was shown above, came into Israel, not passing over Samaria, but when the cause for which it was sent into Samaria was found in Jerusalem, being sent there it also came into the place where the same situation existed. For vengeance follows the cause, not discerning the person.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 13: DEATH SENT INTO JACOB AND ISRAEL

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT DEATH WAS SENT INTO JACOB, THAT IT HAS COME INTO ISRAEL, SINCE JACOB HIMSELF IS ISRAEL? — He gave two names to one people. For the one who was first called Jacob later received the name Israel, when he wrestled with the Son of God and saw Him through understanding, "the man seeing God." (Isa.9:8) Therefore the people whom he calls Jacob, in this passage and for this reason, is understood as not seeing God, but is regarded as carnal, because of its evil works: so that, just as Jacob, before he saw God Christ, was not called Israelite, so these, while they are called the people Jacob, are signified as not seeing God. Israel, however, he calls the people who, by the works of God, are made worthy to see God. Therefore the people Jacob, because it relied on carnal help, despairing of the assistance of God (for it loved idols), is given over to death, when the king of Assyria is stirred up against them. This is understood of Samaria in what was said by the prophet Isaiah, which was the first to do evil before God, establishing calves for sacrifice, having invented new priesthoods through Jeroboam. Therefore death was sent to them: for they were the first to be taken and deported by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, so that by their example the people of Judah and Benjamin and Levi, those two tribes that remained, and the half tribe in Jerusalem under Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, who in the temple of the Lord offered sacrifices through the priests of the Lord, might be warned. These he calls the people Israel because of the tribes of Judah and Levi, who themselves, though they ought to have acted rightly, frightened by the example of Samaria, behaved wickedly, serving idols. Yet there were some kings in Jerusalem who, after the passing of Solomon and his son Rehoboam, followed the way of David, walking rightly in the sight of God. But all the kings of Samaria acted wickedly in the sight of the Lord until their deportation. And therefore they are called by the carnal name. And because Jerusalem followed their wickedness, it too is given over to captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon; and this is "to have sent death into Jacob and to have come into Israel." It was sent to Samaria; but when the cause for which it was sent to Samaria was found in Jerusalem, being sent there it also came into the place where the same situation existed. For vengeance does not follow the place, but the cause.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel. And all the people of Ephraim shall know it, and those who dwell in Samaria, saying in pride and greatness of heart: The bricks have fallen, but we will build with squared stones; they have cut down the sycamores, but we will change them for cedars. And the Lord shall raise up the enemies of Rezin against him, and shall turn his foes into tumult, Syria from the East, and the Philistines from the West, and they shall devour Israel with whole mouth. For all this his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out, and the people has not returned to him who strikes it, and they have not sought the Lord of hosts. We read above (2 Kgs 16) that in the days of Ahaz son of Jotham, son of Uzziah king of Judah, Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel went up to Jerusalem to take it by storm. And (Isa 7) that Isaiah the prophet was sent to meet Ahaz with Jasub his son, to tell him not to fear, and that his heart should not be afraid of the two tails of smoking firebrands, because in them the rule of Syria and of Israel was to be brought to an end. When he did not believe, because of the greatness of the matter and the present danger, he is bidden to ask a sign for himself. And because he was an idolater, he refused to do even this: therefore the Lord gives a sign, not to the king himself, but to the house of David, the sign of his Son who was to be born of the Virgin, at whose invocation they were to be freed from the imminent danger, and the rest, which we have interpreted up to the present place. So, many mysteries having been set in between, he now returns to what he had begun, and prophesies the overthrow of Rezin and Ephraim, that is, of Syria and Samaria: A word, he says, the Lord sent into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel. Among the Hebrews DABAR (דבר), which is written with three consonant letters, DALETH, BETH and RES, according to the nature of the passage signifies word if it is read DABAR, and if DEBER, death and pestilence. For this reason many, deceived by the ambiguity of the term, say that not a word was sent, but death. So the Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel. He willed that Judah should reign, as Jacob prophesies in Genesis (ch. 49); and Israel, that is, the ten tribes, claimed the rule for themselves, of whom it was said: They have reigned, and not through me (Hos 8:4). So the dignity of rule, which had begun in David at Samuel's anointing after Saul was cast off, sent into Jacob, that is, into the twelve tribes, which were once called Jacob, fell upon Israel: not, as the Seventy translated, came: for what had been appointed and directed to the saints fell among the wicked.
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the anagogy, our writers expound this passage thus: God sent his Son to Jacob, that is, to the Jews; and he came to Israel, that is, to the people of the nations, whom the Apostle too says are called Israel (Rom 9). Others, however, thus: The Lord sent his Word to the Church, which supplanted the former people, and it fell upon Israel, that is, upon the heretics, who boast that they see God.
Morals on the Book of Job 2.57

For it is written, "The Lord sent a Word into Jacob, and it hath fallen upon Israel." For Jacob means one that overthrows another, and Israel, one that sees God. And what is signified by Jacob but the Jewish people, and by Israel but the Gentile world? For in that very One Whom Jacob aimed to overthrow by the death of the flesh, the Gentile world, by the eyes of faith, beheld God. And thus the Word, that was sent to Jacob, lighted upon Israel; for Him whom the Jewish people rejected when He came to them, the Gentile world at once owned and found.
Commentary on Isaiah

So the people of Ephraim and those who dwell in Samaria shall know, who because of their multitude are lifted up into pride and say: The kingdom of Judah is small, and in comparison with ours most worthless. So, while they collapse like bricks, let us build ourselves a house of squared stone. When their sycamores, which are cheap wood, have been cut down by hostile incursion, we will build up our rule with cedars, which do not rot, so that they may signify an everlasting kingdom.
Commentary on Isaiah

So let their leaders know, and all who dwell in Samaria, that is, who say that they keep the law of God, and are in an abundance of virtues, and bear the fruits of righteousness (for this is what Ephraim means), who in the pride of their heart despise the Church, and, thinking its simplicity to be want of skill, say: In place of its bricks we will build our churches with squared and very strong stones, and in place of unfruitful trees, soon to perish, we will raise up the loftiest cedars; cedars which the Lord will crush, and which the righteous man, in the person of the wicked, relates that he saw, and their place was not found (Ps 36 [37]).
Commentary on Isaiah

So the Lord says that Rezin, which means worldly wisdom, whose help Ephraim used, will be turned against him, and all his enemies will fight against him, and he will be assailed both from the East and from the West, and they will devour Israel with whole mouth. In place of which the Seventy translated: And let us build ourselves a tower: and God will dash down those who rise up against mount Zion, and will scatter his enemies. For they desire to build themselves a temple in Samaria too, in the likeness of the Temple of God; but although they have moved their feet from the East and said: Come, let us build a tower, and make ourselves a name before we are scattered (Gen 11:4), with the Lord fighting against them their agreement will be dissolved and scattered, and their tongues will be divided against one another, lest by agreeing they become worse; rather they will be destroyed by one another. And when they have been so struck and devoured by their enemies, still they will not return to the Lord; but his hand is still ready to strike, according to what we read in Jeremiah: In vain have I struck your sons: you have not received discipline (Jer 2:30).
Homilies on Ezekiel 2.9.5

Because the prophet recognized that the Jewish people would perish from the faith and because he foresaw that there would arise within the church holy apostles, through whom many of the Gentiles would be established in the strength of faith and life, he spoke with great encouragement, saying, "The stones have fallen, but we will build with square stones." Having foreseen the rise of the apostles, martyrs and doctors of the holy church, he was less troubled by the fall of the stones, which represents the judgment of the Jews, because he also saw the work of Almighty God, which is the holy church built from square stones.Four tables were built from the square stones, therefore, inasmuch as faith, life, patience and kindness were given from the lives of the saints as an example for the people to follow, that they might already have a foretaste of the table. That is, the people might know the virtues through which they can offer a sacrifice of prayer to Almighty God on the altars of their hearts.
Whatever good the faithful people of the holy church have done or continue to do, then, they first received from the exemplary lives of their preachers. For how could they have acquired this foretaste of the table if they had not found the square stones?
Let's look briefly at each of them, dearest brothers. Do you want to see an instance of faith? "For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain." Would you like to know what life is like? "The world is crucified to me and I to the world." Do you want to hear what patience sounds like? "To the present hour we hunger, we are buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our hands. We are cursed and we bless, we are persecuted and we endure, we are slandered and we implore."
Commentary on Isaiah

Let all the people of Ephraim, then, and those who dwell in Samaria know this: that the Syrian, who is now its help, will go over to the enemy. Or certainly, that against the Syrian himself sudden wars of adversaries arise, and all are turned into tumult: so that against Israel Syria moves from the East, and the Philistines, that is, the Palestinians, from the West, and together they devour Israel. And when they have done these things, my hand is nonetheless stretched out, or lifted high, over Israel, and does not cease to strike them. And struck by God they will not return to him who strikes them, nor will they seek the Lord of hosts, worshiping golden calves in place of God.
The Book of Pastoral Rule 3.13

Against them the prophet complains to the Lord, saying, "You have bruised them, and they have refused to receive correction." … Hence again the Lord says, "The people are not returned to him who has struck them." … Hence the Lord reproaches the people of Israel, captive yet not converted from their iniquity, saying, "The house of Israel is become dross to me; all these are brass, and tin, and iron and lead, in the midst of the furnace." This is as though he said unmistakably, "I wished to purify them in the fire of tribulation, and I wanted them to become silver or gold. But they have turned from me in the furnace into brass, and tin, and iron and lead, because even in tribulation they have rushed forward not to virtue but to vices." When brass is struck, it gives off a greater sound than do other metals. He … who when chastised breaks forth into sounds of murmuring has turned to brass in the midst of the furnace. Tin, however, when skillfully treated, presents the deceptive appearance of silver. He therefore who is not free from the vice of pretence in the midst of tribulation has become tin in the furnace. But he uses iron who plots against the life of the neighbor, and he is iron in the furnace when he does not put away in his tribulations the wickedness of doing harm to neighbors. Lead, again, is heavier than the other metals. He then is found to be lead in the furnace who is so weighed down by the burden of his sin that even in tribulation he is not raised above earthly desires.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord will destroy from Israel head and tail, bending and perverting, in one day. The aged and honorable, he is the head; and the prophet who teaches falsehood, he is the tail. And those who call this people blessed shall be leading it astray, and those who are called blessed shall be cast headlong. Therefore the Lord will not rejoice over its young men, and he will not have mercy on its orphans and widows, because every one is a hypocrite and wicked, and every mouth has spoken folly. For all this his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. For impiety is kindled like a fire: it shall devour brier and thorn, and shall be kindled in the thicket of the forest, and shall be rolled together in the pride of smoke. In the wrath of the Lord of hosts the earth has trembled, and the people shall be like food for the fire. A man will not spare his brother, and he will turn aside to the right and be hungry, and he will eat on the left and not be filled: each one will devour the flesh of his own arm. Manasseh Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh, and they together against Judah. For all this his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Not only will the Lord raise up the enemies of Rezin against him, and turn his foes into tumult, Syria from the East and the Philistines from the West, so that they devour Israel with whole mouth; but because it has not returned to him who strikes it, nor sought the Lord of hosts, he will stretch out his hand to strike, so as to destroy from Israel the head, and the tail bending and perverting, namely him who perverts what is right (Jer 2).
Commentary on Isaiah

According to tropology, the Lord will take away head and tail, the greater and the lesser alike. By naming the tail, he shows that the heretics are not men but beasts of burden, which use this member to cover their dung and to keep off small creatures. And after the head he adds the tail bending and perverting, because they overturn the precepts of the law and pervert the right way.
Morals on the Book of Job 14.43-44

Where the head and the tail are said through the prophet to be destroyed, it is clear that priests are designated by the head and prophets by the tail. The crown, therefore, is removed from the head when those who are seen to preside over the body of the church abandon the rewards of heavenly compensation. Once its leaders fall, normally, the army that follows them also succumbs. Hence, soon after the condemnation of the leaders, Job comments on the manifold afflictions of the church: "He destroyed me on every side, and I perish; and he has removed my hope like uprooting a tree." For the church is destroyed on every side and perishes in the persons of its sick members when those who seem to be its strength are corrupted, that is, when the crown is removed from the head because its leaders have abandoned their pursuit of eternal rewards. It is in reference to the sick who have fallen that Job then adds, fittingly: "and he removed my hope like uprooting a tree." A tree is felled by a gust of wind. And what is more similar to a person who falls into unrighteousness as a result of being terrorized with threats than a tree that loses its straightness because of the wind?
Commentary on Isaiah
Who the head is, he himself has interpreted: the aged and honorable. And who the tail is: The prophet, he says, who teaches falsehood, that is, the false prophet.
Commentary on Isaiah

He will also destroy the aged man, because he is the head, and the false prophet, who is set in the tail, both teachers and disciples alike: the one sort who for gifts praise sinners, the other who, being praised, do not perceive their own evils nor do penance.
Commentary on Isaiah

He has spoken of the leaders; now he joins the people as well to the nobles, because teachers and disciples, the learned and the unlearned crowd, will perish alike. For those who called the people blessed are seducers; and those who were called blessed, not for virtue but for gifts, will be cast headlong into death. Hence also we read above: My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray, and trip up the paths of your feet (Isa 3:12).
Commentary on Isaiah

In such a people God will have mercy on no person: not on the orphan, not on the widow, because every one is a hypocrite, pretending one thing and doing another: promising chastity and living luxuriously, making a show of poverty and filling the purse. Hence he adds and says: And every mouth has spoken folly. For all these things the Lord does not cease to be angry, but still raises his hand to strike.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore the Lord will not rejoice in their young men: For woe to the city whose king is a youth (Eccl 10:16). And those who have lost God as Father, or the true Lord, will not obtain mercy. For every heretic is a hypocrite, doing one thing and pretending another, and whatever he says, though it may seem to be wisdom, is nevertheless folly. For these things he stretches out his hand to punish, and the devouring flame will consume all their impieties like thorns. And words without virtues, which are compared to an unfruitful forest, will be wrapped in the pride of smoke.
Commentary on Isaiah

And because they have done these things, impiety will be kindled like fire, so that the ravening flame devours not the tilled field but briers and thorns, and consumes not fruit-bearing trees but the unfruitful forest in which wild beasts dwell. For this reason it is said that the thicket of the forest, when fire is set beneath it, is rolled together in the pride and height of the smoke. For everything that is lofty and rises up on high can be called proud. In place of which the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated: and it will devour all things round about the hills.
Commentary on Isaiah

At their punishment all the ground will tremble, and the deceived peoples will be handed over to everlasting burnings, because for the sake of shameful gain they do not spare even their own, but vie with one another in taking plunder from the peoples they have deceived, leaving good things and lingering in the worst. And though they always find what is on the left, yet they are never sated with their errors, devouring the flesh of their own arm, and fighting against the Church with equal zeal. On account of luxury and pleasures and gains from the peoples they have discord among themselves, so that from one heresy two arise, and these in turn are divided into parts, so that they may lead away flocks of their own and devour the houses of widows and of sinful women, always learning and never coming to the knowledge of the truth (2 Tim 3). In all these things the fury of the Lord will not be turned away, consuming and overthrowing vices; but the more they advance in sinning, the more he stretches out his hand for punishment.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hence also at the wrath of the Lord the earth trembled, and the people became fodder for the fire, because there was such cruelty in it that it did not spare even the dearest name of brotherhood, but, deserting and despising the right, it was sated with the things that were on the left, while it hungers for pleasures and evils, and always longs to join worse things to evil ones.
Commentary on Isaiah

Manasseh and Ephraim too, who were born of one womb and begotten of the same parent, broke out into such madness that they were at odds with one another in hostile hatred. Let us read the volumes of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find the civil wars of Samaria among themselves, while some fight for one king and others for another, and how, when their own kings had been killed, they agree on attacking Judah.

n: Injustice. These great ones excite God's indignation. (Calmet) --- Jeroboam forbidding any to go to Jerusalem; and the Pharisees establishing their wicked traditions, ruined all. (Worthington)

Afar. When Salmanasar shall come from Ninive to destroy Samaria, to punish the people for their idolatry (Calmet) and oppressions. (Haydock) --- Glory. Golden calves, (Osee viii. 5., and x. 5.) or possessions, chap. ix. 8.

Woe. Or come on, Heus, though (Calmet) ho is ordinarily rendered, alas! It here indicates that God makes use of this scourge with regret, and will afterwards consign it to the flames. (Haydock) --- The prophet speaks of Salmanasar, or of Sennacherib. (St. Cyprian; St. Jerome)
Deceitful. Hebrew, "hypocritical," joining my worship with that of idols. (Calmet) --- They had solemnly promised to serve the Lord, Exodus xix. 8. (Worthington)
So. He will not think that he is executing my vengeance, supposing that he conquers by his own power.

As. Literally, "altogether kings." (Haydock) --- Thus Nabuchodonosor kept the conquered princes for derision, Habacuc i. 10., and Judges i. 7. --- Arphad, Arad, or rather Raphanæ, Jeremias xlix. 23. --- Damascus. These two cities were not yet subdued.
Idols. He looks upon the true God as no better than any idols, (4 Kings xviii. 32.) and falsely supposes that the latter were adored in Jerusalem. (Calmet)
Works. Humbling and terrifying Ezechias and his subjects, who were reduced to great distress, in order to avert the impending war. (Haydock) --- Eyes. The Assyrians were punished in their turn.
Nest. Some put these words in the mouth of God. (Tertullian) (Abdias 4.) --- But they shew the insolence of Sennacherib.

Axe. The Assyrian has no right to boast. What can man do without God's assistance? (Calmet) --- Gratiæ tuæ deputo et quæcumque non feci mala. (St. Augustine, Confessions ii. 7.) --- Sennacherib persecuted the Jews of his own free will, though he was God's instrument. (Worthington)
Fire. The Jews assert, that 185,000 perished by an inward burning, so that only ten men were left, ver. 19. (St. Jerome)
Light. God. (Haydock) --- Thorns. Private soldiers. (Calmet)
Glory. Officers. --- Flesh. Or body. All shall perish. (Haydock) --- Fear. Sennacherib escaped alone, and fell by the sword of his own sons.

Israel now submitted to Ezechias, as their kingdom was overturned in the sixth year of his reign, eight years before Sennacherib's arrival. Isaias speaks of this time, and therefore makes no distinction of the kingdoms. Striketh the Assyrian.

Converted. This was partly verified in the children of Israel who remained after the devastations of the Assyrians, in the time of king Ezechias: and partly in the conversion of a remnant of the Jews to the faith of Christ. (Challoner) --- 4 Kings xviii. 3., and Romans ix. 27. The apostle follows the Septuagint, (Calmet) "and if the people of Israel be." --- Converted. Septuagint, "saved, for perfecting the word and abridging in justice. Because God, the Lord of hosts, will make an abridged word in the universe." (Haydock) --- As the apostle has explained this passage, "every other interpretation must cease." (St. Jerome) --- The few who were converted under Ezechias were a figure of those who should embrace the faith of Christ. (Calmet) --- Consumption. That is, the number of them cut short, and reduced to few, shall flourish in the abundance of justice. (Challoner) --- Hebrew, "the desolation is decreed, justice shall overflow." God will treat all with rigour, Nahum i. 8. The incredulous Jews shall be rejected, ver. 23., and Romans ix.
Egypt. He sent Rabsaces from Lachis, when he set out to meet Tharaca, 4 Kings xix.
Little. Twenty-eight years, (Psalm lxxxix. 4.) or he alludes to the destruction which took place in a single night, (Calmet) or in a moment, ver. 16. (Haydock)
Oreb. Judges vii. 25. --- And his. Moses thus let loose the waters of the Red Sea on the Egyptians, by stretching forth his rod. (Calmet)

Oil. That is, by the sweet unction of divine mercy. (Challoner) --- Chaldean, "before the anointed," in consideration of Ezechias and Isaias. In the higher sense, it denotes the victory of Christ over the devil. (Calmet)
Into Aiath, &c. Here the prophet describes the march of the Assyrians under Sennacherib; and the terror they should carry with them; and how they should suddenly be destroyed. (Challoner)
Lodging. Here, say the Assyrians, we will encamp.
Take. Protestants, "gather themselves to flee." (Haydock)

Nobe. He may arrive thither shortly, in the environs of Jerusalem. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "exhort to-day, that they may continue on the road. Comfort with the hand the daughter of Sion, thou rock and hills within Jerusalem." (Haydock) --- Hand. As Nicanor did against the temple, 2 Machabees xv. 32. (Calmet)
Vessel. Like Gideon, when he attacked Madian, ver. 26., and Judges vii. 19. Septuagint, "the nobles." (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "their beauty." The empire of Assyria shall presently fall. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to those who make unjust laws, and who in writing have written injustice, to oppress the poor in judgment, and to do violence to the cause of the humble of my people, that widows might be their prey, and that they might plunder the orphans. What will you do in the day of visitation, and of the calamity coming from afar? To whose help will you flee? And where will you leave your glory? that you may not be bowed down under the chain, and fall with the slain. For all these his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Most think that these things too are still said against the ten tribes which dwelt in Samaria, because they joined these as well to their former crimes. To us, however, it seems that the prophetic word cries out against the judges of the tribe of Judah and of Jerusalem, namely the scribes and the δευτερωτὰς, because they wrote unjust laws against the law of God, and by their traditions overturned the truth of judgment. For when God says: Honor your father and mother (Exod 20:12), they on the contrary taught sons to say to their parents: Whatever gift comes from me will profit you, so that they do not honor father and mother (Matt 15:5-6; Mark 7:11), and other things like these. And they wrote these most evil laws for this purpose, to oppress the poor and the humble of the people, to make plunder of widows and to despoil orphans. They are asked what they will do when the day either of captivity or of judgment has come, and of the calamity coming from afar, which was foretold long before. To whose help, he says, will you flee, when you have offended God, who is the true helper, and where will you leave your glory? For riches will not profit in the day of wrath, to keep the Assyrian from leading you in chains into the enemy's land, to keep you from falling in battle (Prov 11:4). And finally, just as in the preceding passages he had often said against Samaria: For all these his fury is not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out, he speaks so against Judah too, because the final captivity is not the end of their evil, but even in the enemy's land the sword of the Lord will pursue them. According to the anagogy, every heretic writes iniquity in order to deceive the poor and humble of the people and to despoil widows and orphans. For the rich man, of whom we read: A man's own riches are the redemption of his soul (Prov 13:8), does not endure threats, is not quickly caught by them. But the poor man, and he who is humble and small among the peoples, is quickly made to stumble by them. The widow too, who has lost God her husband, and the orphan who has lost his father the Creator, of whom it is written: You have forsaken God who begot you, and have forgotten God your nourisher (Deut 32:18), are easily tripped up. What then will they do in the day of judgment, when they have deceived so many, and of the calamity coming from afar? For just as it is said to the righteous man: The word is near, in your mouth and in your heart (Rom 10:8); and in another place: The kingdom of God is within you (Luke 17:21); so the calamity of the heretics will come from afar, prepared for them over a long time. To whom will they flee for refuge, when the God they have is a fiction? To whom will they hand over their glory, when everything is feigned? Nor will they be able to escape the chain with which they have bound very many. Hence also in the vision of the valley of Zion, which, forsaking the height of God, has been deceived by heretical lowliness, it is said of the teachers of knowledge falsely so called: All your princes have fled, and those who were captured were harshly bound (Isa 22:3); and that they fall with the slain one by one, and perish themselves in the slaughter of others, and though they suffer many things, and the day of visitation has come, their destruction is not their end: but they are ever to tremble at the hand of the Lord hanging over them. Up to this point is God's threat against the ten and the two tribes, that is, against Samaria and Jerusalem, which began among the people while Ahaz was still reigning: of these, two and a half tribes were taken captive under him, and the rest under Hezekiah, who succeeded Ahaz in the kingdom (2 Kgs 16:17). The following prophecy is written against the Assyrians.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to Assur, the rod of my fury, and he is the staff; in their hand is my indignation. Against a deceitful nation I will send him, and against the people of my fury I will give him charge, to take spoils and to seize prey, and to make it a thing trodden down like the mire of the streets. But he does not think so, and his heart does not reckon so, but his heart will be set on crushing, and on the slaughter of very many nations. For he says: Are not my princes all of them kings? Is it not: as Carchemish, so Chalanno and as Arpad, so Hamath? Is it not: as Damascus, so Samaria? As my hand found the kingdoms of the idol, so also their images from Jerusalem and from Samaria. Shall I not, as I did to Samaria and to her idols, so do to Jerusalem and to her images? Let us set down in this place the translation of the Seventy, which disagrees with the Hebrew in very many things. LXX: Woe to the Assyrians: the rod of my fury is he, in their hands; my wrath I will send against a lawless nation, and to my people I will give command to make spoils and prey, and to trample the cities, and to lay them in the dust: but he did not so think, and did not so reckon; but his mind is to crush, and to destroy very many nations. And if they say to him: You alone are prince, he will answer: I have not taken the region which is above Babylon, and Chalane, where the tower was built. But I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria: as I have taken these, so I will take all kingdoms. Howl, you carved images in Jerusalem and Samaria; for as I did to Samaria and to her idols, so I will do to Jerusalem and to her images. First it must be known that in the Hebrew it does not have Chalane, but CHALANNO (כלנו). For the last letter of this name is not IOD, as they supposed, but VAU, letters which differ from each other only in size. Now the tower was built in the plain of Shinar, in which were Erech, Accad, and Chalanne, and Babylon, which received its name from the confusion of tongues (Gen 11). Arabia, moreover, is not found in the Hebrew, but Hamath, which the Syrians to this day call Epiphania. Howl too, you carved images in Jerusalem, they added of their own. And what is written above: If they say to him, You alone are prince, he will answer, I have not taken the region this one and that one, but I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria, suggests this sense: When, he says, those who have been taken captive say to the Assyrian, You are prince of all, he, still feeling himself to be weak, will answer: How do you call me prince, when I have taken only Arabia and Damascus and Samaria, and have not yet brought under my power the nations set far off beyond Babylon? But as I took Arabia, Damascus and Samaria, so I will lay all kingdoms beneath me. Let us pass to the Hebrew, and briefly note what seems right to us. Woe to the Assyrian, that is, Sennacherib, because he is the rod and the staff of my fury, for in his hand is my indignation, and through him I will strike a most deceitful nation, which has always limped between me and the idols, which lied that it would do my precepts; and against the people of my fury I will command him to despoil it and plunder it, and to reduce it to dust, and to trample it like the mire of the streets, that is, to strike it and not kill it, to wound it and not take away its life. But he went beyond the measure of my anger, and raged not only against Israel, against which he had been directed, but against very many nations, so as to crush all the kingdoms round about, and his sword raged even to the slaughter of very many nations. For, lifted up into pride, he dared to say this: My captains are kings of other nations, and, being subject to me, they will rule all nations. As I took Carchemish, so I took Chalanno too; as Arpad, so I gained Hamath too; as Damascus, so I subjected Samaria to myself too. As I have put under my feet the other kingdoms which served the worship of idols, so I will subject to my power Jerusalem too, and Samaria, in which are the same idols. As I took Samaria with its idols, so I will take Jerusalem too, because it worships the same gods. For Carchemish, however, the Seventy, adding of their own, translated the region beyond Babylon, and Chalane where the tower was built, leaving out Arpad altogether. But according to their translation, and with the freedom of tropology, provided it is pious, from what he says, and I will give command to my people to make spoils and prey, and to trample the cities, and to lay them in the dust, we can say this too: that the Lord daily commands his people to reduce to dust the cities of the adversaries, which are raised up against the knowledge of God and have been built by the heretics with enormous labor, and to show that they are nothing. And he, understanding the weakness of the human heart, and that, surrounded as he is with mortal flesh, he cannot have a perfect victory of the virtues nor take all the nations, though others admire him and say: You alone are prince, will answer them: There are many things that I ought to destroy, and have not yet been able to destroy: I know that I do not know. And although I have overcome many arguments of the adversaries, yet there are very many which are still to be overcome. And at the same time, in hope of what is to come, from those which he has overcome he promises himself the victory over the rest as well. Now the images of Jerusalem and of Samaria are bidden to howl: not the things themselves which were fashioned, but those who fashioned them: μετωνυμικῶς, those who made them, by the things that were made: so that not only those who have fabricated idols in the heresies, but those who in the Church through ignorance defend a lie for the truth, may testify by howling and penitence that they have erred.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 8

Long ago, indeed, when the former people sinned, Judah fell away from religion and fashioned "graven images in Jerusalem," and he who was called Israel did so "in Samaria". But if now too someone should consider, out of the multitude of those sinners who are gathered together, he will not be reluctant to say that each one who makes for himself a god — whatever he reckons to be good — and serves sin, is accursed, making a "graven image" and casting a work of the craftsman's hands and setting it up in secret; for in the secret place of the heart we make many idols, if we sin. Hence the word teaches us to do penance and to "wail over the graven images" and idols that are "in Jerusalem and Samaria". And if indeed we sin, we who desire to be of the Church, we make "graven images in Jerusalem"; but if those who are established outside the Church — as heretics — sin, they make "idols in Samaria". Nevertheless God, according to his goodness, calls all to penance, saying: "Wail, you graven images in Jerusalem and in Samaria; for just as I did to Samaria and to the works of its hands, so will I do also to Jerusalem and to its idols". He threatens that whatever things "he did to the Samaritans" he will do also to those who are of the Church.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 8

"But when the Lord has finished doing all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, he will bring judgment upon the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, and upon the loftiness of the glory of his eyes". We are taught what shall come to be for our enemy the devil, whom the prophecy has now called a certain "great mind". For just as "the serpent was wiser than all the beasts that are upon the earth", and "the sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their generation", and "the steward of iniquity acted wisely" according to a wisdom that is not good, in the same way this one, who is figuratively called "the prince of the Assyrians", is a "great mind", and one may marvel at the greatness of his "mind"; which he has misused for the instructing of the wise of this world, who compose the falsehood of their sects with every appearance of truth and with all their power, and put it on display. "When" therefore "God has done all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem" and has rendered those things which have been promised to the just, then "he will bring judgment upon the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, and upon the loftiness of the glory of his eyes". The word knows him to be "wise" as to "high things", and that the beginning of his ruin took its start from being puffed up. Hence, if we too have been puffed up, we "fall into the judgment of the devil", "into" which "the devil himself fell".
Commentary on Isaiah

And it shall be, when the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, I will visit upon the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assur, and upon the glory of the haughtiness of his eyes. For he said: By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood, and I have removed the bounds of the peoples, and I have plundered their princes, and like a mighty one I have pulled down those who sat on high; and my hand has found the strength of the peoples as a nest; and as eggs are gathered which have been left, so I have gathered all the earth, and there was none who moved a wing, or opened the mouth, or chirped. For fruit the Seventy translated sense, or great mind. After the captivity of Samaria, and the victory of the Assyrians, and the threat against Jerusalem, that, because it had imitated the images of Samaria, it must be struck with a like sentence, the Prophet now speaks against the Assyrian himself, who was lifted up into pride and thought that what he conquered was the work of his own strength. For the Assyrian, boasting in the swelling of his heart, said that by the strength of his hand he had conquered all the nations, and by incredible wisdom had taken possession of the bounds of all. And according to the Seventy he was of such power that he overthrew from their foundations the cities of warlike men, and seized the whole world like a nest, and made it his prey like eggs abandoned by their mothers. And because he had once taken a metaphor from birds, from the nest and the eggs, he kept it in the rest, so as to say: There was none who moved a wing, or opened the mouth, or chirped. So great, he says, was the terror of my strength and victory, that the conquered did not freely utter even weeping and groaning. There are those who think these things are said generally against the kingdom of the Assyrians: that after the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that is, after Jerusalem has been overthrown, the empire of the Assyrians is destroyed. To me, however, from what follows, the threat seems to be properly against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians. And what he says: After the Lord has accomplished all his works on mount Zion and in Jerusalem, signifies not the overthrow of the city but its siege, when Rabshakeh, Sennacherib's general, came and did the things which the same Prophet records in later chapters (Isa 37:17). According to tropology, when Samaria and Jerusalem have borne the wrath of the Lord, and have perceived that they erred in fabricating idols, then will the great mind be destroyed, the Assyrian, who was puffed up into such pride against the Lord that he reckoned that all things would yield to his wisdom, and that any lofty doctrines, even those fortified by the art of dialectic, were to be shaken and utterly destroyed: so much so that, like the chicks of birds, they would not be able to rise up on high, and, not yet quickened, would be without sense and torpid, which the example of the eggs shows; and that he would not hear anyone so much as mutter or move his tongue against the reason and strength of his discourse.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 8

But let us also see how great his self-inflation is, that we may guard against it and not permit him to speak true things over us. What, then, does he say? "By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will take away the borders of the nations". He reckons that by his own might he is able to accomplish in us whatever he wishes. And truly, if we are conquered and after these words we sin — if after the Church we go again into the circus and to the horse-races and to the assemblies of the Gentiles — what else happens than that he possesses us as those he has overcome? And what the devil said, "By my strength I will act," comes to pass in us who sin, as he threatened. And also, if we commit fornication after chastity of long duration, after much holiness, what else happens than that he is proved to have spoken true things over us, he who said: "By my strength I will act"? But let us look at what else this boaster promises. "And by the wisdom of my understanding I will take away the borders of the nations". He promises some kind of "wisdom" or other — the wisdom of which the prophet also speaks: "there is a certain alien wisdom in them". There is a certain "wisdom estranged" from the truth, which God destroys. Having this, he reckons himself to be "wise" and says: "By the wisdom of my understanding I will take away the borders of the nations, and I will feed upon their strength". For his working has reached to all the "nations", but the Savior, sending his words into all the "nations", rescues those who by the devil were held captive among all the "nations". "And I will feed upon their strength". He threatens that he will go to plunder our "strength" and to hand it over to those who war against us. And truly one may see him doing this to certain people. For when someone is conquered by the devil and handed over to demons, to most wicked spirits, to the opposing powers, what else has happened than that he who had said, "and I will feed upon their strength", has taken our "strength" and "fed upon" us? "And I will shake the cities that are inhabited". This too the devil threatens: he perceives that the "cities" — the churches of God built in Christ the Lord — are "inhabited", and he gives out that he will "shake" these. And frequently indeed he has shaken the "inhabited cities" with persecutions, frequently he has shaken them with scandals. QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 44: HOW THE PROMISE TO ABRAHAM WAS FULFILLED IN CHRIST

How could it be shown from the testimony of the prophets, already received among the Gentiles in the New Testament, that the promise which God made to Abraham has been fulfilled through the coming of Christ? — It is written in the prophet Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say: The house of God, that is, the synagogue, is open to all. Nor do we object; yet in such a way that, as always, the circumcised join themselves to the Law. For their Law is that by which they were commanded, after the manner of Abraham, to be circumcised. Therefore, nothing new can seem to be signified by this example of the prophet; since anyone coming from any nation has never been forbidden from the beginning of Judaism to join himself to the Law. Nothing new spoken by the prophet can be thought, indeed it would be unessential, if the Gentiles have always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are never found to have been forbidden. And this is true, because those who submit themselves to the Law are never found not to have been received. If, therefore, these things are so, it seems needless that the prophet admonished about what, once handed down, has always been observed. And could anyone so dull be found as to say that the prophet spoke something unnecessary and empty? I do not know for whom it would be safe even to hear this and not oppose it. For since the Jewish people, on account of the sins which they committed against God, seeking help from idols, were often rebuked by the prophets but refused to enter upon the path of repentance so as to return to God, God, in reproach of them, indicated that He would open His house to all nations to pray, so that, the Jews being cast off, He would show that He would place others in their place. For if the nations have always been admitted to the Law, as was said above, how could the prophet say that this would happen in the future, unless he meant something different from what had been previously commanded? He could not speak of a thing which was done daily as though it were going to come. Therefore it is clear that this tends to the ruin of the Jews, to whom the prophet shows that, with them removed, others were to be called and were to receive the house of God’s grace, which had been promised to the Jews. What that promise is, the prophet Isaiah teaches, saying: “There shall come out of Zion one who shall deliver and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them” (Isa. 59:20–21). Therefore this covenant is the removal of sins. This is the New Covenant, which was promised through Jeremiah, who says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will accomplish for the house of Israel and the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I arranged for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I neglected them, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:31–32). This is their transgression, when they made the image of a calf; then they corrupted His covenant. Therefore also the tablets on which the Law had been given were shattered under the mountain (Exod. 32:4, 19), because they deserved to receive more severe precepts. But because God is mild and merciful, He promised through the prophets that He would change the Law, so as to give another Covenant, which would differ from that which He had given before: that not only what was burdensome might be changed, but also those things which were given in figure, that is, the sabbath and circumcision; so that, since they had long been oppressed, being relieved in all things, they might give grateful thanks to God as petitioners. And because, persisting in their fathers’ transgression, they refused to turn their minds away from idols, He testifies that the nations, together with the remnant who kept the faith, will enjoy the Covenant which He had said would come: so that the faithless Jews might be tortured in a twofold way. For they were burdened for a time by the precepts, and in the future they will pay fitting penalties, because they were found faithful neither in the Old nor in the New Covenant. So He said that He would give a New Covenant, so that the Old, which had been given to the Fathers, would cease. And therefore, whoever serves God in this Covenant does not observe the sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions of foods; but has only the fear of God in faith: because he will not be justified by the Law, but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk says: “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4); so that he no longer uses many precepts to gain favor with God, but few. Isaiah again, speaking with the same meaning, says: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of them shall be saved. For the Lord shall accomplish and cut short His word in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short word upon the whole earth” (Isa. 10:22–23). For the remnant who will persevere in the faith of the promise, while the others do not believe, He shows the shortened word of the Law: this is the New Covenant which He promised. It would not otherwise be called a Covenant, unless in a similar way this too were confirmed by the witness of blood, just as the Old Covenant, so that both might have one and the same name: but in the Old, many precepts, in the New, however, few, as He promised. So that, since He had said that Abraham would be the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), in the same way the sons might be justified as the father had been justified: so that, once those things ceased which began after the faith of Abraham, those who receive the faith by which that same Abraham was justified might be sons of Abraham, as was said by the Lord. And this is neither strange nor unheard of, that men should be justified without care for the sabbath and circumcision and the rest of the commandments of this sort. For Enoch did not please God by this, that he might be translated; nor was Noah found righteous in the flood by observing this alone; nor was Abraham himself justified after he was circumcised: “Abraham,” it says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8; Rom. 4:3). Then he was circumcised, so that there might be in him a sign that, though he was old, he believed that he would have a son. Therefore it is not circumcision that commends Abraham, but faith. And so, for those who believe, faith is sufficient for justification, that they may be sons of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision, because they have no need of circumcision. For what Abraham believed is not what is believed in their case. But the Jews were therefore ordered to be circumcised, so that they might have the sign of Abraham’s faith, not of their own faith, but so that they might be known as his sons according to the flesh. Yet if they believe, they will be his sons also in justification. For what advantage is it to be called the son of a powerful man if one is powerless, except that it is even more harmful? For it is a disgrace to be the son of a noble and glorious man without honor. Indeed, bodily circumcision is so far from being a merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that He will take vengeance on all the circumcised in foreskin, if they are not circumcised in heart (Jer. 4:4). Yet He is not angry with those who are circumcised in heart but uncircumcised in flesh, because no one has ever pleased God without the circumcision of the heart. Whoever, therefore, are circumcised in the flesh signify the lineage of Abraham according to the flesh; but those who are circumcised in heart signify the lineage of God according to faith, because, being circumcised from all worldly error, they confess God as their Father. What then does the circumcision of the flesh profit, if, when faith is lacking in the Jew, he cannot attain to the merit of Abraham? Or what harm is there in foreskin, when no one attains to his righteousness except the one who has followed the faith of Abraham? They therefore glory in the circumcision of the flesh in vain, since they see that it has no merit before God. And since, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, the Gentiles are better than the Jews; for the Gentiles have faith, the Jews have circumcision. And whom do you think He recognizes more as sons of Abraham: those who are like him according to the flesh, or those who are like him in faith? But the faith of Abraham bears witness. And therefore he glories not in the flesh but in faith. For this reason he has received as sons those whom he sees to be imitators of his glory. For how can he call those sons from whom he sees a shrinking back from that by which he pleased God and was justified? He will therefore be able to judge them not as his sons, but as his enemies. For they appear to be envious of him, despising the faith through which he was glorified. Nor is it surprising if the Jews are found untrusting, not at all accepting the New Testament, when we know that they were not faithful even in the Old. They were always rebellious and disrespectful against God, and therefore they received such commandments by which their necks, which were unbending, might be pressed down. For they never wished to hope for good things from God, whose such great benefits and such wondrous powers they had come to know. Therefore it is that, among other things, the prophet Ezekiel says: “I lifted up my hand to them in the desert, that they should be scattered among the nations and dispersed in the lands, because they did not perform my ordinances and rejected my commandments.” And in what follows: “I gave them laws that were not good, and judgments whereby they should not live in them” (Ezek. 20:23–25). He shows for what reason such great and so harsh commandments were given to them: because they proved ungrateful for such great benefits, and, justice dictating, they were to be pressed by more severe precepts. Therefore He called them “not good,” although they are just: because they did not lead them to justification, but to destruction; and although a punishment rightly inflicted, yet for the one who suffers it, it is not a good. After these things, however, because God is merciful, He promised that He would give the New Testament, in which the shortening of the Law would justify believers, just as Abraham was justified: so that, with new moons and the sabbath and circumcision and the other precepts ceasing, not those that belong to the natural law, that is, murder, adultery, and such things, they might be justified as Abraham was. For, with the faith of Abraham renewed, He willed that all things should cease, so that the time might be such as it was when Abraham believed. But perhaps the Jews say: “If those things that were given by Moses are said to cease through the shortening of the Law, was circumcision given by Moses so that it should cease? And therefore we have the sign of our father, because we are the sons of Abraham, a sign which, for the sake of the testimony of our lineage, ought not to cease.” Circumcision indeed had to be observed in its time, that is, before the New Testament which had been promised was given. But when, by the grace of God, the burdens of the Law were ordered to cease, what need is there of circumcision? Therefore a new Law was given, that is, a spiritual one, so that carnal things might cease, and those who received it might accept its sign: so that just as in the Old Testament they had the sign of Abraham, from whom the Old Testament began, so also in the New they might have the sign of the Savior, who is the institutor of the New Testament. For just as from Abraham they were called Hebrews, so from Christ they are called Christians. Whoever, therefore, are still called Hebrews have not received the New Testament which God promised, bringing to nothing the kindness and mercy of God: for He no longer wished His people to be designated by the name of a man, but agreed to establish them under the name of His Son. With what courage, then, do the Jews say that we do not use our Law but theirs, when David says, “I will give thanks to you among the nations” (Ps. 17:50), and again, “Rejoice, O nations, with his people”? And to the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you; and I appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jer. 1:5). Judaism certainly has its own particular signs: for this people is signified either in Jacob, or in Samaria, or in Jerusalem, or in Judea, or in Israel. As for the nations, however, it is clear that He signifies them in a different way than He does the Jews. Therefore Jeremiah is our prophet. For although in all the Prophets God showed that the nations would share in His gift, yet to Jeremiah in particular He says that He has given him to us as a prophet. For he signified that the New Testament would come, which would profit the Gentiles more than the Jews, as now appears clearly. For since the preaching of the New Testament is spread over the whole earth, a faithful Jew is so rarely and with such difficulty found that all the Churches of the New Testament are called “of the nations,” as it was said in the prophet Hosea: “I will call that which is not my people, my people; and her that was not beloved, beloved” (Hosea 2:24; Rom. 9:25). Therefore, the Jews having been rejected, He calls the nations with the same mercy and grace with which He agreed to call Abraham. For Abraham did not come to know the Lord without being called. Therefore, He who agreed to call Abraham likewise agreed to call the nations. Why then do they say, “The Law is ours,” when it is clear that the gift of God is for all who are willing? Let this careless violation cease, since the grace of God is common to all. With what shame do they deny that our Christ was promised in the Law, when they see in Him all the signs which the Law foretold as to come? For both according to the promise made to Abraham all nations are justified by believing in Him (Gen. 22:18); and according to the prophet Isaiah He was born of a Virgin (Isa. 7:14) in Bethlehem from the tribe of Judah, as was promised, from the seed of David (Micah 5:2); and in accordance with what Jeremiah prophesied (Jer. 31:31–32), He proclaimed the New Testament which God then promised would come; and after all the signs of power had been shown, He humbled Himself, according to the words of the Prophets; and having suffered all that had been foretold, He rose on the third day, as it is written in the prophet. And if they inquire about the time of the promise, as it is shown in the prophet Daniel (Dan. 9:24 ff.), they will find it fulfilled in the time when Christ was born and suffered: for from the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, down to the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem, which was carried out by Vespasian, chief of the Roman Empire, the seventy weeks were completed, which are four hundred and ninety years, a reckoning made clear through the kingdoms and the successors of the empire. Therefore also it is found calculated by Tertullian in the book which he wrote against the Jews; but, lest this should backfire to his disadvantage, although he calculated correctly, we have passed it over in silence. And who can doubt this number, when now about three hundred years are found in addition to that number? It is therefore shameless, after so many years have been added beyond the time of the coming of the Saviour, to say, “He has not come.” Under the Apostles, or at the time when the Lord was living among men, hatred opposing the truth could still hide itself; so that, although it saw all the signs of the Christ who had been promised in the Savior, it could say that it doubted about the time, to conceal its unbelief. But afterwards, when many years began to exceed the promised number, what shamelessness it is to deny that He has come, whose coming is known to have been fulfilled both by signs and by times! For when something is full and does not overflow, a combative person may say that it is not full; but overflow closes the mouth of the argumentative. So the Jews, in the time of the Saviour, could say, though deceitfully, that the calculation from the time of Darius to the Lord Christ was not correctly made, so that He might not be acknowledged as the one who had been promised. We are mistaken, they might say, in the years and in the months and in the days of the emperors, and we do not make an exact reckoning. But when the times have extended beyond the prescribed number of years of the promised Christ, no excuse can be put forward to deny that He who has come is the Christ, unless, which God forbid, the one who promised is said to have lied. For when the time of the promise has elapsed, and it is denied that the one who was promised has come, what else is charged against the promiser but falsehood? Yet that He who made the promise is truthful, all the signs teach which were foretold in Christ and are known to have been found in Christ. The Jews, however, while they are ashamed to change themselves, do not consider that there will be a judgment to come. For nothing is worse than for someone to deny that a thing is true when he understands that it is not a lie.

Understanding this, the apostle Paul too writes to the Romans: But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved. For he is finishing the word and cutting it short in equity, because a shortened word will the Lord make upon the earth (Rom 9:27). And as Isaiah said: Unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us seed, we would have become as Sodom, and would have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9). And indeed, if we read Josephus (bk. 10, ch. 2), and how great a multitude of men there was in Jerusalem and in Judea when the Lord suffered, we understand that scarcely a few of the Jews were saved, among the Apostles and apostolic men. Now the shortened and perfect word is the word of the Gospel, which in place of all the ceremonies of the long-winded Law gave a very brief precept of love and faith: that what we would not have done to ourselves, we should not do to another. Hence the Lord too in the Gospel: On these two commandments, he says, hangs all the Law and the Prophets (Matt 22:40). To them we shall answer that they do not keep the order of the history, especially since the things that follow are said not against the Babylonians, whose king was Nebuchadnezzar, but against Sennacherib king of the Assyrians.

When God made statements such as "You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness," he was teaching me to refrain from doing to others what I would be unwilling to do to myself. Therefore the precept offered in the Gospel belongs only to the one who first drew it up in ancient times, arranging it according to his own teaching in a formula that could easily be understood. This was predicted in another passage in which the Lord, that is, Christ, was "to make a concise word on the earth."

What wonder, most beloved brothers, if such [the Lord's Prayer] is the prayer that God has taught, who by his instruction has abbreviated our every prayer in a saving word? This had already been foretold by Isaiah the prophet, when filled with the Holy Spirit, he spoke of the majesty and loving kindness of God. He said, "He will finish the word and cut it short in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short word in all the world." For when the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, came to all, and gathering together the learned and unlearned alike, he gave forth the precepts of salvation to every sex and age, he made a concise compendium of his precepts. [This was] so that the memory of the learners might not be burdened in heavenly discipline but might learn quickly what was necessary to a simple faith.

But somebody will perhaps think that we lack nothing for the knowledge of righteousness, since the Lord, when He summarily and briefly expounded His word on earth, informed us that the whole law and the prophets depend on two commandments; nor was He silent as to what these were, but declared them in the plainest words: "Thou shalt love," said He, "the Lord thy God, with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind;" and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts: Do not fear, my people, dweller in Zion, because of Assur: he will strike you with the rod, and will lift up his staff over you in the way of Egypt. For yet a little while, and a very little, and my indignation will be ended, and my fury upon their crime. And the Lord of hosts will raise up a scourge against him, like the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb, and his rod over the sea, and he will lift it up in the way of Egypt. And it shall be in that day: his burden shall be taken from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck, and the yoke shall rot away before the oil. For rock, which Aquila translated according to the Hebrew, Symmachus and Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, SUR OREB (צור עורב). In place of which the Seventy translated place of tribulation: of which we shall speak in its own place. It seems hard to you, he says, O dweller in Zion, that when all the nations round about have been subjugated by the Assyrian, you alone should be freed from his hands. Listen to what I say: do not fear, my people, that you will be taken when Assur conquers. For although in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18) Sennacherib king of Assyria is to go up against all the fortified cities of Judah, to take them, and to send Rabshakeh to terrify the people besieged in Jerusalem, yet you must know this, that he will strike you not with the sword but with the rod, and, marching against Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, and against the Egyptians and the Red Sea by the way of Egypt, he will only lift his staff against you, and will not be able to strike. For yet a little while, and when he has returned from Egypt with an infinite multitude of his army, and wishes to besiege you, he will at once be struck by my indignation, and by that scourge which I once raised up against the Midianites under Gideon (Judg 7), who by another name was called Jerubbaal: when Oreb and Zebah, princes of the Midianites, were slain upon a very hard rock, that is, flint, which in Hebrew is called SUR (צור), so that the place received the name rock of Oreb from the rock and from the king who was slain upon it. So he will lift his rod over the Red Sea when he marches against the Ethiopians, and will lift it when he returns to you by the way of Egypt: but as soon as he has come from Egypt, the burden will be taken from your shoulders, and the yoke of his rule, and you will cease to serve. And this yoke, that is, the power of the Assyrian, will rot away before the oil, that is, the mercy of God. But we can also understand what he said: He will strike you with the rod, and will lift up his staff over you in the way of Egypt; and again: And his rod over the sea, and he will lift it up in the way of Egypt, in this way too: that he struck very many of the tribe of Judah, and took the cities round about the kingdom of Jerusalem, for this reason, because they had their trust not in God but in the Egyptians. Hence Rabshakeh too reproaches them, saying: Behold, you trust upon a broken staff of reed, upon Egypt. If a man lean upon it, it will go into his hand and pierce it (2 Kgs 18:22): so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. The history of the Midianites is written in the book of Judges (Judg 7), and we read it also in the Psalm: Make their princes like Oreb, and Zeeb, and Zebah, and Zalmunna (Ps 82 [83]:12). They err, therefore, who think that the time is signified when in the book of Numbers (ch. 25) the Midianites are reported to have been slain by Israel from the desert of Sur to Oreb, the mountain of God: for these are written among the Hebrews with other letters, and at that time they were not at mount Oreb, but in the wilderness of Shittim. According to the anagogy, the people that dwells in the Church is commanded not to fear the adversaries, who are always ready to fight and have overturned souls by their much disputation. For they receive a little power against the people of God, and strike not so much with the sword as with the rod, that is, not to kill but to threaten, for this reason, because the people have walked in the way of Egypt and have not trusted in the Lord. But when they have returned to God and have left the road of Egypt, then the scourge of God is to be raised up by his judgment against the adversaries. For Midian means from judgment: so that by the spirit of his mouth and by the oil of mercy the yoke of the enemies may rot away.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 26

It is said through Moses: "They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the solid rock." For nothing of this kind is read according to history, if the whole sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed. Nowhere did that people suck honey from the rock, nowhere oil. But because according to Paul's words: "The rock was Christ," they sucked honey from the rock who saw the deeds and miracles of our same Redeemer. But they sucked oil from the solid rock, because by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit after his resurrection they deserved to be anointed. Therefore, as it were, the weak rock gave honey, when the Lord, still mortal, showed to his disciples the sweetness of his miracles. But the solid rock poured forth oil, because, after his resurrection now made impassible, through the breathing of the Spirit he sent forth the gift of holy anointing. Of this oil it is said through the prophet: "The yoke shall decay because of the oil." For we were held under the yoke of demonic dominion, but we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit. And because the grace of liberty has anointed us, the yoke of demonic dominion has rotted away, as Paul attests when he says: "Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty."
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 19, Section 24

It may be that by the designation of oil the actual anointing of the Holy Spirit is denoted, whereof it is said by the Prophet: "And the yoke shall rot at the presence of the oil." For the yoke doth rot at the presence of the oil, because whilst we are anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit, we are set free from the bondage of our captivity; and whereas the proud dominion of the evil spirit is thrown off, the yoke is broken in pieces, wherewith the necks of our liberty were borne down. Of this oil again it is written: "A vineyard was made to my beloved on the horn, a child of oil." For a child of oil, the faithful people is called, which is engendered to the faith of God by the interior anointing of the Holy Spirit. And so at that time let Holy Church, being borne down by countless sorrows, recal to remembrance the gifts of the Spirit and the marvellous preachings which are her's now, and let her bewail her own silence, saying, "The rock poured me out rivers of oil."

He will come into Aioth, he will pass into Magron: at Machmas he will deposit his baggage. They have passed over in haste; Gabee is our lodging (or, as we have found it written elsewhere: they have lodged a lodging); Rama was astonished, Gaba of Saul fled. Neigh with your voice, daughter of Gallim; give heed, Laisa, poor little Anathoth: Medemena has departed: inhabitants of Gebim, take courage. There is still day enough for a halt at Nob: he will shake his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem. LXX: For he will come into the city of Aggai, and will pass into Mageddo: and at Machmas he will set down his baggage: and he will pass through the valley, and will come into Aggai. Fear will seize Rama, the city of Saul: the daughter of Gallim will flee: give heed, Laisa: it will be heard in Anathot: Medemena was astonished, and the inhabitants of Gebim. Be comforted today in the way, so that he may remain: comfort the mount of the daughter of Zion, and the hill of Jerusalem. In this place the Seventy differ much from the Hebrew: for this reason we have set down both editions, so that, with Christ inspiring us, if we have deserved it, we may say what seems right to us on each point. The prophetic word describes the march and the pomp of the Assyrian as he returns from Egypt to Jerusalem, and with how great a din and how great speed he will come to attack it. And first, he says, he will come into Aioth, where, in his excessive haste, unwilling to stay, he will pass into Magron, and he will have such confidence of taking the city that he will leave his packs at Machmas, as one who will soon return when the city has been overthrown: having laid them down, he will pass it in haste; and in Gabee he will have his lodging: and while he halts there a little, to refresh his weary army, Rama, a neighboring city, will be terrified: Gaba, once the city of Saul, will flee. Then the daughter of Gallim too, which in Hebrew is called BETH GALLIM (בת גלים), will wail so that you would think it the neighing of horses. Therefore, O Laisa, and you, poor, or obedient, or humble Anathoth (for it can be interpreted in three ways), take careful heed, and turn aside from the onrush of the runner, if you can: for the city of Medemena has already departed from its seats. But you who dwell in the hills, which is what Gebim means, safe in the height of your places, take courage, that is, seize your arms. There still remained so much of the day that, standing in the little town of Nob, and looking at the city of Jerusalem from afar, he shook his hand and brandished it over mount Zion, either looking down on it and despising it, or insulting and threatening it, and marveling that, when the whole East had been subjected to him, so small a city should dare to resist his power. These things according to the Hebrews, as they were handed down to us by them, we have touched on in brief discourse. Now let us add what the churchmen think about this place according to the edition of the Seventy. When the yoke of the Assyrian, or, as some wrongly think, of the Babylonian, has been taken from your shoulders and broken, the Assyrian Sennacherib, fleeing with a few survivors, will come into Aggai, which is not found in the Hebrew. And so great will be the panic of the fugitive that he will not dare to remain there, but will pass into Mageddo, which the Scripture itself does not contain either. And because, hampered by his packs, he will not be able to flee more swiftly, he will lay down his baggage in Machmas, and with hurried step will pass through the valley, which the Hebrew text does not have either: and he will come again into Aggai, which is set twice in this place and is not found in the Hebrew. At the sound of his flight Rama, the city of Saul, will tremble: which is plainly false. For the city of Saul is called Gaba, as is contained in the Hebrew. Then he will come into Gallim: Laisa will hear, Anathoth will hear, Medemena will tremble. But the inhabitants of Gebim, and the hills which are in Jerusalem, that is, all the lofty men, are called upon to console Jerusalem: not after a long time, but at the present moment, and on the same day, while the Assyrian is on the way; so that they may remain in their places, and, though disturbed by fear, may in no way flee. This according to the letter. But a certain writer in this place, since he could not find the ἐτυμολογίας of the false names according to the Seventy, and testifies that he could not find them in the book of Hebrew Names, sends us off into uncertainty, so as to say that at the last time of the world, and at the consummation of this age, when punishments are imminent, the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, will flee, and through various places and by varied journeys will desire to flee from the wrath of God. And when he has fled, the inhabitants of Gebim, that is, all the lofty powers, are called upon by the prophetic word to console the fugitive, and to teach him not to flee but to remain on the way and wait for the mercy of God; and not only to console the fugitive, but by good works to call back the daughter of Zion from mourning and to summon her to the salvation of penitence; and that these are the hills in Jerusalem of which we read in the latter part of this prophet: Comfort, comfort my people, O priests: speak to the heart of Jerusalem (Isa 40:1). This he said because, constrained by the truth of the matter, he had nothing else to say.
