Do not rejoice, all you Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken: for out of the root of the serpent will come forth a regulus, and its seed swallowing the bird. What we say is natural: when the king of a hostile nation dies, his enemies always rejoice, expecting from the new state of things civil wars and seditions and inexperience in ruling. When Ahaz the sinner died, therefore, who had walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and had been joined to them by kinship, we understand that the Philistines, from close by, rejoiced and mocked Israel, because, having lost a king of mature years, they were subject to the young Hezekiah. Now by Philistines, as we said above, he means the Palestinians, whom the common edition writes as foreigners, although this is the term not for one nation but for all foreign nations. Do not, he says, rejoice, O Philistia, do not mock my people because the rod of Ahaz who struck you has been broken; because the staff which used to strike you seems crushed by death; because the serpent has been slain. For in his place a more harmful one will be born, Hezekiah the regulus, which the Greeks call the basilisk, who will kill you with his gaze and slay you with the breath of his mouth. For just as no bird can pass the gaze of the regulus unharmed, but, however far off it may be, is sucked into its mouth, so you too will perish wholly at the sight of King Hezekiah. And he has kept the metaphor beautifully: for since he had named a serpent and a regulus, he says that birds are devoured by its mouth and breath. And that none of the kings of Judah struck the Philistines as Hezekiah ravaged them, hear the book of Kings: He struck the Philistines as far as Gaza, and as far as its borders: from the tower of the watchmen to the fortified cities (2 Kgs 18:8). And for what we have translated swallowing the bird, where in the Hebrew is written SARAPH MOPHETH (שרף מעופת), it can be interpreted a flying serpent: so that the sense is: from the root of the serpent a regulus will be born, and its fruit, that is, the regulus's, a flying serpent, so that you understand a flying dragon.
Commentary on Isaiah

It is commanded, therefore, to the Philistines, whom they now call Palestinians, and whom the Seventy always translate ἀλλόφυλοι, that is, foreigners; and it is said to them that they should not rejoice nor be glad because they have broken the rod, or the yoke, of him who struck them (Heb 12:6). For whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives. And God instructs us as sons when he visits our iniquities with a rod and our sins with scourges, so as not to take away his mercy from us (Ps 88 [89]). This is the rod of which it is written in another Psalm: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me (Ps 22 [23]:4). This is the rod, and this the yoke, which the Savior wishes to lay upon the necks of all, so that, having put off the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, they may bear the yoke of Christ. But if anyone throws it off and breaks it, at once out of the seed or root of the serpent, who is the crooked serpent, will come forth the basilisk and asps, and out of the asps will go forth flying serpents, or those that swallow birds. For when the yoke of God has been thrown off and the discipline of the Lord broken, first the seed of the serpent takes root in our thoughts; secondly, from the most evil seed is born the basilisk, which is the king of serpents and is said to kill men by its breath and its look; or the offspring of asps, of which it is said in the Psalm: The poison of asps is under their lips (Ps 13 [14]:3; and 139 [140]:4), which are the various sins, and they burst forth from the most evil treasury of thoughts into evil works. And when they have reigned in foreign men, who are estranged from God, at once winged serpents come forth; so that it is not enough for them to have thought and done what is evil, unless they also seek a defense of their evil works and fashion various heresies. I think the winged serpents are those who exalt and lift themselves up against the knowledge of God and set their mouth against heaven: or those who swallow birds, that is, who with poisoned mouth devour in their jaws all who desire to fly and rise to the heights. And this, for the present, concerning the wicked.
MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 6:33.62

But because this Leviathan is called in another place not merely a serpent, but also a basilisk, because he rules over unclean spirits, or reprobate men, as Isaiah says, Out of the serpent's root shall come forth a basilisk, we must attentively observe how a basilisk destroys, that by the doings of the basilisk, his malice may be more plainly made known to us. For a basilisk does not destroy with its bite, but consumes with its breath. It often also infects the air with its breath, and withers with the mere blast of its nostrils whatever it has touched, even when placed at a distance.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the firstborn of the poor will feed, and the poor will rest in confidence. When the regulus has struck you, and the flying dragon has laid waste your borders, you will by no means lie in wait for Judah, nor terrify my poor little people with your treachery; but, hard pressed by your own straits, you will weep over your calamity. And the humble and the poor, who trusted not in riches and in power but in my name, will rest in secure peace, and will dread the onslaught of no enemy.

And I will make your root perish by famine, and I will slay your remnant. He speaks entirely in figures. And the sense is that, while the people of God rest in confidence, the root of the Philistines is dried up, and all its remnant will be consumed.
Commentary on Isaiah

But those who have not broken the rod and yoke of him who struck them, but have submitted their neck to the Lord, and are poor in spirit, will be fed, and will say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing (Ps 22 [23]:1). And they will hear from the Lord: In most rich pastures I will feed them (Ezek 34; John 10); and they will go in and go out and find pasture. And the poor will be fed through him who strikes them in order to amend them: and they will rest in peace, or, with a careful shepherd, they will live confidently and will rest with Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16). But those who have broken the yoke and rod of him who struck them will suffer perpetual famine, so that they are not nourished by the word of God: but all their remnant will perish, lest anything sprout from the evil seed.
Commentary on Isaiah

Howl, O gate; cry out, O city: all Philistia is laid low. For smoke comes from the North, and there is none who escapes its column. And what will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in him the poor of his people will hope. For messengers, that is, Angels, which Symmachus alone translated, all have translated kings, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, because, except for the one letter ALEPH, which is added in the word for Angels, kings and Angels are called by the same name among the Hebrews, that is, MALACHE (Kings מלכי, Angels מלאכי). In the book of Hebrew Names I have found that Philisthiim means falling by the cup. Those, therefore, who have been made drunk with the cup of Babylon and have drunk the wine in which is debauchery, and, among the other vices, have not obtained the kingdom of God because of drunkenness, according to the Apostle (Eph 5), are commanded that their gate should howl and their city cry out. The gate I take to be the mouth of the heretics, with which they blaspheme; the city, the soul, which is a treasury of evil thoughts. This ought to howl and lament, because it is wholly laid low and cast down to the ground, and there is nothing in it of sound understanding and of the wisdom of God. Why does the gate howl? for what cause does the city cry out? because all Philistia is laid low. And why it is laid low the following verse shows: Smoke comes from the North, and there is none who escapes its column. This smoke is raised by the burning darts of the devil; it is harmful to the eyes and contrary to light, and it rises from the North, from which in Jeremiah the pot is set on fire (Jer 1:14), and from which evils blaze forth upon all the inhabitants of the earth, who cannot say: I am a sojourner and a stranger, as all my fathers were (Ps 118 [119]:19); but they dwell in the earth. Hence in Proverbs too it is read: The North is a harsh wind (Prov 25:23; Sir 43). But by another name it is called the right-hand wind; for although of itself it is harsh and left-handed, and with a most hard neck will not receive the yoke of God, it is called right-handed by those who put sweet for bitter and bitter for sweet; who put darkness for light and light for darkness. And there is no one who escapes the column of this smoke; for no one is without sin, not even if his life be of a single day (Job 25).
Commentary on Isaiah

Howl, O gate, cry out, O city, all Philistia is laid low: for smoke will come from the north, and there is none who escapes its column. He says the gate for those who are in the gate, and the city for the inhabitants of the city. And he directs his speech to the cities of the Palestinians, that they should wail and mourn as Sennacherib comes and lays everything waste like a torrent. For under King Hezekiah the Assyrian came, and among the other nations laid waste the Philistines. To them Jeremiah speaks: Behold, waters will rise up from the north, and they will be like an overflowing torrent: and they will cover the land and all that fills it, the city and its inhabitants (Jer 47:2). For from the north came the Assyrian, and those who went forth from its heat, subjugating Nineveh and the other nations. At the time when these things were being sung, the smoke was rising on high, that is, a rumor was spreading among the peoples, through the whole range of the nations, that the Phoenicians too and the Palestinians were to be laid waste.
Commentary on Isaiah

What will be answered to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in her the poor of his people will hope. Because he had said, There is none who escapes its column, Judah too seemed to be included in the general statement. If, he says, the messengers of the Assyrian nation ask why Judah alone has escaped, answer them that the Lord has founded Zion, and has himself protected the humble people by his power. For messengers (מלאכי) the Seventy translated kings (מלכי), misled by an error over a single letter, ALEPH.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when Philistia has fallen, and its smoke has penetrated all things, so that no one can escape it, what will be said to the Angels who preside over the several nations, who wonder and desire to know why Zion alone, set on a watchtower and on the heights, has escaped the bitterness of this smoke? What, then, will be said to them? Surely what follows: That the Lord has founded it, and he himself is its foundation. And he has founded it upon the foundation of prudence, righteousness, fortitude and temperance, under which names Christ is understood, of whom the Apostle also says: For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, Jesus Christ (1 Cor 3:11). But he who is foolish, and speaks foolish things, and whose heart understands vain things, builds his house upon the sand, which has no foundation. In this Zion, therefore, which has been founded by the Lord, the poor, or the meek and humble of his people, will hope, of whom it is said: Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land (Matt 5:4): and who have heard the Lord saying: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart (Matt 11:29). They have been humbled before glory, and have heard the apostle Peter saying (1 Pet 5:6): Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation. And these are the poor of whom we read above: The firstborn of the poor will be fed, and the poor will rest confidently.

n: Moab. Which would be visited in three years' time (chap. xvi. 14.) either by Ezechias, or by Sennacherib, though history be silent on this head. The Moabites had been very cruel, Amos i. and ii. --- Night. Suddenly. (Calmet) --- Their misery was so much the greater. (Worthington) --- Ar. The capital. (Calmet)

House. Protestants, "he is come up to Baiith," (Haydock) or the royal family is gone to the temple of their idol, Chamos, to lament. (St. Jerome) (Menochius) (Calmet) --- Shaven. As in mourning, Jeremias xlviii. 37.
Itself. Every one shall deplore his own distress.

My. A charitable heart will grieve for the misfortune of an enemy. (Worthington) --- I shall join in the general lamentations, though Moab has always been so great an enemy of Israel. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "the heart of Moab cries in itself to Segor." (Haydock) --- We will retire thither. (Chaldean) --- Bars. Princes. Protestants, "his fugitives shall," &c. --- Heifer. Strong and ungovernable. Hebrew, "to Heglath and to Shelishia for," &c., though we may as well adhere to the Vulgate, Septuagint, &c.
Nemrim. Or Nemra, (Numbers xxxii. 3.) to the north of Segor. (Calmet) --- The country around hence became barren. (St. Jerome)
Willows. That is, as some say, the waters of Babylon; others render it a valley of the Arabians, (Challoner) or "of crows," to which their bodies will be exposed, chap. lvii. 6.
Cry. Of iniquity, or rather of grief.

Dibon. Septuagint, &c., read, "Dimon," which signifies, "blood." I will give it a better claim to this appellation. --- Lion. Nabuchodonosor. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "I will bring the Arabs up on Dimon, and will take away the seed of Moab, and Ariel, and the remnant of Adama." (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Moab: because in the night Ar was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent: because in the night the wall was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent. Let it suffice to have spoken once about burden and weight. I give only this brief reminder: that sad things always follow a burden, whereas a vision is followed either by glad things at once, or by glad things at the end after the sad. Moab is a province of the Arabs, in which was Balak son of Beor (Num 22), who hired the soothsayer Balaam from Mesopotamia to curse Israel; where also the people were initiated into Baal-peor (ibid., 25). Its metropolis is the city AR (ער), which today is called Areopolis, a name compounded from the Hebrew and the Greek tongue; not, as many suppose, because it is the city of ἄρεος, that is, of Mars. And Ar also means ἀντίδικος, that is, adversary. How great its power was, Jeremiah testifies (Jer 48:2, 7ff.), saying: There is no more exultation in Moab. And again: You have trusted in your fortifications and in your treasures. And again: Moab has been fruitful from his youth, and has rested on his lees, and has not been poured from vessel to vessel, and has not gone into exile; and therefore his taste has remained in him, and his scent has not been changed. And in another place (ibid., 17): How has the strong rod been broken, the glorious staff? And a little later: We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud. His loftiness, and arrogance, and pride, and the haughtiness of his heart I know, says the Lord, and his boasting. Just as, therefore, the Prophet prophesied against Babylon and the Philistines because they had oppressed the people of the Jews, so now the devastation of the Moabites, that is, of Arabia, by the Assyrians and the Babylonians is foretold. For they were laid waste by both nations, at the time when Sennacherib led Israel captive, and when Nebuchadnezzar overthrew Jerusalem (2 Kgs 17 and 25). For at the coming of each enemy he had mocked Ephraim and Judah, as Jeremiah says: Moab will strike his hand in his vomit, and he too will become a derision. For Israel was a derision to you, as though you had found him among thieves (Jer 48:26-27). Because of your words, therefore, which you have spoken against him, you will be led captive. And when he says: In the night AR was laid waste, Moab has fallen silent, it is a fitting beginning for the invective, that he who was conceived at night from his father's incest should be laid waste in darkness. Unless perhaps we take night for the greatness of the terror; and it is to be believed that, because the city trusted in its walls, it was overcome by stratagems and mines. I have heard a certain man of Areopolis say, and indeed the whole city is witness to it, that in a great earthquake in my infancy, when the seas passed over the shores of the whole world, the walls of this city collapsed on that same night.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Moab. LXX: The word against the land of Moab. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Moab. Just as circumcision is both carnal and spiritual, and of the spiritual it is said by the Apostle: For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit, and glory in the Lord, and put no confidence in the flesh (Phil 3:3); and again, to distinguish the spiritual Israel, it is said of the carnal: Behold Israel according to the flesh (1 Cor 10:18): and, You Gentiles in the flesh (Eph 2:11); so Moab is to be taken spiritually, which means from the father, or paternal water, conceived of incest and drunkenness, because he would seem to have been begotten in a manner in the absence, or rather without the knowledge, of the father. In many places of the Scriptures we read of Moab, and especially in the volume of Numbers, when Balak, king of the Moabites, invited Balaam the soothsayer to curse, who among other things prophesied also this mystical word against Moab: A star will rise out of Jacob, and a man will rise up out of Israel, and will strike the princes of Moab (Num 24:17).
Commentary on Isaiah

Because by night Ar has been laid waste, Moab has fallen silent; because by night the wall has been laid waste, Moab has fallen silent. LXX: By night the land of Moab perished, for by night the wall of the land of Moab perished. For AR (ער), which Theodotion alone set down thus, as it is read in the Hebrew, Aquila and Symmachus translated city, not considering that between the Hebrew letters AIN and RES it does not have the letter JOD, which, if it were there, would rightly be read as city. Worldly wisdom, of which the Lord speaks through the Prophet: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject (Obad 8; 1 Cor 1:19), because it has as its author the mind, which is begotten by God's creating, seems indeed to be born of the father, which is what Moab means; but because it is adulterous and an adversary to the people of God, it is begotten of incest, of a cave and of night. Hence it perished by night, namely in everlasting error. The Egyptians too in the Red Sea were overwhelmed by the waves at the morning watch, which indicates the time of night (Exod 14). And Lot, while the Sodomites were perishing by night, came to Zoar, and the sun rose for him (Gen 19). Understanding this, the blessed Apostle writes of the saints and the perfect (1 Thess 5:6, 7): We are not of the night nor of darkness, but we are sons of the day. For those who sleep sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night. But let us who are of the day keep watch, clothed with the breastplate of faith and love. And because he had left the night and had already begun to be a son of the day, he says to believers: The night has gone before, and the day has drawn near; let us walk honestly as in the day, not in revelings and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness (Rom 13:12). And when the land of Moab perishes by night, its wall too, which was built by the art of dialectic, was laid waste and destroyed in the same night, and fell silent in eternal silence. Moreover Ar, which means ἀντίδικος, that is, adversary, shows this: that this wisdom, which is the adversary of God, has been overcome by the Church's preaching fighting against it.
Commentary on Isaiah

The house has gone up, and Dibon, to the high places to lament over Nebo, and over Medeba Moab will howl. Do not let it be irksome to you that I walk along the road of the history; for you yourself wished me to do this. Now what is understood is the royal house; and the city of Dibon goes up to the idols set on the heights: over Nebo and over Medeba, noble cities, the whole province will howl. For in Nebo was consecrated the idol Chemosh, which by another name is called Baal-peor.

On all its heads baldness, every beard will be shaved. Among the ancients the shaving of the beard and the head was a sign of mourning. By these things, therefore, the greatness of the grief is shown, as Jeremiah cries out the same things against Moab: Every head baldness, and every beard will be shaved, and on all hands a binding, and on every back haircloth (Jer 48:37).
Commentary on Isaiah

The house has gone up, and Dimon, to the high places, to lament. LXX: Be sorrowful within yourselves, for Dimon will perish, where the altar is: thither you will go up to weep. The whole house of hostile wisdom, and Dibon, which means their flowing, goes up to the high places in which it had grown proud: not to sacrifice victims, but to lament the things in which it had formerly sinned. And truly falsehood passes like a river, and flows by, and can never stand firm in a stable dwelling. But the word of God, which is compacted, is stable. Hence the manna too, which is seen like ice upon the face of the earth, does not flow away, but stands firm. Moreover, according to the Seventy, the Moabites are commanded to grieve and lament, not over others (for this belongs to the perfect) but over themselves, because their Dibon too, that is, their composed discourse, which flowed like a torrent, is to perish: in which they had, as it were, the altar of their consecration, and all worldly riches. Hence it is said in the psalm too: If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them. And the beginning of salvation is to understand and weep over one's own sins.
Commentary on Isaiah

Over Nebo and over Medeba Moab will howl: on all its heads baldness, every beard will be shaved. In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth: and upon its roofs and in its streets everyone howls: he will go down in weeping. And Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out: their voice has been heard as far as Jahaz: for this the armed men of Moab will howl, his soul will howl to itself. My heart will cry out to Moab: its bars as far as Zoar, a heifer of three years: for by the ascent of Luhith he will go up weeping, and on the way of Horonaim they will raise a cry of crushing: for the waters of Nimrim will be desolate: because the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished. According to the greatness of the work is also their visitation: they will lead them to the brook of the willows: for the cry has gone round the border of Moab: its howling as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim: because the waters of Dimon are filled with blood. For I will set upon Dimon additions, for those who have fled from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land. Since the whole of this prophecy has almost a single sense, lest I tear it apart by setting it forth piecemeal, I have set it all down together, and I shall run through in brief discourse what seems to me, according to the anagogy, to be meant in each part. Nebo means sitting or prophecy; Medeba, from the forest; Heshbon, thoughts; Elealeh, ascent; Jahaz, deed or command; Zoar, small; Luhith, cheeks; Horonaim, hole of grief; Nimrim, leopards or transgressors; Eglaim, calves or mounds of sand; Elim, rams or strong ones; Dimon, sufficient grief. Since, then, every doctrine contrary to the truth, which is born without the inspiration of God from human sense in the darkness of error, has been laid waste by night, and its arguments, which are understood as walls, have been destroyed by the Church's preaching, so that they have fallen silent in eternal silence, insomuch that their whole faction has been turned to penance and tears, over Nebo, that is, the prophecy and the sitting, that is, their teachers, and over Medeba, where there are no fruitful trees but a barren forest in which wild beasts dwell, of which it is written in the twenty-eighth psalm: And he will uncover the thickets of the forest: there will be howling and lamentation, and all the ornaments of eloquence will be taken from their heads, so that they remain naked and unsightly. And if they seemed to have anything of manliness in the beard, shaved by the churchman, it is shown to be effeminate and weak.
Commentary on Isaiah

In its crossroads they are girded with sackcloth; on its roofs and in its streets all howling will go down into weeping. The tears will not be private; public laments will resound for a public grief; neither matrons nor virgins, nor the tender age of children, nor the broken steps of old men will be kept within doors: the extremity of captivity will know neither shame nor weakness.
Commentary on Isaiah

In their crossroads too, that is, in the byways of errors, while each one according to his own will fashions what he wishes, he is girded with the sackcloth of penance; and upon the roofs and housetops, on which at first they believed themselves to be lofty, and in the streets (because they do not enter by the narrow way that leads to life, but by the broad way that leads to death), there will be howling. And they will by no means go up into pride, but will go down into weeping.
Commentary on Isaiah

Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out. These are names of cities of the province of Moab, of which Heshbon was once the city of the king of the Amorites, about which the same Jeremiah says: Fire has gone forth from Heshbon, and flame from the midst of Sihon. Now Heshbon means thought, and so Jeremiah, alluding to the name: Against Heshbon, he says, they have thought evil things (Jer 48:2).

Even to Jahaz their voice has been heard. The city of Jahaz overlooks the Dead Sea, where the border of the province of the Moabites lies. This, then, indicates that the howling of the province will resound to its farthest borders. Hence Jeremiah too says: From the cry of Heshbon, up to Elealeh and Jahaz they have uttered their voice (Jer 48:34).

Over this the lightly armed of Moab will howl, its soul will howl for itself. The Hebrew word ELUSE (חלוצי), for which Aquila translated ἐξώμους, that is, lightly armed and with shoulders bared, and Symmachus girded, some think is to be understood not of men but as the name of a city, which today is called Eluza and is situated in the region of Moabitis. But we can also say this: that the whole strength of the fighting men has collapsed, and the whole land has resounded with their weeping for one another. If, however, ELUSE is understood, as Aquila would have it, as with shoulders bared, this sense is suggested to us: that all have bared their breasts to beat them in mourning.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then they will understand all their thoughts to be vain, which is the meaning of Heshbon, and the ascent of pride to be empty, which is what Elealeh sounds, so that their voice is heard as far as the evil works which they have done, and the command which they thought was God's, condemning themselves by their own confession. Therefore the bars, that is, those who have been firm in Moab and have understood their error, will howl, and will begin to have hope of progress, when their soul has howled to itself.
Commentary on Isaiah

My heart will cry out to Moab. The Prophet speaks with the feeling of one who grieves, either because the enemies too, upon whom so many evils come, are God's creatures, or because they were to be crushed by such great calamities that they become pitiable even to their enemies. Jeremiah says the very same: Therefore my heart will sound for Moab like a flute.

Its bars, as far as Segor, a heifer of three years. And Jeremiah: From Segor, he says, as far as Horonaim, a heifer of three years. Of this city we have spoken in the books of Hebrew Questions as well, and now we note briefly that it is the fifth city after Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which, being small, was preserved at the prayers of Lot. And it is called Bala, that is, swallowed up, the Hebrews relating that it was overthrown by a third earthquake. It is the city which today in the Syrian tongue is called Zoora, in the Hebrew Segor: in both, the little one. We can take the heifer of three years as signifying full age. For as the thirtieth year is the strongest in men, so the third is in cattle and beasts of burden. Understand the bars, too, as borders and strength, because Segor is situated at the borders of the Moabites, dividing the land of the Philistines from them.

For by the ascent of Luhith he will go up weeping. And Jeremiah: By the ascent of Luhith, weeping, he will go up in tears. We understand it to be the slope of the road that leads to the Assyrians, and by this captivity is signified.

And on the road to Horonaim they will raise a cry of crushing. Again Jeremiah: The voice of a cry from Horonaim, devastation and great crushing. It would take long if I wished to speak about each one, since it is plain that these are the names either of cities in Moab or of places which those who are carried away into exile are leaving.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hence the Prophet, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, speaks to those whose soul was howling to itself, and says: My heart will cry out to Moab, that I may call them to penance. And their bars and all the supports which they seemed to have in their heresies will come as far as Zoar, that is, as far as the little one: and they will be shown to be not strong but fragile. And this Zoar, that is, small penance, if it perseveres, will lead them to perfect salvation: which is what the heifer of three years signifies, according to what we read in Genesis, where Abraham is commanded to offer a heifer, a ram and a goat of three years, namely a perfect sacrifice, so that he might deserve to be the heir of the Lord (Gen 15). And when they have done penance, they will climb to higher things by Luhith, that is, by the tears of the cheeks. And by this, as it were, hole and entrance of grief, they will raise the cry of contrition to the Lord, so that they can say: A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit: a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise (Ps 50 [51]:19).
Commentary on Isaiah

For the waters of Nimrim will be deserted. This town lies above the Dead Sea, with salt waters, and barren for that very reason. And either he has alluded to the name, or what had not been so before came about after the devastation: that even the waters were turned to bitterness.

For the grass has withered, the shoot has failed, all greenness has perished. It is not, as some think, that all the grass truly dried up because of the barren waters of Nimrim; rather, Scripture is speaking by metaphor. And the sense is: in all Moab there will be the salt and bitter waters of Nimrim; as no grass springs up there, so drought will overtake the whole province, that is, from Segor to Horonaim, from border to border. Jeremiah says the very same: The waters of Nimrim will be very bad (Jer 48:34).
Commentary on Isaiah

And this will come about because the waters of Nimrim, that is, the doctrine of the heretics, which is compared to leopards and transgressors, will be desolate and will be brought to nothing. They are leopards whose varieties and spots, in Jeremiah, are not changed (Jer 13), and apostates, of whom we read in the Psalms: I have counted all the sinners of the earth transgressors (Ps 118 [119]:119). Every grass too, and shoot, and whatever seemed green in their discourse, has withered.
Commentary on Isaiah

According to the greatness of the work, so also their visitation: they will lead them to the torrent of the willows. For willows we read in the Hebrew ARABIM (ערבים), which can also be understood as Arabs, and can be read ORBIM (עורבים), that is, a village situated on their borders, whose inhabitants are said by many to have provided food for Elijah on Mount Horeb: a name which, because of its ambiguity, is also translated as ravens, and as the West, and as level places. And the sense is: the visitation will be according to the greatness of the disease. Take visitation here not as a remedy but as a blow. I will visit, he says, their iniquities with the rod, and their sins with stripes (Ps 88 [89]:33). The torrent of the willows understand as the rivers of Babylonia, of which David says: On the willows in the midst of it we hung up our instruments (Ps 136 [137]:2); or else as the valley of Arabia through which one passes to the Assyrians.
Commentary on Isaiah

And they have been visited by God according to the greatness of their sins, so that him whom they had not perceived through benefits they might come to know through scourges. Accordingly they will be led to the valley or brook of the willows, so that no fruit may remain in them. For they say this is the nature of the seed of these trees: that whoever drinks it in a cup is without children. Hence the saints too, who because of their sins have come to be in the confusion of this world, hang their instruments on the willows of the rivers of the Babylonians (Ps 136 [137]).
Commentary on Isaiah

For the cry will go round the border of Moab, its howling as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim. Jeremiah too writes almost all the same things. And these are cities and places of the Moabites, in which the crying and wailing of the captive people is described.
Commentary on Isaiah

A cry goes round all the borders of the Moabites, either of those who call them to repentance, or of those who lament for their error: so that through their howling they may be able to offer the calves of the lips, and come as far as the fountain of the Lord's rams, or of the strong: because Elim signifies both.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood. Where formerly there was luxuriance because of the watered fields and the ever-flowing springs, there, because of the multitude of the slain, streams of blood will flow.

For I will set additions upon Dibon: for those who flee from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land. Lest anyone think it a fault of the scribe and, in wishing to correct an error, make one, the one city is written both with the letter M and with the letter B: of these, Dimon is interpreted as silence, Dibon as flowing. Both names having been given it because of the waters that flow silently, to this day this little town is called indifferently both Dimon and Dibon. And as for his saying: I will set additions upon Dibon, since it seemed to raise the question what these might be, he showed it in the following line, saying: For those who flee from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land: so that even those who have slipped away in flight are consumed by beasts. Although by metaphor we can also understand the lion as the king of the enemies, so that no one can escape his power, as though it were a roaring.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the waters of Dimon, which means sufficient sorrow, or grief, which had polluted many by their sprinkling, will be shown to have been to the deceived peoples not for salvation but for blood. Hence the prophetic word promises that upon the flowing tears, which is the meaning of Dibon, they will redouble not one grief but many additions of grief: so that, after they have done full penance and have fled from Moab, they may have as their prince the lion, God, whom the Seventy called ariel, which means lion of God: whose edition I have forborne to discuss in this place, because it disagrees in very many points with the Hebrew truth, and from what we have translated its sense too can be understood.

n: Petra. Hebrew selah, "the rock." (Haydock) --- Our Saviour sprung from Ruth, the Moabitess. (Menochius) --- The original may insinuate, that the king of the country had neglected to pay the usual tribute to Juda, 4 Kings iii. 4. (Calmet) --- "Send the lamb to the ruler," &c. (Tournemine.) Amid scenes of distress, the prophet perceives that the Saviour will proceed from one of this nation. (Worthington)
Arnon. They shall not be able to fly over, or to escape the conqueror.
Night. Seek a retreat in the darkest places; or protect Israel when they shall flee before the Assyrians. Their cruelty is thus insinuated, Amos i.
Dust. Theglathphalassar. I need not exhort you to receive my people, as I know your dispositions, and they are out of danger. (Calmet)
Just. This regards Christ, (St. Jerome) prefigured by (Haydock) Ezechias. (Calmet)
Walls. Hebrew, "Kir-hareseth," chap. xv. 1. (Haydock)
Lords. Princes of Jerusalem, (Lamentations i. 1.) or of Assyria. (Calmet) --- Sea. Of Sodom, even as far as Jazer, (Haydock) in the tribe of Ruben. (Calmet)

My tears. Chap. xv. 5. (Haydock) --- I announce a different sort of music from that which is customary in times of harvest, and of vintage. The liquor shall be tears, chap. lxiii. 2., and Jeremias xlviii. 32, 33. (Calmet)
Carmel. This name is often taken to signify a fair and fruitful hill or field, such as Mount Carmel is. (Challoner) --- It means, "the vine of God." (Calmet)
Wall. Kir-hareseth, ver. 7. I am grieved at your misfortunes. (Calmet)
Prevail. Chamos shall not be able to help them.
That time. A long while ago, Psalm xcii. 2.

Not many. It was laid waste in the third year of Ezechias. But its final destruction took place only five years after that of Jerusalem. (Calmet) --- The wars against Moab continued three years, after which it was reduced to servitude. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Send forth the Lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. What we are interpreting is not history but prophecy. And every prophecy is wrapped in enigmas, and with abrupt sentences passes, while speaking of one thing, to another: lest, if Scripture kept to order, it should be not prophecy but narrative. And the sense is: O Moab, upon whom the lion is about to rage, and from whom not even a remnant will be able to be saved, have this consolation: from you will go forth the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, who will rule over the whole world. From the rock of the desert, that is, from Ruth, who, widowed by the death of her husband, bore Obed by Boaz, and from Obed came Jesse, and from Jesse David, and from David Christ. And the mountain of the daughter of Zion we shall interpret either as the city of Jerusalem itself, or, according to the sacred understanding, as the Church, which is set upon the summit of the virtues.
Commentary on Isaiah

Send forth the lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert, to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. And as a bird fleeing, and as young ones flying from the nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon. Enter into counsel, call a council: make your shadow like night at midday: hide those who flee, and do not betray the wanderers. My fugitives will dwell with you; Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the destroyer. For the dust is at an end, the wretch is consumed; he has failed who trampled the earth. And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and one will sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just. What we have translated from the Hebrew, send forth the lamb, the ruler of the earth, can be read thus: send forth the lamb to the ruler of the earth, in the sense, namely, that the lamb itself is not the ruler of the earth, as we interpreted according to the history, but that the lamb is to be sacrificed to the ruler of the earth. This lamb, then, which either is itself the ruler of the earth or is sacrificed to the ruler of the earth, is of the nation of the Moabites, and of those who have fled from Moab and have deserved to have the lion as their prince. And it signifies Ruth, from whom Christ was begotten (Matt 1:5), whom he calls the rock of the desert, because according to the precept of God the Moabites and Ammonites do not enter the Church of God even to the tenth generation and forever (Deut 23).
LETTER 53.8

Then, as for Job, that pattern of patience, what mysteries are there not contained in his discourses? Commencing in prose the book soon glides into verse and at the end once more reverts to prose. By the way in which it lays down propositions, assumes postulates, adduces proofs and draws inferences, it illustrates all the laws of logic. Single words occurring in the book are full of meaning. To say nothing of other topics, it prophesies the resurrection of humankind's bodies at once with more clearness and with more caution than anyone has yet shown. "I know," Job says, "that my redeemer lives, and that at the last day I shall rise again from the earth; and I shall be clothed again with my skin, and in my flesh shall I see God. Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another. This my hope is stored up in my own bosom." I will pass on to Joshua, son of Nun3—a type of the Lord in name as well as in deed—who crossed over Jordan, subdued hostile kingdoms, divided the land among the conquering people and who, in every city, village, mountain, river, hill-torrent and boundary which he dealt with, marked out the spiritual realms of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, of the church. In the book of Judges every one of the popular leaders is a type. Ruth the Moabite fulfills the prophecy of Isaiah: "Send you a lamb, O Lord, as ruler of the land from the rock of the wilderness to the mount of the daughter of Zion." Under the figures of Eli's death and the slaying of Saul, Samuel shows the abolition of the old law. Again in Zadok and in David he bears witness to the mysteries of the new priesthood and of the new royalty. The third and fourth books of Kings called in Hebrew Malachim give the history of the kingdom of Judah from Solomon to Jeconiah, and of that of Israel from Jeroboam the son of Nebat to Hosea, who was carried away into Assyria. If you merely regard the narrative, the words are simple enough, but if you look beneath the surface at the hidden meaning of it, you find a description of the small numbers of the church and of the wars that the heretics wage against it. The twelve prophets whose writings are compressed within the narrow limits of a single volume have typical meanings far different from their literal ones. Hosea speaks many times of Ephraim, of Samaria, of Joseph, of Jezreel, of a wife of whoredoms and of children of whoredoms, of an adulteress shut up within the chamber of her husband, sitting for a long time in widowhood and in the garb of mourning, awaiting the time when her husband will return to her. Joel the son of Pethuel describes the land of the twelve tribes as spoiled and devastated by the palmerworm, the cankerworm, the locust and the blight. He predicts that after the overthrow of the former people the Holy Spirit shall be poured out upon God's servants and handmaids;8 the same spirit, that is, which was to be poured out in the upper chamber at Zion upon the 120 believers. These believers rising by gradual and regular gradations from one to fifteen form the steps to which there is a mystical allusion in the "psalms of degrees." Amos, although he is only "a herdsman" from the country, "a gatherer of sycamore fruit," cannot be explained in a few words.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will be: as a bird fleeing, and young ones flying away from the nest, so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon. He returns to the order he had begun: When I have set, he says, a most savage lion upon those who flee from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land, to break their limbs and bones, then they will fly away in terror, and all the daughters, that is, the villages and cities of the province of Moab, will migrate at the crossing of the Arnon, which is the border of the Amorites and the Moabites. And by putting crossing here too, he signifies captivity.
Commentary on Isaiah

But he who has fled from the desert of Moab (to return from the prophecy to the anagogy), and, despising falsehood, has stood on the mountain of truth, will be like a bird fleeing; and like young ones flying from the nest, lest they be devoured by the Moabite serpents. Thus, he says, will all the daughters, that is, the Moabite souls, be at the crossing of the Arnon, which means their illumination: when, having abandoned their errors, they have crossed over to the knowledge of the truth.
Commentary on Isaiah

Take counsel, call a council: make your shade like night at midday, hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. My refugees will dwell with you: Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the devastator; for the dust is at an end, the wretched one is finished, he who trampled the land has failed. For wretched one in the Hebrew one reads SOD (סד), which can also be understood as devastator. And he speaks to Moab, that it should find counsel for its safety, and, gathering its elders, convene a council for its salvation. Do you wish, he says, to be saved and to merit the mercy of God? In the clear light and the open flight of my people, be like night and shade; take in the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. And why he said this he adds at once: My refugees will dwell with you. For when Jerusalem has been laid waste, and all Judea, which borders on the Moabites, my people will migrate to you. Be therefore their hiding place, and do not fear the onslaught of the devastator, because he will quickly pass like dust; and the despoiler of the whole land, who trampled it and subjected it under his feet, will perish as a breeze blows. Some wrongly interpret this place of the Antichrist, so as to suppose that at that time the saints will cross over to the Arabs because of their nearness to the city of Jerusalem, and that the Arabs are now commanded not to betray those who flee to them.
Commentary on Isaiah

It is said therefore to Moab himself, or to him who has escaped from Moab: Do nothing without counsel (Prov 13): and do not be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but follow him who is the Angel of great counsel (Eph 4): and call a council, so that out of the wandering and straying you may make a Church of God. And your shade and tabernacle, in which you formerly thought you were resting, which belonged to night and darkness, set it at midday, that is, in the brightest light, in which you ought to hide those fleeing from error, and no longer betray those who were formerly wanderers.
Commentary on Isaiah

For, O Moab, my fugitives who had forsaken me, who had gone out of the Church and, abandoning the teaching of the Holy Spirit, were following their own sense; or those who had dwelt with you, when the destroyer, the devil, begins to persecute them, do you, turned with your whole mind to the fear of the Lord, offer them hiding places: and know that after the coming of the Lamb, who arose from the rock of the desert as ruler of the whole earth and came to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, all the power of the devil, which is compared to dust, is at an end. And the wretch is consumed who made many wretched: and he has failed who trampled the whole earth, namely those who were earthly.
Commentary on Isaiah

And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just. The Hebrews interpret this place thus: When the Assyrian has been put to flight, Hezekiah, a righteous man, will reign over Judah and will hold the throne of David, judging in truth the people of God subject to him. Others understand it of Christ: when the dust of the Antichrist is at an end, and the devastator who trampled the whole earth has been taken away, Christ the king will come, who will sit in the tabernacle of David, and in the day of judgment will render to all according to their works. Nor is there any doubt that this passage prophesies of Christ. But we can understand the same thing of his first coming, and show it in the tabernacle of the Church: that throughout the whole land of Moab the trophies of the Churches as they rise bear witness to the dominion of Christ.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when he has been consumed and brought to nothing and has utterly failed, a throne and an everlasting kingdom will be prepared. First in mercy (for we are all (Rom 3) under sin, and need the grace of God); and he will sit in the tabernacle of David, which had fallen and has been raised up, who after mercy will judge, and seek righteousness, and render to each according to his works. Let us consider from the beginning of the Burden, or of the word, of Moab, in which it is said: By night Ar of Moab has been laid waste, and the rest up to this place; and we shall see how by steps and in the order of penance Israelites are made from Moabites, and flee like birds and fly away like young ones from the nest, so as to cross over by the Arnon and dwell on the mountain of the daughter of Zion: and, all the power of the devil or of the Antichrist having been crushed, Christ reigns in them and sets his throne among those who have been saved by mercy and righteousness. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5).
Commentary on Isaiah

We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud. His pride and his arrogance and his indignation are more than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of him will howl: to those who rejoice over the wall of baked brick, speak of his wounds: for the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted, the vineyard of Sibmah. LXX: We have heard of the insolence of Moab: he is exceedingly insolent: his pride and his insolence and his fury are not like your divination: not so will Moab howl: for in Moab all will howl: but for the inhabitants of Deseth you will meditate, and you will not be confounded: the plains of Heshbon will mourn the vineyard of Sibmah. In how many obscurities this passage is wrapped according to the Seventy translators is evident from the fact that it can scarcely be read. Let us speak, therefore, according to the Hebrew. It is the custom of the Scriptures, after they have relieved the despair of the human mind with glad tidings, to deter again by threats the negligent and those unwilling to do penance, lest the goodness of God harden our heart. Of this let us set down only one example. In the hundred and forty-fourth psalm we read: The Lord is sweet to all, and his compassions are over all his works (Ps 144 [145]:9). And a little after: The Lord upholds all who fall, and raises up all who are dashed down. The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them their food in due season. And when he had said first, The Lord keeps all who love him, lest he make the hearer negligent, he added: And all sinners he will destroy. Since, then, he prophesied that when the Antichrist and his parent the devil, who trampled the whole earth, have been consumed, a throne is to be prepared in mercy, and he who is to sit in the tabernacle of David, the prophet speaks in the person of the saints who have been saved from Moab and have learned his pride by their own experience: We have heard of the pride of Moab, or the insolence, as the Seventy translated. For which of the heretics is not proud? who, despising the simplicity of the Church, regards the men of the Church as brute animals, and is lifted up by such a swelling of pride and insolence that he arms his mouth against the Creator himself, disparaging his prophets as though on the authority of the testimony of the Gospel, in which the Savior says: All who came before me were thieves and robbers (John 10:8): so much so that he even calls Moses, the servant of God, a murderer, and disparages Joshua the son of Nun as a bloodthirsty man, who was of such holiness that at the command of his word the sun and moon stood still: and calls David, of whose seed Christ was born (Matt 1), a murderer and an adulterer, not regarding his penance and his meekness, by which the clemency of God is obtained. But although he is proud and arrogant, and exults in his fury, yet he dares more than his strength allows.
Commentary on Isaiah

We have heard of the pride of Moab, he is exceedingly proud: his pride, and his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, all of it will howl: to those who rejoice over the walls of baked brick, tell of its wounds. Again he returns to the present, and accuses Moab of pride, because it was lifted up far more than its strength warranted; and because of this pride Moab will howl to Moab, that is, the people to the city, or the metropolis to the province, and the whole land will resound with howling over the walls of baked brick, of which Jeremiah too says: Therefore I will wail over Moab, and to all Moab I will cry out, to the men of the earthen wall, lamenting (Jer 48:31). And by these things he shows both the power of its former prosperity and the wounds of its sudden overthrow.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore Moab will howl to Moab, that is, one to another: namely, all the varieties of the heretics and of worldly wisdom will bellow against one another when they are in torments (1 Kgs 6). For this reason, to those who have walls not built of squared stones, of which the Temple was built, and so polished that hammer and axe were not heard in the house of God, O you teachers of the Church, or you who have been saved from the error of Moab, announce their wounds, with which they have been wounded by the darts of the heretics. For all their thoughts, which is what Heshbon signifies, do not belong to the dwelling of the Lord's city, of which it is written: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps 45 [46]:5); but they are suburbs, so that they may be believed to belong to the city of the Lord: and these suburbs are deserted by the protection of God, or burnt by the divine fire, especially the vineyard of Sibmah, which means lifting up height, because it raises itself on high and tries to build the tower of its pride up to heaven. And what is set down in the Seventy, for the inhabitants of Deseth, is not found in the Hebrew; but in its place is read ARES (חרש), which signifies potsherd, or baked brick.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted: the vine of Sibmah. Between Heshbon and Sibmah there are scarcely five hundred paces; and by the metaphor of the vine he signifies the devastation of the whole province.

The lords of the nations have cut down its shoots. He keeps the metaphor he had begun, showing that the kings of the nations who had laid Moab waste ravaged all its hamlets and fortresses.

They have reached as far as Jazer: they have wandered in the desert: its offshoots have been left behind: they have crossed the sea. Understand the shoots and offshoots as its people and its fugitives; and the crossing of the sea as the captivity into Babylon, about which we shall read later: The burden of the desert of the sea.
Commentary on Isaiah

The lords of the nations have cut down its branches: they have reached as far as Jazer. They have wandered in the desert: its shoots have been left: they have crossed the sea. For this I will weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vineyard of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh: for upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. And gladness and exultation will be taken away from Carmel: and in the vineyards he will not exult nor shout for joy: he who was accustomed to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. The suburbs of Heshbon, of which we spoke above, are deserted, and the vineyard of Sibmah, which can be interpreted not only as lifting up height but also as some conversion: because in the region of Moab it seems in some part to wish to be converted to the service of the Lord. Of this vineyard of Sibmah, therefore, the lords of the nations, the Apostles and apostolic men, have utterly cut off the branches and shoots, lest from some heresies other heresies should be born and an infinite multitude of the straying should come to be. And they not only cut off the shoots of Sibmah, but reached as far as Jazer, which means their strength: that is, to all the strongest doctrines of the heretics, built by the art of dialectic, in which they seemed to have the strength of their error; and their sword raged so far that at last they wandered in the wilderness and had no one to slay. And though they cut off its branches, yet, through the fault of the most evil root, some shoots remained. But the lords of the nations crossed the sea, that is, the temptations of this world, of which we read in the psalm: I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest swallowed me (Ps 68 [69]:3); and in another place: Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters: they have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep (Ps 106 [107]:23). These, then, crossed the sea, so as to behold the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep of temptations, while they are delivered from them.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore I will lament with the weeping of Jazer, the vine of Sibmah: I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh. This is the voice of the Prophet lamenting, and attesting the greatness of the devastation by the greatness of his tears, and weeping for the vine of Jazer and of Sibmah, and for Heshbon and Elealeh, cities once most strong, cut down as the Assyrian pruned them.

For upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. Understand the treaders of the grapes, gathering in the joy of the vintage, as the armies of the enemies; and that in the very season of joy the season of captivity has come.
Commentary on Isaiah

And so the prophetic word laments the strength of the heretics, that is, Jazer, and the vineyard of Sibmah, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God. And I will drench you with my tears, Heshbon, namely their thoughts, and Elealeh, by which they climb to the heights. And why does he lament Jazer and the vineyard of Sibmah, and drench Heshbon and Elealeh with his tears? So that, while he himself weeps, he may teach them also to weep. For, he says, upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has burst in. For the vineyard of the Moabites, because of the nearness of the place, is such as is the vineyard of the Sodomites too, of which it is said: For their vine is of the vineyard of the Sodomites, and their shoot of Gomorrah (Deut 32:31). And in Psalm 77 (78) we read of the Egyptian vine which God struck with hail. The harvests of Moab too grow in the valleys which are called Rephaim: and its false vintage is of the vineyard of which it is said above: The lords of the nations have cut down its branches. For these crush the most bitter grapes and tread them with their feet, lest the poisons of the dragon be pressed out of them and all who drink be killed.
Commentary on Isaiah

And joy and exultation will be taken away from Carmel. It is an idiom of the Scriptures always to liken Carmel, a rich and wooded mountain which overlooks Ptolemais and on which Elijah prayed, to fertility and abundance; and by this it signifies that all joy and fertility are to be taken away from cities once most fruitful.

And in the vineyards he will not exult, nor shout for joy. What is understood is the former vintager, that is, the husbandman of the province of Moabitis. Accordingly he immediately added:

He who used to tread will not tread wine in the press: I have taken away the voice of the treaders. By no means will the joyful vintager sing the vintage shout at the vintage; but everywhere hostile devastation and the clamor of the victors will arise.
Commentary on Isaiah

The gladness and exultation of the heretics, in which they had formerly been accustomed to rejoice, will also be taken away: so that, after they have done penance, they may deserve to hear: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:5). And what he added, from Carmel, signifies this: not that the heretics truly have Carmel, that is, the knowledge of the spiritual circumcision, but that they falsely boast of having it. And when the vineyards have been cut down, and gladness and exultation taken away from the knowledge falsely so called, then there will be none of the former treaders to tread the grapes which he had trodden before: and their voice will be struck dumb in eternal silence.
Commentary on Isaiah

Moreover, according to the Seventy, who translated: The inner parts of the prophet, like a wall renewed by God, and that he is put to shame, that is, Moab, and enters to the altars and to the things that are made by hand, we can discuss it thus, saying that the inward parts of the prophet are always renewed and made stronger by God, so that the adversaries are confounded, and understand the things which have been fabricated by human hand to be empty and of no profit for salvation.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inmost parts for the wall of baked brick. Lest anyone should think the Prophet's lament a sign of exultation, by which he rejoiced that the enemies of the people of Israel were captives, he says that it is out of affection, and out of the inmost grief of his heart, that he mourns the overthrow of a city once most mighty.
Commentary on Isaiah

For this my belly will sound for Moab like a harp, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick. And it will be, when it has appeared that Moab has labored on his high places, he will enter into his holy places to entreat, and he will not prevail. This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. When the error of Moab has been destroyed, or rather its false gladness changed into mourning and tears, my belly, the prophet's, which is composed with musical art like a harp, and which, conceiving from the fear of God, has begotten many children, so that there is no string that does not give back its sound, will resound with the mourning of Moab doing penance: and all my inward parts for the wall of baked brick: for which Theodotion translated for the scattered wall. For all the defenses of the adversaries, in which they formerly trusted, will be destroyed and will fall. And these are the inward parts and the inner things of the prophet, of which David too spoke in the Psalm: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all my inner parts his holy name (Ps 102 [103]:1). For just as a harp does not give forth a tuneful and well-composed sound if even one string is broken, so the spiritual belly of the prophet, if one string of the virtues is lacking in it, will not be able to sound forth a sweet melody, nor to cry out with all its inward parts to the brick wall. It is also the opinion of the philosophers that the virtues cleave to one another; and of the Apostle James, that he who lacks one lacks all the virtues.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will come to pass, when it has become apparent that Moab has labored over its high places, it will enter its sanctuaries to pray, and it will not prevail. It is the last misery not to have help even in those whom it has always worshiped. Deserted, he says, by your own strength, and with all your defenders slain, you will go to the idols, you will venerate the shrines, and you will find no help in those upon whom the devastation will come together with you.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when Moab has understood that he has labored in vain at the doctrines which he formerly thought lofty, he will enter into his holy places, not those which are holy of themselves, but those which in his error he thought holy, and he will not be able to find help. Or surely, having abandoned the error of falsehood, he will try to enter into the holy places of the Church, to make them his own, and to pray and entreat, but he will not prevail. For we cannot take hold of perfect virtue as soon as we wish.
Commentary on Isaiah

This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time. From what time, do you suppose? Clearly from the time when Moab was created. And the Lord says: The Moabites and the Ammonites shall not enter into the Church of God (Deut 23:3). Or we may understand from that time as of ancient time: that these things were decreed long ago by the divine sentence; not that the foreknowledge of God brought about the cause of the devastation, but that the future devastation was known beforehand to the majesty of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what he adds: This is the word which the Lord spoke to Moab from that time, let us know that an epilogue has been given back to the proem in which he had said, the word against Moab, or the burden, so that what he had begun there he has completed here. And from that time is to be understood as from when he began to speak to him, so that all that he said is one word of God, that is, one sentence.
Commentary on Isaiah

And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away, above all its great people, and it will be left small and slight, by no means many. This prophecy, as we said above, is directed against the Moabites after the death of Ahaz, in the reign of Hezekiah, under whom the ten tribes were led into captivity by Sennacherib king of the Assyrians. So, just as a hireling waits for the setting of the sun, and day and night looks for the end of his work so as to receive his fixed wage, so too after three years Moab will be destroyed when the Assyrian comes, and scarcely a few will be left in the land to inhabit the overthrown cities and to till the deserted fields. It can also be a prediction about the Babylonian captivity: that after Jerusalem had been taken and three years had passed, Moab was to be laid waste by the Chaldeans; or else that within the space of three years no rest was to be given them.
Commentary on Isaiah

And now the Lord has spoken, saying: In three years, like the years of a hireling, the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, and he will be left small and slight, by no means many. The three years in which the glory of Moab will be taken away over all his great people, or great riches, as the Seventy translated, are to be understood mystically. For just as the mercy of the Lord is in weights and measure, so torments and punishments too have their measure, so that after three years have passed, in which he will be left small and slight and by no means many, he may then cease to be without glory. And this is to be noted, that according to the prophecy of Ezekiel, when days are counted for years to Israel (Ezek 4), that is, to the ten tribes, which had sinned more grievously, three hundred and ninety years are reckoned in punishments, as it is contained in the Hebrew, not a hundred and ninety, as the common edition has: and to Judah, in which was the Temple of God, forty years. For he who is small deserves mercy: but the mighty will suffer torments mightily (Wis 6). And the servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12). Moab, therefore, because he was an outsider and not of the people of God, but was converted after leaving his error, will be left small and slight and without glory, not for many years, but for three only. These are the years of which we read elsewhere too: Remember the days of the age (Isa 46), and again: I thought upon the days of old, and I had the eternal years in mind (Ps 76 [77]:6). For if Israel according to the flesh served the shadow and the patterns, and every solemnity of theirs was a type of things to come, why should not the years of the present time also prefigure the times to come? of which we read in another place too: What will you do in the days of the assembly, and in the days of the festival of the Lord? And what is joined to it, Like the years of a hireling (Hos 9:5), shows this: that false doctrine does everything for gain and profit. For every hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, when he sees the wolf coming, flees, because he is a hireling and the sheep do not belong to him (John 10). For this reason I think that the stranger and the hireling do not eat of the holy things, nor are servants partakers of the holy things. For it is not for love of the Lord but for wages that they do all things, who devour the houses of widows and lead off flocks of their own, to be clothed with their wool and to milk their milk (Matt 23). What we have said of hireling doctrine, let us refer to the rest as well. If I give alms in order to be glorified by men, I have received my reward and am to be called a hireling. If I pretend to be chaste, and there is something else in my conscience, I have not the glory of a hireling but the punishments of a sinner. And in the comparison of two evils, it is a lighter evil to sin openly than to feign and counterfeit holiness. But in this too Moab has made progress: that he who formerly had many companions in his error is afterward reduced to a few; or he who formerly was great in the riches of sins is, after penance, small and poor in malice.

n: Damascus. When it was taken by Theglathphalassar, or rather by Sennacherib, chap. x. 8. It was again ruined by Nabuchodonosor, Jeremias xlix. 24. But after the first taking, it never regained its power. Magni nominis umbra. (Calmet)

Aroer. Chaldean, "abandoned, shall be folds for sheep." Septuagint, "left for ever a resting place for flocks and herds, and none shall pursue." The tribes on the east of the Jordan shall be led captive, as well as those on the west, Ephraim, &c. (Haydock)
Damascus. Their too great union proved their ruin. Sennacherib took Damascus, as Salmanasar had done Samaria.
Lean. All the power of the kingdom shall fail, as in a mortal illness.
Raphaim. Near Jerusalem, 3 Kings xxiii. 13. Septuagint, "of stones." (Calmet) --- It will be equally difficult to find any men left in the kingdom of Israel. (Haydock)
Israel. They obeyed the summons of Ezechias and of Josias, (2 Paralipomenon xxx. 1., and xxxiv. 6.) and every after followed the same worship as Juda. (Calmet)
Left. By the Chanaanites, when the children of Israel came into their land. (Challoner) --- Their consternation was become proverbial, Josue ii. 9., and v. 11.
Good. Septuagint, "fruitless." Israel had abandoned the Lord; and could expect nothing but the fruits of death. (Calmet)
Much. Thou hast laboured earnestly, but reaped no benefit. (Haydock)

Multitude, &c. This and all that follows to the end of the chapter, relates to the Assyrian army under Sennacherib, (Challoner) or rather to that of Israel and its allies. (Calmet) --- After the Assyrians had afflicted Israel, they were also punished. (Worthington)
Not be. Phacee and Rasin were presently exterminated. --- Spoiled us. The kingdom of Achaz, 4 Kings xvii. 5.

f: Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Damascus: Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city, and it will be like a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks, and they will rest there, and there will be none to frighten them. And help will cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. After Babylon and the Philistines and Moab, the discourse turns to Damascus, that is, Aram, which itself was once a royal city too, and held the primacy in all Syria: Antioch and Laodicea and Apamea were not yet flourishing, cities which we know to have grown after Alexander and the empire of the Macedonians. Because, then, it always gave help to the ten tribes against Judah, as the history of Kings and Chronicles relates, he signifies that devastation by the Assyrians is drawing near to them too, as the king of the Assyrians says: I have taken Arabia, and Damascus, and Samaria. For as I have taken them, and all kingdoms, I will take you too. And in the volume of Kings we read: The king of the Assyrians went up to Damascus, and took it, and carried it away to Cyrene (2 Kgs 16:9). He also slew Rezin, who was king of Damascus: all of which it suffered while Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem. Behold, he says, Damascus will cease to be a city: already captivity is near, already the Assyrian has set his army in motion. And it will be like a heap of stones in ruin, so that only broken walls and traces of its former power are to be seen in the vastness of the ruins.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Damascus. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Damascus; the LXX: The word against Damascus, adding something of their own, as they did at the beginning of Moab. We first read the name Damascus in Genesis: he was Abraham's home-born servant before Isaac, and was thought to be his heir, had not the son of Sarah been begotten by promise (Gen 15). Now it means either kiss of blood, or drinking blood, or blood of sackcloth, all of which suit the people of the heathen, who before the faith of Christ were friends of blood and cruelty, and did works worthy of lamentation and of sackcloth. In the book of Days (2 Chr 24) the history relates that when the year was completed the army of Syria went up against Joash king of Judah, and came into Jerusalem, and slew all the princes of the people, and sent all the spoil to the king of Damascus; it had come with few men, and God had delivered into their hand a very great multitude, because they had forsaken the Lord God of their fathers. This must be considered according to the anagogy and as a type of things to come, whether we may refer it to the time of the Lord's advent. For after the end of the acceptable year, in which the Gospel was preached by the Savior, the army of the nations went up from Damascus with few men against Judah and Jerusalem, who had forsaken the Lord; and they carried off all their riches of the Law and the Prophets, and sent them to the king of Damascus: namely, churchmen and men of the Gospel teaching, who, in comparison with the whole world, still unbelieving at that time, and with the Jews scattered through the whole earth, were few; and yet the Lord delivered Jerusalem into their hands, because they had forsaken the Son of God, who had been foretold beforehand through the prophets (Acts 9). Therefore I think that for this reason Saul too, who afterwards received the name of Paul from his virtue, went to Damascus because he was a zealot of the Law, and wished to fight against the believers from the nations; and that, overcome there, he followed those who lived in Damascus, so that from there he might go up again to Jerusalem to do battle with the Jews. Nor should it seem contradictory to anyone if in the book of Paralipomenon glad things are foretold of Damascus, and now in Isaiah sad things; for of Israel itself, which is surely the portion of God, now adverse things, now prosperous things are announced. And as it is said to Israel according to the flesh and to the nations: You nations according to the flesh, who are called uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh; so, on the contrary, there is an Israel according to the spirit, and there are nations according to the spirit, and among the other nations there is a Damascus according to the spirit, lest we rest content with Jewish fables alone.
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city, and shall be as a heap of stones in ruin. The cities of Aroer shall be left for flocks, and they shall rest there, and there shall be none to make them afraid; and help shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts. As was shown in the title, by Damascus is signified the calling of the nations, which loved or drank blood; and once they have believed in Christ, they will cease to be cities of their former way of life, and will be as a heap of stones in ruin. For as heaps of stones that are scattered over the fields are carried together into one mound, so out of all the nations a heap of believers has been gathered at the ruin of the people of the Jews, they falling and we rising.
Commentary on Isaiah

Some think that this prophecy is the same as the one we read in Jeremiah: Damascus is dissolved, it has turned to flight, trembling has seized it, anguish and pains have held it like a woman in labor (Jer 49:24, 27). And again: I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus, and it will devour the ramparts of Ben-hadad. But it must be known that Jeremiah describes the Babylonian captivity of the city of Damascus, that is, of the few whom the king of the Assyrians had left in it; whereas Isaiah announces the captivity by the Assyrians that is close at hand. Others suppose that the Roman captivity is foretold, since the people of the Jews too was taken captive, and Damascus, over which Aretas ruled, endured a like servitude: so that all that is written about it is to be transferred to the time of Christ and to the mysteries of the Apostles.
Commentary on Isaiah

The cities of Aroer, abandoned, will be for flocks. Aroer means tamarisk, which is properly a tree that grows in the wilderness and in salty soil; and by this the devastation is shown. They will rest there: the flocks is understood; and there will be none to frighten them. For the solitude will be so great that not even a robber lying in wait is to be feared.
Commentary on Isaiah

The forsaken cities of AROER (ערוער), that is, of the tamarisk, shall also be for the flocks of the Church, so that we may inhabit those which the Jews forsook; or else, idolatry being destroyed, the Gospel shall be built up. This too we see fulfilled in our own times: the Serapeum at Alexandria and the temple of Marnas at Gaza have risen up as churches of the Lord, and the cities of Aroer have been made ready for the flocks of the Gospel. Aroer, that is, tamarisks, grow in desert places, according to what is written in the curse of the man who trusts in man, and whose heart departs from the Lord: He shall be, it says, like the tamarisk in the desert, and shall not see good when it comes; but he shall dwell in dryness, in the desert, in a land of salt and uninhabitable (Jer 17:6). Others again say that from this tree, by the arts of sorcerers, μίστρα, that is, hatreds, are stirred up. Therefore those who were formerly in the desert of the Gentiles, and in hatred of the Christian name, shall serve the flocks of Christ, which shall rest in them, and there shall be none to make them afraid, because the Lord shall dwell among them, and with the Shepherd present they will not be able to fear the wolf.
Commentary on Isaiah

And help will cease from Ephraim: by no means will the ten tribes have help in it against Judah. And the kingdom from Damascus: ἀπὸ κοινοῦ [from the common or popular edition] will cease is understood. But when he says that the kingdom ceases and rests, he does not signify a perpetual devastation, but takes away for the present the power by which it formerly reigned in all Syria. And the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the sons of Israel, says the Lord of hosts.
