As, he says, the ten tribes were destroyed when the Assyrian ravaged them, and all their glory was led into captivity, so the few who remain in Damascus will imitate them, and will have the glory of their allied nation. Take glory as said by irony, for ignominy. And all this will happen because the Lord has spoken, whose words cannot be made void.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then the help of God shall cease from Ephraim, by whom in this place are understood the Scribes and Pharisees, according to the prophecy of Hosea, who names Ephraim those who are opposed to the people of God (Hos 5 and 8). And the kingdom shall cease from Damascus, so that sin, and the prince of sin, the devil, may no longer reign in Damascus, which formerly loved blood; but the remnant of Syria, that is, those from the nations who have believed, are to be as the children of Israel formerly were, the kingdom of God having been taken from them and given to the nations which bring forth its fruit, as the Lord God of hosts has spoken through all his prophets.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will come to pass in that day, the glory of Jacob will be made thin, and the fat of his flesh will waste away. When, he says, Damascus has been taken and has ceased to be a city, and such glory has crowned it as crowned Israel, that is, the ten tribes, then all the defense, and the fattest flesh, and the refuge of Jacob will waste away: for by no means will he have allies to join with him in laying Jerusalem waste. We have read above that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, and that it was announced to the house of David: Syria has rested upon Ephraim; of whom the Prophet speaks to Ahaz: Do not fear, and let not your heart be afraid of these two tails of smoking firebrands, in the wrath of the fury of Rezin king of Syria and of the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah have taken most evil counsel against you.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it shall come to pass in that day that the glory of Jacob shall be made thin, and the fatness of his flesh shall waste away. And it shall be as one gathering in the harvest what remains, and his arm shall glean the ears, and it shall be as one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there shall be left in it as a cluster of grapes, and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five at its summits, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. After the remnant of Syria has become as the glory of the children of Israel once was, and through their trespass salvation has been given to the nations, then all the glory of the Jews, by which they were glorious in the whole world, shall be made thin, and the fatness of their flesh shall waste away, since they have no prophets, no signs and mighty works, no present help of God, no dignity of the priesthood; but the whole body of their nation shall wither and be brought to nothing.
Commentary on Isaiah

And since it is said of the calling of the nations: The harvest is great, but the labourers are few (Matt 9), those poor ones shall glean the remnants of the harvest, which were saved through the Apostles, and the scantiest ears, not from the mountains and lofty places, but in the valley of Rephaim, that is, in the lowliness of the letter. And consider that Rephaim, which means giants, signifies the Pharisees and Scribes, as Ephraim did above. Indeed, for the valley of Rephaim the Seventy translated the hard valley, to express the hardness of the Jewish heart.
Commentary on Isaiah

And it will be like one gathering in the harvest what has remained, and his arm will gather the ears: and it will be like one seeking ears in the valley of Rephaim. And there will be left in it as it were a cluster, and as at the shaking of an olive tree two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five on its topmost boughs, its fruit, says the Lord God of Israel. Those who understand the present devastation of Damascus as under the Roman empire maintain that these words signify the Apostles: that just as a few ears and olives are wont to remain in the field or on the trees, so the remnant of Israel is saved; especially since there follows: In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, that is, to Christ. The two olives, and three, and four, and five they interpret as fourteen Apostles: that is, the twelve who were chosen, and a thirteenth, James, who is called the brother of the Lord, and also Paul the Apostle, the vessel of election (Acts 9:15). But those who think that what was said was fulfilled in the times of the Assyrians would have it understood thus: that under the Assyrian captivity Damascus was not entirely destroyed, but, when some had been carried away to Cyrene, another part of the tillers of the land was left behind, which itself was afterwards destroyed when the Babylonian laid it waste; until under the Macedonians and the Ptolemies it was restored again, and at the coming of Christ it was indeed a city, but not of such power as it had been before. And the sense is: as few will remain in Damascus as the few ears that commonly remain after the reapers, which the poor are wont to glean in the very broad and very rich valley of Rephaim; or the few olives on the olive tree that have escaped the diligence of the gatherer.
Commentary on Isaiah

Out of their lowliness those who shall be saved are chosen like ears among the stubble and like clusters at the vintage; and as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three olives, or four or five. For when the smiting of the people of the Jews came, that olive tree of the people of Israel, which under Moses had six hundred thousand armed men (Num 26), and under David, when Joab numbered them, a countless people (2 Sam 24), could scarcely offer a few fruits to the Lord the Savior: two olives, Paul and Barnabas; and three olives, Peter and James and John (Acts 13), who both beheld the Lord transfigured on the mountain and were found worthy to go with the Lord to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Matt 17). The four and five olives make up the remaining nine Apostles, among whom Matthias took the place of Judas the betrayer; and these, according to a diversity of graces unknown to us, are divided into four and five olives, so that they might show in themselves the number of the Gospels and the volumes of the Law, as preachers of both Testaments (Acts 1).
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel. And he will not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought: and they will not look to the groves and the shrines. They think that this was fulfilled in the times of Christ, when, the kingdom of Damascus having been destroyed, the everlasting empire of the Savior succeeded, and the error of idolatry was diminished. The intention of these interpreters is indeed pious, but it does not keep the order of the history. We, however, say that, when Damascus had been overthrown and the ten tribes had been led away to the Assyrians, those who were left of the tribes that belonged to Israel turned, at Hezekiah's letters, to the worship of God, and came to the temple at Jerusalem, as the history of Chronicles relates (2 Chr 30). When Damascus has been destroyed, therefore, men will turn to their maker, that is, to him who created them, and their eyes will look by no means to the idols which they had made in Bethel and in Dan, but to God, despising the shrines and altars which their fingers had wrought.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day man shall bow down to his maker, and his eyes shall look to the Holy One of Israel. And he shall not bow down to the altars which his hands have made, and which his fingers have wrought; they shall not look to the groves and the shrines. At that time, when from the people of Israel, to whom it was formerly said, The Lord your God has called you a fruitful olive tree (Jer 11:16), and of whom we read in the Psalms, Your children like young olive plants round about your table (Ps 127 [128]:3), the Lord in his hunger shall scarcely have found, for the drought of spiritual grace, two olives, and three, or four, or five, the fullness of the nations shall come in, and shall bow down not to idols made with hands but to its God, and looking to the Holy One of Israel they shall despise altars and groves and shrines, knowing what is written: Every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Matt 15:13).
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day the cities of its strength will be abandoned like ploughs, and the crops that were abandoned before the face of the sons of Israel, and it will be deserted. He does not say this against Damascus, but against the ten tribes, which were called Israel: that just as, at the coming of the people of God out of Egypt, all the nations that inhabited the land of promise, struck with sudden terror, abandoned their ploughs and the heaps of grain and their work half done, seeking safety in their feet, so the land of Israel too should remain desolate for a long time. Hence I wonder that for ploughs and heaps of grain Aquila chose to translate potsherd and Emir; Symmachus, forest and Amir; the Seventy, the Amorites and the Hivites. Theodotion alone set down the Hebrew word, ARS ET EMIR: which among them is read more correctly HORES (חרש) ET AMIR (והאמיר), that is, ploughshares and heaps of crops.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day the cities of his strength shall be forsaken like ploughs and standing corn, which were forsaken before the face of the children of Israel. And it shall be desolate, because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. LXX: In that day your cities shall be forsaken, as the Amorites and the Hivites forsook them before the face of the children of Israel. And they shall be desolate, because you have forsaken God your Savior, and have not remembered the Lord your helper. As under Moses and Joshua the son of Nun the Amorites and the Hivites, and the other nations that dwelt in the land of promise, forsook their ploughshares and standing corn and the heaps in the fields and fled, lest they be seized by their enemies, so the land of Judea and all its strongest cities were forsaken by their inhabitants when the Romans laid Judea waste and besieged Jerusalem.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore you shall plant a faithful plantation, and shall sow a strange seed. In the day of your planting wild grapes, and in the morning your seed shall flower: the harvest is taken away in the day of inheritance, and he shall grieve grievously. LXX: Therefore you shall plant an unfaithful plantation and an unfaithful seed, and in the day on which you plant you shall go astray. But if you sow in the morning, it shall flower for harvest in the day of inheritance, when, as the father of a man, he gives an inheritance to his sons. Where we, following Aquila and Symmachus and the Seventy, have translated in the day of inheritance, which in Hebrew is BIOM NEHELA (ביום נחלה), one can read in the Hebrew in the worst day. And where Aquila and Theodotion translated and man shall grieve, we, taught by the Hebrews, instead of man, which in their tongue is ENOS, have rendered ANUS (אנוש), that is, grievously. Of the ambiguity of this word we shall treat more fully, if the span of this life allows, in Jeremiah, where according to the Seventy it is said: And he is a man, and who shall know him? Let me say, then, what I set out to say. Because you have forgotten, land of Judea, God your Savior, and have not remembered him who always gave you strength, therefore you shall indeed plant a faithful plantation, or as Aquila and Theodotion translated, a beautiful one, or as Symmachus, a good one, preaching one God; but you shall sow a strange seed, not receiving the Father because you do not receive the Son. For whoever believes in the Father believes also in the Son. And because you have sown the strange seed of blasphemy against Jesus in the synagogues of Satan, therefore you shall not gather the grape at the vintage, but the wild grape. And when your seed shall seem to flower, and to have some shadow of piety, while you draw men away from idols, yet when you come to gather the fruits in the day of inheritance you shall grieve grievously, seeing the people of the nations preferred to you. Whence the Apostle also says: I have great sorrow and unceasing grief in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption of sons, and the giving of the law, and the glory, and the covenant, and the promises; whose are the fathers and so on (Rom 9:2ff.). This not only Paul but every saint says, wishing that, together with the branches of the wild olive, the root too may be saved. Now that inheritance is the one we obtain from the Lord, of which the Apostle says: Now there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all in all. Someone may wonder why, where Aquila and Theodotion and Symmachus translated beautiful and good plantations, we have said a faithful plantation. The Hebrew word NEEMANIM (נאמנים), if it is written with the letter ALEPH, sounds πιστοὺς, that is, faithful; but if with AIN, and pronounced NEAMENIM נעמנים, it signifies beautiful. Hence Naomi too, whose name is written with this letter, says in Ruth (Ruth 1:20): Do not call me NOEMI (נעמי), that is, beautiful, but call me bitter.
Commentary on Isaiah

Because you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper. These things, he says, you will suffer, O Israel, because you have abandoned God your Savior, who freed you from Egypt, who subjected hostile nations to you: and you have not remembered your helper.

Therefore you will plant a faithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot. This is to be read more pointedly and as irony. Because, he says, you have forgotten God your Savior, and have not remembered your strong helper: will you on that account have to plant a faithful planting, and not rather sow a foreign shoot, for the enemy to snatch away? Or certainly thus: my sons, who were begotten from the stock of my people, you have established in the land for this purpose, that you might make them foreign and most wicked.
Commentary on Isaiah

And an apostrophe is made to the land of Judea itself, that is, to those who dwelt in it: You have suffered all these things because you have forgotten God your Savior, which means Jesus, whose coming to you the Law and the Prophets continually announced; and you have not remembered your strong helper, who was always your succour. The cause, then, of the desolate cities of Judea is forgetfulness of the Savior, who had said at the beginning of this Prophet: Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood.
Commentary on Isaiah

In the day of your planting, wild grapes, and in the morning your seed will flower. The harvest has been taken away in the day of inheritance, and it will grieve grievously. These, he says, are the fruits of your works that you will reap: your vine of Sorek will degenerate into wild grapes, your seed will hold out hope in the blade; but when ripeness has come, it will be reaped by another. And then you will grieve grievously, when you lose what you hoped for and almost already held.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to the multitude of many peoples; like the multitude of the roaring sea, and the tumult of the crowds, like the sound of many waters, they shall roar. The peoples shall roar like the multitude of overflowing waters; and he shall rebuke him, and he shall flee far off, and he shall be carried away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the tempest. At eventide, behold, trouble; in the morning, and he shall not stand. This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. Above, under the name of Damascus, we read of the calling of the nations, and the casting off of the Jews, and, through the Apostles and in the Apostles, the election of the few of the Jews who believed. And since, in comparison with the whole world and all the nations, only a small part believed of the Christian people, of whom it was said above: And the remnant of Syria shall be as the glory of the children of Israel (for many (Matt 22:14) are called, but few are chosen); and: Not all have faith (2 Thess 3:2): now there follows in due order, not a lament, but a woe to those nations which had refused to believe and persecuted the Christian people. And they are compared to the masses of the waves and to the raging sea, which, as far as in it lies, longs to overwhelm and seize everything.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to the multitude of many peoples, like the multitude of the roaring sea: and the tumult of crowds, like the sound of many waters: the peoples will roar like the sound of flooding waters: and he will rebuke him, and he will flee far off: and he will be snatched away like the dust of the mountains before the wind, and like a whirlwind before the storm. At eventide: and behold, confusion in the morning, and he will not endure. This is the portion of those who have laid us waste, and the lot of those who plunder us. Those who suppose that the earlier captivity of Damascus was brought on by the Romans refer this also that is written: Man will bow down to his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, to the times of Christ and of the Apostles. And what follows as well: You will plant a faithful planting, and you will sow a foreign shoot: in the day of your planting, wild grapes, and the rest, they take to concern the unbelief of the Jews. And this passage which we have now set out they interpret of the heathen, who persecute the Church. What follows too, He will rebuke him, and he will flee far off, they take of the devil, showing by a tropological interpretation the devastation of the persecutors and of the demons. But we follow the order we have begun, and cover historical foundations with a historical roof. Woe, he says, to all the nations that have made war against my people, whose onslaught was so great that it must be likened to the waves of the sea. But when they have come raging and have flooded my land, then their prince Sennacherib will flee from him, rebuked; and as dust is scattered when the wind snatches it, and a whirlwind is rolled on high in a storm, so he will indeed approach Jerusalem, besieging it, but he will be struck by the Angel; he will come in the morning, and will see the army of his power destroyed. And this will be the portion of those who have laid us waste. The Prophet says this either in the person of the people, or joining himself to his nation (2 Kgs 19:35-36). Afterwards we read: The Angel of the Lord went out, and struck in the camp of the Assyrians one hundred and eighty-five thousand: and they arose in the morning, and behold, all were the corpses of the dead. And Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went out, and departed, and returned, and dwelt in Nineveh.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the peoples shall roar in the spectacles of theatrical licence, and in the cruelty of the amphitheatre, and in the frenzies of the circus, like the sound of overflowing waters, when with a voice concordant in impiety they blaspheme and cry that the Christians be thrown to the lions and the beasts, and other things of the kind. But while they rage like the sea, the Lord shall rebuke the author of their sedition and drive him away from his people. And as dust stirred up on the mountains is carried off the more violently the higher it is, and as a whirlwind that rises from the earth is borne aloft by a sudden tempest, so he too shall be carried off and separated from the people of God and shall flee, lest he be banished to the abyss.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when the day of consummation comes, which is what evening means, then there shall be trouble for him as he recognizes his own sins. And at morning time, that is, on the day of the resurrection, he shall not stand, which the Seventy translated shall not be. But if he shall not be, what will they answer who grant the devil repentance and, as far as in them lies, promise him the summit of an archangel? This is the portion of those who have wasted us, and the lot of those who plunder us. These words are spoken either by the Christian people, or by the prophet in the person of the believing people: that their persecutors, who oppressed the saints of God with exiles, prisons and confiscations of goods, shall have eternal destruction and shall possess everlasting punishments.

n: Cymbal. Or sistrum, commonly used in Egypt. Septuagint, "ship sails." --- Ethiopia, or Chus, lying between the Nile (the branches of which are styled rivers) and the Red Sea. He alludes to the kingdom of Tharaca, 4 Kings xix. 8. (Calmet)

Ambassadors. Hebrew, "images," (Bochart) in honour of Adonis; (St. Cyril) or rather Ezechias, or Tharaca send to demand troops. (Calmet) --- Bulrushes. Literally, "paper." (Haydock) --- Formed of rushes which grow on the banks of the Nile. (Pliny, [Natural History?] vii. 56., and xiii. 11.) --- Angels. Or messengers. --- Pieces. With factions after the death of Sabacon, or by the inroads of Sennacherib. --- Other. He derides the vanity of the Egyptians. (Calmet) --- Expecting the overflowing of the Nile. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "of line," (Calmet) with which they marked out each person's property, after the waters had subsided. (Strabo 17.) --- Foot. They worked their dough with their feet, and sent swine to trample on the seed, which required no more cultivation. (Herodotus ii. 14., and 36.) --- Spoiled. The Nile made considerable alterations.

Place. God rules all with ease. --- Harvest. The allies shall comfort my people, (Calmet) or Sennacherib shall threaten ruin. (Haydock) --- But I will frustrate his evil designs. His army shall perish unexpectedly, ver. 5. (Calmet) --- The Egyptians had sent messengers to assure the Israelites that they would come to assist them: but the prophet informs them of their own ruin. (Worthington)
Them. Their bodies shall lie unburied.
Sion. Egypt shall send presents to the Lord, 2 Paralipomenon xxxii. 23. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to the land, the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia. The Hebrew word SELSEL (צלצל), which Symmachus interpreted as sound and Theodotion as birds, we have rendered as cymbal. Aquila translated double shadow. But it must be known that a shadow is called SEL (צל), and here the syllable itself is doubled. From this we can understand the saying thus: Woe to the land that promises help in the shadow of its wings. And whereas Scripture says: He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven (Ps 90 [91]:1), for which in the Hebrew is written, He will abide in the shadow of the Almighty, this land, boasting that it has the very likeness of God, promises, though itself set in dangers, to give support to others. And it signifies either No, the city of Egypt which is now called Alexandria, or Egypt, on which Jerusalem always leaned as on a shaken reed, which, when it breaks, pierces the hand of the one who leans on it. And here the order is most beautiful: that just as in the former Vision the prophetic word threatened Damascus, because the ten tribes had help in it, asking God's mercy, so now too devastation is foretold to Egypt, for the sake of whose help the invocation of God was neglected. For this is the land which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, that is, beyond the streams of the river Nile, which no one doubts flows from Ethiopia into Egypt. Egypt can be called the cymbal of wings because of the swiftness of its crops: for the swift and rapid flight of birds gives back the sound of a cymbal. Some, from what follows: Who sends envoys by sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters, understand the Roman empire, and refer the whole history to the times of Vespasian and Titus, by whom Jerusalem was overthrown. But it does not accord with our faith that the Lord should threaten the Roman empire for having overthrown an impious nation, and then say that gifts are to be brought to Mount Zion; unless perhaps we take these things too spiritually, of the Church.
Commentary on Isaiah

Woe to the land, the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors by the sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters: go, swift Angels, to a nation torn away and rent asunder, to a terrible people, after which there is no other, to a nation waiting, waiting and trodden down, whose land the rivers have plundered. All you inhabitants of the world, who dwell on the earth, when the sign has been lifted up on the mountains you shall see, and you shall hear the blast of the trumpet. LXX: Woe to the land of the wings of ships beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, you who send hostages by the sea, and letters of papyrus upon the water. For swift messengers shall go to a lofty nation, and to a foreign and most wicked people, which is beyond it: a nation without hope, and trodden down; now the rivers of the whole earth as a region that is inhabited: their region shall be inhabited, as if a sign were lifted up from the mountain, and the voice of the trumpet were heard. I have set down both editions in a most obscure prophecy, so that nothing may seem to be lacking to those who wish to understand what is written. And at the same time I greatly marvel at those who think that our faith and Christian hope are content with simplicity, because it is written: The commandment of God is clear, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9), and that we ought to seek nothing more than that what is commanded be done; whereas the whole of Scripture, and the Prophets especially, are wrapped in the mysteries of things to come precisely in order to rouse us to understanding, and to what is said in the Gospel: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. Since, then, I have expounded it in the fifth book according to the history and what is contained in the Hebrew, I shall now set out what seems to me according to the anagogy. A prudent reader may perhaps ask what is meant, in the Vision or Burden of Damascus, by the cymbal of wings and the other things that follow. After it had been said of the calling of the nations, of the casting off of the Jews, and of the election of those who believed through the Apostles, and afterwards of the multitude of the nations and the persecutors, who were compared to the waves of the sea, it followed that the prophetic word should also announce the heresies which have troubled the Church and lay it waste to this day, which, while the householder slept, oversowed tares in the field of the Church (Matt 13). And they are called a cymbal, as not having the love of God, according to that saying of the Apostle: If I speak with the tongues of men and of Angels, but have not love, I have become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal (1 Cor 13:1). And they are called not only a cymbal clashing with a harsh sound, but, because of the lightness of heretical speech running off in different directions, a cymbal of wings, or according to the Seventy, wings of ships, since, promising great merchandise, they sail on the waves of this world. By the wings of ships understand the sails by which they are lifted and drawn along. And he fittingly said wings of ships, for every heretic promises lofty things, and though he boasts that he has wings, he nevertheless sticks fast in the salt waves, and does not go far from land, and in mid-course suddenly suffers shipwreck. Hence Aquila translated, instead of cymbal, shadow of wings, for they do not have wings, but a likeness of wings. And what he adds, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, signifies that the heretics surpass all in their impiety. For example: Epicurus says that there is no providence, and that pleasure is the highest good. In comparison with him Marcion is more wicked, and all the heretics who tear the Old Testament to pieces. For while they admit providence, they accuse the Creator, and assert that he erred in very many of his works and did not make them as he ought to have made them: for to what benefit of men, they ask, do serpents, scorpions, crocodiles, and fleas, bugs and gnats belong?
Commentary on Isaiah

But according to the Seventy the wings of the heretics are bewailed, which flit like ships over the sea of this world and surpass the impiety of the heathen, whom the Scripture now calls Ethiopians; and it is said to their teaching and speech: You who send books on the sea of this world, the hostages of your perversity, and letters to deceive those who will read them. Swift messengers go to a lofty nation, and to a foreign and most wicked people. For none of the churchmen has as much zeal for good as the heretics have for evil, and they think they gain a profit if they deceive others, and, being lost themselves, destroy the rest. Now the nation is called lofty on account of its pride, and foreign and most wicked because it is estranged from God. Truly a nation without hope, and trodden down, whose rivers throughout the whole earth imitate the dwelling of the Church, so that they may find themselves a lodging and a region in which to lift up the sign of their teaching, in which to sound the trumpet of the Scriptures.
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 2:3.18

Someone might wonder and say to himself, "Why does the prophetic oracle addressed to Damascus now mention the land that is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia?" At certain times the Israelites foolishly abandoned God the Savior of all and fell into the error of worshiping many gods. Paying no heed whatsoever to the law given by Moses, they were chastised by God, at times through foes who rose up against them and at times by other catastrophes. Although they should have repented and been healed, ceased their wicked way, walked in the commandments and sought help from God, they made alliances with their neighbors, first with the kings in Damascus, then with those in Egypt. Not only this. They also embraced the gods of the nations that had come to their aid and wasted no time in emulating their ways. Hence the prophet now turns his attention to the Egyptians.The Israelites, in particular those living in Jerusalem, had approached the Egyptians and pleaded with them to become allies. They needed their support because they were being invaded by the Babylonians. As God says in the words of the prophet, "Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who trust in horses and chariots." The Egyptians were zealous in their devotion to idols. Therefore he calls them a people desperate and beaten down. Desperate because they did not know the one who is by nature truly God, beaten down because they had allowed their minds to become subject to the deceptions of demons, trodden down under their feet.
Commentary on Isaiah

Who sends envoys by sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters. Go, swift messengers, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a terrible people, after whom there is no other, to a nation waiting and trampled down, whose land the rivers have plundered. Among the Hebrews Egypt, and the Egyptian, and the Egyptians are all called by one word, MESRAIM (מצרים). Let this be said lest anyone stick at the word when he finds the masculine in place of the feminine, that is, the man in place of the land; for now too it is said: Who sends envoys by sea, that is, Mesraim herself, the Egyptian himself: because from Alexandria, which was then, as we have said, called No, envoys were sent to Jerusalem, and, in vessels of papyrus, that is, in letters, or else in ships, promising them their help, they said: Go swiftly to the Jews' convulsed nation, torn by the attack of the Assyrians: to a people once terrible, which enjoyed the command of God, to whose power no other is to be compared: to a nation which always waited for the help of God, and nevertheless is trampled down by men: whose land the rivers, that is, various kings, have ravaged. Others, however, think that the apostrophe is directed to the Lord, and that the sense is: O God, who send the Prophets into the sea of this world, and, admonishing the people through letters as if by men under sail, command your messengers: Go swiftly to my nation, torn and convulsed, to a most mighty people, which was once a terror to all the nations round about, which always waited for the help of God, and, because of the greatness of its sins, does not deserve to receive what it hopes for: whose land the kings of various nations have laid waste, and the rest that follows. Eusebius of Caesarea, promising a historical interpretation in his title, wanders off into various senses; and when I read his books, I found something very different from what he promised in the heading. For wherever the history fails him, he passes over to allegory, and joins together things so far apart that I marvel at his combining stone and iron into one body by a new architecture of speech. I have given this brief warning lest anyone think that we have borrowed what we say from his springs; for in the present passage too he says that the prophecy is directed against the Jews and Jerusalem, because at the beginning of the Christian faith they sent letters to all the nations that they should not accept the passion of Christ, and sent them as far as Ethiopia and the Western region, and filled the whole world with the spreading of this blasphemy.
Commentary on Isaiah

These, then, are beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and they send ambassadors on the sea of this world, that is, their disciples, who, carrying their volumes, are rightly said to carry vessels of papyrus, that is, of paper, upon the waters, which are quickly blotted out. For as books by water and damp are soon dimmed, blotted out and perish, so their speech and teaching, though at the beginning it seemed to possess some strength, passes away and slips by. And so it is said to them ironically: O Angels of the heretics, go swiftly. These the blessed apostle Paul calls false apostles, deceitful workers, who transform themselves into Apostles of Christ (2 Cor 11). And go to a nation torn away and rent asunder: torn away from God and mangled by the bites of the heretics. To a terrible people; for nothing is more terrible than blasphemy, which sets its mouth on high. After which there is no other people: for every sin, compared with blasphemy, is lighter. A nation waiting, waiting and trodden down. For all the heretics promise themselves heavenly things and pledge great things, and yet they are trodden down by demons. Whose land the rivers have plundered, rivers which have their waters not from heaven but from the earth. For what corner is there, what remotest wilderness of the earth, which the turbid speech of the heretics does not reach?
Commentary on Isaiah

All you inhabitants of the world who dwell on the earth, when the signal has been raised on the mountains, you will see, and you will hear the blast of the trumpet. All you nations round about, he says, when you hear my command like a signal raised on the mountains, and my order like the blast of a trumpet resounding on high, then you will see what I have commanded.
Commentary on Isaiah

And so all who inhabit and dwell in the world lift up their eyes to the sign of the heretics, which is lifted up as it were on the mountains, and hear the blast of the trumpet, that is, of their teaching. So much according to the Hebrew.
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus says the Lord to me: I will rest, and I will consider in my place. What is it that the Lord spoke to the Prophet? What follows: until the things I have commanded come about, I will rest in my seat: as the Jews think, in the Temple; as we think, in the heavens. And I will consider, he says, what end of things is coming.

As the noonday light is clear, and as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest. Just as in the whole day nothing is clearer than noon, when the sun glows from mid-heaven and lights up the whole world alike; and just as in the heat and scorching warmth, when the naked reaper is baked and his panting attests the greatness of his labor, the coolness of the dew is most welcome, if the morning moisture makes the dry stalks easy to cut: so my word, which I will consider in my place, will come welcome to all who believe in me.
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus says the Lord to me: I will rest, and I will consider in my place, as the noonday light is clear, and as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest. For before the harvest it has all blossomed, and an unripe perfection shall bud, and its twigs shall be cut off with sickles; and what is left shall be cut away and shaken off. And they shall be left together to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth, and the birds shall be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon it. At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn away and rent asunder, from a terrible people, after which there was no other, from a nation waiting, waiting and trodden down, whose land the rivers have plundered, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion. God rests and contemplates in his place, or according to Aquila, in his firmament, that is, in the Church, of which the apostle Paul says: The pillar and firmament of truth (1 Tim 3:15). And he contemplates the things that are done in the Church, and as the noonday light is clear, so he surveys all things, according to what is said in the eighteenth Psalm, according to the anagogy, of the sun of righteousness: Nor is there anyone who can hide himself from its heat (Ps 18 [19]:7). And as a cloud of dew in the day of harvest and in the burning summer is most welcome, so the Lord refreshes the dwellers of his Church, and in his presence all things flourish.
Commentary on Isaiah

For before the harvest it has wholly blossomed, and an unripe perfection has budded, and its little branches will be cut off with pruning hooks, and what is left will be cut away and shaken off. And they will be left together to the birds of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth, and the birds will be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts of the earth will winter upon it. Because he had spoken of noon, and had mentioned beforehand a cloud of dew in summer and harvest, and had taken his metaphor from husbandry, he keeps it in the rest, describing the pride of Egypt and the devastation of its people, and the corpses throughout the whole province which are to be devoured by birds. For as crops that burst forth before ripeness quickly perish, and, budding before the fullness of their time comes, are useless, so, he says, the peoples of Egypt will be cut off with pruning hooks like useless branches, and all the offshoots will be stripped bare.
Commentary on Isaiah

And before the time of the consummation comes, since now we know in part and prophesy in part, many will be found perfect, of whom the Apostle says: Let as many of us as are perfect be of this mind (1 Cor 13; Phil 3:15). But the twigs that are useless shall be cut off with sickles, as the Savior says in the Gospel: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take it away; and every one that bears fruit he will prune, that it may bear more fruit (John 15:2).
Commentary on Isaiah

And lest you should think he speaks of a vine and not of men, he turns the metaphor into the truth of history: And they will be left, he says, together to the birds of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth. For birds and beasts devour not the cut branches of trees, but corpses. Let us read Ezekiel more fully, where he prophesies against Pharaoh and against Egypt, and we shall find all these things written most plainly (Ezek 29). And when he says: The birds will be upon it all summer long, and all the beasts will winter upon it, he either truly signifies the multitude of the slain, or shows through the same metaphor that it is to be laid waste by all the nations.
Commentary on Isaiah

And those that have been cut off shall be left to the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth: to the birds which ravage what is sown by the wayside, and to the beasts to which the soul that does not confess God is delivered; so that whoever has been cut off and cast away by the Lord, and separated from his body, which is the Church, becomes, in summer as in winter, that is, in prosperity and adversity, the dwelling of birds and beasts.
Commentary on Isaiah

At that time a gift will be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn away and torn apart, from a terrible people, after whom there has been no other: from a nation waiting, waiting and trampled down, whose land the rivers have plundered, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion. After the devastation of Egypt and the destruction of its empire, Israel will by no means trust in the vanity of its shadow, but will return to the Lord, and will bring its gifts to Mount Zion, that is, to his temple, entreating him alone, whose protection is true and eternal. And we understand this to have been done under Zerubbabel and Joshua, and Ezra and Nehemiah. The Seventy, for what we have said, waiting, waiting, where in the Hebrew is written hoping, hoping, translated to the contrary ἀνέλπιστον, that is, not hoping. And for this reason they gave Eusebius occasion to think that this is to be understood of the nations, which have neither hope, nor the Testament of God, nor the Prophets, rather than of the Jews: that gifts were afterwards to be sent by them to the Church, which is set upon a watchtower, and spiritual victims offered.
Commentary on Isaiah

But as those who are useless and unfruitful in the Church are cut off and cast out, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump, so on the contrary it may come about that those who had been deceived by heretical error, torn away from the Lord and rent, terrible on account of blasphemy, vainly awaiting lies, trodden down by demons, and scattered by the rivers in various directions, when they remember their God and forsake their most wicked masters, may offer a gift to the Lord of hosts nowhere else but on Mount Zion, and in the watchtower, which is interpreted as the Church. We speak more briefly because we have already said much in the book of the historical explanation.

n: Egypt. Many refer this to the coming of Christ, (Calmet) at whose presence the idols fell down, and many saints adorned the country. (Worthington) --- But the prophet may also literally refer to the wars of the Assyrians against Egypt. Sabacon having retired, after reigning fifty years, Anysis, and afterwards the priest of Sethon, succeeded to the throne. The latter was attacked by Sennacherib. After his death, twelve kingdoms were formed, but Psammitichus reunited them, and had Nechao for his successor. (Herodotus ii. 141, 158.) --- Behold. The prophet speaks fourteen years before the attack of Sennacherib. --- Cloud. Psalm xvii. 11. Some Fathers explain it of the blessed Virgin [Mary]. (Calmet) --- Moved. Plundered by the Assyrians. (Menochius)
Kingdom. Under the twelve kings. (Calmet)
Egypt. Septuagint, "of the Egyptians shall be troubled within them." (Haydock) --- Soothsayers. Feeble but too common resource of superstitious people!
Masters. Twelve kings. Psammitichus, one of them, shall gain the ascendancy.
Dry. The lakes and the Nile shall not afford sufficient moisture. (Calmet) --- If the Nile rose less than twelve or more than sixteen cubits famine ensued. (Pliny, [Natural History?] xviii. 18.)
Fountain. The Nile rises in Ethiopia. But the canals alone were left dry. (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "the achi, every green herb along the river, and every," &c. (Haydock)
Fishers. The lake Mœris produced a talent every day for the revenue, and so great was the abundance of fish, that they could hardly be salted. The Nile was also well supplied with fish.
Linen. Greek, "silk." Ezechiel xvi. 10. (Calmet)

All they. Septuagint, "and all who make strong drink (secer) shall be in sorrow, and shall afflict their souls." (Haydock) --- This version is perhaps the best, as the Egyptians used much ale or wine distilled from barley. (Calmet)
Tanis. Or of the twelve kings, ver. 1. They are disconcerted at the approach of Psammitichus, (Calmet) or at the want of water. (Haydock)
Memphis. The seat of many kings, and a very ancient city. Hebrew, "Noph." --- Stay. Literally, "angle," denoting the chiefs, or all the land, Judges xx. 2.
Back. King and subject are equally confused, chap. ix. 14. (Calmet)
Terror. Hebrew also, "a rejoicing," (St. Jerome) on account of Sennacherib's defeat there, chap. xviii. 7.

Chanaan. Hebrew. The Israelites had a connection with Egypt, which the prophets often blame, chap. xxx. 2. Ezechias trusted in their aid, when he refused to pay tribute to the Assyrians. Many at that time, or afterwards, retired thither, and served God unmolested, chap. xi. 2., and Jeremias xlii. More established themselves in the country under Alexander [the Great] and the Ptolemies. (3 Machabees viii.) But this prediction was more fully accomplished by the propagation of the Christian religion. Grace no where shone forth more brightly than in this country, once the seat of superstition. --- Sun. Hebrew, "of desolation." But the copies have varied. It is supposed to denote the city On, Genesis xli. 45. (Calmet) --- Prideaux (p. 2. b. 4.) accuses the Jews of willfully corrupting this text in the Septuagint. (Kennicott)

Altar. If the Jews were forbidden to have any other than the one at Jerusalem, how can the prophet announce this as a blessing? Onias being excluded from the high priesthood, retired into Egypt, and obtained leave to build the temple Onion, in the Nome, though not in the city of Helipolis, above Bubaste, on the Nile, alleging that Isaias had foretold this event, and that one was already built at Leontopolis. (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities xii. 15., and xiii. 6.) --- But we must allow with the fathers and Jews in the days of St. Jerome, that this prediction regarded the Messias, when altars might be lawfully erected in every nation. See Misna, tr. Moneuth, xiii. 10. --- Monument. The cross is set up wherever Christ is adored. (Calmet) --- The Egyptians shall embrace Christianity, and St. Anthony of Thebes, &c., shall live a holy (Worthington) and austere life. (Haydock)
Them. The Jews were miraculously rescued from the hands of Philopater, (Josephus, contra Apion ii.) or rather Christians are delivered from sin and Satan.

Egypt. The kings often caused sacrifices to be offered for them; but they were not acceptable, as long as they continued idolaters. The country was converted to Christianity, (Calmet) and the Anchorets performed their vows and penitential exercises, to the admiration of all. (Haydock)
Scourge. By means of Sennacherib, Cambyses, and Ochus. Afterwards the country was quietly subject to the kings of Persia, Alexander the Great, the Ptolemies, and the Romans. (Calmet)
Land. The apostles, who were true Israelites, (Haydock) procured the blessing of faith for these nations, (Calmet) to serve God with concord. (Haydock)

f: AN ANSWER TO THE JEWS 9
Egypt is sometimes understood to mean the whole world in [Isaiah], because of superstition and malediction.
Hippolytus Exegetical Fragments

Under Egypt he meant the world, and under things made with hands its idolatry, and under the shaking its subversion and dissolution. And the Lord, the Word, he represented as upon a light cloud, referring to that most pure tabernacle, in which setting up His throne, our Lord Jesus Christ came into the world to shake error.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 50

Consider also, in the vision of Egypt, Isaiah saying: "behold the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and he will come into Egypt", whether he means this Egypt which is commonly understood, or the whole world. For according to John himself, the place "in which their Lord was crucified" "is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt", whether the whole world or Judea is called Sodom and Egypt. But he who upon a light cloud will come into Egypt, will first make his ascent into Judea (for it is according to reason that, when he comes again, it should first happen there). But it is called "Sodom" "where their Lord was crucified", just as also once it was said to that people and their princes: "hear the word of the Lord, princes of Sodom; attend to the law of God, people of Gomorrah".
Exposition on Psalm 118, 19.6

Hear, for the flesh of the Lord was a shadow: Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and will come to Egypt. And David says: Protect me under the shadow of your wings. Therefore, he became a shadow emptied for us, whom the sun of iniquity had burned. We saw him in the shadow when faith first advanced. But now he illuminates the whole world: and yet we still see him through the shadow of his body, which is the Church, not yet face to face; for the eyes of the body are unable to receive the brightness of divinity. This shadow also protects the entire world every day. Therefore, the conclusion is beneficial; For God has concluded all in unbelief, that he may have mercy upon all.
Homily 56 on the Gospel of Matthew

What then? He Himself speaks nothing, nor Moses, nor Elias, but He that is greater than all, and more worthy of belief, the Father, uttereth a voice out of the cloud. Wherefore out of the cloud? Thus doth God ever appear. "For a cloud and darkness are round about Him;" and, "He sitteth on a light cloud;" and again, "Who maketh clouds His chariot;" and, "A cloud received Him out of their sight;" and, "As the Son of Man coming in the clouds." In order then that they might believe that the voice proceeds from God, it comes from thence. And the cloud was bright.
Homily 2 on the Acts of the Apostles

That it was Jesus himself [at the ascension] they knew from the fact that he had been conversing with them (for had they seen only from a distance, they could not have recognized him by sight), but that he is taken up into heaven the angels themselves inform them. Observe how it is ordered, that not all is done by the Spirit, but the eyes also do their part. But why did "a cloud receive him"? This too was a sure sign that he went up to heaven. Not fire, as in the case of Elijah, nor fiery chariot, but "a cloud received him"; which was a symbol of heaven, as the prophet says, "Who makes the clouds his chariot"; it is of the Father himself that this is said. Therefore he says, "on a cloud"; in the symbol, he would say, of the divine power, for no other power is seen to appear on a cloud. For hear again what another prophet says: "The Lord sits upon a light cloud."
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt, and the images of Egypt will be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt will waste away in its midst. It is the custom of the Scriptures to append plain things to obscure ones, and to bring out in open speech what they had first said in enigmas. Hence in the present place too, because he had threatened Egypt: Woe to the land that overshadows with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and the rest that the prophetic discourse wove together, he now makes the understanding plainer, and speaks with threats to Egypt itself: that not through angels but the Lord himself comes upon a light cloud, that is, a swift one, and enters Egypt, and the idols of Egypt tremble, and the heart of the strong wastes away, and the prophecy of Ezekiel is fulfilled: I will destroy the images, and I will make the idols cease from Memphis (Ezek 30:13). Some refer this whole prophecy to the times of the Savior, when he entered upon a light cloud, that is, the human body which he had taken from the Virgin, weighed down by no seed of human intercourse; or that he was carried by a light cloud, that is, by the virginal body, and at his entry all the demons trembled, and then came the first ruin of the idols, unable to bear the presence of the Lord.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Egypt. Symmachus and Theodotion: The taking up of Egypt. LXX: The vision of Egypt. Where in the Hebrew is written MASSA MESRAIM (משא מצרים), which we have translated The burden or weight of Egypt, for which Aquila rendered ἄρμα Αἰγύπτου, we may say that because the prophet takes up and carries the yoke of the Lord, he proved worthy to behold, or to bear, the prophecy of Egypt. Hence I marvel that the Seventy, both in Babylon translated Vision for Weight, and in Philistia and Moab and Damascus Word, and now in Egypt Vision, when in the Hebrew in all these places what is set down is not Word and Vision but MASSA (משא), that is, Burden and weight. And as for Symmachus and Theodotion always translating λῆμμα, that is, a taking up, we ought to know that the prophet received spiritual grace from the Lord to know the mysteries of Egypt, or to behold them with the eyes of the mind, as the Seventy translated. But this Egypt is not the one the Jews suppose, as Josephus thought, who relates in the books of the Antiquities that the priest Onias fulfilled the oracle of Isaiah by building in the district of Heliopolis, which the Egyptians call a νομὸν, a temple after the likeness of the Temple of God, and an altar. For suppose we grant that these things were said of Onias and the altar he built in Egypt: what will be the five cities in Egypt that speak the Canaanite tongue, of which one according to the Seventy is called ἀσεδὲκ, and according to the other translators the city ARS or ARES, or the city of the sun? And who will be this savior who was sent to the Egyptians to save them, so that the Egyptians might know the Lord? When did they worship him with sacrifices and gifts, and pay their vows? When did the Lord strike Egypt and heal it? At what time shall we be able to show it happened that there was a way from Egypt to the Assyrians, and that the Assyrians entered Egypt, and the Egyptians the Assyrians, and that the Egyptians served Assur? When was Israel the third in Egypt, and among the Assyrians as a blessing in the midst of the earth, so that the Lord should say: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands the Assyrian? It is plain that these things do not belong to that Egypt which the Jews suppose. And so this place which we inhabit, and the world which lies in the evil one, we may call Egypt, especially because MESRAIM (מצרים), which is called Egypt, means ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, afflicting, or reducing to straits. Yet we must know that many things of the Burden, or Vision, of Egypt belong to the province of Egypt, which is inhabited and seen to this day. But both in this and in other places of the Scriptures very many things are set down which could not stand according to the history, so that by the necessity of the matter we are compelled to seek a higher understanding.
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, the Lord shall go up upon a light cloud, and shall enter into Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt in the midst of it. And I will make the Egyptians clash against the Egyptians, and a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, city against city, kingdom against kingdom. And the spirit of Egypt shall be broken in its bowels, and I will cast down its counsel; and they shall consult their idols and their diviners, and those with familiar spirits, and the soothsayers. And I will deliver Egypt into the hands of cruel lords, and a strong king shall rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts. Most of the prophecy of Egypt, which Isaiah took up or saw, I touched upon in the historical explanation; so now, according to tropology, only the chief points are to be gathered. The Lord went up upon a light cloud, the body of the holy Virgin Mary, which was weighed down by no burden of human seed; or certainly his own body, which was conceived of the Holy Spirit. And he entered into the Egypt of this world, and at once all the idols of Egypt were moved, so that divinations and the whole fraud of idolatry, which held possession of a deceived world, felt itself broken; so much so that the magi from the East, taught by the demons, or understanding from the prophecy of Balaam (Num 24) that the Son of God was born who would destroy all the power of their art, came to Bethlehem, and, the star showing the way, worshipped the child (Matt 2).
Commentary on Zechariah

And in Isaiah we read that the Lord came into Egypt on a light cloud. Egypt is taken as the world, into which the Lord is recorded to have descended in the flesh, which, brought forth from a virginal womb, was weighed down by no weight of human seed and of sins.
City of God 8.23

It is relevant to recall that holy Isaiah uttered a particular prophecy concerning Egypt: "And the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt within them" and the rest.In the same class with these prophets were those who rejoiced because they knew he had come whom they had been expecting. Such were Simeon and Anna, who recognized Jesus when he was born, and Elizabeth, who, in the Spirit, realized that he had been conceived, and Peter, who, by revelation of the Father, affirmed, "You are the Christ, the son of the living God."
Homilies on the Gospels 2:15

The psalmist spoke of this solemnity [when he said], "God has ascended with a shout of jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet." He ascended with a shout of jubilation, since he sought heaven as the disciples rejoiced in the glory of his being lifted up. He ascended with the sound of the trumpet, since he went up to the throne of his heavenly kingdom as the angels heralded his return to judge the living and the dead.How God, who is present always and everywhere and does not change from place to place, ascended, the same [inspired writer] declares elsewhere, saying, "He who makes a cloud his stairway and walks upon the wings of the winds." He calls the substance of human weakness with which "the sun of righteousness" clothed himself, that [the sight of him] might be borne by human beings, a cloud. Hence Isaiah says, "Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before his face." The Lord ascended upon a swift cloud so that when he entered Egypt he might overturn its idols when "the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us." He took upon himself a body immune from all stains of iniquity and entered the world in it, so that he might destroy the cult of idolatry and make clear the true light of divinity to the shadowy and dark hearts of the Gentiles. He who is not enclosed in a place willed to go from place to place by means of this cloud, his human nature; in it he who always remains invisible in his divinity willed to suffer mockery, scourging and death; by means of it he who fills the heavens in the power of his divinity ascended into heaven, crowned with the power of his resurrection.
Commentary on the Song of Songs 3:4.15

Such brief downpours are rightly compared with the shallow, inflated boasting of secular teaching which often seems to pour forth an endless, deep river of eloquence and broad learning but soon dries up entirely, as though it had never existed at all, where the sun of justice and the summer of evangelical radiance shine. The Lord himself laments this state of affairs through the prophet: "They abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns which cannot hold water." Isaiah also says, "Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will come to Egypt," and again, "The water of the sea will dry up and the river will be desolate and arid." "A well of living waters," he said, "which flows from Lebanon," that is, from the church, whose life is both clear and deep. For Lebanon, which means "clarity," fills its camps with saving streams of wisdom for its subjects, as though they were an audience, like the Lord promises in the Gospel: "Whoever believes in me, as Scripture teaches, 'rivers of living water will flow from his heart.' " Explaining this, the Gospel adds, "He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him would receive."
On the Gospel of Luke 1:1.35

The blessed Virgin, being purely human, was unable to receive bodily all the plenitude of divinity. But the power of the Most High overshadowed her, that is, her body received the incorporeal light of divinity. The prophet comments on this beautifully: "Behold, the Lord will ascend upon on a light cloud and will come to Egypt," which is to say, Behold, the coeternal Word of God the Father, the light from light who was born before the ages, will receive at the end of the age a flesh and soul not burdened with any sin, and he will enter the world from a virginal womb, like a bridegroom from his chamber. Therefore, what will be born will be called holy, the Son of God. In distinction from our holiness, Jesus alone is said to be born holy.
On the Gospel of Luke 4:12.51

But if the entire world is divided against itself with respect to faith in Christ, each home contains both infidels and believers. A good war is waged, therefore, to disrupt an evil peace. Isaiah also announced prophetically under the figure of Egypt: "Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will come to Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence and the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them, and I will cause Egyptians to attack Egyptians." Clearly this refers to a struggle between proponents of the faith and its enemies.
Commentary on Isaiah

And I will make Egyptians rush against Egyptians, and a man will fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom. When the Lord has entered Egypt and destroys a most powerful nation by his presence, the first victory will be that Egyptians fall out with Egyptians and fight one another with rebellious hatred: which, it is clear, came about in the times of the Assyrians and of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, some sitting still and others resisting. And that he foretells these things of the Babylonian captivity, Jeremiah is witness, saying: Egypt is a choice and beautiful heifer; a goader will come to her from the North. And again: The daughter of Egypt has been put to shame, and delivered into the hand of the people of the North (Jer 46:20, 24). Ezekiel too, agreeing with equal authority of prophecy: And I will make the multitude of Egypt cease, he says, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. And again: I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I will put my sword into his hand, and I will break the arms of Pharaoh. And they will know that I am the Lord, when I have put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he has stretched it out over the land of Egypt, and I will scatter Egypt among the nations (Ezek 30:10, 24ff.). But if we refer these things to the times of the Savior, let us take this example from the Gospel: Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth: I have not come to send peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his neighbor, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies will be those of his own household (Matt 10:34ff.). And again in another place: Two will be divided against three, and three against two: father against son, and mother against daughter, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law (Luke 12:52-53).
Commentary on Isaiah

Then the whole heart of Egypt melted, and Egyptians rose against Egyptians, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: Do not think that I have come to send peace upon the earth; I have not come to send peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law (Matt 10:34ff.). At that time this too was fulfilled: A man's enemies are those of his own household (Mic 7:6). And a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his friend. For in one house they were divided, two against three and three against two, and father was divided against Son and son against father, city against city and kingdom against kingdom: those who did not believe against those who believed, or else those who believed, longing to save their neighbours.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the spirit of Egypt will be broken in its inward parts, and I will cast down its counsel: and they will consult their images and their diviners, and those with pythonic spirits, and the soothsayers. When sedition has arisen in Egypt, some desiring to serve the Babylonian, others unwilling to submit their necks to his yoke; or else some believing in Christ, and others resisting, the spirit of Egypt will be broken and torn apart, since not all wish the same things, and all their counsel will be brought to nothing. Then they will go to their images; and they will ask the diviners, and the soothsayers, and the seers, and those schooled in the magic arts, why these things have happened.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the spirit of Egypt was broken in its bowels, so that they were no longer of one mind; but, separated against themselves by the spiritual sword, they came to know that all their counsel had been cast down; and nonetheless, remaining in their former error, those who had refused to receive the truth of the faith consulted their idols and their diviners, and those with familiar spirits, and the soothsayers.
Commentary on Isaiah

And I will deliver Egypt into the hand of cruel masters, and a mighty king will rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts. We follow a twofold understanding: either of the Chaldean times, when Egypt was conquered by Nebuchadnezzar; or of the Roman empire, when, after Antony and Cleopatra had been overcome, Augustus Caesar subjugated Egypt. That the Babylonians were cruel all Scripture testifies: they did not spare little ones, and wounded them with their darts, and had no pity on pregnant women. And that the Roman kingdom was most mighty the Scripture of Daniel also testifies (Dan 7), setting forth the fourth beast, which has teeth and claws of iron.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when they had done this, the Lord delivered them into the hand of cruel lords, according to that saying of the Apostle: Whom I have delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim 1:20), so that, oppressed by that hardest servitude, they may return to the most merciful Lord. And fittingly he calls the demons cruel lords, for nothing is crueller than they. The strong king also, who is their lord, is plainly understood as the devil, whom the Lord in the Gospel too calls the strong man; and when he is bound and overpowered, the vessels of his house and the spoil are plundered.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the water shall dry up from the sea, and the river shall be laid waste and dried up, and the rivers shall fail; the streams of the embankments shall be diminished and dried up. The reed and the rush shall wither; the bed of the stream shall be laid bare from its source, and every watered sowing shall be dried up; it shall wither and shall not be. And the fishers shall mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river shall lament, and those who spread a net upon the face of the water, and they shall wither away. And those who work flax shall be confounded, plaiting and weaving fine things, and its watered places shall be drooping, all who made pools to catch fish. Foolish are the princes of Tanis; the wise counsellors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel. When the strong king, the harsh one, has ruled in Egypt, all the learning and beauty of worldly eloquence shall dry up, and the devil himself, the source of all the rivers, from whom all lies spring, shall be laid waste, so that the other rivers and streams, which used to be filled from the turbid waters of the Nile, shall fail. The reed and the rush too shall wither from excessive drought. For rush the Seventy translated papyrus, from which paper is made, adding of their own green achi, which is not found in the Hebrew. And when I asked learned men what this word signified, I heard that the Egyptians in their own tongue call by this name everything green that grows in a marsh. Now the reed, according to tropology, is empty speech, having nothing solid in itself; and the papyrus is that which seems indeed to have pith and is not empty, and yet is fragile and quickly withers.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the water will dry up from the sea, and the river will be desolated and dried up, and the streams will fail; the channels of the embankments will be diminished and dried up. The reed and the rush will wither, the bed of the stream will be laid bare from its source, and every watered sowing will be dried up, will wither, and will be no more. It is natural that, when captivity has come through the wrath of God, pestilence should follow upon his indignation, and all the elements together should rage against those who have offended God. Hence it is written in another Prophet (Jer 12) that both the birds in the air and the fish in the waters fail, so that all things are withdrawn from human use. This we say if we choose to take it simply of a drought of the river Nile and its streams. But if by metaphor: in the river we understand the kingdom, and in the streams its leaders; and in the greenery, the rush and the papyrus the whole abundance of Egypt, so that through these things the riches of Egypt are described, in which Egypt is most fertile. Let us read Ezekiel, where King Pharaoh is described as a great dragon dwelling in the rivers, and he says: The river is mine, and I made myself. And he hears: I will put a bridle in your jaws, and I will make the fish of your rivers stick to your scales, and I will draw you out of the midst of your rivers, and all your fish will cling to your scales, and I will cast you into the desert (Ezek 29:3-4). At the coming of Christ, however, all these things are to be understood τροπικῶς, in keeping with what we read above: The Lord will make the sea of Egypt desert. And again: The Lord will lay his hand upon the violent river of Egypt, and will strike it in seven valleys, so that one may pass over it with shod feet: namely, that all the error of the Egyptian waters, and the evil arts by which they deluded the peoples subject to them, are dried up at the coming of Christ. And as for his saying: The water will dry up from the sea, we can also take it historically: that what is signified is not the great sea, but Lake Mareotis, because Scripture calls all gatherings of waters seas. These things can also be understood as said hyperbolically. And what follows: The bed of the stream will be laid bare from its source, describes the stream and the source drying up together.
Commentary on Isaiah

All the streams too, once the head of the streams has dried up, shall be dried up, and whatever was formerly watered by the Egyptian waters shall be dried up and shall not be; so that the fishers of Egypt shall mourn, who are utterly opposed to the fishers of the Lord, and those shall lament who used to cast a hook into the river and spread a net upon the face of the water. Those who deceive people one at a time cast a hook into the turbid waters; but those who deceive many at once, speaking publicly in the synagogues of Satan and leading away whole flocks of the peoples, cast a net upon the Egyptian waters.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the fishermen will mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river will lament, and those who spread a net upon the face of the water will waste away. And those who work flax will be confounded, plaiting and weaving fine things: and its watered places will be withered: all who made pools for catching fish. Take this too in two ways: that when Egypt has been laid waste and the whole province dried up with drought, the fishermen mourn, and those who used to cast a hook into the river lament, and those who worked nets and dragnets and wove little vessels of various kinds out of rush, that is, the princes and those of royal stock, and the rulers; and that at the coming of Christ all the fishermen of a perverse kind, who, contrary to the apostolic discipline, caught men for perdition, and with a foolish wisdom wove nets and dragnets in which to ensnare the lost, were confounded, and that there is no such fisherman, or a rare one, in the land of Egypt. We see this fulfilled in fact, in that the trophies of the Churches are rising, and throughout Egypt the idols have fallen.
Commentary on Isaiah

Those too shall be confounded who used to work flax to make the vestments of the priests, plaiting it and weaving fine things, which belongs properly to the art of the dialecticians. For fine things the Seventy translated byssus, which itself also is woven into the vestments of the priests.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, And its watered places shall be drooping, all who made pools to catch fish, signifies that all the snares of the fishers of Egypt shall be destroyed and perish. Where we, following the sense, have translated pools made to catch fish, both in the Hebrew and in all the translators souls are set in place of fish, so that we may be drawn from the history to tropology: namely, that these fishers who made pools and pits made them for this purpose, to ensnare souls in them. It should be noted that for pools the Seventy translated ζύθον, which is a kind of drink made from grain and water, and is commonly called sabaium in the provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia, in the heathen and barbarian speech. The Egyptians use this most of all, so that they give those who drink not pure waters but turbid ones, like dregs mixed in; so that by a drink of this kind is shown the teaching of heretical depravity.
On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, 11.49

And the Father says to him: Return to me, calling him from the earth to heaven, whom he had sent for our salvation. Therefore, raising up his only-begotten Son, he frustrated the plan of the slanderers. Hence, Isaiah also says: The futile plan of your spirit. And the one who had been accusing and directing arrows like a hunter, has disarmed everything: he has crushed the power of those who relied on their own strength and not on God.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then the princes of Tanis shall be foolish, which means a lowly command. For all the heretics teach a lowliness contrary to loftiness, and drag men down to the underworld, and are princes of a lowly and abject command. The counsellors too of Pharaoh, who is the king of Egypt, and is rightly rendered scatterer and divided, and separated into various parts, shall be convicted of having given foolish counsel, when the Lord destroys the wisdom of the wise and rejects the understanding of the prudent (1 Cor 1).
Commentary on Isaiah

How do you say to Pharaoh: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? Where now are your wise men? Let them tell you, and declare what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools, the princes of Memphis have withered; they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples. The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of giddiness, and they have made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man errs and vomits. And there shall be no work for Egypt which may make the head and the tail, bending and curbing. The heretics are accustomed to say to their king, or Pharaoh: We are sons of the wise, who handed down the Apostolic teaching to us from the beginning; we are sons of ancient kings, who are called the kings of the philosophers, and we have the knowledge of the Scriptures joined to worldly wisdom.
Commentary on Isaiah

The princes of Tanis are foolish; the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel: how will you say to Pharaoh: I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings? Where now are your wise men? Let them announce to you and show what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools, the princes of Memphis have withered: they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples. That Tanis was the metropolis of Egypt the Psalmist also declares, because Moses worked there the many signs which are described in Exodus: He set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the plain of Tanis (Ps 77 [78]:43). That Memphis too was given over to the magic arts, the traces of its old error show to the present time. And this is briefly indicated: that when the Babylonian devastation came, all the counsels of the Magi and of those who promised knowledge of the future were convicted of folly; and that at the coming of Christ all were brought to nothing, since the seers of Egypt could find no counsel how to suppress the Christian doctrine. It is an idiom of the Scriptures to put corner for kingdom, because it holds the peoples together, and is, as it were, the strongest part of the whole house. Hence Christ too, who holds together the walls of the two peoples, is called the corner stone (Eph 2). And his adding: How will you say to Pharaoh, I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings, signifies that the Egyptians feign heroes and gods as the founders of their race: Horus, and Isis, and Osiris, and Typhon.
Commentary on Isaiah

These he now asks, or the very king of the heretics, where are his wise men who despised the simplicity of the Church; and he compels them to answer what the Lord Sabaoth has purposed concerning the Egypt of this world, and what he will do at the consummation.
Commentary on Isaiah

The princes of Tanis, who held the lowly command of the heretics, are proved to be fools. All the princes of Memphis have withered, who were tainted with the boasting of eloquence and of the mouth. For Memphis means mouth or from the mouth, and μεταφορικῶς signifies speech. And what follows: They have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples, or according to the Seventy: they shall deceive Egypt by tribes, signifies that the kingdom of worldly wisdom is shown to be foolish, and the princes of the several doctrines, who are interpreted as the tribes, are convicted of having had foolish teachers.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of giddiness: and they have made Egypt err in all its work, as a drunken man errs and vomits: and Egypt will have no work to do, head and tail, bending and bridling. Let us speak first of the translation, and afterwards we shall discuss what is written. For spirit of giddiness one can also translate spirit of error. In what we have translated, bending and bridling, we can also say bent and wanton, so that we understand the old man and the boy. For we, while translating what is written in haste, misled by its ambiguity, rendered the Hebrew word AGMON (אגמון) as bridling, which Aquila translated more expressively στρεβλοῦντα, that is, one who does nothing rightly but everything perversely, so as to signify a boy.
