The sense, then, is: The princes of Tanis have become fools, and the wise counselors have given Pharaoh foolish counsel, and the princes of Memphis have withered, and they have deceived Egypt, the corner of the peoples, because the Lord has mingled in them a spirit of error and giddiness, so that they do not know what they are saying, and make Egypt err. And as a drunken man, vomiting, brings up what he had taken in, and does not know where he is, but lies out of his mind: so Egypt will have no work or counsel that has either a head or an end, or that suits either the old or the young, of whom the former, through excess of age, are foolish and rave, and the latter, through wantonness and infancy, do not know what they are doing. And whether you wish to take this of the Babylonian devastation or of the coming of Christ, both according to the letter and according to the spiritual understanding, it will hold together.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the Lord has mingled for them a spirit of giddiness, or of errors, according to what is written: And as they did not see fit to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate mind (Rom 1:28). And as he who is holy can say with Isaiah, We shall make the spirit of your salvation upon the earth, so he who is a sinner will make a spirit of error, that is, a spirit of wickedness, according to what we read also in Jeremiah: Your own transgression shall reprove you, and your wickedness shall rebuke you (Jer 2:19). But if the heretic who does not receive the Old Testament is scandalized that the Lord is said to mingle a spirit of error or of giddiness, let him hear what is written in the Apostle, that is, in the New Testament: God delivered them up in the desires of their heart to uncleanness (Rom 1:24). And again: For this reason God delivered them up to passions of ignominy. And again: God delivered them up to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not fitting. Now they are delivered up in the desires of their heart because they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things. This we read not only in the Epistle to the Romans, but also in that to the Thessalonians concerning Antichrist: Because they did not receive the love of the truth, that they might be saved, God shall send them the working of error, that they may believe a lie, and that all may be judged who did not believe the truth, but took pleasure in the lie (2 Thess 2:10); which I think the apostle Paul took from the present reading of Isaiah, in which he says: The Lord has mingled for them a spirit of error, and they have made Egypt err in all its works, as, he says, a drunken man errs and vomits, one who is drunk with vices. Of such drunkards Joel speaks: Woe to those who are drunk without wine. And not only drunk, but also vomiting the fury of dragons and the incurable fury of asps; so that, after they have vomited up wine of this kind, they may understand their drunkenness, and recognize that as long as they were drunk they had neither beginning nor end, that is, neither head nor tail, but were an animal maimed at both ends. For beginning and end, as both Symmachus and the Seventy translated, Theodotion, after his custom, set down the Hebrew words themselves, CHAPHPHE (כפה) and AGMON (אגמון), which Aquila translated bent and perverse: wishing old men to be understood by bent, and by perverse wanton boys, who do everything perversely; and hence the sense is that in Egypt not only head and tail are lacking, but also old men and boys, that is, both beginning and end.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day Egypt shall be like women, and shall be amazed, and shall fear before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he shall shake over it. And the land of Judah shall be a festival to Egypt; everyone who remembers it shall tremble before the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has purposed concerning it. At that time (for that, as we have often said, is what day signifies), when the Lord has mingled a spirit of error and giddiness, so that Egypt vomits up the wine of dragons and the incurable fury of asps, understanding its error and its former drunkenness, Egypt shall fear like a woman: not with the chance fear that is wont to befall men, whom Egypt does not love but strangles and kills, but with the fear of women, whom alone Pharaoh wishes to live. And it shall fear the shaking, or lifting up, of the hand of the Lord, by which punishments are signified, which he will shake and lift up to strike Egypt.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day Egypt will be like women, and they will be astonished and afraid before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he will shake over it. And the land of Judah will be a festival to Egypt: everyone who remembers it will tremble before the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has devised against it. I think it better even to censure one's own error than, while blushing to confess one's inexperience, to persist in error. In what I translated, And the land of Judah will be a festival to Egypt, for festival one reads in the Hebrew AGGA (חגה), which can be interpreted both as festival (whence Haggai too is rendered festive) and as fear; this Aquila translated more expressively γύρωσιν, as when someone, afraid and trembling, casts his eyes about and dreads the approaching enemy. If, then, we choose to take it in a good sense, that the remembrance of Judah is a joy to Egypt, it is rightly called a festival. But if, as I judge, festival is turned into fear, let us understand dread or terror: that when Nebuchadnezzar has come, and all the hands of the brave men have been loosened like those of women, even the name of Judah is a terror to Egypt, because, in wishing to bring it help, it has suffered such great evils. Concerning our own times no one doubts that, in comparison with the Christians, all the heathen are like women, holding feeble opinions, and that whatever they say is turned into folly, while they are astonished at so great a conversion of the nation, and marvel at and understand the hand of the Lord; and whoever of the Gentiles remembers the Christian name confesses with fear the weakness of idolatry.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then the land of Judah, that is, the knowledge of the Scriptures, the Law and the Prophets, the Gospels and the epistles of the Apostles, shall be a festival to Egypt, if it comes to know them; or a fear, if by comparison with their teaching and truth it understands that it has held a lie. Everyone who remembers this land shall tremble with that trembling which leads to life: For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Prov 9:10). And we can take this not only of the consummation of the world, but of the present time as well: that every heretic fears a churchman learned in heavenly teachings, and is terrified at the remembrance of him. And he shall fear and tremble at the counsel of the Lord, which he has purposed concerning the Egypt of this world. We run through each point briefly, so as to pass on to the rest.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan, and swearing by the Lord of hosts: one will be called the city of the sun. For city of the sun the Seventy, meaning I know not what, translated asedec, which one of our writers interprets as city of righteousness; and, led astray by error, because according to the Hebrew ARES (חרס) is written, he thinks it means earth, which is written with other letters. Symmachus, then, translated better: one will be called the city of the sun; for ARES, an ambiguous word, means both potsherd and sun, because both are parched and dry. Onias, not understanding this place, built a temple in Egypt in the town of Ἡλιοπόλεως. Read the Histories of Josephus (Josephus, book 12, chapter 9). Others would have Ares, that is, ὄστρακον, that is, potsherd, understood as the city of Ostracine, and the other cities near Rhinocorura and Casium, which, it is clear, speak to this day in Egypt the Canaanite tongue, that is, Syriac; and they think that Syrians and Arabs from the neighborhood were transported into that land by Nebuchadnezzar. Further, those who expound the prophecy of the coming of Christ and of the Roman empire take the five cities either as the law of the Lord, which was first translated in Alexandria, or as the five orders of the Church: bishops, presbyters, deacons, the faithful, catechumens; or certainly as the spiritual understanding of the law, of which the Apostle too says: I would speak five words in the Churches with my understanding, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue (1 Cor 14); and they take it that one of the five cities is called the city of the sun, namely of righteousness, in whose wings is healing.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the Canaanite tongue, and swearing by the Lord of hosts: one shall be called the city of the sun. The hand of the Lord lifted up or shaken over Egypt is of great profit, so that the land of Judah becomes a fear to it, and everyone who remembers it trembles. At that time five cities in the land of Egypt shall speak the tongue of Canaan, which most of our writers understand as the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. When we look on a woman to lust after her, our sight speaks the Egyptian tongue. When we hear a judgment of blood, though the Lord says, You shall not receive a vain report (Exod 23:1, LXX), our hearing speaks the Egyptian tongue. When, according to the prophet, we live in delights, and lie upon beds of ivory, and are anointed with the chief ointments, our smell speaks the Egyptian tongue. When our belly is our god (Phil 3), our taste speaks the Egyptian tongue. If we do not hear what the Apostle says, It is good for a man not to touch a woman (1 Cor 7), but on the contrary are joined to a harlot, our touch speaks the Egyptian tongue. But if, on the contrary, we lift up our eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvest, and are no longer bent toward the earth, but, like the woman in the Gospel who for eighteen years could not look up at heaven (Luke 13), lift up our eyes and say, To you have I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens (Ps 122 [123]:1), our eye and sight speaks the Canaanite tongue. If we circumcise our ears and hear the Lord saying, He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Luke 8:8), our hearing speaks the Canaanite tongue. Whoever can say to the bridegroom, We run after you in the fragrance of your ointments (Song 1:3), and, We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place (2 Cor 2:15), his smell speaks the Canaanite tongue. Taste too is taken in a good sense, of him who eats the bread that comes down from heaven, the living bread and not the dead, and who hears that saying, Taste and see how sweet the Lord is (Ps 33 [34]:9): at once it speaks the Canaanite tongue. And there is a spiritual touch also, of which the apostle John says, Our hands have handled of the Word of life (1 John 1:1); and he has it who touches Jesus by faith, so that the Savior can say of him, Someone has touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me (Luke 8:46). We have learned how great the good things are which the uplifted hand of the Lord bestows; let us ask why the five cities of Egypt speak not the Hebrew tongue but the Canaanite tongue. To this we shall try to answer thus. Hebrew sounds περάτην, that is, one who passes over, who passes from place to place. Therefore we too, though we be saints, as long as we are in Egypt and live in the darkness of this world, cannot speak the Hebrew tongue, but the Canaanite tongue, which is midway between the Egyptian and the Hebrew, and for the most part borders on the Hebrew. Canaan means as it were a moving, or as it were answering. When, therefore, we withdraw from Egypt and wish to go out from the power of Pharaoh, so that our land and our confession are fearsome to Egypt, then we are moved and as it were answer to the will of the Lord; and yet, because we are still in the present world, we cannot yet speak the Hebrew tongue. And what follows, five cities swear by the Lord of hosts, signifies that even while placed here we call to mind not demons but almighty God. Of these five cities, the names of the other four being passed over in silence, one is called the city of the sun, which seems to me to refer to sight. For as a city needs the sun and the moon in order to be seen, so we need the sun of righteousness in order that our eyes may be enlightened.
On the Gospel of Luke 5:19.17-19

The servant is "faithful in very little" who does not defile the word of God but speaks as though he were speaking from God and with God in Christ. For whatever gifts we receive at present are very little and very poor in comparison with those of the future, since "now we know only partially and prophesy only partially, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away." The ten cities are souls coming to the grace of the gospel through the word of the law. And because he must be glorified, the one who will invest the money of the word worthily for God is placed over them. Hence one successful investor addressed the cities over whom he presided, that is, the souls whose governance he had accepted, asking, "What is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord Jesus?"20"And another came, saying, 'Lord, your mina has made five minas.' " This servant is representative of those who were sent to evangelize the uncircumcised. The Lord had given him one mina for preaching, which means one and the same faith which is also believed by the circumcised. He made five minas because people who had previously been enslaved to their bodily senses he converted to the grace of evangelical faith. "And he said to him, 'You will be over five cities,' " that is, you will shine greatly and on high with the faith and conversion of those souls whom you imbued. Isaiah also spoke mystically about this: "In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt who speak the language of Canaan." The five cities in the land of Egypt are the five senses of the body we use in this world, namely, vision, hearing, taste, smell and touch. He who looks at a woman with concupiscence, he who shuts his ears not to hear the poor, he who gets drunk with wine, which is dissipation, he who delights in crowning himself with fresh roses, whose hands are covered with blood and whose right hand is filled with bribes, represents the five cities that speak the language of Egypt, that is, that perform the works of darkness with all of their senses, for Egypt sings of the darkness. But he who blocks his ears not to hear of blood and closes his eyes not to see evil, he who tastes and sees how sweet is the Lord, who castigates his body and makes it his slave, who is able to say with the apostle "we are the fragrance of Christ to God," represents the cities of those who speak the altered language of Canaan. And the one who delivered them from darkness by his teaching is rightly rewarded with the leadership of five cities because he is being honored not only for his own progress but also for that of those whom he called to the light.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER ELEVEN

[Daniel 11:13-14] "And the king of the North shall return and shall prepare a much greater multitude than before, and in the end of times and years he shall come in haste with a large army and great resources. And in those times many shall rise up against the king of the South." This indicates that Antiochus the Great, who despised the worthlessness of Ptolemy Philopator (for he had fallen desperately in love with a lute-player named Agathoclea and also her brother, retaining Agatho-cles himself as his concubine and afterwards appointing him as general of Egypt), assembled a huge army from the upper regions of Babylon. And since Ptolemy Philopator was now dead, Antiochus broke his treaty and set his army in motion against Philopator's four-year-old son, who was called Epiphanes. For so great was the dissoluteness and arrogancy of Agathoclea, that those provinces which had previously been subjected to Egypt rose up in rebellion, and even Egypt itself was troubled with seditions. Moreover Philip, King of Macedon, and Antiochus the Great made peace with each other and engaged in a common struggle against Agathocles and Ptolemy Eprphanes, on the understanding that each of them should annex to his own dominion those cities of Ptolemy which lay nearest to them. And so this is what is referred to in this passage, which says that many shall rise up against the king of the South, that is, Ptolemy Epiphanes, who was then a mere child.

"Moreover the children of the transgressors of thy people shall lift themselves up, that they may fulfil the vision, and then fall to ruin (Vulgate: and they shall fall to ruin)." During the conflict between Antiochus the Great and the generals of Ptolemy, Judaea, which lay between them, was rent into contrary factions, the one group favoring Antiochus, and the other favoring Ptolemy. Finally the high priest, Onias, fled to Egypt, taking a large number of Jews along with him, and was given by Ptolemy an honorable reception. He then received the region known as Heliopolis, and by a grant of the king, he erected a temple in Egypt like the temple of the Jews, and it remained standing up until the reign of Vespasian, over a period of two hundred and fifty years. But then the city itself, which was known as the City of Onias, was destroyed to the very ground because of the war which the Jews had subsequently waged against the Romans. There is consequently no trace of either city or temple now remaining. But as we were saying, countless multitudes of Jews fled to Egypt on the occasion of Onias's pontificate, and the land was filled with a large number from Cyrene as well. For Onias affirmed that he was fulfilling the prophecy written by Isaiah: "There shall be an altar of the Lord in Egypt, and the name of the Lord shall be found in their territories" (Isaiah 19:19). And so this is the matter referred to in this passage: "The sons of the transgressors of thy people," who forsook the law of the Lord and wished to offer blood-sacrifices to God in another place than what He had commanded. They would be lifted up in pride and would boast that they were fulfilling the vision, that is, the thing which the Lord had enjoined. But they shall fall to ruin, for both temple and city shall be afterwards destroyed. And while Antiochus held Judaea, a leader of the Ptolemaic party called Scopas Aetholus was sent against Antiochus, and after a bold campaign he took Judaea and took the aristocrats of Ptolemy's party back to Egypt with him on his return.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and an inscription to the Lord at its border. And it will be for a sign and for a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they will cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he will send them a Savior and a defender to free them. And the Lord will be known by Egypt, and the Egyptians will know the Lord in that day, and will worship him with victims and gifts, and will vow vows to the Lord and pay them. From this place to the end of the Egyptian Vision, or Burden, both the Jews and our writers would have it understood of the coming of Christ; but they put off their hopes into the future, while we hold them as already accomplished. Take day for time: although Josephus maintains that these things were done under Onias, who, fleeing into Egypt with a very great crowd of Jews, built a temple and an altar, and with vain rashness tried to fulfill the prophecy of Christ. But one altar is spoken of in the way that there is one faith, and one baptism, and one Church. And an inscription to the Lord at its border: there is no doubt that this signifies the Gospel and the writings of the Apostles. For just as above, according to the tropological understanding, the land of Judah, fearful or festal to Egypt, is understood as the Old Testament, so too the inscription at the borders of Egypt is shown to be the history of the Gospels.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar of the Lord at its border. And it shall be for a sign and for a witness to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they shall cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he shall send them a Savior and a defender to deliver them; and the Lord shall be known by Egypt. In sequence to what he had said above, In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the Canaanite tongue, and swearing by the Lord of hosts, there now follows: There shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, which Onias, according to Josephus (Antiquities, book 13, ch. 6), misunderstanding it, tried to fulfil. And the title of the Lord containing his passion, on which was written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin letters, Jesus of Nazareth, king of the Jews (John 19), for a sign of the Cross, and for a witness to all the nations, which are now called Egypt. And when persecution has grown at the hands of those who afflict the Christian name, then they shall cry in their hearts: Abba, Father (Rom 8). And the Lord of hosts shall send a Savior, that is, Jesus, and a Judge, or defender, to deliver them, so that, delivered, they may know the Lord, and themselves be known by the Lord; and where sin abounded, grace may abound the more (Rom 5). Now one altar of Egypt, that is, of this world, is spoken of, so that we may know that all the altars which are raised up against the altar of the Church are not the Lord's. In the book of the Historical Explanation we said that, up to the end of the vision of Egypt, since the prophecy was manifest, all things are to be referred to Christ.
LETTER TO THE CATHOLICS ON THE SECT OF DONATISTS 16:41-42

The prophet Isaiah says this about Egypt: "In that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the land of the Egyptians and an inscription to the Lord at its border. It will be a sign forever to the Lord in the land of the Egyptians, for they will cry to the Lord against their assailants, and the Lord will send them a savior who will be determined to save them. And the Lord will be known to the Egyptians, and they will fear the Lord in that day and make sacrifices to him and promise vows to him and fulfill them. And the Lord will strike the Egyptians with plagues and heal them by his mercy, and they will turn to the Lord, and he will listen to them and heal them." What do they [i.e., members of the Donatist sect] say to this? Why do they not share with the church what was foretold of the Egyptians? Or, if Egypt signifies the world by prophetic prefiguration, why are they not in communion with the church of the world? Consequently, they search the Scriptures and, against so many sure and clear witnesses through which the church of Christ is shown to be diffused throughout the entire world, they offer just one witness in an attempt to demonstrate that the church of Christ perished from all other peoples and remained only in Africa, as though from another beginning, not from Jerusalem but from Carthage, where they first elevated one bishop against another.
On the Sacraments, 2.2.7

He said, I do not have a man; that is, because through a man is death, and through a man is the resurrection of the dead. He could not descend, he could not be saved, who did not believe that our Lord Jesus had taken flesh from the Virgin. But this one who was waiting for the mediator between God and men, the man Jesus Christ, expecting him of whom it was said: And the Lord will send a man to save them; he said: I do not have a man; and therefore he deserved to come to health, because he believed in the one who was coming.
Commentary on Isaiah

Next he adds: And it will be for a sign and for a testimony, namely of the Lord's passion. Then those who have believed, when Egyptians rush against Egyptians, and a man fights against his brother, and city battles against city, when the time of persecution has broken upon them, will implore the mercy of the Lord, and at once the Savior will come, that is, Jesus, for that is what it means in our language.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord will be known by the Egyptians, and they will know him, whether the persecutors who have been overcome, or the believers set free by his present help. And they will worship him with victims and gifts, and will vow vows to the Lord and pay them. Let the Jews answer: It is commanded in the Law that no altar be made except in the one place which the Lord God has chosen, and that victims be sacrificed only by priests of the Levitical race (Deut 26). Behold, Isaiah teaches openly that the Egyptians know the Lord and worship him, and offer victims and gifts, and vow vows and pay them. If the Egyptians have a priesthood, the testimony of Paul is fulfilled in them as well, who says: When the priesthood is changed, there must of necessity be a change of the law (Heb 7:12).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Egyptians shall know the Lord in that day, and shall worship him with sacrifices and gifts, and they shall vow vows to the Lord and pay them. And the Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague, and shall heal it; and they shall return to the Lord, and he shall be appeased toward them, and shall heal them. After the Egyptians have come to know the Lord, they shall worship him with spiritual sacrifices and gifts; and they shall vow vows to the Lord and pay them, and shall say with David: A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit (Ps 50 [51]:19), and: The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice (Ps 140 [141]:2); when, believing in the Nazarene, they themselves have become Nazirites, drinking neither wine nor strong drink (John 19), nor the vinegar which was offered to the Lord to drink, nor whatever is made from the grape of Sodom. And when they have paid their vows with Abel, and God has had regard to them, the elder brother Cain, that is, the people of the Circumcision, will envy, and will shed Christian blood, which shall cry out to the Lord (Gen 4); and therefore he shall go out from the face of God, saying of the Savior: Crucify, crucify him (Luke 23:21), and: We have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). He who is holy in body and spirit offers a vow and pays it to the Lord. Zacchaeus too offered a vow, who promised half of his substance to the poor (Luke 19).
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord will strike Egypt with a blow, and will heal it: and they will turn to the Lord, and he will be appeased toward them, and will heal them. For whom the Lord loves he rebukes, and he chastises every son whom he receives. Persecution serves not for the denial of believers, but for their proving and their crown.
Commentary on Isaiah

It is asked: if a savior and defender was sent to the Egyptians to deliver them from their straits, how is it now said, The Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague? But let us consider what follows: And he shall heal it. For whom the Lord loves he chastens (Heb 12). And the Savior himself in Psalm 68 (69) says to the Father: For they have persecuted him whom you struck, and they have added to the pain of my wounds (Ps 68 [69]:27). If, then, he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us, that by his bruise and wounds we might be healed (Rom 8), the Lord delivered up the martyrs too to suffering, but he will heal them again in the resurrection, so that by their wounds the faith of believers may be confirmed. Hence it is said also to Job: Do you think that I spoke to you otherwise than that you might appear righteous? For he himself causes pain and restores to former health; and he visits his servants with the rod, so as not to take away his mercy from them. Hence the daughters and daughters-in-law who have sinned greatly, and have spread their feet to everyone who passed by, are not visited or chastened, for the Lord says: I will not visit your daughters when they commit fornication, nor your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery (Hos 4:14). The Lord, then, strikes the Egyptians, not with fire, not with the sword, but with the rod. For what son is there whom his father does not train? So that, after they have been healed, they may return to the Lord, and he may be appeased toward them, and heal them once more. For we always need the mercy of God, and there is no end to his clemency.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day there will be a road from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Assyrian will enter Egypt, and the Egyptian the Assyrians: and the Egyptians will serve Assyria. Before the coming of Christ each nation had its own king, and no one could go from one nation to another; but in the Roman empire all things have been made one. Let the learned reader turn over the ancient histories, and he will find that the whole region from the Euphrates to the Tigris, and all between, belonged to the Assyrians. Those, therefore, whom the ancients called Assyrians we now call Syrians, naming the whole from the part. And when it is said: The Egyptians will serve the Syrians, it is to be taken either thus: that Roman legions furnished with Syrian soldiers guard Egypt; or that the two nations trade with each other, and the cities of Syria receive the abundance of Egypt, just as, conversely, Egypt is watered with the goods of Palestine and Phoenicia. Some of our writers wrongly refer these things to the thousand years, and in the Jewish manner declare that they will come to pass at the consummation of the world, when the Antichrist, coming from the Assyrians, has taken possession of Egypt and Ethiopia.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day there shall be a way from Egypt to the Assyrians, and the Assyrian shall enter into Egypt, and the Egyptian into the Assyrians; and the Egyptians shall serve the Assyrians. As we have shown that the other things which go before befell the Egyptians in a good sense, namely, five cities in their land speaking the Canaanite tongue and swearing by the Lord, and the altar of the Lord set in the midst of the land of Egypt, and the pillar, and the witness, and the sign, and the savior who should deliver them; and that the Lord should be known by the Egyptians, and they themselves should know him; and that they should offer sacrifices and gifts, and pay their vows, and, being struck, be healed, and return to the Lord, and he be appeased toward them, and they be healed again: so this too which follows, that the Egyptians serve the Assyrians, is to be taken in a good sense. For the Apostle too serves believers, that he may gain them (1 Cor 9). And Esau is made subject to his brother Jacob (Gen 33), that he may become a sharer in his blessings. Therefore those from the nations who are saved first, and have the altar of the Lord within them, will by their service save those who persist in hardness; and by mingling and fellowship with them they will themselves go to the Assyrians, in order to lead the Assyrians to Egypt, and so that afterwards they may be able to reach the people of Israel. For this reason, I think, the believing wife too serves the unbelieving husband, so that little by little she may draw him from Egypt and from the Assyrians to Judea.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day Israel will be the third with the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands to the Assyrian: but my inheritance is Israel. By no means will Israel be crushed in the middle between Egypt and the Assyrian, now with the Antiochi and Demetrii dragging the kingdom of Judah to themselves, now with the Ptolemies claiming its possession for themselves; but it too, established under the Roman empire, and through this under the empire of Christ, will be of the same condition as Egypt and the Assyrians, and will be blessed in all the earth. For out of Zion will go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.
Commentary on Isaiah

In that day Israel shall be the third to the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: Blessed is my people of Egypt, and the work of my hands the Assyrian; but my inheritance is Israel. Israel shall be the third in Egypt and among the Assyrians, that he may mingle the whole lump with the leaven of his blessing, and that those who formerly were at hostile variance with one another may be joined together by this clasp of blessing; and that Egypt may be the people of God, and the Assyrian the work of his hands, but Israel his inheritance. The Egyptian is blessed by the Lord, because he is blessed through fellowship with Israel. And the Assyrian is the work of his hands, because in him he has shown his clemency. But Israel alone can say: The Lord is my portion (Lam 3:24), he who beholds God with the mind, and is called his inheritance.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then it will be said by the Lord: Blessed is my people of Egypt: when, led not by Moses but by Christ the Lord, countless thousands of men have filled the deserts and, with Pharaoh drowned, have said in the desert: Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified: horse and rider he has cast into the sea (Exod 15:1). Then also the work of the hands of the Lord will be among the Assyrians; for these nations above all, Egypt and Mesopotamia, flourish with swarms of monks, and vie with one another in equal piety. And the inheritance of Christ is Israel, that is, the places of his nativity, and of his cross, and of his resurrection and ascension, to which men flock from the whole world.

n: Year. Eighteen after the preceding predictions. (Calmet) --- Sargon. Sennacherib, (St. Jerome) Salmanasar, (Sanctius) or Assaradon, who intended to revenge Sennacherib, and sent his "collector of taxes" to take Azotus from Ezechias, and then to proceed farther. (Calmet) --- Psammitichus having obtained the sole dominion of Egypt, besieged Azotus for 29 years. (Herodotus ii. 157.) (Amos i. 8.)

Sackcloth. The prophets lived in poverty, Zacharias xiii. 4. Their persons were prophetic. It is not agreed whether Isaias went quite naked, or only without his upper garment. The former supposition would represent better the condition of slaves, (ver. 4.) and is adopted by St. Jerome, &c. (Calmet) --- People are said to be naked when they are almost so, 2 Kings vi., and John xxi. (Haydock) --- Yet "nothing is more honest than to obey God." (St. Jerome) (Worthington)
Years. Isaias went so long, or perhaps only three days undressed, Numbers xiv. 34., and Ezechiel iv. 5. Egypt and the Arabian Ethiopia were to be abandoned to the Assyrians, in or during three years.
Shame. Thus captives were generally exposed to sale, chap. xlvii. 2., and Nahum iii. 5.

Glory. The alliance of these nations shall not avail the Jews, who are said to inhabit an island, because they neglected God's service no less than the most distant and abandoned nations. (Calmet) --- The changes in empires must convince us to depend only on God, since Damascus and Egypt could not save the Hebrews, nor even themselves. (Worthington)

f: Letter 58.10-11

Someone perhaps will say, "Was it not disgraceful for a man to walk naked among the people since he must meet both men and women? Must not his appearance have shocked the gaze of all, but especially that of women? Do we not ourselves generally abhor the sight of naked men? And are not men's private parts covered with clothing that they may not offend the gaze of onlookers by their unsightliness?" I agree, but you must consider what this act represented and what was the reason for this outward show; it was that the young Jewish youths and maidens would be led away into exile and walk naked, "as my servant Isaiah walked," he says, "naked and barefoot." This might have been expressed in words, but God chose to enforce it by an example that the very sight might strike more terror, and what they shrank from in the body of the prophet they might utterly dread for themselves. Wherein lay the greater abhorrence: in the body of the prophet or in the sins of the disbelievers?
Letter 58.13

That it may be more fully clear that prophets look not to themselves or what lies at their feet but to heavenly things, Stephen, when he was being stoned, saw the heavens open and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. Then he did not feel the blows of the stones, he did not heed the wounds of his body, but, fastening his eyes on Christ, he clung to him. So, too, Isaiah did not notice his nakedness but made himself the instrument of God's voice, that he might proclaim what God spoke within him.
Letter 58.4-6

Truly I grieve that while falsehood is so respected, there should be such negligence as regards the truth, that many are ashamed of seeming too devoted to our holy religion, not considering his words who says, "Whosoever shall be ashamed of me before men, of him will I also be ashamed before my Father which is in heaven." But Moses was not thus ashamed, for though invited into the royal palace he "esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt." David was not thus ashamed when he danced before the ark of the testimony in the sight of all the people. Isaiah was not thus ashamed when he walked naked and barefoot through the people, proclaiming the heavenly oracles.…But the things that viewed corporeally are unseemly, when viewed in regard to holy religion become venerable, so that they who blame such things will involve their own souls in the net of blame. Thus Michal reproves David for his dancing and says to him, "How glorious was the king of Israel today, who uncovered himself today in the eyes of his handmaids!" And David answered her, "It was before the Lord, who chose me before your father and before all his house to appoint me ruler over the people of the Lord, over Israel."
LETTER 40
Isaiah goes naked without blushing as a type of captivity to come.
Commentary on Isaiah

And this is to be noted, that before Ashdod is taken the Prophet is clothed in sackcloth and has his feet shod, so that he may indeed lament those who have been wounded by the fiery darts of the devil and serve lust, but may nonetheless himself go shod, so as to be able to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and walk safely through the desert of this world, in which there are serpents and scorpions and thirst for good things. But after Ashdod has been taken, as a type of the captivity of Egypt and the exile of Ethiopia, he walks barefoot and naked. For in the holy Land, to which he hastens to go, he could neither stand nor walk clothed in sackcloth and with his feet covered with skin, for the Lord says: Loose the shoe from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground (Exod 3:5).
Commentary on Isaiah

In the year in which Tartan came into Azotus, when Sargon king of the Assyrians had sent him, and he had fought against Azotus and taken it. At that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah son of Amos, saying: Go and loose the sackcloth from your loins, and take your shoes from your feet: and he did so, walking naked and barefoot. And the Lord said: As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot, a sign and portent of three years will be upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia. So will the king of the Assyrians drive off the captivity of Egypt and the exile of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. And they will be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their hope, and of Egypt their glory. And the inhabitant of this island will say in that day: Behold, this was our hope, those to whom we fled for help, to free us from the face of the king of the Assyrians; and how shall we be able to escape? We have set down the whole content of this passage so that we may discuss each point part by part. Azotus, which in Hebrew is called ESDOD (אשדוד), was a most powerful city of Palestine, one of the five cities: Sargon king of the Assyrians, who is called by seven names, sent the commander of his army, whose name was Tartan, and took it and held it.
Commentary on Isaiah

In the year that Tartan came into Ashdod, when Sargon the king of the Assyrians had sent him, and he had fought against Ashdod and had taken it, at that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying: Go, and loose the sackcloth from your loins, and take your shoes off your feet. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot. And the Lord said: As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent of three years upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia. So shall the king of the Assyrians lead away the captivity of Egypt and the exile of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. And they shall be afraid and ashamed of Ethiopia their hope, and of Egypt their glory. And the inhabitant of this isle shall say in that day: Was this our hope, to whom we fled for help, that they might deliver us from the face of the king of the Assyrians? And how shall we be able to escape? For Tartan the Seventy translated Thanatan, and for Sargon, Arna: what these mean we cannot know. For we cannot invent false etymologies for false names. Now these are not Hebrew names but Assyrian, and of them we have learned that they sound thus: Tartan, he gave a tower, or superfluous, or putting far off; and Sargon prince of the garden. This king of Assyria, whom we read of above as the great mind, has very many generals, of whom one is Tartan, lifted up in pride, and going far in wickedness, and greater than the rest; and he is sent to attack Ashdod, which in Hebrew is called ASDOD (אשדוד), and means fire of generation; and the general of the king of Assyria overcomes those who serve generation and lust. And the king of the Assyrians, Sargon, prince of gardens, is fittingly said to be given over to pleasure and luxury. Indeed Ahab king of Israel too desired to turn the vineyard of Naboth into a garden (1 Kgs 21); and Naboth, understanding this according to the laws of tropology, chose to die rather than do it, lest his father's inheritance and ancient possession be turned into the delights of an impious king.
Commentary on Isaiah

At the time, then, when the neighboring city was taken, Isaiah is commanded to lay aside his tunic of sackcloth (for this was the garb of the prophet lamenting the sins of the people), and the shoes from his feet, which the Seventy call caligae, and to go about naked and barefoot, presenting a type of the captivity of the Egyptians and of the Ethiopians, who had been a help to the Egyptians: that just as Isaiah walked naked and displayed his unsightliness to the onlookers with bare buttocks, so all Egypt and Ethiopia, when the Assyrian ravaged them, should become naked, and nothing at all should remain in the land. And let no one think this contrary to the prosperity promised above to the Egyptians: for there, after the evils, future blessedness is foretold; whereas here the present captivity is narrated, in which, having destroyed Israel and Damascus and the Philistines, he went straight on to Egypt, and overcame them and the Ethiopians alike. And lest this seem doubtful to anyone, let us set down the testimony of Isaiah himself: And Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah: for he had heard that he had set out from Lachish: and he heard men saying of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia: He has come out to fight against you (2 Kgs 19:8-9). And at the same time we learn the obedience of the prophets: that a man of noble birth (for the Hebrews relate that Isaiah was the father-in-law of Manasseh son of Hezekiah king of Judah) did not blush to go about naked, but, judging nothing more honorable than the commands of God, laid aside the sackcloth, and when it was thrown off he was naked, having had before only one tunic, and that of haircloth.
Commentary on Isaiah

Now the Prophet is commanded to lay aside the sackcloth and the shoes and walk naked and barefoot, and to be a sign and portent to the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, who persecuted the people of God and were made low on account of their pride. For Egypt means persecuting or afflicting; Ethiopians, lowly and cast down; for everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled (Luke 14:11). These are to be led into captivity and to suffer torments of three years (Exod 12), of which years we read in the Psalms: I thought upon the days of old, and I had the eternal years in mind (Ps 76 [77]:6). Let us not think these are small punishments, but punishments drawn out over long ages.
Commentary on Isaiah
And when it is said: A sign and portent of three years will be upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia, this signifies that Egypt and Ethiopia were to be laid waste by the Assyrians for three years.
Commentary on Isaiah

And in that very captivity and exile of Egypt shall go the young and the old, who have been hardened in wickedness and have come to the vices of full age: naked, so that all their crimes may be laid bare (for nothing (Luke 8:17) is hidden that shall not be revealed), and barefoot, because they will not be able to eat the Passover of the Lord; for whoever eats it has his loins girded, and holds a staff in his hand, and stands with shod feet, lest, passing through the wilderness of this world, he be bitten by serpents (Exod 12). Then their buttocks, through which dung is voided, shall be uncovered, and all the shame of Egypt shall be shown, so that those shall be confounded who had their hope in Egypt and in Ethiopia, and shall see their glory changed into confusion; so much so that the inhabitant of this isle, that is, of the world, who is not a stranger and a sojourner, but longed to have a perpetual possession of the world, shall say in his confusion: Is this Egypt, and is this Ethiopia, whose help we hoped for, that they might deliver us from the prince of this world? How then shall we be able to escape, when those in whom we had our hope are taken captive?
Commentary on Isaiah

Then, he says, the inhabitant of this island will say, that is, Jerusalem, which is beaten by the waves of the neighboring nations: Was this our hope? And did we flee to these to give us help, who could not rescue themselves from the evil of captivity? This, then, is the order of the providence of God, who disposes the whole race of men by his ineffable judgment. Against the wrath of God Israel hoped in Damascus: let the city be destroyed which, against his will, gives help to the impious. Judah hoped in the Egyptians: let Egypt too be destroyed. The Egyptians trusted in the Ethiopians: let the Ethiopians too be conquered by the Assyrians. The Assyrians grew proud, thinking the victory to be not God's but their own strength's: let them too be conquered by the Babylonians. Babylon lifted up its head against God: let it too be overcome by the Medes and Persians. The Persians and Medes in part persecuted the people of God, and the most savage ram tossed all the peoples toward the East and the West: let the he-goat Alexander come and trample him under his feet. And let him who was lifted up beyond measure perish by poison, and his kingdom be divided into parts; and when it has long been dashed against itself, let it be ravaged as the Roman conquers. The Roman himself has torn the flesh of the saints with iron teeth and claws and with bloody mouth: let a stone be cut from the mountain without hands, and let it crush like potsherds the kingdom that was first most mighty and of iron, and then brittle and weak (Dan 2).

n: The desert of the sea. So Babylon is here called, because from a city as full of people as the sea is with water, it was become a desert. (Challoner) --- After its fall, it was mostly inundated, chap. xiii. 20. --- Land. Media and Persia, which lay to the south, and were not so beautiful as the environs of Babylon.

Spoileth. Baltassar is incorrigible, or his opponents must proceed. (Calmet) --- Elam; that is, O Persia: (Challoner) Cyrus, and Darius, the Mede. (Calmet) --- The former nation was weak, and the latter strong. (Worthington) --- Cease. The enemy will shew no pity; nor shall I; as Babylon did not heretofore. (Haydock)
Pain. He bewails the crimes and the fall of Babylon, which at this time was in amity with Ezechias, ver. 10. (Calmet)
Babylon. Protestants, "the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me." Septuagint, "My soul is turned into fear." (Haydock)
Drink. Persians refresh yourselves. --- Take up. Hebrew, "anoint." He may also allude to the Babylonians, who were feasting.
Camel. These two riders are the kings of the Persians and Medes. (Challoner) --- The sentinel, placed by Isaias, in spirit, or rather by the king of Babylon, brings these tidings. (Calmet)
Out. Literally, "He cried, a lion." (Haydock) --- Cyrus appears like one. Septuagint, "And call Urias to the watch-tower," &c., chap. viii. 2.
Horsemen, drawn by the ass and camel, ver. 7. This was verified long after.

Floor: you who must shortly be reduced to the utmost distress. Baladan was friendly to Ezechias. But Assaradon having seized Babylon, took Manasses prisoner; and the city thenceforward continued to fill up the measure of its sins. (Calmet)

Duma. That is, Idumea, or Edom. (Challoner) --- It was a city of that country, twenty miles from Eleutheropolis. (St. Jerome) --- Assaradon desolated Idumea the year following, ver. 16. The Jews absurdly apply to Rome what is said of Edom. (St. Jerome) (Calmet)
Night. Instead of joy, I must announce dreadful things. (Haydock)
Arabia. This sentence is not in the Roman (Calmet) or Alexandrian Septuagint, (Haydock) and Dedan is a city of Idumea. (Calmet) --- The Ismaelites are threatened. (Worthington)
Water. To neglect this was to be accessary to another's death, in those dreary regions, chap. xvi. 3., and Deuteronomy xxiii. 2.
Hireling; counting precisely, chap. xvi. 14. (Calmet) --- Cedar: Arabia, (Challoner) near to Edom. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

As whirlwinds come from the southwest, it comes from the desert, from a terrible land. A hard vision has been announced to me. The voice of the Babylonian people in fear is brought in, or of Babylon itself, because it hears that the Medes and Elamites are preparing an army against it and are coming from the wilderness; and it sets forth an example by way of comparison. As, it says, a violent storm usually comes from the southwest wind, so devastation comes upon me from the wilderness, from a terrible land, whose very name I cannot hear without dread. A hard vision has been announced to me: for what is harder than captivity at hand?
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of the desert of the sea. If I did not read in what follows in this chapter: Babylon, my beloved, has become a wonder to me; and again: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground; and above: Go up, Elam, and besiege, O Mede, I would be in doubt what this Burden is that is laid upon the desert of the sea. It is plain, therefore, that Babylon is called the desert of the sea, as Jeremiah says in the person of God: And I will make her sea desert, and I will dry up her land, and Babylon will become heaps of sand (Jer 51:36-37). And it is called sea because of the multitude of its inhabitants. Hence above, too, the multitude of Egypt was compared to the sea: The Lord will make the sea of Egypt desert. And that the Medes and Persians fought against Babylon and overthrew it, we read in the aforesaid Jeremiah: Sharpen the arrows, fill the quivers. The Lord will rouse the spirit of the kings of the Medes, and his mind is against Babylon, to destroy it, for it is the vengeance of the Lord, the vengeance of his Temple. Upon the walls of Babylon lift up a signal, strengthen the watch, set up watchmen, prepare ambushes: for the Lord has purposed, and has done all that he spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon. And again: Lift up a signal in the land, sound the trumpet among the nations, sanctify the nations against her, proclaim against her to the kings of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz, number Tapsar against her, bring up the horse like the stinging locust. Sanctify the nations against her, the kings of Media, its leaders and all its magistrates, and all the land of its dominion. And the land will be shaken and troubled, because the thought of the Lord has kept watch against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon desert and uninhabitable (Jer 51:11ff.).
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of the desert of the sea. As whirlwinds come from the south-west, it comes from the desert, from a terrible land. A hard vision has been told to me: he who is unbelieving deals faithlessly, and he who is a spoiler lays waste. Go up, Elam; besiege, O Mede: I have made all its groaning to cease. Therefore my loins are filled with pain; anguish has taken hold of me, like the anguish of a woman in labour. LXX: The vision of the desert of the sea. As a tempest passes through from the desert, coming from the desert. From a terrible land a hard vision has been announced to me: the transgressor transgresses, and the wicked man does wickedly. Against me come the Elamites and the ambassadors of the Persians: now I shall groan, and comfort myself; therefore my loins are filled with anguish, pains have seized me, as a woman in labour. What we think according to the History we have said briefly; now let us gather the chief points of tropology. The vision, or weight, is seen against the sea of this world; and it is seen by the Prophet with how many temptations this world is filled. That the world is called the sea (to pass over many things), I am content with a single testimony of the Psalm: They who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in many waters, these have seen the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep (Ps 106 [107]:23). For those who do the work of God in this world, and say with the Prophet, I have come into the depth of the sea, see his wonders in the deep; and, delivered from temptations and straits, they say that they have heard a terrible and hard vision. Now this very tempest comes from the desert, in which the Lord too was tempted (Matt 4), and Israel lay open to the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions (Num 21).
Commentary on Isaiah

And rightly, according to the Hebrew, whirlwinds and tempests come from the desert and from a terrible land, where God is not the inhabitant, and where all things are earthly; and whoever is unbelieving does a thing in keeping with his faithlessness, and he who is a spoiler lays waste. Hence he speaks boldly against his adversaries: Go up, Elam; besiege, O Mede: I have made all the groaning of the desert of the sea, and of the terrible land, and of the hardest vision that has been told, to cease. For my loins, doing penance, are full no longer of pleasure, as before, but of pain; and I shall no longer say: My loins are filled with illusions (Ps 37 [38]:7). For anguish and tribulation have taken hold of me, as it is wont to hold a woman in labour. The common edition and the Hebrew differ greatly from each other in this place; therefore we shall touch briefly on both, lest we leave the φιλεγκλημῶσιν some little occasion of carping at us.
Commentary on Isaiah

He who is unbelieving acts faithlessly: and he who is a despoiler lays waste. In the Hebrew it can be read thus: You who slay, slay; and you who lay waste, lay waste, so that the prophetic utterance is directed to the Elamite and the Mede himself, urging him to accomplish what he has begun, to go up fearlessly, to besiege the most mighty city. But if it is read as we have translated, as though spoken of a third person, he who is unbelieving acts faithlessly: and he who is a despoiler lays waste, it is to be joined with what precedes, in which Babylon declares that a hard vision has been announced to it.

Go up, Elam, besiege, O Mede: I have made all its groaning cease. Do not fear, he says, O Persian and Mede, the multitude of Babylon; do not dread its past power: I have made to cease all its groaning and the weight with which it used to oppress you before; either because no one now groans and grieves, oppressed by the power of Babylon; or because Babylon itself is oppressed by such great evils that it does not even have freedom to groan.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when it has come, it passes through and goes by; and then he who endures it understands that none transgresses but the transgressor, and none does wickedly but the wicked. That we are overwhelmed, then, by the waves of the sea, and that a savage tempest overpowers us, is our own fault, who were transgressors and wicked before the tempest. And what he says, Against me come the Elamites and the ambassadors of the Persians, has this sense: Elamites means despisers; Persians, tempters. Let those come, then, who are wont to despise, to scorn and to tempt: but I shall groan, and my groaning will be my consolation.
Commentary on Isaiah

But my loins too are filled with anguish, and pains have taken hold of me as of a woman in labour, so that from the fear of the Lord I may conceive and bring forth, and make the spirit of his salvation upon the earth.
Commentary on Isaiah

I fell down when I heard, I was troubled when I saw; my heart withered, darkness stupefied me; Babylon my beloved has been made a wonder to me. Set the table, behold in the watchtower those who eat and drink: rise up, princes, seize the shield. LXX: I did wickedly so as not to hear, I hastened so as not to see; my heart goes astray, iniquity has overflowed upon me; my soul stands fast in fear. Prepare the table, watch the watchtower: eat, drink; rise up, princes, prepare the shields. At the hearing and at the hardest vision which the Prophet saw coming from the desert of the sea, he says that he fell down and was troubled, and that with his eyes almost darkened and his mind stupefied he did not know what he was seeing. For that Babylon (for which Aquila and Theodotion translated darkness, to signify this world, which lies in the evil one (1 John 5), and whose princes, according to the apostle Paul (Eph 6), are the rulers of this darkness), which was once dear either to the Prophet or to God, has become a wonder in its overthrow. Hence the Prophet is commanded, eating at the table of the Lord and filled with his food, to contemplate more carefully what is to come upon the world; and through him it is said to all believers that, eating and drinking the body and blood of the Lord, they should be turned into princes of the Church, and hear with the Apostles, Rise up, and seize the shield of faith from the armour of the apostle Paul (Eph 6), with which they may quench the fiery darts of the devil. This according to the Hebrew and the interpretation begun concerning the world. Let us pass on to the edition of the Seventy, which differs greatly from the foregoing. The Prophet reproves himself, or rather in his own person confesses the error of others, who, following the letter that kills, despise the spirit that gives life; and he says that he did wickedly so as not to hear the law spiritually, but on the contrary hastened not to see the mysteries of God, and did not say with David: Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law (Ps 118 [119]:18). Therefore his heart goes astray, and, filled with Jewish superstition, stands fast not in the love of God but in fear, so that he has the spirit of bondage in fear, and by no means the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, Abba, Father (Rom 8). Hence he is commanded to come to the table of spiritual food, and that all who follow his example should eat and drink at it; and that, having scorned the old error, those who lay in the letter should rise up in the spirit and become princes, and say with the Prophet: Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will (Ps 5:13).
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore my loins are filled with pain: anguish has possessed me, like the anguish of a woman giving birth: I fell down when I heard, I was troubled when I saw. My heart has withered, darkness has stupefied me. Babylon, my beloved, has been made a wonder to me. The Prophets are obscure for this reason, that the persons in them change very often. So now too the voice of Isaiah is brought in, lamenting Babylon in the prophetic spirit: that such great evils are to come upon it that he who tells of them, overcome by fear, cannot burst out into words, seeing the blood of so great a multitude shed; and, moved by the feeling of pity (for he is a man speaking of men), he grieves no less than a woman is wont to howl in childbirth; but, troubled and trembling, and falling to the ground, with his eyes darkened, he does not know what he is saying. And for what we have rendered: Babylon, my beloved, in the Hebrew one reads NESEPH ESCI (נשף השקי); and it is the very word which we set down at the beginning of the Babylonian Burden, upon a misty mountain: for there Neseph is written for misty or dark. And this city is properly so called because of its height and the summit of its pride raised up to heaven.
St. Jerome, Commentary on Daniel, CHAPTER FIVE

[Daniel 5:30-31] "On that same night Belshazzar, King of the Chaldeans, was slain, and Darius the Mede succeeded to his kingdom at the age of sixty-two." Josephus writes in his tenth book of the Jewish Antiquities that when Babylon had been laid under siege by the Medes and Persians, that is, by Darius and Cyrus, Belshazzar, King of Babylon, fell into such forgetfulness of his own situation as to put on his celebrated banquet and drink from the vessels of the Temple, and even while he was besieged he found leisure for banqueting. From this circumstance the historical account could arise, that he was captured and slaughtered on the same night, while everyone was either terrified by fear of the vision and its interpretation, or else taken up with festivity and drunken banqueting. As for the fact that while Cyrus, King of the Persians, was the victor, and Darius was only King of the Medes, it was Darius who was recorded to have succeeded to the throne of Babylon, this was an arrangement occasioned by factors of age, family relationship, and the territory ruled over. By this I mean that Darius was sixty-two years old, and that, according to what we read, the kingdom of the Medes was more sizable than that of the Persians, and being Cyrus's uncle, he naturally had a prior claim, and ought to have been accounted as successor to the rule of Babylon. Therefore also in a vision of Isaiah which was recited against Babylon, after many other matters too lengthy to mention, an account is given of these things which are to take place: "Behold I Myself will rouse up against them the Medes, a people who do not seek after silver nor desire gold, but who slay the very children with their arrows and have no compassion upon women who suckle their young" (Isaiah 13:17-18). And Jeremiah says: "Sanctify nations against her, even the kings of Media, and the governors thereof and all the magistrates thereof and all the land under the power thereof" (Jeremiah 51:28). Then follow the words: "The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing-floor during the time of its treading; yet a little while, and the time of its harvesting will come" (Jeremiah 51:33). And in testimony of the fact that Babylon was captured during a banquet, Isaiah clearly exhorts her to battle when he writes: "Babylon, my beloved, has become a strange spectacle unto me: set thou the table and behold in the mirrors those who eat and drink; rise up, ye princes, and snatch up your shields!" (Isaiah 21:4-5).
Commentary on Daniel

And in testimony of the fact that Babylon was captured during a banquet, Isaiah clearly exhorts her to battle when he writes: "Babylon, my beloved, has become a strange spectacle unto me: set thou the table and behold in the mirrors those who eat and drink; rise up, ye princes, and snatch up your shields!"
Commentary on Isaiah

Set the table, watch in the watchtower those eating and drinking: arise, princes, seize the shield. This place is taken in two ways. O Medes and Elamites, to whom I said above: Go up, Elam, besiege, O Mede, take food, prepare yourselves for the coming battle, lest, when the time of fighting has come, weariness hold you back. And when you have eaten and drunk, arise, seize your arms, vanquish the Babylonian. And his saying, watch in the watchtower, is read in this sense: look out diligently for what is to come. It can also be understood thus: O Babylon, prepare a table and a banquet for Belshazzar your king, son of Evil-merodach, grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, and see what happens after the meal, at which he will drink toasts to harlots and concubines from the vessels of the Lord. O princes, who recline at table with the king (and he means the Medes and Persians), arise and seize your arms to kill the king. We learn this more fully in the volume of Daniel (Dan 5).
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set a watchman, and let him declare whatever he sees. And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel; and he gazed diligently with much attention, and a lion cried out. LXX: For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set for yourself a watchman, and whatever you see, declare it. And I saw two horsemen riding, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel; I heard much hearing, and I called Uriah to the watchtower. The Prophet is bidden to set a watchman in his heart, and to gaze more carefully at what is to come upon the world; and he saw two horsemen, a rider on an ass and a rider on a camel. These someone has interpreted so as to call the rider on the ass, according to the Gospel reading (Matt 21) and the prophecy of Zechariah (Zech 9), Christ; and on the contrary the rider on the camel the opposing power, on account of the foulness of that crooked animal. Others again refer the two riders, of the letter and of the spirit, to the two Testaments.
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus the Lord said to me: Go and set a watchman, and let him announce whatever he sees. And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass, and a rider on a camel. And he gazed diligently with much attention, and the lion cried out: Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand continually by day, and upon my watch I stand whole nights. Behold, there comes this rider, a man of the two-horsed chariot; and he answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground. My threshing, and son of my threshing floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you. He gives the reasons for the fear above: why anguish possessed him like a woman in labor, and he fell down on hearing, and was terrified and surrounded with dark horror. Thus, he says, the Lord said to me: Go and appoint a watchman, to foretell the future to you in the prophetic spirit; and when I had set him in the watchtower, he saw a two-horse chariot coming, and a charioteer upon it, and an ass and a camel drawing the chariot. And he signifies Cyrus king of the Persians and of the Medes, coming with a small and a great empire. For before Cyrus the Persians were obscure, and were held of no account among the nations; the Medes were always most mighty. This one rider, then, supported by the army of two nations, comes against Babylon: and that watchman who had been set to look out for what was to come cried out like a lion; or else the prophet himself is called a lion.
Commentary on Daniel

[Daniel 5:1] "Belshazzar the king made a great feast for his one thousand nobles; and each one drank in the order of his age." It should be known that this man was not the son of Nebuchadnezzar, as readers commonly imagine; but according to Berosus, who wrote the history of the Chaldeans, and also Josephus, who follows Berosus, after Nebuchadnezzar's reign of forty-three years, a son named Evilmerodach succeeded to his throne. It was concerning this king that Jeremiah wrote that in the first year of his reign he raised the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and took him out of his prison (Jeremiah 52:31). Josephus likewise reports that after the death of Evilmerodach, his son Neriglissar succeeded to his father's throne; after whom in turn came his son Labosordach. Upon the latter's death, his son, Belshazzar, obtained the kingdom, and it is of him that the Scripture now makes mention. After he had been killed by Darius, King of the Medes, who was the maternal uncle of Cyrus, King of the Persians, the empire of the Chaldeans was destroyed by Cyrus the Persian. It was these two kingdoms which Isaiah in chap. 21 (Isaiah 21:7) addresses as a charioteer of a vehicle drawn by a camel and an ass. Indeed Xenophon also writes the same thing in connection with the childhood of Cyrus the Great; likewise Pompeius Trogus and many others who have written up the history of the barbarians. Some authorities think that this Darius was the Astyages mentioned in the Greek writings, while others think it was Astyages' son, and that he was called by the other name among the barbarians. "And each one of the princes who had been invited drank in the order of his own age." Or else, as other translators have rendered it: "The king himself was drinking in the presence of all the princes whom he had invited."
Commentary on Isaiah

And because there was doubt about the person of the watchman who had seen Cyrus coming up, he himself explains it more plainly, and says: Upon the watchtower of the Lord I stand continually by day, declaring himself to be the watchman of the Lord, who, always set in the prophetic office, and obeying the command of the Lord by day and by night, speaks whatever he commands.
Commentary on Isaiah

But what the Seventy interpreters meant in this place, in translating uriam for lion, which in Hebrew is called ARIA (אריה), I do not well understand, especially since the aforementioned priest Urias, who is called to bear witness, is written with other letters.
Commentary on Isaiah

And for what is said in the Hebrew, ARIE (אריה), for which Aquila and Symmachus translated lion and lioness, the Seventy, meaning I know not what, set down οὐρίαν, which a certain man thinks is to be interpreted light of the Lord, though light of the Lord, which is not found here, is written with other letters, and lion, which is read here, with others. And he would have this watchman, whom the Prophet is bidden to set in his heart, be called Uriah, and by the interpretation of the name he refers it to the understanding of Christ, so that, with him dwelling in us, we may be able to see what is to come. This indeed could also be fitted to the lion, since Jacob (Gen 49) and Balaam (Num 23 and 2) name the lion under the mystery of Christ.
Commentary on Isaiah

I am upon the watchtower of the Lord, standing continually by day, and I am upon my guard, standing whole nights. Behold, this man comes, the rider of a chariot of horsemen, and he answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken to the ground. My threshing, and the sons of my floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you. LXX: The Lord said: I stood all day, and upon the camp I stood all night; and behold, he comes, the rider of a chariot, and answering he said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all her idols and the things made with hands are broken to the ground. Hear, you who are left and are grieving; hear what I have heard from the Lord Sabaoth; the God of Israel has declared it to us. The Prophet stands on the watchtower of the Lord, and, set in his light, looks forward to what is to come. And this is the guard he keeps, this the office entrusted to him: to see, in the darkness of this world, what is to come.
Commentary on Isaiah

What, then, did the lion cry out? Behold, there comes this rider, a man of the two-horsed chariot: there is no doubt that Cyrus is indicated. And the lion himself, who had cried out above, answered and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all the graven images of her gods are broken on the ground. For when the rider of the two-horse chariot laid it waste, Babylon was destroyed forever, and the temple of Bel and all the idols were leveled to the ground.
Commentary on Isaiah

Behold, he says, this man comes, signifying by what follows that he saw the Lord the Savior coming, seated on a chariot of two, and yoking to one car two horses, or rather two animals, the ass and the camel. And this rider of the chariot answered the Prophet, who longed and desired to hear his words, and said: Fallen, fallen is Babylon, the confusion of the whole world; it fell at my coming, when I took a human body, and it will utterly collapse at the consummation of the world. And all her graven images are broken to the ground. For which the Seventy translated idols and things made with hands, signifying the scripture of the heretics and the various errors of heresies, who are makers of idols and worship what they have fashioned out of their own heart.
Commentary on Isaiah

And in what follows: My threshing, and son of my threshing floor, he makes an apostrophe to Jerusalem, and to the Temple which stands on the threshing floor of Ornan, and says to her: O Jerusalem, and you people, son of my Temple, let not what I have said seem incredible to you: for they are not my words but the Lord's, and it is his words that have resounded through my mouth. Some think, but wrongly, that this is said not to Jerusalem but to Babylon, of which he said above as well: Babylon, my beloved, has been made a wonder to me; and that the sense is: You who have crushed me will yourself be crushed too, not by my word, but by the power of the Lord, which foretells to you that these things will come.
Commentary on Isaiah

And what follows, in the person of the Prophet saying, My threshing, and the sons of my floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you, has this sense according to the Hebrew: O people, who are to be stored in my granaries, whom I have therefore threshed in various straits, that I might shake the chaff from you, and the purest wheat might be stored in my granaries: what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, is to come upon the whole world, this I have declared to all of you who are in the world. Others again say that the person is still the earlier one, namely the Lord the Savior, and that he himself speaks to the Apostles: What I have heard from the Father I have declared to you (John 15:15). And since in place of this the Seventy read, hear, you who are left and are grieving, this seems to me the sense according to their translation: O Apostles, of whom Isaiah writes, Unless the Lord had left us seed, we should have been as Sodom, and should have been like Gomorrah (Isa 1:9), whose remnant the Apostle too, writing to the Romans, teaches has been saved (Rom 9): you who were left of the people of the Jews that you might be saved, and grieve over the perdition of your nation, of which we read elsewhere also, There is sorrow in my heart, and continual grief for my brethren, who are Israelites according to the flesh (Rom 9:2, 3): these things which I have heard from God the Father I declare to you, which the God of Israel foretells to you as things to come.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Duma. He calls to me out of Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? And the watchman said: The morning comes, and the night: if you seek, seek; turn, come. For Duma the Seventy put Idumaea. But Duma is not the whole province of Edom, but a certain region of it which lies toward the south, and is twenty miles distant from the city of Palestine which today is called Eleutheropolis: near it are the mountains of Seir, which took their name from their founder; for Seir means shaggy and hairy, which Esau was. In the prophet Obadiah we have discussed this nation more fully: there it was necessary to go over the ancient history, and to draw in as testimony the same Visions of Ezekiel and Jeremiah, and especially the prophecy against Mount Seir (Ezek 25 and 35; Jer 49); and that saying from the Psalms: Into Edom I will stretch out my shoe; and elsewhere: The tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek (Ps 59 [60]:10; Ps 82 [83]:7-8). Amos also says: For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he pursued his brother with the sword, and violated his mercy (Amos 1:11), or, as Symmachus translated, his bowels: because he dared to fight against kindred peoples, and to be at variance with them in hostile hatred. Now the region of Esau was in the region of Duma, that is, in the mountains of Seir. We believe that this, as a metropolis, in keeping with the order of the preceding Visions, was conquered by the Assyrians or by Nebuchadnezzar, and that, mindful of its former stock, since it was begotten of the line of Abraham and Isaac, it implored the help of God, and under the compulsion of necessity begged for his clemency. Now, therefore, the Lord recounts: He who is besieged in Seir and surrounded by enemies implores my help, and says: O watchman of Israel, who guard your people with an everlasting watch, and, as it were in the night, keep vigil while they sleep, lest the enemy break in, why do you not protect us also, who are of his seed, with like clemency? To them I reply, the watchman and keeper of whom it is written: He who guards Israel will not slumber nor sleep (Ps 120 [121]:4). Morning comes for my people, and night for the nation of the Edomites; to them I will give light, you I will leave in darkness. Or certainly thus: the light has come, the night being past; if you call upon my help, and are of the stock of my servant Abraham, do not seek me only in your necessities, but turn to me with your whole mind. Come, and I will receive you as penitents. Let this be said according to the history. For the rest, because of the similarity of the letter, and because RES and DALETH differ little from each other, some of the Hebrews read Roma for Duma, wishing the prophecy to be directed against the Roman empire, by the frivolous persuasion by which they always think that the Romans are pointed out under the name of Edom: but Duma means silence.
Commentary on Isaiah

The Lord therefore speaks to the choir of the Apostles and commands it: Call to me those who are of Seir, so that the multitude of the nations may serve me, which, after the likeness of Esau, has nothing in itself soft and smooth and sleek, but is shaggy, wild, intractable. And you, O Apostles, after you have called the nations to me out of Seir, guard the ramparts of the Church, lest the enemy break in easily; lest the lion, roaring and going about, seeking an entrance by which he may get in, tear and scatter the flock shut up in the Church. And the multitude of the Church answered: Not only in prosperity but in adversity, that is, both by day and by night, I will keep your commandments, O God.
