To her God says: If you truly seek me, show by your works that you seek me; and let it not suffice you to have sought once, but seek always him whom you have found; and to hold him more perfectly, forget your people and your father's house, and, having forsaken the error of the Gentiles, abide with me in the Church. This we would say according to the Seventy, who put in the title the vision of Idumea, that is, of the earthly, to show that those are called who formerly served earthly works. Further, according to Aquila, who set down Dumah, that is, silence, or likeness, we can understand it thus: that the multitude of the nations is roused to the likeness of the people of Israel, and that where formerly there was silence of the law of God, there the cry of confession should be, and the wild olive be grafted into the good olive. We read also in the parable of the Gospel that servants were sent to call good and bad, and to fill the householder's banquet with whomsoever they found, because the first guests refused to come (Matt 22). The Church too can relate that the Lord cries aloud to her out of Seir, that is, out of earthly places, and calls her forth to salvation; and she may say to the Lord himself: O watchman, why, rising by night, do you dwell in darkness? Why are you, without sin, in the flesh of sin? For what reason did you will to take a human body? The watchman answered, that is, the Samaritan, who in the Gospel carried the wounded man on his shoulders to the inn (Luke 10): The morning comes, and the night. And the sense is: For the multitude of the nations the sun of righteousness has risen, and for the Jews darkness has come; according to what is said by the Lord: For the judgment of this world I have come, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind (John 9:39). And the watchman himself, who had said, The morning comes, and the night, speaks to the multitude of the nations: If you seek me, seek more earnestly. Turn to me, you returning sons, and I will heal your bruises; and come to me. The passages are difficult, and since according to the history they are by no means plain, we are compelled to follow various opinions according to the ἀναγωγὴν.
Commentary on Obadiah

The Jews dream in vain that this prophecy is made against the city of Rome and the Roman empire; and that in what is written in Isaiah, The burden of Dumah, with the stroke of a letter slightly changed, res can be read in place of deleth, and it sounds Rome, since the letter vau in their language is taken both for u and for o.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of Dumah: he calls to me out of Seir: Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said: The morning comes, and the night. If you seek, seek; turn, and come. LXX: The vision of Idumea: he calls to me out of Seir: Guard the ramparts; I keep guard morning and night; if you seek, seek, and dwell with me. The Hebrew word ELAI (אלי), which all have translated to me, if you choose to read it ELI, means my God or my strong one. And what we have rendered he calls or he summons, that is, καλεῖ, may, by the ambiguity of the Hebrew and the Greek speech, be read call! or summon!; and the sense is: God, who is my watchman, calls me day and night to repentance, so that, leaving Seir, which means shaggy and hairy, I may return and dwell with him. Dumah sounds either likeness or silence; but Idumea is rendered earthly.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 6.34

Again he says, "Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The watchman said, 'The morning comes, and also the night.' " For "the watchman came by night," in that the guardian of the human race even showed himself manifest in the flesh, and yet Judea, being close pressed by the darkness of its faithlessness, never knew him. Where it is well added in the voice of the watchman, "The morning comes, and also the night." For by his presence has a new light shone out upon the world, and yet the former darkness remained in the hearts of unbelievers. And it is well said, "They shall grope in the noonday as in the night," for we search out by groping that which we do not see with our eyes. Now the Jews had seen his undisguised miracles, and yet they still went on seeking him, as it were groping for him, when they said, "How long do you make us to doubt? If you be the Christ, tell us plainly." See, the light of miracles was before their eyes, yet stumbling in the darkness of their own hearts, they continued to grope in seeking for him."
Commentary on Isaiah

Since we have understood what Kedar is, and what Arabia, and what Hazor, let us see what the prophet Isaiah says: In the forest at evening you will sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. The word ARAB (ערב), as we have often said already, is used for evening, and Arabia, and raven, and plain, and the West. And for what we, following the Seventy, have translated you will sleep, one can render you will stay or you will dwell, that is, αὐλιθήσεσθε, which in Hebrew is THALINU (תלנו). DODANIM (דדנים) too is rendered as kinsmen and relatives. So it is now foretold to the Jews who have been able to escape the Babylonian siege, and to cross from the devastation of the whole province to the neighboring desert, that they will dwell in the wilderness of Arabia, on the road that leads to their brothers.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden in Arabia. This is not found in the edition of the Seventy Translators; but what follows, In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in the paths of Dodanim, is joined to the preceding vision, so that it reads, if you seek, seek, and dwell with me in the forest. Arabia in our tongue sounds evening, which is the beginning of night and of darkness; and everyone who has the beginning of sins dwells in the evening. But he who comes to the height of them stands in the middle of the night. Hence in Egypt too the firstborn are slain at midnight (Exod 12). And the apostle Peter denied the Lord three times before the cock crew, which is understood as midnight (Matt 26); but after the night was far spent and the day began to draw near, when the darkness of midnight had been overcome and the cock, herald of the light, sounded, he wept bitterly and understood his sin, and at that time he could say: In the evening weeping shall linger, and in the morning gladness (Ps 29 [30]:6). So much meanwhile on the present place. But the name of Arabia, that is, of evening and of the West, receives different meanings in other places of the Scriptures.

In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. LXX: In the forest at evening you shall sleep, in the way of Dedan. Those who have begun to be in wickedness, and are entering on the way of sins, do not sleep or linger in sown fields and fallow lands, nor in meadows and cornfields, which the Savior teaches are white for harvest, nor among fruit-bearing trees, but in fruitless forests, where there are brambles and thorns and where beasts dwell. Of such a forest we read also in the volume of Kings, that the wood or forest devoured more than were slain by the sword, when Absalom rose up as a rebel against his father (2 Sam 18). And rightly, since evening is the beginning of evils, they are said to dwell in the way and in the paths, and in the way of Dedan, which means judgments. For as many kinds of sins as they have, so many sentences of judgment do they deserve. But Dedan can also be interpreted great judgment.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden in Arabia. In the forest at evening you will sleep, in the paths of Dodanim. Meeting the thirsty, bring water: you who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of the swords, from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the bent bow, from the face of grievous battle. For thus says the Lord to me: Yet in one year, as in the year of a hireling: and all the glory of Kedar will be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the sons of Kedar will be diminished: for the Lord God of Israel has spoken. As I sought, and long turned over with deliberation, what Arabia this was to which the prophetic word is directed, whether the Moabites, or the Ammonites and Edomites, and all the other regions which are now called Arabia, what follows in this same Vision gave me occasion to see that the Ishmaelites must be understood: All the glory of Kedar will be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the sons of Kedar will be diminished (Isa 21:16-17). The book of Genesis teaches that from Ishmael were born Kedar and the Hagarenes, who by a perverted name are called Saracens. These dwell throughout the whole wilderness; of them, I think, the poet too speaks: And the Barcaei, roaming far and wide (Virgil, Aeneid 4); and the aforesaid volume: He will dwell over against the face of all his brothers (Gen 16:12): because a very broad desert stretches from India as far as Mauretania and the Atlantic Ocean. This, I think, is what the title in Jeremiah expresses: To Kedar and to the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck (Jer 49:28); and at once there follows: Thus says the Lord: Arise and go up to Kedar, and lay waste the sons of the East: they will take their tents and their flocks; they will carry off for themselves their skins and all their vessels and their camels (ibid., 29); and again: For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has taken counsel against you, he has devised plans against you. Arise and go up against a nation at ease, dwelling confidently, says the Lord: no doors, no bars for them: they dwell alone. And their camels will be for plunder, and the multitude of their cattle for a prey. And I will scatter to every wind those who have the hair of their head cut round: and from all their borders I will bring destruction upon them, says the Lord: and Hazor will be a dwelling of dragons, deserted forever; no man will remain there, nor will a son of man inhabit it (ibid., 30ff.). I have set down the whole testimony of the prophecy from Jeremiah, so that you may understand without doubt what Kedar is. And consider how he has described exactly the nation of the Ishmaelites, that is, of the Saracens: because they dwell in tents; they hold whatever abodes the night drives them to; they have herds, and flocks, and droves of camels; they have neither doors nor bars, for they do not live in cities but dwell in the wilderness. These too, then, were destroyed by the Babylonians, in that they overthrew to the ground the city of Hazor, which was the metropolis of that nation in the desert; and yet, though their droves of camels and sheep were taken, and their skins and tents divided by lot, the destruction of that whole nation is not signified, because on dromedary camels they are wont to flee a hundred miles and more in a single day through the vast wilderness. All the glory of Kedar, he says, will be taken away; and when the number of the archers has been diminished, since they excel above all in that art of fighting, the rest who have fled will remain.
Commentary on Isaiah

And again the discourse turns to the Ishmaelites, and urges them to mercy: Run, and go to meet your brothers, weary and in peril from burning thirst, and bring them water: for so great is the heat of the sun that, unless you come to their aid, they will perish in the wilderness; and bring not only water but bread too to the fugitives, so that your clemency may relieve those whom the siege has worn out.
Commentary on Isaiah

Moreover, that place in which we have translated: You who dwell in the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread, and have read it in the imperative mood, as if in the person of the Lord, they affirm can be read in the Hebrew thus: Those who dwell in the land of the south met the fugitive with bread; so that, when God had said to them, Meeting the thirsty, bring water, they with hostile mind brought bread without water, to increase their thirst with food.
Commentary on Isaiah

Coming to meet the thirsty, bring water, you who inhabit the land of the South; meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of the swords, from the face of the threatening sword, from the face of the bent bow, from the face of the grievous battle. LXX: To meet the thirsty bring water, you who dwell in the region of Teman; meet those who flee with bread, because of the multitude of the slain, because of the throng of those who go astray, because of the multitude of the sword, and because of the multitude of the bent bows, and because of the multitude of those who fall in war. You who are in Teman, which means South and perfection, and who dwell in that place of which it is written, God shall come from the South (Hab 3:3), and who are consummated and perfect, and have within you the light of the knowledge of the Scriptures: meet those who flee from Arabia and from the forest with water and bread, and do not wait until they come to you, but imitate that father of the Gospel parable who ran to meet his returning son. And he indeed gave the robe and offered the ring (Luke 15); but you, offer water and bread to those who flee, so that those who were weary and spent may be sustained by your mercy and pass the more quickly to your dwellings. For they have fled the swords of the heretics, the teaching of the Gentiles, the blasphemies of the Jews. And because they have seen many slain by their darts, and very many fallen in battle, they themselves long to be delivered by your help. This place may properly be understood as directed against those who, giving themselves to leisure and sloth, are content with their own salvation and do not stretch out a hand to the penitent and converted.
Morals on the Book of Job, Book 23.49

Again, by bread is set forth the instruction of heavenly doctrine, as is said by the prophet, "You who dwell in the land of the south, meet with bread him that is flying away." For they dwell in the land of the south who, placed within [the] holy church, are breathed upon by the love of the Spirit from on high. But he is flying who is wishing to escape from the evils of this world. He then who dwells in the land of the south should meet with bread him that is flying; that is, he who is already full of the Holy Spirit within the church should console with words of instruction the one who is endeavoring to escape from his evil ways.
Commentary on Isaiah
And at the same time he gives the reason why he commands this to be done, saying: They have fled the Babylonian sword, they have fled the bows of the Elamites, they have fled the threatening battle.
Commentary on Isaiah

Some, from the words yet in one year, and all the glory of Kedar will be taken away, would have it that what is foretold is not the Babylonian captivity, of which Jeremiah too speaks, but that of the Assyrians, who, one year after the devastation of Judea, pursued the Saracens far and wide.
Commentary on Isaiah

And do not despise the wretched: your captivity too will come quickly. For as the hireling's year is swift, and he thinks all labor short until he reaches the wage he longs for, so all the glory of the sons of Kedar will be taken from you, and your arrows will be broken, and a small number of fighters will remain.
Commentary on Isaiah

For thus says the Lord to me: Yet within one year, as in the year of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar shall be taken away, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers of the children of Kedar shall be diminished. For the Lord God of Israel has spoken. I tell you to meet with water and bread those who flee from the forest and from Arabia because the Lord has promised that these things shall be. As the year of a hireling passes quickly, who every day looks for nothing but the wage of his labour, or certainly is always at work and toil in order to receive the wage of his labour, so all the glory of Kedar, which means darkness, of which we read in the Psalm too, I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar (Ps 119 [120]:5), shall swiftly be taken away; and the whole number of the archers, that is, of the various doctrines, which used to wound those placed in the forest of Arabia, shall be brought to nothing, once those fleeing from the forest have been delivered, and have received the water of saving baptism, and have eaten the heavenly bread. For the Lord of all, and properly the God of Israel, that is, of those who behold God with the mind, has spoken that these things shall be.

n: The valley of vision: Jerusalem. The temple of Jerusalem was built upon Mount Moria, or the mountain of vision. But the city is here called, the valley of vision, either because it was lower than the temple, or because of the low condition to which it was to be reduced, (Challoner) during the captivity. (Worthington) --- Vision. Septuagint, "Sion." (Haydock) --- This prophecy regards the devastation caused by Sennacherib, (St. Jerome) Nabuchodonosor, (Sanctius) the Romans, (Eusebius) or by Assaradon, when he took Manasses, 2 Paralipomenon xxxiii. 11., and 4 Kings xxi. 10. --- Tops, to weep.
Battle. He taxes the king with cowardice.
People. He saw this in spirit, though he might not live to witness it. (Calmet)
Searching. That day beheld the Assyrians (Haydock) undermining the wall, and behaving with haughtiness (Calmet) on Mount Sion. (Haydock)
Wall. Arms were frequently hung thereon, Canticle of Canticles ix. 4. (Calmet)

Covering. Hebrew masac, (Haydock) "shade," for the convenience of the people, 4 Kings xvi. 18. --- Forest, built by Solomon. Ezechias has also procured store of arms, which were now delivered out to the citizens.
Many, but you have neglected them, (Calmet) till it be too late. (Haydock) --- Pool, communicating with Gehon on the west.
Walls. Manasses enclosed the pool within walls, forming a second town, 4 Kings xxii. 29. --- Ago. You have not imitated the piety of Ezechias.

Die. Thus the pagans encouraged themselves to feast. (Calmet) --- Ergo vivamus dum licet esse bene. (Petronius) --- This conduct betrayed an entire want of faith. (Calmet) --- "Nothing offends God so much....as contempt proceeding from despair." (St. Jerome)
Die. The repentance of Manasses, and the piety of Josias, could not avert the storm. Discite justitiam moniti et non temnere divos.
Temple, in the place of Eliacim. He had been secretary before, (Calmet) and had intruded himself into some office in the temple, which he abused. (Worthington)

Cock. St. Jerome's master assured him that the word which is usually rendered a warrior, has this meaning. (Haydock) --- The comparison agrees well with a proud man reduced to misery. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "With the captivity of a man, and he will cover thee." Septuagint, "he will cast out and bruise the man, and will take away thy comely robe, and throw thee into," &c. (Haydock)
Lord; Manasses, who hath exalted thee. (Calmet)

Eliacim, who had been displaced, ver. 15. He acted as regent after the departure of Manasses, who always followed his counsels at his return, Judith iv. 5. The priesthood was not then incompatible with civil and military functions.
Girdle, the badge of power, Job xii. 18.

Shoulder. Here the marks of dignity were worn. Eliacim was appointed master of the palace, over all the other servants. (Calmet) --- Thus we may gather what power Christ conferred on St. Peter, when he gave him the keys of heaven, Matthew xvi. 19., and Apocalypse iii. 7. (Haydock)
Peg, on which whatever is placed shall be secure, 1 Esdras ix. 8.
House. He shall be the ornament of the priesthood. --- Music. All affairs in church and state shall be at his disposal.
Fall. Sobna shall lose all his employments, and ruin others. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of the valley of Vision. The Seventy, although it is not found in the Hebrew, translated more plainly, the word of the valley of Zion. For this city is the seedbed of the prophets, in which the Temple was built and the Visions of the Lord were multiplied. Because, then, it is placed among the other nations and reckoned as one of many, it is by no means called a mountain, according to that prophetic saying: Its foundations are on the holy mountains: the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob (Ps 86 [87]:1); but a valley, because it has been humbled. Jeremiah says this very thing in other words, when he receives the cup full of wine and gives it to all the nations, and last of all holds it out to Jerusalem, that it may drink and vomit and fall and go mad: signifying that it too was to be laid waste by the Babylonians (Jer 25). The history of Kings and of Jeremiah tells this more fully. From this we understand that God is equally the creator of all, and disposes all things by the same judgment, according to what he himself says through Amos: Are you not to me as the sons of the Ethiopians, O sons of Israel? says the Lord. Did I not bring Israel up out of the land of Egypt, and the Palestinians from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene? Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the sinful kingdom (Amos 9:7). Lest the Jews should think that they had a privilege of merit because they had been led out of Egypt, he says that the other nations too had been transferred to other lands by his command.
Commentary on Isaiah

The burden of the valley of vision. LXX: The word of the valley of Zion. In the book of Hebrew Names we have set down that Zion means watchtower, which, set on high places, beholds from afar the things that are coming. Since, then, Zion, according to the laws of tropology, is referred to the Church, as in that saying of the second Psalm in the person of the Lord the Savior, But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain (Ps 2:6); and, Those who trust in the Lord are as Mount Zion (Ps 124 [125]:1); and, The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob (Ps 86 [87]:2); and more plainly the Apostle: You have come, he says, to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22): we ask why in the present vision it is called the valley of Zion. And by the very sequence of the words we are drawn to a spiritual understanding: that we should know that all the princes of perverse doctrines, who have fallen from the loftiness of the sense of the holy Scriptures and have rolled down to low things, dwell in the valley of Zion. Something of this kind I think Solomon too says in the Proverbs: The eye that mocks its father and despises the old age of its mother, let the ravens of the valleys dig it out, and the young eagles eat it (Prov 30:17). For as soon as the mind of the heretics has mocked the Creator, the Father, and despised the old age of the Church, its mother, it is dug out by foul and unclean birds, which are referred to the opposing powers. Nor can such men say, I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me (Ps 120 [121]:1); but, like brute beasts, they are bowed down to earthly things.

What is the matter with you also, that you too have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops? LXX: What has happened to you now, that you have all gone up onto vain housetops? That which, according to the Seventy translators, is asked in the volume of Kings, what is meant when Elisha says (2 Kgs 2:14), Where is the God of Elijah APHPHO (אפא), is set down more plainly in the present place: where the Seventy translated now, the Hebrew has APHPHO, which we have translated now also; and Aquila, wishing to preserve the Hebrew idiom, set down καίπερτοι, a conjunction which the Latin tongue cannot render. And when he says, What is the matter with you also?, he asks why she too goes up among the others, and, with the reputation of lofty things, abides in low ones. And the sense is: Since the Philosophers are puffed up, and all worldly wisdom, disputing about lofty things, despises the simplicity of the Church, why do you too pursue high things? These the Seventy, σημαντικώτερον, translated δώματα μάταια, that is, vain housetops, to show that there is also another housetop, from which the Savior forbids us to come down (Matt 24), which is not, however, a vain housetop. Indeed the apostle Peter too went up onto the housetop at the sixth hour of prayer (Acts 10). But now, to show the great variety of heresies, he has named not one housetop but very many housetops.
Commentary on Isaiah

What is it with you too, that you also have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops, full of clamor, a crowded city, an exultant town? A Hebrew used to tell me that the present Vision does not belong to the time when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and led Zedekiah, bound and deprived of his eyes, to Babylon, but to the times of Sennacherib, when Shebna the high priest betrayed a great part of the city, and only Zion, that is, the citadel and the Temple, and the nobles remained, after the example of the city of Rome, which, when the Gauls burst in, preserved its patricians and the flower of its youth in the citadel. But we can also speak of it as of the Babylonian captivity; although Eusebius refers everything to the coming of Christ, and thinks it was fulfilled in the times of Vespasian and Titus. Let us then pick out each point, touching briefly on the threefold exposition. What is it with you too? What do you have, he says, O Zion, that you too have gone up, all of you, onto the housetops? When he says, you too, he shows that the others had gone up before. Have you also been reckoned among the nations, that you are besieged by enemies and climb onto the housetops, full of the howling and lamentation of wretched women, you who were once a royal city?
Commentary on Isaiah

Full of clamour, a crowded city, an exulting town. LXX: The city is filled with those who cry out, an exulting city. The teaching of the heretics consists not in sense but in much speaking and clamour. Hence, on account of the multitude of those deceived, it is called a crowded city, and exulting on account of its pride. For being puffed up they swell, and boast that they have found holier things.

Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in battle. LXX: Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead dead in battle. The greatest part is overthrown by the deceptions of the heretics without any struggle or debate, and this is a very great crowd. The slain, then, or as the Seventy translated, the wounded of the valley of Zion are not slain and wounded by the sword, but have gone over to the heretics of their own will; and in comparison with those who are overcome after battle, he is the more unhappily wounded and slain who has surrendered of his own accord. Just as in martyrdom too, he who yielded after torments is liable to a lighter penalty than he who denied Christ without any necessity and without the pain of tortures.
Commentary on Isaiah

Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in war. All your princes have fled together, and have been harshly bound. All who were found have been bound together: they have fled far away. If you refer it to the times of Sennacherib, when the city was partly taken, they are rightly said not to have been conquered by the sword nor slain in war, but by treachery, some fleeing from the city, and others, whom the enemy overpowered, bound in chains. But if to the Babylonian captivity, which is also the truer view, we shall say that they were overcome not by battle but by siege. And if you wish to understand it tropologically, with Eusebius, of the coming of Christ, you will say that they were slain not by the sword but by unbelief, and that all their princes withdrew from God and were bound with the cords of sins, and that there was none of the Pharisees who was not bound in the nets of the devil.
Commentary on Isaiah

All your princes have fled together, and have been harshly bound. In this place we have followed the translation of the Seventy, because in sense it is not far from the Hebrew. But to translate word for word from the Hebrew, it reads thus among them: All your chief men have departed together, they have been bound by the bow; and the other translators also followed this edition. For all the princes of the heretics have departed from the Church of Christ to the synagogue of Satan, and have gone over together, discordant in faithlessness, concordant in desertion; and they have been bound by the bow, of which it is written in the Psalm: Behold, the sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart (Ps 10 [11]:2), and to send the fiery darts of the devil, which both wound and bind. And therefore they have been harshly bound, because they have stopped their ears like deaf asps, and stopping their ears, which will not hear the voices of the charmers, nor of the sorcerer charming wisely. For this reason the apostle Paul too commands that a heretic be left to his perversity after one admonition (Titus 3), because he is perverted and condemned by his own judgment. For they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us (1 John 2:19). Of these fugitive princes the prince is he whom the same Isaiah calls the fleeing dragon, the crooked serpent, who, when he has sent deadly words into the ears of the deceived, binds them harshly and does not suffer them to escape from his bonds. Delivered from these, the saint rejoiced in the Psalm: My soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the fowlers (Ps 123 [124]:7). And in another place, rejoicing that he has escaped, he says: You are my upholder and my refuge. My God, I will hope in him. For he has delivered me from the snare of the fowlers, and from the harsh word (Ps 90 [91]:2-3), or the turbulent word, which properly signifies the teaching of the heretics.

All who were found in you are bound together; they have fled far off. LXX: And the strong in you have fled far away. The Prophet's speech is still against the valley of Zion, whose inhabitants have gone up onto vain housetops and have cried out with a confused clamour, and have been wounded without battle; all of whose princes have fled and been harshly bound, and those who were strong among them have fled further away. For the more prudent a man is in heretical perversity, the further he withdraws from the Lord. And as for what he says according to the Hebrew, All were found in you, we ought to note this: that the heretics too say they have found those whom they have deceived; but their finding is perdition. Accordingly they are bound together and flee far off. Nor am I pleased with that exposition which holds that, according to the diversity of the heresies, the distances of those who flee are also diverse, since the holy Scripture says (Luke 11:23) that all who have been found by the heretics are bound together and have fled very far, the Lord saying: He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters. Hence it is said of Moses (Exod 24): Moses alone drew near to God, but the rest did not draw near. For to his saints God is a God who draws near, and not from afar, says the Lord.
HOMILIES CONCERNING THE STATUES 18:8

Grief is often capable of refreshing distressed souls, and of rendering a burdened conscience light: consider how often women, when they have lost their most beloved children, break their hearts, and perish, if they are forbidden to mourn, and to shed tears. But if they do all which those who are sad, are wont to do, they are relieved, and receive consolation. And what wonder that this should be the case with women, when you may even see a prophet affected in a similar manner? Therefore he was continually saying, "Suffer me—I will weep bitterly—labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people." So that, oftentimes, sadness is the bearer of consolation; and if it is so with regard to this world, much more with regard to spiritual things.
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore I said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: do not press to console me over the devastation of the daughter of my people. If at the devastation of Babylon the Prophet weeps with the feeling of a mourner, and says: Anguish has possessed me, like the anguish of a woman giving birth: I fell down when I heard, I was troubled when I saw, my heart has withered, darkness has stupefied me: Babylon my beloved has been made a wonder to me, how much more now, at the ruin of his own city, can he accept no consolation, giving himself wholly to lamentation!
Commentary on Isaiah

Therefore I said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly; do not press to comfort me over the devastation of the daughter of my people. For it is a day of slaughter and of trampling and of weeping from the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision, searching the wall, and magnificent upon the mountain. LXX: Therefore I said: Let me alone, I will weep bitterly; do not strive to comfort me over the breaking of the daughter of my race; for it is a day of tumult and of perdition and of trampling, and error from the Lord God Sabaoth in the valley of Zion; they err from the least to the greatest, they err upon the mountains. Samuel too mourned for Saul (1 Sam 15), and the Lord and Savior wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19; 2 Cor 12:21); and the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: Lest, when I come to you again, God humble me, and I mourn for many who sinned before and have not done penance. Hence, with the feeling of one who suffers with them, he says to others also: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn? (2 Cor 11:29). So the Prophet too, seeing the people that was once of vision climbing the vain housetops and living in clamour, and all its princes fled and bound with the chains of sins, bursts into tears, and drives away those who would console him, and testifies that he weeps with most bitter weeping, not over the sons but over the daughter of his people, which has lost the dignity of manhood.
Commentary on Isaiah

For it is a day of slaughter, and of trampling, and of weeping, for the Lord God of hosts in the Valley of vision. He gives the reasons, according to the threefold understanding, why he said: Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: because Zion has been trampled down, once the mountain of visions and now the valley of weeping.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the day of judgment and slaughter and trampling will by no means be Jerusalem, which means vision of peace, but of its ancient name Jebus, which means trampling; a day of weeping too, or of error, as the Seventy translated, from the Lord Sabaoth: not that weeping and error come from the Lord, but through the occasion of the holy Scriptures, which the Lord gave to be read, an occasion of error arises for those who can say: Why have you made us err from your way? (Isa 63:17). And in another place: The Lord has mingled for them a spirit of error (ibid. 29:10): so that they should stand not on the mountain of Vision but in the valley of Zion. And this very day, which arises from the Lord of hosts in the valley of Vision to show the works of each, searches the wall of the heretics, which they have built against the Church like a most solid rampart; and it searches the magnificent and glorious one, that is, their teachers, who boast that they stand upon Christ the mountain, of which we read elsewhere: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare to us his way (Isa 2:3). Further, as for what the Seventy translated, they err from the least to the greatest, they err upon the mountains, we ought to understand this: that those who are greater are in greater wickedness, and yet that all err from the least to the greatest, and err upon the mountains: Moses, Jeremiah and the other Prophets, the Evangelists and the Apostles. And though they dwell in the valley, they err in a wondrous way upon the mountains.
Commentary on Isaiah

Searching the wall, and magnificent upon the mountain: and Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of a horseman, and the shield laid bare the wall. The army of Babylon is described entering the city, occupying the temple, and proudly driving through the streets in four-horse chariots. And that the shield, which is wont to cover other things, laid bare the gilded doorposts and the walls clad with marble facing, sounds elegantly in the Hebrew, and the sense is most beautiful: that the shield protected no one, but laid bare, since all the riches were torn out by the strength of the soldiers. If, however, the Elamites are set in the battle, Elam being a city of the Assyrians, it cannot be referred to the times of the Roman overthrow, unless perhaps we interpret everything allegorically.
Commentary on Isaiah

These Elamites, according to the edition of the Seventy, have not one quiver but several; and they are riders of men, on whose souls they ride; and there is a very great multitude preparing itself for battle against the Church, so that all its valleys are filled; and the horsemen stop up their senses, and by their combat challenge to the contest the churchman, who is interpreted Judah; and when he brings forward the testimonies of the Scriptures and refutes all lies, the heretics will see the houses of the city of David, and will come to know all the things formerly secret: how in the citadel of David, which means strong of hand, that is, of Christ, are all the doctrines of truth. The places are obscure, not only according to the history but according to the ἀναγωγὴν. Those, then, whom our views displease ought to bring forward their own, so that we may acquiesce in their explanation, if it is true.
Commentary on Isaiah

And Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of a man, a horseman, and the shield laid bare the wall. And your choice valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set their seats in the gate. And the covering of Judah shall be uncovered, and you shall see in that day the armoury of the house of the forest; and you shall see the breaches of the city of David, that they are multiplied. LXX: But the Elamites took quivers, riders, men upon horses, and a gathering of fighters; and your choice valleys shall be filled with chariots, and horsemen shall throng your gates; and they shall uncover the gates of Judah, and they shall look on that day into the choice houses of the city; and they shall uncover the hidden things of the houses of the citadel of David, and they shall see that they are many. Elam, which means their ascent, or the Elamites, as the Seventy translated, whom we render despisers, took up the quiver to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart; they are horsemen of men in a chariot, to lay bare with their shield and their assault the wall of Zion and the strongholds of the Church.
Commentary on Isaiah

And your choice valleys will be full of chariots, and the horsemen will set their seats at the gate. And the covering of Judah will be uncovered, and you will see in that day the armory of the house of the forest, and you will see the breaches of the city of David, that they have been multiplied. He plainly describes the captivity which took place in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, of which Jeremiah too speaks: Behold, I will call together all the families of the kingdoms of the North, says the Lord, and they will come, and each will set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its walls round about (Jer 1:15). And lest we should think this foretold in word and not fulfilled in deed, the same Jeremiah says: In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month, the city was opened, and all the princes of the king of Babylon entered, and sat in the middle gate (Jer 39:2). Then, therefore, a countless army was poured out round about the city of Jerusalem, and the Holy of holies was opened, and the armory, which was planted with a grove, was thrown open by the enemy's ravaging, and, the walls having been breached, the enemy entered through all parts of the city.
Commentary on Isaiah

And your choice valleys, he says, and your lowly doctrines, O valley of Zion, shall be full of chariots, those which the Lord sank with Pharaoh, whose horsemen and riders shall set their seats in your gates, so as not to let those besieged and shut up in you go out.
Commentary on Isaiah

Then almighty God, through churchmen, shall uncover the coverings of Judah and all the secrets of those who stand in the confession of the faith; and then, O valley of Zion, in that day and in the clear light of truth, you shall see the whole armour of the Apostle, and of the house of the forest, in which the throng of the nations stands; as it is sung also in Psalm 131 (132): Behold, we have heard of it in Ephrathah; we have found it in the fields of the forest (Ps 131 [132]:6). And when the covering and secret of Judah, which formerly was hidden on account of the mystery, has been uncovered, and you have seen the armour of the Church, then you will understand the schisms of the city of David, which you have multiplied in order to gather to yourself deceived peoples.
Commentary on Isaiah

And you gathered the waters of the lower pool, and you numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and you destroyed houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the two walls, and the water of the old pool: and you did not look up to him who had made it, and you did not see its maker from afar. He relates how they prepared the city for the siege: they transferred the waters of the lower pool, which could be captured, to the upper fortification; they destroyed houses and built walls; family by family they reckoned up how much water each house should receive; they made a cistern between the two walls, and restored the old pool to store the waters; and they did not rather call upon the help of God, who is the founder of the city and the Lord of the pool; as if he had said in other words: You have placed your trust in man, and not in God, who is the maker of man. Some, according to mystical senses, understand the old pool as the shadow of the Law, and the reservoir built between two walls, namely the New and the Old Testament, as built by the traditions and commandments of the Pharisees, one that cannot hold water: and that they did not look to the Son of God, nor believe in the presence of him whom they had not seen of old, because they had always been unbelieving toward the precepts of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And you gathered the waters of the lower pool, and you numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and you pulled down houses to fortify the wall. And you made a reservoir between the two walls, and the water of the old pool; and you did not look to him who had made it, and you did not see its maker from afar. LXX: And they turned the water of the ancient pool into the city, and they pulled down the houses of Jerusalem to strengthen the walls of the city; and you made yourselves water between the two walls within the ancient pool; and you did not look to him who made it from the beginning, and you did not see its creator. You who will see, or do see, the breaches of the city of David, that is, of the Church, which have been multiplied throughout the whole world; who have gathered the waters of your pool and teaching, not the upper but the lower, and have numbered, or pulled down, the houses of Jerusalem in order to fortify your wall: you have not dug wells which might have living and eternal waters, but broken cisterns, which cannot hold water. And you have made them between the two walls of the New and the Old Testament, and have neglected the water of the old pool, and have not considered God the giver of the law, and have utterly neglected the maker of the world. This according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy, the heretics considered that they were many, and trusting in this multitude they turned the teaching of the Old Testament away from the city of God, which is the Church, and pulled down the houses of Jerusalem in order to build assemblies of the wicked; and while they reject the Old Testament, they have not followed the New either, because the New is strengthened by the testimonies of the Old Testament. Therefore between the two walls, the old and the new, they have made themselves new waters, which they think are more inward and contain greater mysteries than are contained in the Old Testament; and they did not look to God, who is the founder of the Old Testament, and would not see its maker even from afar.
Commentary on Isaiah

And in that day the Lord God of hosts shall call to weeping and to mourning, to baldness and to the girding of sackcloth; and behold joy and gladness, killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: Surely this iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die, says the Lord God of hosts. Daily the Lord God of hosts calls to repentance the heretics, who, despising the water of the old pool between the two walls, have dug themselves a reservoir and gathered the water of the lower pool, which has its waters not from heaven but from the earth; and he calls them to weeping, for blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh (Matt 5:5); and to mourning, lest afterwards they hear: We have lamented to you, and you have not mourned (ibid. 11:17); and to baldness, that they may shave off all the works of death, and remove from their body whatever does not live in the body; and to the girding of sackcloth, lest afterwards, according to Jerusalem, they be girded with a rope instead of a girdle.
Commentary on Isaiah

And the Lord God of hosts will call in that day to weeping, and to lamentation, and to baldness, and to the girding of sackcloth. And behold, joy and gladness, slaying calves and slaughtering rams, eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And it has been revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: If this iniquity will be forgiven you until you die, says the Lord God of hosts. When the captivity was at hand and Jerusalem besieged, while sword, famine and thirst pressed hard upon the city, Jeremiah called the people to repentance (Jer 34); and on the contrary the kings and princes, and the wretched multitude, with the despair of men perishing, gave themselves over to feasting. But nothing so offends God as a stiff neck after sins, and contempt born of despair. This he says through Amos too: For three and for four impieties I will not turn him back: because he both devised it and did it, and did not repent, and moreover taught evil. Hence now too it is said: If this iniquity will be forgiven you until you die (Amos 1:4). The allegorical interpreters think this was foretold of the passion of Christ: that God called the unhappy people to repentance even after the cross of the Lord Savior, and nevertheless they gave themselves over to despair and pleasure. For the beginning of this vision, where he says: Full of clamor, a crowded city, an exultant town, they refer to that time when the people, stirred up by the Pharisees, resounded with one voice against Jesus: Crucify, crucify such a one: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:6, 7). The Apostle too made use of the example of this testimony, writing to the Corinthians about the resurrection: If the dead do not rise, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die (1 Cor 15:32).
Treatise XII. Three Books of Testimonies Against the Jews 3:60

That too great lust of food is not to be desired. In Isaiah: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. This sin shall not be atoned for to you, even until you die." Also in Exodus: "And the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play." Paul, in the first [letter] to the Corinthians: "Food does not commend us to God; neither if we eat shall we abound, nor if we do not eat shall we lack." And again: "When you come together to eat, wait one for another. If any is hungry, let him eat at home, that you may not come together for judgment." Also to the Romans: "The kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit." In the Gospel according to John: "I have food of which you don't know. My food is that I should do his will who sent me and should finish his work."
Commentary on Isaiah

But they, on the contrary, instead of weeping and mourning, baldness and haircloth, had joy and gladness, and, as if all things ended with death, killing calves and slaughtering rams, to eat flesh and drink wine, they spoke the words of blasphemers: While we are in the present world, let us abound in delights; for tomorrow, that is, the time to come, will be without sensation. While they were saying these things, the Lord heard the words of blasphemy, and threatened that he would not forgive this iniquity until they either die to sin and vices, or are dragged down to the underworld with their offences. This indeed can be understood not only of the heretics but of every sinner who, neglecting his sins, becomes worse through despair, and, ensnared by pleasures, joins blasphemy to sin, so as to think that all the sensation of the living ends with death, saying that saying of Epicurus: "After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing."
Commentary on Isaiah

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna who is over the temple, and you shall say to him: What are you doing here, or as whom are you here? For you have hewn yourself a tomb here; you have hewn a memorial on high carefully, a tabernacle for yourself in the rock. Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away as a cock is carried away, and he will lift you up like a garment. Crowning, he will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will cast you into a land wide and spacious: there you shall die, and there shall be the chariot of your glory, the shame of the house of your Lord. And I will drive you from your station, and depose you from your ministry. And it shall come to pass in that day that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and I will give your power into his hand; and he shall be as a father to those who dwell in Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah. And I will lay the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; and he shall open, and there shall be none to shut; and he shall shut, and there shall be none to open. And I will fasten him as a peg in a sure place, and he shall be for a throne of the house of his father. And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, divers kinds of vessels, every small vessel, from the vessels of bowls even to every vessel of the musicians. In that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that was fastened in the sure place shall be taken away, and shall be broken and fall; and what hung upon it shall perish, for the Lord has spoken. LXX: Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: Go to the pastophorion, to Somnas the treasurer, and you shall say to him: What are you here? Or what have you here? For you have hewn yourself a tomb, and have made yourself a memorial on high, and have marked out for yourself a tabernacle in the earth? Behold, the Lord Sabaoth will cast out and crush a man, and will take away your robe and your glorious crown, and will cast you into a great land, and without measure, and there you shall die; and he will set your excellent chariot in shame, and the house of your prince for trampling. And you shall be removed from your stewardship and from your rank. And it shall come to pass in that day that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your robe, and will give him your crown with strength, and will give your stewardship into his hands; and he shall be as a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and of Judah, and I will give him the glory of the house of David, and he shall rule, and there shall be none to gainsay. And I will lay the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; and he shall open, and there shall be none to shut; and he shall shut, and there shall be none to open. And I will establish him as a prince in a sure place, and for a throne of glory of his father's house; and every glorious one in his father's house shall trust in him, from the least to the greatest. Every small vessel, from the vessels aganoth; and they shall hang upon him. In that day thus says the Lord Sabaoth: The man who was established in a sure place shall be moved, and shall be taken away and shall fall, and the glory that was upon him shall perish, for the Lord has spoken. The prophet Isaiah is commanded to go in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, which in Hebrew is called SOCHEN (סכן), to Shebna who is over the temple, or as the Seventy translated, ταμίαν, that is, the treasurer and steward of the treasures of the house of God. Now Sochen is interpreted either tabernacle or pastophorion, that is, the chamber in which the one set over the temple dwells. And who else is it that dwelt in the tabernacle of the Jews, and in what was once the house of God, but the word and reasoning of the Jewish law, which was occupied with the reading of the Old Testament?
Commentary on Isaiah

And what almost escaped us in the haste of dictation: Shebna means turn now, or conversion. It is said, therefore, to the prince of the Jews, that he should turn from the Law to the Gospel, and, forsaking the images of the victims, pass over to the truth of the spiritual sacrifice.
Commentary on Isaiah

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna, who is over the Temple, and you will say to him: What are you doing here? or as whom are you here, that you have hewn out a tomb for yourself here? You have hewn out a monument on high, a tabernacle for yourself carefully in the rock. Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away, as a cock is carried away, and he will lift you up like a cloak. Crowning, he will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will throw you into a broad and spacious land: there you will die, and there will be the chariots of your glory, the shame of the house of your Lord. And I will drive you out from your station, and depose you from your ministry. And it will come to pass in that day, I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah. And I will clothe him with your tunic, and strengthen him with your girdle, and I will give your power into his hand: and he will be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. And I will lay the key of the house of David upon his shoulder, and he will open, and there will be none to shut: and he will shut, and there will be none to open. And I will fix him as a peg in a sure place, and he will be for a throne of glory to his father's house. And they will hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, vessels of various kinds: every small vessel, from the vessels of bowls even to every vessel of the musicians. In that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, and what had hung upon it will perish, because the Lord has spoken. We said above that Shebna was the high priest who betrayed the city to the Assyrians. But since this belongs to Hebrew tradition, and Scripture does not say it, let us understand him as proud, swollen and given to pleasure, trampling the peoples under his feet; and that, because he had done all the things the Prophet describes, his priesthood was transferred to Eliakim son of Hilkiah, so that, with him cast out, a new high priest might be made. From this we understand that pride, which offends God, is to be shunned with all zeal, and that it cannot be safe even with the privilege of the high priesthood. This is the Shebna (as some think) and the Eliakim of whom the same Prophet wrote further on: The king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, to King Hezekiah, with a heavy force: and he stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller's field; and there went out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the house, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder (Isa 36:2ff.).
Commentary on Isaiah

The Prophet, then, is commanded to go in to the high priest, who dwelt, according to the Seventy, in the pastophorium; according to Aquila, in the tabernacle; for which Theodotion, following the Hebrew truth, says: Go in to this Socen, which can be interpreted fair and upright (so that, namely, κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν, unjust and crooked is to be understood), to the high priest of the temple, and you will say to him: You who dwell in the house of God, whose crimes run riot through the whole city, why are you secure in your works, as though you did not fear captivity? Have you hewn yourself a tomb in the rock, and built so proudly that your ambition should follow you even in death?
Commentary on Isaiah

Those who take everything according to ἀναγωγὴν would have the priesthood of the Jews fall in the high priesthood of Shebna, and the mysteries of the Gospel worship shown in the succession of Eliakim, which means God rising again: so that what follows: In that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, pertains to the ruin of the former people. And no one doubts, both according to the history and according to the allegory, that, because he had said peg, the metaphor is kept in the hanging up of vessels of different kinds; and that when the former have been broken, others are hung up.
Commentary on Isaiah

To this tradition and teaching, then, it is said: What are you doing here? Why do you wish to build yourself a house in the letter that kills, and to fix your tabernacle, which has no foundation, in the firmness of the rock, which ought to be called not so much a tabernacle and a house as a tomb and a memorial?
Commentary on Isaiah

And I tell you this because you ought not to toil at hewing a tomb, since the Lord will carry away your priesthood, as GEBER (גבר) is wont to be carried, which all have translated man. But the Hebrew who instructed us in the reading of the Old Testament rendered it cock. As a cock, he says, is carried from one place to another on the shoulder of a porter, so the Lord will lightly carry you away from your place.
Commentary on Isaiah

Hear what the Lord's sentence upon you is: as a cock is carried off on the shoulder of the one carrying it, and men each lift their cloak onto the shoulder, so your removal into captivity will be easy. You will have a crown, not of the golden plate and of the sanctification of the Lord, but of tribulation and anguish. For as a ball, if it is thrown down a slope, cannot stand still but rolls on in swift course, so you too will be led away to a most broad land, which we may understand as either Egypt or the plains of Babylonia, and there you will die; and there will be the chariots of your glory, all the powers and riches on which you now lean as you go about. There you will feel the shame of the house of your Lord: because you will suffer these things on account of your evil works and the violation of the Temple of your God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And you who once had the crown of the high priest, and the sanctification on the plate of gold on which the name of God was written (Exod 28), shall be crowned with tribulation and distress. And as a ball, if it is thrown down a sloping and spacious place, cannot stand still but rolls on without end, so all your people shall be scattered to the ends of the world. And there you shall die with your letter, and all your glory, and the chariots in which you were formerly borne in renown; and the splendour of the house of God shall be turned into shame.
Commentary on Isaiah

For the Lord shall take you away from your station and from your ministry, that is, from the ceremonies of the victims, so that what is written to the Hebrews may be fulfilled: For when the priesthood is changed, there must of necessity be a change of the law also (Heb 7:12).
Commentary on Isaiah

I will drag you down from your rank and cast you out of the office of high priest, and in your place I will clothe Eliakim my servant, son of Hilkiah, with your garments, and adorn him with your girdle, just as Eleazar was clothed with the garments of his father Aaron. To him I will give the authority of the Temple, so that he may have the people, not subject to him as a slave, but loving him as a son.
Commentary on Isaiah

And when you have been cast out of your ministry, I will call my servant Eliakim, to whom I have said in another place also: It is a great thing for you to be called my servant (Isa 49:6, LXX). Eliakim means God rising again, or the resurrection of God. This God rising again, then, who is the son of Hilkiah, that is, of the portion of the Lord, shall receive your place, and shall be clothed with your robe and strengthened with your girdle, so that what you had in the letter he may possess in the spirit; and he shall be the father of those who dwell in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, which is interpreted as the Church, and to the house of Judah, where the true confession of faith is. Hence he himself says to the Apostles: Little children, yet a little while I am with you (John 13:33). And to another: Son, your sins are forgiven you (Matt 9:2). And to another woman: Daughter, your faith has made you whole (Luke 7:50).
COMMENTARY ON ISAIAH 22:10-14

When he says, "I will call my servant Eliakim" (the name Eliakim means resurrection of God), then everyone who is glorious in the house of his father will trust in him [Eliakim]. Yet what is the house of Christ's Father if not the church? And who are glorious there? Those who put their trust in Christ, and they are not just those who are glorious according to the judgment of this world. On the opposite they may be very small people according to that judgment. But God is just and unprejudiced. He repays everyone according to the measure of their spiritual age [maturity], as in that respect some are fathers yet others are still toddlers, babies and teenagers.
Commentary on Isaiah
He will receive the key of my house, and carry it on his shoulder; he will have authority over all the ceremonies.
Commentary on Isaiah

I will give him, he says, the key of the house of David, he who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Rev 3). And this very key shall be upon his shoulder, that is, in his passion, according to what is written in another place: Whose government is upon his shoulder (Isa 9:6). For what he has unlocked by his passion cannot be shut; and what he has shut in the ceremonies of the Jews shall be opened by no one else.
Commentary on Isaiah

And as, when a peg is fixed in the wall of the Temple and set in a very firm place, all the vessels of the priests and Levites are hung upon it, both those needed in the sacrifices and those of the musicians of every kind, so the whole people will hang upon the authority of Eliakim my servant.
Commentary on Isaiah

For I will fasten him as a peg in a sure place, where the assembly of the Faithful is; hence too those who believe in Christ are called the faithful. And he shall be for a throne of glory of his father's house, that is, of the Church; and they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house. Hence it is written in the Gospel also: All the people hung upon him (Luke 19). And this indeed was done not only at that time, but is fulfilled to this day, so that there hang upon him, as it were, divers vessels of God: wisdom and righteousness and all the things by which Christ is called. Divers kinds of vessels: for these Aquila translated SASAIM (צאצאים) and SEPHOTH (הצפעית), which Symmachus rendered grandsons and mixed ones, so that the Apostles and all believers, that is, the sons of sons, and those mixed from all the nations, may hang upon him. From the vessels of bowls, for which Theodotion set down AGANOTH (אגנות): for both small and great shall believe in the Lord. And I think the bowls are the Apostles, full of living waters, of whom it is said: Bless God from the fountains of Israel (Ps 67 [68]:27), in which bowls wisdom has mingled her wine. And every vessel, he says, of the musicians, of those who at all times resound in the praises of God.
Commentary on Isaiah

And as for his saying: In that day the peg that had been fixed in the sure place will be removed, and it will be broken and fall, and what had hung upon it will perish, because the Lord has spoken, many refer it to Shebna: that when Eliakim had been fixed as a peg, the former peg, which had been fixed, collapsed. But since there follows: And what had hung upon it will perish, which by no means happened when Shebna was cast down, we understand this to be said: that when Shebna was deposed, Eliakim received the high priesthood, the dignity of whose priesthood the final captivity overthrew.
Commentary on Isaiah

What follows seems contrary to our sense: how this peg, which had been fastened in a sure place, is taken away and broken, and what had hung upon it falls and perishes, and this happens because the Lord has spoken. This can be resolved thus, if we read that saying of the Gospel, that in the last days the love of many shall grow cold (Matt 24), and the Lord himself says: Do you think the Son of man, when he comes, will find faith upon the earth? (Luke 18:8). It is not, then, the peg that will be broken and fall and perish, which it is impious to say; but the peg will be taken away from the sure place, that is, from the Church, through the impiety that daily grows up, and those who before hung upon him by faith will afterwards through unbelief be broken and fall and perish. And this shall happen in the last days, because the Lord has spoken. For peg, which in Hebrew is called JATHED (יתד), and is rendered alike by all, the Seventy alone translated above prince, and here man.

intro: < Previous Chapter ----- Next Chapter > ON THE PROPHETS. We come now to another division of the Bible, specified by our Saviour: All things must needs be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms, concerning me, Luke xxiv. 44. He more frequently comprises all the Scriptures under the titles of Moses, or the Law and the Prophets; (Luke xxiv. 27) as in effect, all the sacred writings refer ultimately to him, who is the end of the law; (Romans x. 4.) and the Jews comprise under the name of the first prophets, the histories of Josue, &c. (Haydock) --- God has kept up a succession of prophets from the beginning, who either by word of mouth or by writing, established the true religion. Their predictions are the most convincing proof of its divine origin, Isaias xli. 23. They contain many things clear, and others obscure: having, for the most part, a literal, and a mystical sense. (Calmet) --- Yet some relate solely to Christ, while others must not be applied to him. (Bossuet) --- The Fathers, in imitation of the ancient Jews, and of the apostles, discover frequently a spiritual sense, concealed under the letter, as Christ himself declared that Jonas, in the whale's belly, prefigured his burial and resurrection on the third day. See Matthew xii. 39., Mark ix. 11., and Galatians iv. 24. When the figurative sense is thus authorized, it may serve to prove articles of faith; and such arguments must be more cogent in disputes with the Jews, than what can be drawn from their authors. They must confess that the New Testament contains a true history, or they cannot require that we should pay greater deference to the Old. Tertullian (Præs.) well observes, that heretics have no right to the Scriptures: But if they will quote them, they must receive them all, and adopt the sense given to them by the Church. (Calmet) --- The providence of God, in giving prophets, and other guides to direct his people, was ever an object of admiration and gratitude. The prophets were enabled, by a supernatural light, superior to that of faith, though beneath that of glory, to announce the secrets of futurity, as eye-witnesses; whence their predictions are styled visions, as such witnesses deserve the utmost credit. We have the writings of the four great, and the twelve less prophets. In these, many things are hard to be understood, which must not be interpreted by the private spirit, 2 Peter i. A large commentary would be requisite to explain these to the bottom, and we must refer the curious to the works of the Fathers, &c., as the subsequent notes will be rather briefer than usual. (Worthington) --- The Septuagint varies much from the original in Isaias. But we cannot specify every particular. (Calmet) --- St. Jerome has frequently given a double version in his learned comments on the prophets, as he would not peremptorily decide which exhibited the sense of God's word more accurately. (Haydock) =============================== THE PROPHECY OF ISAIAS. INTRODUCTION. This inspired writer is called by the Holy Ghost, (Ecclesiasticus xlviii. 25.) the great prophet; from the greatness of his prophetic spirit, by which he hath foretold, so long before, and in so clear a manner, the coming of Christ, the mysteries of our redemption, the calling of the Gentiles, and the glorious establishment, and perpetual flourishing of the Church of Christ: insomuch that he seems to have been rather an evangelist than a prophet. His very name is not without mystery: for Isaias in Hebrew signifies the salvation of the Lord, or, Jesus is the Lord. He was, according to the tradition of the Hebrews, of the blood royal of the kings of Juda; and after a most holy life, ended his days by a glorious martyrdom; being sawed in two, at the command of his wicked son-in-law, king Manasses, for reproving his evil ways. (Challoner) --- He began to prophesy ten years before the foundation of Rome, and the ruin of Ninive. His style is suitable to his high birth. He may be called the prophet of the mercies of the Lord. Under the figure of the return from captivity, he foretells the redemption of mankind (Calmet) with such perspicuity, that he might seem to be an evangelist. (St. Jerome)
